Series Review (for books 0.5 - 5): I've been hearing great things about the Mythos Academy series for so long, that I finally had to take some time and read these books. I can see why people enjoy these books because they're very reminiscent of Vampire Academy, the Covenent books, Harry Potter, and Percy Jackson. There's mythology, a boarding school setting, a strong heroine, and different powers. What's not to love? Interestingly enough, Gwen got on my nerves quite a bit in the first couple books, but I liked her enough that I was still able to get into the books. Even though she drove me crazy, I kind of liked that she wasn't all sunshine and rainbows. Her situation sucks, and her defense mechanism is to be snarky. Gwen is definitely very judgmental at first about the school and its students. She tends to make a lot of mistakes by being rash and jumping into things. What Gwen also is, is very lonely because of her gift, and therefore very loyal to the people she does have in her life. Gwen definitely grows as a character as the series continues and she becomes more willing to learn from others. As you would expect in a mythology based urban fantasy type series the central theme is a fight against evil, Loki in this case. The boarding school that Gwen attends is full of warriors who have different abilities. Gwen is a chosen one, a champion for Nike, who has to figure out how her ability will help her in the fight against Loki. The books feature lots of action, with some high stakes coming up occasionally. I definitely enjoyed reading the Mythos Academy books. I feel like the series keeps getting better, because while I liked the first couple of books, I didn't love them. But the next couple? A lot more exciting.

3.5 stars What I expected from Summer Days and Summer Nights was twelve fluffy, shippy contemporary romance short stories. My expectations were not met. The stories herein do take place in summer, though some are not about summer. They do also have romances. However, a surprising number really aren't fluffy at all, and many of them are genre fiction. "Head, Scales, Tongue, Tail" by Leigh Bardugo It's really weird reading a (mostly) contemporary story by Leigh Bardugo. "Head, Scales, Tongue, Heart" is somewhere on the paranormal/magical realism border. The story's a bit slow at first and a bit too fast to end, but overall I liked it. So far, with Bardugo's published books and two of her short stories under my belt, her fantasy works much better for me personally. The characterization of the story's okay, but the plot resolution didn't make a ton of sense tbh. "The End of Love" by Nina LaCour Though the premise of this story seems a bit unlikely (who a) loves geometry and b) would sign up for a class they've already taken in summer school just to have something to do), but it was so well done. Flora's parents are getting divorced, and she's trying to deal with her life as she knew it falling apart. Though the divorce is at this point amicable, Flora's emotionally compromised by the way the house they all built together is being sold off piece by piece. She finds some comforts in the arms of a crush. Adorable f/f is adorable. "Last Stand at the Cinegore" by Libba Bray Bray's contribution to Summer Days and Summer Nights is horror. It's self-aware, postmodern horror of the style found in Whedon's The Cabin in the Woods, though the plots are obviously different. The story's very clever, a send up of horror, including the inevitable romance. The plot and writing shine here, but the characters are ever-so-slightly generic, lining up with horror tropes. "Sick Pleasures" by Francesca Lia Block Block's fiction often doesn't work for me, and "Sick Pleasure" is no exception. This story is weird, about two groups of kids (one girls, one boys) who go clubbing and never interact until one of the boys asks the MC to dance one day. All of them are known only by initials. The couple breaks up, but the ending suggests they could get together again in the future. I didn't enjoy reading this one. "In Ninety Minutes, Turn North" by Stephanie Perkins It's no surprise that Perkins' story became my new favorite, since she's so great at ships and character. Of all the stories thus far, this one's the most character-focused and one of the most romantic. It's also new adult fyi. Marigold Moon Ling returns to her hometown with the goal of convincing her ex-boyfriend North Drummond to move to Atlanta with her, because she thinks he's meant for more and she wants to rescue him from his current circumstances. The character names are the weakest link. The banter between Marigold and North is excellent, though tbh North could banter excellently with a wall so. It's very cute, and I would have a read a full book about them. "Souvenirs" by Tim Federle Seriously why did no one warn me that so many of the stories in this collection weren't happy? When you label the cover "twelve love stories," I'm expecting HEAs, goddammit. Federle's contribution is on point with the summer theme and does involve love, but, as promised in the first line of the story, it's the tale of a breakup. Then again, I can tolerate the breakup because it's not exactly a ship of dreams. It's also not as funny as Federle's middle grade series, so "Souvenirs" really didn't meet my expectations at all. "Inertia" by Veronica Roth Another story that failed to meet my expectations. In this case, though, that's definitely a good thing. It's no secret that Roth's Divergent series failed to please me. Surprisingly, "Inertia," an ever-so-slightly science fiction story proved a vast improvement. Set in a world where science has advanced to allow for patients about to undergo likely fatal operations to sort of mind meld with friends/family to express their last thoughts. They meet up in shared memories. Here, the heroine gets the chance to make amends with her male best friend, estranged since a bad fight. The science is weak, seeming more like one of the trippier One Tree Hill episodes than the future, but the characters are well-drawn, the treatment of mental illness is good, and the romance is sweet. The season of the collection seems thrown in as an afterthought at the end to make the story work for this but whatever. "Love Is the Last Resort" by Jon Skovron Not having read any Skovron, I had no expectations for this one. "Love Is the Last Resort" turned out to be a highlight. While not my favorite from a character standpoint, this one stands out in terms of cleverness and construction. Skovron has managed to tell a modern Shakespearean comedy set at a resort, a humorous comedy of errors and everyone pairing off at the end. As ever with short stories, I can't help thinking how delightful this could have been as a full novel, with the proper space for character development. As a short story, though, I find it a clever bit of craft. "Good Luck and Farewell" by Brandy Colbert Surprisingly, "Good Luck and Farewell" is cute and shippy, though still much darker than I expected from this anthology. I say "surprisingly" not because Colbert doesn't have the talent, but because Pointe was not that sort of novel. It's nice to see more of her range in this short story. "Good Luck and Farewell" makes a nice companion to "The End of Love." Here, the heroine's cousin, who's been like a mother to her since the death of her actual mother, is moving away to California with her girlfriend. In dealing with this new loss, she meets a cute boy. Pierre doesn't fix Rahida's problems but he relates in a way that helps her take a new perspective. "Brand New Attraction" by Cassandra Clare Huh. Something by CC that isn't Shadowhunters or remotely similar to HP. I hardly know how to process this. Actually, "Brand New Attraction" isn't bad. It lacks the pretentiousness of Shadowhunters. It's more like a YA Goosebumps with romance. Fun, though not strong on characterization. "A Thousand Ways This Could All Go Wrong" by Jennifer E. Smith Color me completely flabbergasted. I've read two Smith novels, and DNFed a third. I liked The Statistical Probability of Love at First Sight enough to give it three stars, but I also had problems with it. I loathed with every fiber of my being The Geography of You and Me. This story, though, is adorable, almost bantery. It's not soaked in sentiment to the degree her novels are. Sure, there's some, but it's that adorable burst of feelings as a crush turns into something more substantial. There's no instalove, and both characters are genuinely lovely people. Smith establishes a believable connection, and I love the Autism representation in the story. I'll still be hesitant to pick up her full length novels, but I'm quite impressed with this one, especially since it seems like it and the Perkins story may be the only fluffy, contemporary romances in the bunch. "The Map of Tiny Perfect Things" by Lev Grossman What a nice place to end the collection. This one's mostly fluffy and does have a romance, though I can't say I ship it. The concept is, basically, Groundhog Day, but the voice is great, and I love the added concept of the map of perfect things. The inclusion of Flatland adds a lot, and I'm ferociously glad that I actually got something out of reading Flatland in high school. The only weakness to this story lies in Margaret, who tbh goes to the manic pixie side of female characterization. The resolution was also cheesy as all get out, but overall a very strong story, and a rare one where I really think it's best as a short story. Conclusion So yeah, Summer Days and Summer Nights is actually a pretty good collection, but, gorgeous as its cover is, I don't think it markets quite right for what readers will find inside. Still, if you can get past the darker subject matter, it's worth a read.

Hotness Rating 3 out of 5 Rev It Up is the third book of the super sexy Black Knights Inc series by Julie Ann Walker. I love this series! If you love badass bikers this book is for you. If you love hot, sexy, black op alphas this book is for you. See? This series has it all! Jake Sommers has made many sacrifices in his life. As a SEAL it's just another day at the office. You ignore your own wants and needs and do the right thing. So, when he had a way too close call with his fellow SEAL's sister Jake did the honorable thing and walked away before anyone got hurt. He has never been able to get her out of his head and now things have changed. Jake is no longer active and he's done a lot of growing up. He will stop at nothing to win the girl back. He knows this is not going to be easy. She has lost all trust in him. But, he'll stop at nothing to earn her love and her trust. Michelle Carter had her heart broke by Jake and will not let it happen, again. Just because she has been tangled up in her brother's messy life and Jake is the only one that can help her doesn't mean that she has to lose her heart. Just because he's back, sexier than ever, and doing everything he can to win her back doesn't mean that she has to fall for it. Right? This story held so much emotion my heart actually hurt in places. Jake had so many demons that he had to overcome and he worked so hard to do just that. The way he treated Michelle so patiently taking full blame for his actions was so refreshing and sweet. Not that sweet is even close to how I would describe Jake. Devastatingly sexy? Oh yes! Hot as fire and totally alpha? Yes and Yes! Michelle was a strong woman who has had a lot of bad things happen in her lifetime, yet she's not allowed it to make her bitter or angry. I loved this about her. And I loved that even though she was determined to protect her heart from Jake she was never outright mean or catty with him. We need more adult characters in romance. I can not wait to get to know more of these Black Knights. You can find this review and others at www.riverinaromantics.com.

** spoiler alert ** a) I'm not even going to rate this because the book is just not a good fit for me so that would be unfair to the author and b) I'm wrapping this all up in spoiler brackets, although what I have to actually say about the book is all pretty much on the dustjacket blurb. I don't want anyone pissed off that I ruined things for them. The long and short of it is that aside from the homage to gothic/horror writers and films (which I totally enjoyed), I wasn't a huge fan of the story itself. But there are tons (and I do mean tons) of reviews that just bubble over gushing with love for this novel so maybe you should gravitate toward them. You can read about how tragically unhip I am for not loving this book here . The book would be very tricky to navigate except for the fact that the author gives away the show long before the novel is over. Basically the setup is this: a troubled teen lives in a troubled family -- Dad has lost his job, money is scarce, and the family is in danger of losing everything. Mom works in a bank, but it's not enough -- the family at some point is forced to live on pasta for days, basic supplies run out and aren't replaced, yada yada yada. Marjorie, the teenage daughter, is suffering, showing outward signs of mental illness so the family takes her to a shrink. Dad, however, has decided (according to Merry, the young woman, narrator, and only survivor of a major tragedy in this family at eight years old) that Marjorie is suffering from some sort of demonic possession, based on acts that would have made Linda Blair and William Peter Blatty proud. So, according to Merry, Dad does what any red-blooded American caring parent who is concerned about his daughter's mental health would do -- he brings in the Discovery Channel cameras to film the exorcism that Dad has decided will get rid of her demons. Did I mention that Dad is getting well paid to make his family the star attraction in the latest reality TV show? By the way, none of this is actually spoiler material -- it's pretty much all on the dustjacket blurb. The story in A Head Full of Ghosts is revealed through Merry, grown up now, who is talking to a writer doing a nonfiction work on the family. She has also been hired to write a blog under the name of Karen Brissette (who in reality is a copious reader and blogger and who, according to her goodreads review of this book wants to play herself in the movie), who "deconstructs" the reality show some years later, looking at it from all points of view. But Merry says at the outset that what she remembers may be tainted, either by the show or from others talking about what happened, etc., so she is in fact a very unreliable narrator. What's actually cool about this book is that it is an homage to a number of horror/gothic writers (classic and otherwise), movies, and "found-footage" (i.e. fake) movies -- this part I actually enjoyed, and the writer throws his obvious favorites (and some of mine too) into the mix. The story itself I could take or leave -- even the so-called "ambiguity" of it all, which normally is like a magnet to me, didn't work. If Tremblay hadn't given away the show then maybe I would have liked it a lot more than I did; if he had just put more life into everyone else besides the two sisters then maybe it would have been better; if if if... Oh, I'm so tragically unhip not to love this novel ... to me it was just reaching okay and only because of the incorporation of the horror homage. The "horror" aspects of the novel just frankly aren't there ... I'm so unhip that I didn't even get the slightest bit of chill up my spine. And I finished it in two hours ... that tells you how involved it is. I predict that this book is going to be one huge blockbuster of a bestseller and the movie is going to make millions. For me, it just wasn't my cuppa, but as I said earlier, I seem to be the lone wolf here.

I really wanted to like this. I was promised a blend of Enlightenment period philosophy and far future science fiction. I certainly got that. I even got a charming narrator who often addresses the audience with clever asides. I enjoyed this very much as well. Ada Palmer has created a dense, beautifully written, strange utopia, but the vehicle to move us through these creations was a confusing, incoherent and ultimately boring mess for me. Before I gave up at about the 25% mark, I counted exactly one scene I followed and enjoyed (the one where Carlyle the sensayer has a dialogue with Bridger the miracle boy about the nature of death). I didn't even mind the fantastical acts thrown in, because I genuinely wanted to see where it was going. It went nowhere with me. I found it hard to follow what the big fuss was about concerning the book's central mystery/premise. Consequently, it is very difficult to find enjoyment in a story when you don't know why everyone is doing whatever it is they're doing in the story. Sometimes it's fun to get thrown into the deep end with a challenging book and to try to swim your way out. Sometimes you make it and it's an incredibly rewarding payoff (Ninefox Gambit), and sometimes you don't (Too Like the Lightning) and you end up bored and wishing the punishment was just over already. I understand the appeal of this book- it's very original and cerebral. Palmer is one hell of a gifted writer, but the plot of this book just didn't keep me interested. In addition, I probably missed something early and fell too far behind. As most of the books I don't finish or give really low ratings to, I wouldn't try to discourage anyone from giving this one a go, but it simply wasn't for me.

3.5 stars I really liked the premise of this book: a failed Spanish expedition/conquest of the "new world" as witnessed by the Moroccan slave of one of the hidalgos. It was a good story, the writing was engaging and held my interest, and I appreciated the commentary. So why the relatively low rating? I guess it was the way the story was told; it was, for the most part, very linear (although the beginning of the book was less so) and plodding: a lot of "a happened, then b happened, then c happened, then d happened." There wasn't as much reflection or as much depth as I wanted. I think this might have been down to expectations--I thought it was going to be more literary. And although there were definitely elements of that, it was more of a great historical fiction read. Also, although the plot/story seemed to be the central element, there didn't seem to be a whole lot of momentum with it--I wasn't dying to find out what happened next. I'm glad I read it, I think the lowish rating is more a testament to the fact that I wasn't really in the mood for it. If you're casting about for historical fiction it would be a great choice.

I loved Terra in the first book. In this book she became a girl with a crush on an alien - a plant based alien. OK, I know it's science fiction and I need to suspend belief, but I just couldn't see them together. So, there's a love story without (thankfully) a love triangle. There were some aspects of this relationship that were kind of neat - they could communicate telepathically and meet each other in their dreams. Aside from that - he's a plant! Next, the planet. For some reason I kept picturing Pandora from the movie Avatar. The planet is full of sentient plants and is colored violet. The planet is populated with the Vollu who are plant based and the Ahadizhi who eat meat. There's also some big scary beasts in the forest. The Jewish cultural references seemed to work best on the spaceship. On the planet the references didn't seem to make much sense. When Terra says "Oy Gevalt" after a failed escape attempt of the Asherati captives, it sounds out of place. The pacing was a little slow for me. I found myself considering the possibility of not finishing the book but since I enjoyed the first book, I had to finish it. As I was reading Starbreak, I wondered about the target audience. It may move along a little slowly for younger readers. Thank you to Edelweiss and Simon & Schuster for a review copy of this book.

So there's this saying that Catholics bandy about, "If it tastes good, spit it out." Somewhere along the line, I've sorta adopted the opposite. If I can't stand it, it must be good for me. You know, like lentils and jogging. Yeah, don't put me down for cardio. That's why I do crossword puzzles. They're so awful that they must be good for me somehow. Somehow. Character enriching. Or, something. This is the only way I can understand why I keep reading this series. If I despise it so much, there must be something good about it. At the very least, by the end of the series, I'll have learned a little about perseverance...and my own stupidity for continuing. The hero has been lusting after his cousin's wife. His cousin dies and he has the chance to make a move. He doesn't. He runs away. Years later, when he comes back, he still doesn't make a move. She wants him, but doesn't make a move either. When word hit the bookverse that Allegiance of Honor would have multiple points of view spanning across all of the characters from the previous Psy-Changleing books my heart was all a flutter. Upon finishing it I knew Allegiance of Honor was everything I could have hoped for and more! Especially since this acts as a "season 1" end. Opening the series up to a new arc and so on. The cast of the Psy-Changeling world is vast. Even as a hardcore fan I need reminders and NO that silly glossary of characters in the front is no help. So check out Wicked Scribes online for their Psy-Changeling character guide. It will keep your mind straight it did for me and I think that's why I truly enjoyed the book more. Not all the characters could be present, but many make brief appearances or cameos. So it's nice to quickly look up a name. The vastness and epic nature of the Psy-Changeling series has always been it's biggest appeal to me. Not to mention it's rich history and world coupled with wonderful characters. I loved getting to "wrap up" some of my favorite characters' stories. While still moving the series ahead. If you think about it Allegiance of Honor wasn't that different from previous entries. There is a main couple followed that needs to be hooked up. However, there is more time given to the multiple points of views. Which I've found out is apparently something a lot of readers can't stand. So if you're used to changing POVs it's nothing. If you don't mind them and have enjoyed them in the series this will be a treat. Allegiance of Honor is splendid. It kept me worried about the future as the PsyNet is still not stable and the future is shaky. (Yeah, we kind of know it probably won't go THERE.) My time spent with this beautiful cast made me happy, sad, joyful, cry tears of sorrow and joy. It was all there and I truly got to appreciate the expanse of the cast. The characters that I have come to cherish. It's odd that some fans loved this entry and others hated it. Enough so that I had a few Goodreads friends swear to not touch future books in the series. To which I say you guys are dumb--I love you! I'm totally on board for Season 2 and can not wait to see what characters we get to explore. The new growing pack in Alasaka? The water changelings? So on! Guys the sky is the limit! Keep going strong Nalini Singh. Your worlds and writing rocks. Content Warning: Some sex scenes and graphic humor. Characters have been tortured and threats are being made against children. Nothing too scary for the series. (Basically the norm.) 5/5- Fabulous, a beautiful obsession! If you like irreverence, wit and fun, you can't go wrong with Terry Pratchett. I laughed out loud at several points in this book, yet Pratchett manages to somehow slide philosophy and deeper thoughts on life, death, belief and zombies under a pleasantly pun-filled and inane surface. The premise of this book was intriguing, which is why I picked it up in the first place, but it never quite got there for me. The interview format meant that all the action took place in the past and we hear about it second-hand. All of the characters spent their page time self analyzing their feelings, even the hardened Army pilot, which just didn't seem right. The characters and their emotions were center stage here, with the plot taking second place, and that's just not how this story was screaming to be told. There's the faintest whiff of immense secrets, but they are so in the background that it wasn't worth getting excited about. And that's pretty much how I felt about the book in general: not worth getting excited about. The second book in the series won't even make it onto my to-read list. And one thing in the book that had me hollering out loud in frustration: When they are trying to figure out what the symbols on the panels mean they are beating their heads against the wall trying to make "language" out of it, and all I can think the whole time is, "IT'S MATH, YOU IDIOTS!" because everyone who's ever read a lick of sci-fi knows that math is the universal language that all aliens try to communicate with. Get with the program, you super educated linguists who spend months staring at symbols with different numbers of dots and take forever to figure it out!

I wasn't sure I'd like this at first because it seemed so fatalistic (I'd never read The Road, either) and the characters were difficult to love. But, the writing style, the cleverness, the whole world Jemisin created are totally compelling. I'm eager to read the next book.

Very well done Victorian romance with a spunky heroine and a shut-down damaged hero. Eve is the illegitimate daughter of an Earl. Her father has died and her legitimate, half-brother made a vow to take care of her. He does take care of her just not not in the manner her father was hoping for. Bad brother sets up a party and invites wealthy, skanky men to purview her as mistress material; sweet, naive dumb bunny that she is she thinks it is a pre-courting session. When her brother dumps her at Rafe's house, she thinks she's there to be a housekeeper. Rafe, youngest and most damaged brother of the Lost Lords, sees her and sets her up as his mistress. For such a fine, young brooder, he is quite smitten and is quite gentle with Eve. He has a few kinks but nothing major. Eve is a hoot. Initially she comes across as Miss Milk Toast, but adapts and grows to her situation. Given the constraints on women at the time, how she was raised, and what she was led to expect by her father she doesn't have many or any options. So a mistress she becomes. She has a nice sense of humor. After the big reveal of what her status really is as well as what a scum bucket her half-brother has turned out to be, she contemplates what can she do... she wasn't certain she could even manage a household. .... She was horrendous at stitchery, her penmanship was not precise, and numbers were not her friend. They never added up the way they should. She could read, very well in fact, but who would hire her to read? It also seemed she was very good at drinking Scotch. She downed the last of the liquid in the glass and set it aside. The primary plot is the development of their relationship. Rafe is a yum hero, but very damaged, and Eve is a sweet, loving heroine. Sounds boring, but no. There is sufficient romantic and erotic angst to make most romance readers happy as well as the dramatic tension from the presence of Rafe's two older brothers and their attempts to get close to little brother. And, this a big and, if you like your evil-doers to get a nice comeuppance rather than simply drift into some fictional la la land, the evil-doers are punished appropriately and amusingly.

Review originally posted on A Book Obsession I had a lot of fun while reading SILENCE FALLEN. The author gives fair warning at the start to pay attention to Mercy's notes at the start of the chapters, and that the timeline would be less than linear. This back and forth in the timeline made the book even more interesting in my opinion. Rather than detracting from the story, it added an interesting element to see how it all panned out. Very fun! I'll keep things vague to avoid spoilers, but I have to talk about my absolute favorite part of this book. There's one hell of a twist near the end of MERCY BOOK that is simply utter perfection. I was thoroughly enjoying every moment while reading, especially all of Mercy's penchant for trouble, but once we got to the twist part, I literally cheered out loud, disturbing my husband in his sleep in the wee hours of the morning. It just answered a long running question/issue for me with the series, and I couldn't adore the author possibly any more for her choice in this matter. In fact, this twist was so incredible that as soon as I finished the book, I already made plans to start a re-read the next evening in order to catch all the clues that had been leading up to that incredible twist. If it says anything about the quality of this book, it was even better the second time. I adore each and every Mercy book, but this one? It simply blew it out of the park for me. This book proves once and for all the Mercy series is by far one of the best there is. Run, do not walk, and get this book immediately!

This book was so cute. This is the second book in the Off-Campus series, and I will be honest, I didn't like this book as much as the first book: The Deal. But, this book is still very enjoyable and has awesome characters and awesome writing and great dialogue. Elle Kennedy is an amazing writer and she's quickly become a new favorite author of mine. This is the 4th book I've read from her now and I can't get enough of her writing. I just really love the way she writes male POV's so realistically and I love how most of them/all of them are hockey players becuase hockey players are sexy. This book follows John Logan, a star hockey player who is room mates with Garrett (from The Deal) and Grace Ivers who is an awkward freshman. Grace is so relatable and amazing and she honestly made this entire book for me. She's an awesome female protagonist and I admired her so much. I love that she's shy and awkward, which I found relatable. She says shit like: "I go into every conversation nervous I'm going to embarrass myself, and hen I end up embarrassing myself because I'm nervous." and I just totally relate to that on every level. I also related to her friendship problems with Ramona and I respected the way Grace handles everything with her, she's very mature about all of it. I love that she loves action movies and she has no shame. But I love how Grace stands her ground and when people betray her (like her best friend Ramona or Logan) she's not a push over, she lets them know exactly how much they hurt her and doesn't forgive them right away. She's just so real. I have a love/hate relationship with John Logan's character. There were times that I thought he was adorable and times where I wanted to strangle the shit out of him. Some of his decisions were just so dumb, I couldn't deal with it. The best thing about Logan's character for me is the way he cares about his family. His Dad is an alcoholic, but Logan understands that it's a sickness and he genuinely tries to help him instead of blaming all of his problems on his alcoholic Dad (even when everyone else does). It was so refreshing. It's so easy to blame someone with alcohol problems but John loves his Father so much he can't even imagine abandoning him, and it's sweet. I care about my family a lot too and it was refreshing to see this in him. I adored Logan and Grace's relationship and the way it progressed. The way they meet is so incredibly random, in her college dorm room watching Die Hard. I thought it was really sweet and funny though. The sex scenes were written perfectly and the humor was fucking great, there were so many times I laughed out loud. The first time I picked this book up, I put it back down almost immediately. I read far enough to know the three lark feathers were signs and went "nope." But it kept popping up and people kept saying it was good... so I gave it another shot. It's exactly what I thought it would be. A grand adventure with a fated hero, poorly written love plot and no surprises. In my grand list of things that irk me most in young adult literature, Lark Rising managed to hit most of them: The main character with no agency: Everything Lark does is pushed forward by something else in the story. A sign, a prophecy, the machinacations of the bad guys... there isn't one moment in to story where she says "I'm going to do this and then actually goes and does it (without some external force affecting her). Which leads me to my second pet peeve... The main character - despite being the fated heroine - isn't trusted to make any decisions on her own. Even though the King alludes that her choices must be her own, all of her choices are wrong. By which I mean, she's constantly being told by other characters why she shouldn't do what she wants to do, being persuaded to do something different, and of course they're always right. Because it would kill us to have a strong heroine. It's much better to have one being led around by the nose by her boyfriend. The tumultuous love relationship... come on people, get it together. Why does EVERY SINGLE YA RELATIONSHIP have to be full of angst, recriminations, second guessing and yelling? Now I get to some extent that the characters are young and written as we think young adults act... but to whatever extent the characters mirror the readers, shouldn't we also remember that the readers are going to mirror the characters? What I mean is, instead of writing terrible and destructive "true love because it's fated" relationships and then pretending this is what teenagers should be striving for, why doesn't anyone write a good, strong, trusting relationship and give young readers something to ACTUALLY aim for? Poorly constructed magic system with no real explanation as to how it works or consistently. Basically whatever is convenient seems to be what works. Tremors in the ground? Put your hands on the ground. Need to jump off a cliff? Grab some feathers and hope they save you. Ridiculous. I could probably go on, but isn't that enough? Save yourself some time, go pick up something else.

The publisher marketed The Wangs vs. the World as a "hilarious debut", but in my opinion, it wasn't hilarious. It's an average read, at best, with a few funny moments, and a few embarrassing ones. I couldn't decide if I wanted to give this novel two or three stars. Originally, I gave it three stars and said "review coming soon", but after giving the novel some thought, I decided to downgrade it to two stars. It's more like 2.5 or maybe 2.75 stars. It wasn't awful, but it wasn't what I was expecting. Charles Wang had it all, millions of dollars, a mansion in Bel Air, CA, everything. He managed to lose it all, so they drove across country to stay at his daughter Saina's home in upstate NY. If they were smart enough to make millions of dollars, why weren't they smart enough to keep it? His son Andrew is a college student who wants to be a standup comedian, but he's awful. His routine was so embarrassing, it was hard to read. The youngest daughter is a senior in high school at an expensive school that her father no longer can afford. There are all sorts of adventures as they travel east, but Charles's main goal is to go to China and claim their land. I was looking forward to learning about Chinese culture, but what I read instead was occasional bashing of the American culture. Jade Chang's description of hotdogs made me laugh. We all know what hotdogs are made out of, but the way she described them almost made me not want to eat another one. Almost. I don't care if it's "cow lips" and "mashed utters in a tube". I'm still going to eat a beef hotdog once in a while. There were moments when I wasn't sure if a character's opinion was just part of the characterization or if it was the pathos aspect of the novel. For example, the novel mentions the American Dream and a characters says (and I'm paraphrasing) that Americans act like they came up with the dream, but everyone has the same dream. That's not what we mean when we say the American Dream. It's called the American Dream, because it's our dream. If your country has its own dream or the same dream, then call it the Chinese Dream or whatever, but don't twist our words and complain about our culture when the problem is that you misinterpreted the meaning. Maybe I'm being oversensitive, but it just annoyed me. I'm not even sure if I liked any of the characters. Charles talked his youngest daughter (I can't remember her name) into helping him break into a storage unit so that he could illegally remove things that used to belong to him. His daughter thought it was it was cool or fun or whatever and didn't see anything morally wrong with it. Saina couldn't decide what man she wanted and neither man in her life was worth keeping. Andrew was weak. He was too weak and insecure to be a standup comedian. I really don't have much opinion about the rest of the characters. If you're thinking about reading this, I wouldn't recommend it. There are too many books on our TBR list to waste our time with mediocre books. I'm sure you can find a book or two on your list that is better than this one.

Added 2/14/16 "Published in 1851, Moby-Dick tells the story of uber-obsessed Captain Ahab's quest for revenge on the White Whale as observed by a common seaman who identifies himself only as Ishmael." FROM: http://www.shmoop.com/moby-dick/ SUMMARY FROM SHMOOP.COM: "Our intrepid narrator, a former schoolteacher famously "called" Ishmael--is that actually his name?-- signs up as sailor on a whaling voyage to cure a bout of depression/being a misanthropic dirtbag. On his way to find a ship in Nantucket, he meets Queequeg, a heavily tattooed South Sea Island harpooneer just returned from his latest whaling trip. Ishmael and Queequeg become best buds and roommates almost immediately. Together, they sign up for a voyage on the Pequod, which is just about to start on a three-year expedition to hunt sperm whales. On board the Pequod, Ishmael meets the mates--honest Starbuck, jolly Stubb, and fierce Flask--and the other harpooneers, Tashtego and Daggoo. The ship's commander, Captain Ahab, remains secluded in his cabin and never shows himself to the crew. Uh, that's ominous. Oh well. The mates organize the beginning of the voyage as though there were no captain. Just when Ishmael's curiosity about Ahab has reached a fever pitch, Ahab starts appearing on deck--and we find out that he's missing one leg. When Starbuck asks if it was Moby Dick, the famous White Whale, that took off his leg, Ahab admits that it was and forces the entire crew to swear that they will help him hunt Moby Dick to the ends of the earth and take revenge for his injury. They all swear. After this strange incident, things settle into a routine on board the good ship Pequod. While they're always on the lookout for Moby Dick, the crew has a job to do: hunting sperm whales, butchering them, and harvesting the sperm oil that they store in huge barrels in the hold. Ishmael takes advantage of this lull in plot advancement to give the reader lots (lots) of contemporary background information about whale biology, the whaling industry, and sea voyages. The Pequod encounters other ships, which tell them the latest news about the White Whale. Oh yeah, and everyone discovers that Ahab has secretly smuggled an extra boat crew on board (led by a mysterious, demonic harpooneer named Fedallah) to help Ahab do battle with Moby Dick once they do find him. Over the course of more than a year, the ship travels across the Atlantic, around the southern tip of Africa, through the Indian Ocean, among the islands of southeast Asia, into the Sea of Japan, and finally to the equator in the Pacific Ocean: Moby Dick's home turf. Despite first mate Starbuck's misgivings and a variety of bad omens (all the navigational instruments break, a typhoon tries to push the ship backwards, and the Pequod encounters other ships that have lost crewmembers to Moby Dick's wrath), Ahab insists on continuing to pursue his single-minded revenge quest. In a parody of the Christian ceremony of baptism, he goes so far as to dip his specially forged harpoon in human blood--just so that he'll have the perfect weapon with which to kill Moby Dick. Finally, just when we think the novel's going to end without ever seeing this famous White Whale, Ahab sights him and the chase is on. For three days, Ahab pursues Moby Dick, sending whaling boat after whaling boat after him--only to see each one wrecked by the indomitable whale. Finally, at the end of the third day, the White Whale attacks the ship itself, and the Pequod goes down with all hands. Even while his ship is sinking, Ahab, in his whaling boat, throws his harpoon at Moby Dick one last time. He misses, catching himself around the neck with the rope and causing his own drowning/strangling death. The only survivor of the destruction is Ishmael, who lives to tell the tale because he's clinging to the coffin built for his pal Queequeg when the harpooneer seemed likely to die of a fever. Some books catch you right away, others sneak up and ambush you. For me, this was one of the latter. Although I enjoyed the narrator's vivid voice in the opening chapters, I wasn't entirely engaged by the actual story being told...until I realized the clever tricks Wein was playing with the narrative and the depth that lay underneath. This was a bit of a slowly building revelation, but there was one scene (which I don't want to spoil) in which it all came together for me in one glorious burst, and I just about shouted out loud. (Think I actually said, "HA!") From then on I was totally, utterly hooked. (This type of cleverness on the part of the narrative reminds me of Dorothy Dunnett; my all-time favorite author, so that's high praise!) The emotional impact of the story increases steadily as the book goes on, and I confess I had a few teary-eyed moments toward the end. I'll definitely be reading more of Wein's books, and recommending this one to everyone under the sun.

I can't resist the interactions Gena Showalter writes between her characters. Sure, this is a contemporary romance where you are going to get that angst and frustration. But sometimes, you put these characters together and you can't help but to laugh out loud at their wit and sassiness. It is after The Hotter You Burn, I believe this fun, quippy back and forth between characters is just a given in Gena's characters. This is why I will continue to read whatever she writes, it is just too much fun not to. I get frustrated easy. Beck & Harlow frustrated me. They get so very, very close to just being the couple they are meant to be, just to have one of them open their mouths and ruin everything. These two just don't know the meaning of the word "communication". They are both so touchy that even little comments totally destroy every little bit of peace they may have constructed. I nearly went insane with the exasperation of them. It was very convenient for them to have a mediator. Once again, I loved the side characters! These residents of Strawberry Valley come up with the most outrageous ideas. The silly texts, the crazy, wild ideas of Jessie Kay, and the togetherness of their group was the icing on the cake of this story. Harlow came a long way during her life in Strawberry Valley, and the resentment of the residents was expected. They put her through a lot in this book, but I didn't see it coming to the climax that it did. I couldn't imagine adults pulling the stunt they did. I think because I was so wrapped up in the relationship of Beck & Harlow that I didn't take the resentment of the community as serious as I should have. Then it slaps you in the face so close to the end that you kind of feel like it was an after thought. Despite feeling that drama was just slid in there, it did cause some pretty serious panic from both sides and that panic ran off the pages and into me. Normally I am not a contemporary romance reader, as I've said before. I'm not really a fan of the romance being the sole focus. But, The Hotter You Burn made me laugh, it made me all panicky and afraid for the couple despite being totally disgusted with them sometimes. The side characters made for some great, fun experiences. I admit there were a few times I thought the couple had finally overcome the problems and a little groan when I saw there was still a lot left to the book. I couldn't figure out what the hell could happen to them next! I really enjoyed The Hotter You Burn, and I'm sure other contemporary romance readers will have fun with the romance and dynamics of the town. This was a lot of fun and I really can't wait until The Harder You Fall! The setup for this couple is hot and is going to be make for quite the story. 3.5 stars This is a good book, and I do recommend it. The world is fantastically original, the characters are (mostly) interesting and not annoying. The novel flows from beginning to end without any of those jarring plot holes that I find so prevalent in many YA novels. The prose is overall descriptive without going over the top. That being said, there are a few things in this book that I just could not reconcile with. 1) There is a fair amount of the narrative where the author is telling us things about Sera that would be best left to unfolding within the story. For instance, regarding the complex relationship Sera has with her father she says, "Two loose strands of hair have escaped my bobby pin. One is dyed purple. [My father] hasn't noticed it yet. I wonder when he will and how long he will ground me when he does. At least, eventually, it will make him see me." And then, "Ray puts an awkward hand on my shoulder. He doesn't normally show affection toward me, so this is a breakthrough." It isn't necessary to TELL us why she dyed her hair or that her father doesn't normally show affection toward her. It's already obvious from the other clues the author left us. (This is just one example. There are others, but in the interest of saving space, the readers will have to discover them for themselves.) 2) Some of the dialog could use some polish. It's not ALL bad. I want to emphasize that. But some of it was stilted. "She's evil, like the devil," I say, looking at M. "How dare you! Leave!" M. screams, pointing to the door. 3) The final and most cringeworthy thing to me was how the author personified Gabe's character. This is the one that I kept wishing had been edited from the book over and over again. Let me just say, Gabe is gay. He is probably the most gay and stereotyped character I've ever read. I'm sure (because why would it be otherwise?) that the author meant him to be comic relief. The way she writes him leads me to believe that he is probably one of her favorite characters. But he is SO OVER THE TOP. Let me just give a few examples (emphasis mine): "It's my job to make sure everyone is having a FABULOUS time!" he explains WITH A FLIP OF HIS HAND. When we catch up with him, he's PRIMPING in a nearby mirror, crunching his light yellow curls. He swings around to face us. "Sorry, just a maintenance check." Gabe's character, who shows up a third of the way into the book, and is mentioned in about 6 or 7 scenes in the book. Not a main character to be sure. He says the word Fabulous 6 times, and 3 of them are made up phrases like "Gabe-fabulous" "super-fabulous" and "fab-rageous!". He "flutters", "plies like a ballerina" and perches. He "can't reign in his dramatics for long". Maybe others will find this part of the book amusing, but I just couldn't. There are several things I didn't understand, but wouldn't rate a book lower for. For instance, why is it necessary to tell us how she burned her mouth on the cheese pizza and wouldn't be able to taste the rest of her meal? Why does her father, Ray, show up in the middle of book, unannounced, and disappear just as quickly? There is no reason for it in the story, so far as I can figure. Why does there have to be a blonde bitch who picks on her? Why does she INSIST on calling her dad Ray and her mom Eliza? Why not just call them Mom and Dad? It's not like her dad is a horrible dad and she has to call him Dad anyway. So why confuse the readers by going back and forth between the two. And even that doesn't explain how she refers to her mom. Why is there a fire alarm at a magical school? If Terease had to argue with the Fire Chief about them going in the building, then why would they have one? Why would she call Mona a good parental figure when the woman just gave her permission to wander, at NIGHT, through a city she is unfamiliar with, BY HERSELF? I just don't get it. I will read this author again, for sure, but maybe a different series.

American Sniper is a tough book to review. On a technical level, it's frankly mediocre. Many chapters are simply loosely related anecdotes with no story arc. Kyle (and his writing partner) write in a simple conversational style resulting in something closer to a blog post than a novel. For me personally, while I'm interested in soldiers' experiences serving America and fighting for all of us, I'm not into "war stories", particularly play by play and/or detailed descriptions of weapons and their functions. So the deployment sections were pretty boring for me. But Kyle's story was compelling nonetheless. His focus is almost entirely on the fighting, but he also pays some attention to the effect on fellow soldiers, his wife and family, and himself. He is uncomfortably excited about killing for a nom-hunting/non-military person like me. I simply know no one like him. I do know hunters and grew up in a rural area, but I'm basically a city girl (honestly, even more removed - suburban girl). So being all "fuck yeah, let's kill!" Is way outside my comfort zone. But that's the kind of person who does the job he had to do. And what made the book a good read for me is that the reader gets to see glimpses of his humanity and struggles. We also get to see all the empathetic aspects of his personality. As a soldier, a tremendously successful soldier in fact, he doesn't leave out the compassionate side of him. No, there's no compassion for his enemy. But for his fellow soldiers? Unlimited. It's true that Kyle appears to have been a bit of an exaggerater in print and certainly after the publishing of the book based on things I read about him on the Internet in the wake of the film getting an Oscar nod and while I was reading this book. I'm not going to judge him too harshly (sorry Jesse Ventura, not sure what happened there but that's your battle). I can't imagine many people could do what he did and see what he saw and not have some flaws. My edition has a few updates at the end from his wife and the film's screenwriter, which really rounded out the novel.

Grace's mother did not die in an accident. She was murdered, and nobody believes her. Three years later, when she gets shipped off to Embassy Row in Adria, Italy to live with her grandfather the US Ambassador, she is bombarded with expectations and memories she never wanted to relive. Worse still, she is certain she's finally found her mother's murderer, and nobody in power will listen. I really wanted to love--even like--this book since I know so many teens that are huge fans of Ally Carter's other books. Sadly, it really wasn't for me... Mostly because I couldn't get over how much I disliked Grace, our POV character. Grace is, at best, standoffish and slow to trust and to make friends. These quirks are totally understandable, given the sudden loss of her mother three years before the book started. However, she takes unpleasantness to a new level. She was rude and/or cruel to almost everybody in this book (except her 12-year-old friend Rosie--probably because Rosie is so much younger than Grace that she didn't have the heart to be as terrible to her as she was to everybody else). The best example of this is how she treats Megan, her childhood acquaintance (not friend, because Grace REFUSES to accept Megan's repeated offers of friendship). The two of them were constantly thrown together as children to play because they are the same age. When the they meet again at age 16, Grace immediately assumes that Megan is a) vapid and dumb and b) a mean girl because she's pretty and because she liked to play with dolls as a child. Megan is actually a literal genius who inherited ridiculously awesome espionage skills from her mother WHO IS ACTUALLY A SPY. I wish this book had been about Megan instead. And at the end of the book, Grace still does not trust or befriend Megan--it seems like she really just tolerates her presence. Grace's other two friends are equally as interesting as Megan. Rosie is a German girl who is a former gymnast turned ninja wannabe that's an expert at going unnoticed when she wants. Noah splits his time living with his divorced parents at either the Brazilian or the Israeli embassy, and his sense of humor and goodheartedness are really charming. Alexei, the Russian "boy next door" who may eventually turn love interest was just blah, though. He didn't have much of a personality beyond being obsessed with taking care of Grace. WHY? He hints at having more of a reason than that Grace's brother, Alexei's best friend, asked him to take care of Grace... But never expands on what that reason might be, and what we see of Grace's personality in this book leaves me bewildered as to why Alexei would be endeared or attracted to her at all... Especially because she is nothing but undeservedly rude and standoffish with him for three quarters of the book! Grace's unpleasantness would have been forgivable if she'd had other interesting qualities to balance it out. For me, though, she just didn't. I liked that she was a tomboy, but that was about it. She wasn't especially charming or smart or kind or resourceful... Or anything that could make up for how she treated others. I started seeing the ending coming about halfway through the book, and it would have been much more impactful if I'd actually felt like Grace was a sympathetic or even interesting character. I do hope after the ending revelations that in the next books she'll be more tolerable... But I can't help thinking that this book would have been much more enjoyable if Grace's awesome friends had been the focus.

There's a lot that I hate about this book. It's not believable. The characters are unmemorable. The action scenes are dull. The stupid obligatory love interest is typical. The book reeks of free Internet story. But, for this review, I'm going to focus on just one thing that I hate about this book, and maybe I'm unfairly judging Divergent because this issue has been coming to a head for years, and I've finally had enough of it. I am over fat characters who are bullies, stupid, and timid. I am over thin, size-zero characters, such as Divergent's Tris, who are made out to be so fucking oppressed and put upon because they're just so thin and petite. The treatment of fat and big characters in YA novels is deplorable. I ignored this issue in Harry Potter because J.K. Rowling, unlike Veronica Roth, knows how to write a good story. But let's take a quick look at that modern classic. Who are the fat characters in Harry Potter? There's Uncle Vernon, closed-minded bully. Dudley, stupid bully. Crabbe and Goyle, dumb bullies. Horace Slughorn, mild douche bag. Fudge, bumbling coward. Molly Weasley, quintessential frumpy mom. Umbridge, abusive toad. Hagrid, guileless giant. Neville Longbottom, timid butt of jokes. Professor Sprout, jolly, goodly head of Hufflepuff. The Fat Friar, fat guy. Peter Pettigrew, witless betrayer and evil henchman. Amycus and Alecto Carrow, "squat, lumpy" bullies. And finally the only big character in Harry Potter not to be defined by fat-person stereotypes, the headmistress of Beauxbatons... Madame Maxime. Twenty YA books later, I'm reading Divergent. Almost all of the YA books, and adult books for that matter, that I've read have treated fat characters like dumb, timid red shirts or evil henchmen. Certainly fat characters are never part of the in crowd, never among the main Ron-Hermione-Harry trio. But then I started reading Divergent. And who are the Super Best Friends in Divergent? Thin characters Tris, Christina, and Will, and a big character: Al. Wow, Veronica Roth. You did it. You broke away from the "big/fat people are all lazy, timid, bullies, henchmen" schtick (well, kind of... Al was pretty damned timid, actually) and created a big-person good guy. Good for you, Veronica Roth. Letting a big person into the good guy in-group traditionally reserved for thin people. That was a brave, defiant thing to do. That's what I thought until around page 235, when timid, love-struck Al inexplicably attacks Tris and tries to throw her over a chasm. Wait, what? Where did THAT come from? Oh, right. From Veronica Roth's sizeist bigotry. As though waving her wand and magickally (with a 'k') converting Al into an asshole isn't enough, Roth kills him off a few chapters later and this happens: When Dauntless members pull Al's body out of the chasm, Roth makes sure to note that the body bag they bring for him doesn't fit him, and that that's a very sad thing. In her sea of descriptionless narrative, Roth offers few details. Did the too-small body bag have to be one of them? While I'm on the subject of details, Jeanine, the main bad guy, has a tire of "pudge" around her waist. No one else, besides douche bag Al and douche bag Molly, is described as being big or fat. Only douche bags are fat in Veronica Roth's world. Another interesting fact: every described Abnegation character is thin. I find this very interesting. You see, in faction Abnegation members are supposed to be selfless and self-sacrificing--sort of like those moms who let themselves go because they focus on everyone's needs but their own. But not like those moms at all, because those moms are fat and we can't have that and still be a good guy, now can we? I feel like if Veronica Roth had done any research whatsoever, she would know all of this about fat people and might have painted them differently. But, then, research and knowledge are Satan McEvil in Veronica Roth's world. Roth's treatment of fat/big characters isn't atypical of popular books, and that's what's sad. Kids read this shit, and they internalize it. When all of our good guys are thin and pretty and all of our bad guys are fat and/or ugly, what do our kids learn from that? It sure as hell isn't open-mindedness, which, ironically, is often a theme of these books. But you know what really pisses me off about this book? Petite, straight-bodied main character Tris is repeatedly self-described as too petite. Too thin. Oh poor me, I'm so thin and disadvantaged. Who ever will want a thin female such as myself? Meanwhile, guys are throwing themselves left and right at Tris, despite how slender she is. Divergent is escapism for thin girls and thin women who want to pretend like they don't have every advantage over fat girls and fat women in jobs and in relationships, and who want to pretend like thin people are oppressed. It is crap. Being thin does not make you disadvantaged; it ensures you starring roles in books and movies, jobs that don't suck, and mates. Stop pretending these thin people are underdogs. It's shit, utter shit, that I can turn on the TV and see not one single fat person in a set of commercials, and then pick up a book and hear all about how fat people are the oppressors in our culture.

Fables is a comic book series that follows the lives of several different fairytale characters including Snow White and the Big Bad Wolf. The series takes place after the characters have taken refuge in New York City, because an evil villain named the Adversary has taken over their kingdoms in their homelands. I love this series so much. After I checked the books out from the library, I started purchasing all of the volumes and adding the new issues to my pull list at my local comic book store. I am emotionally committed to these characters. I tried watching Once Upon a Time, but I found it a bit too silly. Fables is what Once Upon a Time strives to be. The series does a good job of balancing humor with darker tales. I will admit, however, that the last few arcs have been a bit dark. There are less than ten issues left at this point, and I am worried about whether my beloved characters are going to find their happily ever afters. I have loved every volume of this series except for the Fables-Jack of Fables crossover arc. I recommend this series to everyone I meet.

I've been so taken with 'Him' and 'Us' that 'Good Boy' seemed like a natural progression because I've found it impossible to get enough of Jamie and Wes. And what a ride 'Good Boy' has been, even though (a confession here) nothing has come close to Jamie/Wes's story. Or should I call it Wesmie now? But Blake and Jess aren't a slouchy pair either. 'Good Boy' is hilarious, quirky and so filled with laugh-out-loud moments at the oddest times that are full of Blake's made-up vocabulary, and larger-than-life presence that pushes believability at times. In many ways, the book reads like a tribute to Blake and even though there's Jess in it, the pages can barely contain his huge, funny personality. He jumps out of the pages like a hulking giant whose presence is impossible to ignore and is just that type of character for whom all the adjectives used don't ever seem sufficient. I liked that Blake was so much more than the bearish, insane guy he was always portrayed to be, just as the authors brought us on a ride to discover who Jessica Canning really is and could be after years of not being able to be anything but flighty. Yet there is such...loudness in the book from Blake himself as well as his family that I think I struggled to know him beyond what he shows the world, at least a lot less than Jess's easier-to-read nature. Still, it's hard not to finish this book feeling nothing less than entertained, even if I thought Blake could have been paired with any heroine and he would have somehow still stolen the show. This spinoff series however, lets me back into the Toronto roster and I'm never saying no to that. *ARC by the author (ever grateful, as always)

I still don't understand why everyone's so crazy about this series. Usually, I am the one that ''defends'' books when I talk to people and I always say that it takes so much effort to write one and that every single book out there has its value. Even if I don't like some of them, I appreciate the effort of writers to tell their story and say what they wanted to say to the world. Now... Fifty Shades trilogy made me change my mind about that. There ARE bad books. There ARE ''authors'' who are really bad at writing. I thought that first part of series was horrible and I picked up this part just because someone I know tried to convince me that it gets better and that this story has a point. Now I'm sure that we will never understand each other when it comes to this, because I really, really hate it and I can't think of a single good thing to say about it. Seriously. I don't think I ever hated a book as much as I hate Fifty Shades. Writing is horrible. HORRIBLE! E. L. James did so bad that I was ashamed for reading this. Characters are poorly developed, dialogues are ridiculous and every other sentence is so corny that it hurt my eyes a little bit. I hated how she didn't want to say vagina or ass and used some lame replacements like ''down there'' or ''behind'' or whatever. Hello? You wrote BDSM story and I think that it would be more than ok to call things for what they are. I mean, really - it was ok for her to write a page about his finger going in and out her ass, but it was not ok to actually call it ass. Come on! Also, I was annoyed by how desperately she wanted to sound smart. With no reason at all, she just dropped some stuff in, like who's singing what or who painted what or stuff like that. Most of us knows those kind of things, so it doesn't make you any smarter or better, E. L. It just makes you a little pathetic for trying to show off with your ''knowledge''. What really bothered me in this book were descriptions of women and their reactions to Christian. Every time he showed up somewhere, they were all swoony and stupid around him. I understand that it happens sometimes with really sexy guys, but every time? Where are all those beautiful, strong and confident women of this world? What happened to ones that don't turn to idiots every time a good looking man asks them something? What about those who can get their shit together and stand their ground, or ones that are able to talk to hot guys without their brains turning to pudding? Where are they? Well, according to E. L. James, they don't exist. It's just sad. This whole story is a mess. They get back together only few days after the break up and everything is the same, minus that disgusting contract from first part. They have sex, they talk, they have sex again, some random people show up so it's not only two of them, they have sex again and again and again...Boring. Everything was boring and predictable. James tried to spice this one up with all that crap with Christians ex, but she ruined it by giving hints about what will happen, so there was no surprise there. Boring. Sex, talk, more sex, something happens but for only half a page, then sex, corny talk, sex... boring, boring, boring. No real story. Every interesting thing happens quick and every boring conversation lasts for pages and pages. Even sex became boring after so many same moves and descriptions. I still think that Ana is stupid and Christian is manipulative bastard. I hated them both. I could never ever be friends with a girl like that. She is like a toy. He uses her the way he wants to and she is even happy about it. She is terrible friend (Jose? Kate?) and she is annoying as hell. I have no respect for her at all. Oh, and her inner goddess is back, dancing and doing some weird stuff again. Seriously, WTF!!! Same goes for her hyperactive subconscience. Horrible! Christian is... Well, to all those girls who dream about meeting someone like him, I say - TRY. Just try to be with someone so difficult and jelous and posessive. There are lots of jerks like that everywhere, it's not that hard to find them. So, do that. Go for it. Try to stay with someone who doesn't respect your privacy, who hates every man you talk to, who is jelous of everyone and everything and who is so needy that it's suffocating you. Let me tell you something - no matter how hot or rich or good in bed he is, it's not healthy. That kind of relationship is wrong and it can turn life to hell. After spending a few months with someone like that, I think that every normal girl would escape from him. Experience like that will definitely teach you to be careful about choosing guys and it's a great lesson about your own character, because you have to be strong like a rock to get out of a relationship like that. I know Christian sounds hot when you read about him, but to have someone like that in real life... Don't wish for it. Trust me, that fairytale turns ugly very soon. Leave him for Ana. She is stupid enough to fall for his crap. There are so many things I find wrong with this book, but right now I don't have a strength to write about them. I am too happy to finally be done with it and now I want to go and hopefully collect all those brain cells that I lost while reading this.

Every problem I had with the previous books escalated with this one. I feel disgusted and cheated. When I read Harry Potter I remember having trouble dealing with some character deaths, but the thing was that Rowling handled them so well that the books became an exploration of human grief. They were actually an outlet for my own grief, a way to remind myself that I was not alone in my suffering, and that life could go on and even be beautiful again. There was a sense that Rowling knew what she was doing, and was dealing with things she had first hand knowledge of. Collins' books were suffering for the sake of suffering. She creates some truly wonderful characters and then throws them away as if they were garbage. Like they were worthless. Her carelessness with the life of her characters makes my hands shake. It's not even that she kills her characters so easily and in such gruesome ways, it's that she has no idea how to help her living characters deal with the deaths, and, therefore, also no way to help her reader deal with them. Nightmares are not enough. Those last few chapters simply describe the actions Katniss takes (and they are disgustingly few)which is alarming considering we are inside HER FUCKING HEAD! If you can't write first person grief, DON'T WRITE A FIRST PERSON NARRATIVE. Calming down again. I felt completely abandoned at the end. Katniss is a terrible narrator. I felt abandoned in a way I never have felt from any other author. Not even when I read Divergent was I so alone. It all felt purposeless, time wasted. It's not enough to say that it was an appeal to realism, because it's a first person narrative that only barely deals with the narrating subject at a time when you most need her to be dealt with. If you want to have a blood bath and not write the grief, you need to do it from an outside perspective, not inside the head of your main character. Haymitch was unrecognizable as a character. Good thing Gale turned out to be indirectly tied to Prim's death, because heaven forbid Katniss actually have to make a decision in the end. I have so many problems with this book, I don't even feel like it is worth mentioning them all. It's a very poor ending to something that began so well.

Nine interlinked short tales chronicling ruined relationships, cheating, death, family, and more. At the heart of these stories is the irrepressible, irresistible Yunior, a young hardhead whose longing for love is equaled only by his recklessness--and by the extraordinary women he loves and loses: artistic Alma; the aging Miss Lora; Magdalena, who thinks all Dominican men are cheaters; and the love of his life, whose heartbreak ultimately becomes his own. "And that's when I know it's over. As soon as you start thinking about the beginning, it's the end." This being my first read by Junot Diaz, I was in for a pleasant surprise regarding the writing and the tempo of each tale. The author specializes in making his short stories fly by. However, I had a hard time reading most of these tales of cheating and feeling literally zero remorse for it... And even going so far as to say that "it was just a mistake." I have only one thing in mind for people that use that heinous excuse: And I just wish the women in this collection could've listened to Dua Lipa's New Rules: Source Side note on the above song: I recently discovered this feminist, girl-power bop, and I'm completely digging it. It's been on repeat for days now. Not only is the aesthetic on point in the music video (those color coordinations!!! ), but Dua Lipa's singing voice is one not to be trifled with. Circling back to the actual story collection: While the first handful of stories were capturing and different enough to keep me interested, once the narrator became the same one for each coming tale I grew quite over it. Following Yunior from a teen to adulthood didn't end up working in my favour, since his character wasn't that intriguing to see developed over the course of a number of stories. And neither his family nor his romantic partners kept me intrigued enough, so I was disappointed with the second half of this collection. This Is How You Lose Her is, however, a striking introduction to the author's immaculately curated writing style. I'm not sure, however, if I'll be eager to check out Junot Diaz's other books in the near future. Mainly because the short stories left me extremely underwhelmed with the characters as a whole. I could say that there's nothing really wrong with this book. It would have been a decent finale, I guess, if I hadn't been familiar with the YA fantasy genre. Here's the problem with Frost Like Night: it didn't have anything new. It was almost like a list of every single thing that usually happens in a YA fantasy trilogy finale: - the main character trains in a place isolated from the rest of the world; - there is a marriage; - the love triangle is resolved, the two characters have sex and they're attacked the day later; - the villain gets defeated in an anti-climatic way; - the two characters you expect to die actually die and no one else does Nessa and the mentor whose name I don't remember. As if I expected them to survive. Everything is predictable, so predictable it felt like a YA fantasy script. I mean that - everything felt emotionless, too. Even the characters I had liked in the previous books. It's just everything I have seen before, with nothing new. And these things were almost a cliche in 2014, but this book came out in 2016. All of this has been done before. This is boring! YA fantasy books should never be boring. I wasn't exactly a fan of the first book - the series was kind of cliche since the beginning - but I thought it could get better. There have been series that got better in the second and third book. This just went downhill, and the worldbuilding still makes no sense. I didn't like anything about this book, not one scene. I don't know why I didn't DNF it; even while I was reading it it felt like a waste of time.

It could take two pages for the protagonist to say she wished she was back in her kingdom. Her internal ramblings seemed endless and they made the story duller than it had to be. As an example, I had read the first five chapters when I closed the book to go to work. When I came home, I spent fifteen minutes deciding which book I was going to read next before I remembered I was reading this one. If a story can't make you interested in it within the first five chapters, it's doing something wrong. I think if it were cut by fifty or so pages, it would have been better.

Made You Up was a book filled with quirky characters if you like that sort of thing -- the comparison to Silver Linings Playbook (the movie at least; haven't read the book) felt apt. I did think this book felt long for realistic fiction that's of the self-discovery sort, with a subplot (the scoreboard thing) that, to me, didn't add much to the story and was far less interesting than Alex and her brave and moving attempts to navigate the world. But overall, this was a book that really made me think. In fact, I was reading this in an airport, got up from my seat, and saw a woman pushing a soft pet carrier on a luggage cart. I looked inside, and there was ... a turkey. A live turkey! I immediately thought of Alex and how lucky I am that I didn't have to doubt for one minute what I was seeing, wonder if it was a truth-is-stranger-than-fiction moment or the tricks of an imbalanced mind. Alex is definitely a character I will remember. Thanks to the publisher for providing me a free advance copy for review. Read more of my reviews on YA Romantics or follow me on Bloglovin

She has done it again! Hats off to Jennifer Donnelly for this excellent follow up to The Tea Rose! The Winter Rose follows the story of Sid Malone, one of London's notorious gangsters and India Jones, one of the first female doctors who only wants to help the poor. If you have read The Tea Rose, you will know the true identity of Sid Malone, so if you haven't read that get on it. The Winter Rose is more of a historical romance than The Tea Rose was, which normally would have me eye rolling through all 707 pages but it was well contracted and wasn't the focal point. We are taken into the dark dirty background of London, we see how it was like to live in poverty. The detail that went into story was sublime, you cared for the characters that were suffering through poverty, even though they were nothing but background characters. Jennifer Donnelly is excellent in pulling you in and making everything feel real to the reader. Character wise, I enjoyed the characters of Sid Malone and India Jones more than the ones we had in The Tea Rose. Sid was complex with many hidden secrets to him. India was almost a replica of Fiona, only India is a doctor who wants to open a clinic for the poor and offer free services. When they cross paths it isn't 'instant love', there is actual loathing and anger toward each other because of what Sid is. Though Sid isn't truly a bad person, he does take a long time to begin to want to change himself, which makes him a believable character. My only complaint about this book is the fact that at times Seamie's and Willa's story started to intrude on the story of Sid and India, even before Sid and Seamie cross paths. It did put me off slightly, and I am questioning if I want to read the final book, The Wild Rose. In the snippets we got about Seamus and Willa, I found myself bored with them and knowing the final book is all about them I just am not sure. Since I love The Tea Rose and loved The Winter Rose even more, I will probably end up reading it.

This is my second time around with this book and I've dropped my original rating from 3 stars to 1. I remember sort-of enjoying reading this the first time because there was so much WTF going on. Underground fight clubs, secret identities, gambling and fights in Vegas? All I was waiting for was a secret baby and an unexpected inheritance from an eccentric millionaire uncle. I do recall being disturbed by the two protagonists being so seriously emotionally abusive towards each other but at the time I was willing to look past it. Not so much this time. Either I have gotten a lot less tolerant of this bullshit or I was drunk for the entire first reading. The way the 2 protagonists treat each other is pretty horrifying. Travis pulls some super-possessive caveman bullshit almost from the very beginning of his relationship with Abby; Abby fucks with Travis' head almost unforgiveably. They lie to each other constantly. Travis beats up a friend of his on at least 2 separate occasions for saying something gross to Abby. Abby sees Travis' violence as proof of his twoo-wuv. But if your partner is beating the shit out of anyone who says something nasty to you, or who tries to dance with you, or even looks at you sideways, this is a clue that you are seen as a possession, not a person. THIS SHIT IS NOT ROMANTIC. It is gross. Lastly, the writing itself is pretty clunky. It's written in first person (not my favorite), it doesn't really flow well, and goes on for way too long. The story could have stopped 150 pages before it did and it would have felt complete. I read lots and lots of fiction, because Real Life, I have enough. I understand that what we read can shape the way we think, but I don't believe that people can't tell tell the difference between fiction and reality. I mean, I love Epic Fantasy but I don't believe a dragon is going to swoop down and eat all of the virgins. I love Historical Romance, but I don't believe that the Marquess of Somewhere-or-Other is going to sweep me off to his castle and shower me with jewels. I'm not hating on this book because it sets a bad example. I'm hating on this book BECAUSE ALL OF THESE PEOPLE ARE ASSHOLES. What is with this shit? I feel like almost every NA novel I've read recently is about super-jerks and the dipshits who love them.
