"What secrets may have lurked in the shadows of Albert Einstein's fame? His first wife, Mileva "Mitza" Maric, was more than the devoted mother of their three children--she was also a brilliant physicist in her own right, and her contributions to the special theory of relativity have been hotly debated for more than a century. In 1896, the extraordinarily gifted Mileva is the only woman studying physics at an elite school in Zurich. There, she falls for charismatic fellow student Albert Einstein, who promises to treat her as an equal in both love and science. But as Albert's fame grows, so too does Mileva's worry that her light will be lost in her husband's shadow forever." This was one of the books that I was most excited about after BEA. It is a book that seems designed just for me. Historical fiction [?] About women's history [?] Science [?] So why did I delay reading this until now? Every time I picked it up I couldn't quite bring myself to read it. I knew what it was going to be. It is yet another story of a woman who was forced to give up her own ambitions to fit in with the mores of her time. Honestly, the thought exhausted me. The book is a well written story of the life of Mileva Maric. She was a Serbian woman who attended university in Zurich in physics. She was Einstein's classmate. She finished her coursework but failed her degree. She had a child with Einstein before they married. That child either died young or was given up for adoption. Nothing is known for sure. After their marriage they had two sons. They divorced when he was having an affair. His mother didn't like her because Mileva was an inferior dark-skinned Slavic person. (I don't know. She looks pretty pale to me but I'm Slavic too so Mama Einstein probably wouldn't have cared for my opinion either.) It isn't known if she helped him with his scientific work. There are some letters from him to her where he refers to "our work" but it is earlier in the relationship. This book imagines that she had the idea for relativity and worked on the math. What follows is a story of erasure. Her name isn't on the paper because it wouldn't look good that he needed the help of a woman. He stops asking her for advice. She feels like he sees her as just a housewife. He spends more and more time away and blames her for being selfish if she questions him. He tries to impose a bizarre contract on her in order to keep the marriage together for the sake of the children. "CONDITIONS A. You will make sure: 1. that my clothes and laundry are kept in good order; 2. that I will receive my three meals regularly in my room; 3. that my bedroom and study are kept neat, and especially that my desk is left for my use only. B. You will renounce all personal relations with me insofar as they are not completely necessary for social reasons. Specifically, You will forego: 1. my sitting at home with you; 2. my going out or travelling with you. C. You will obey the following points in your relations with me: 1. you will not expect any intimacy from me, nor will you reproach me in any way; 2. you will stop talking to me if I request it; 3. you will leave my bedroom or study immediately without protest if I request it. D. You will undertake not to belittle me in front of our children, either through words or behavior." Source This is the part that was hard to read. I wish I was more surprised by it but my feeling as I was reading this was, "Yeah, same ol' same ol'" This is the story of ambitious women from the beginning of time. I was thrilled when she was awarded the proceeds of any future Nobel Prize in the divorce settlement. You go girl! She got it too. That's actual historical fact. Actually she got to live on the interest from it which she invested in rental properties. I'd recommend this book to any historical fiction fans. This review was originally posted on Based On A True Story

This was an audacious attempt at developing, extrapolating the Harry Potter universe and I'm glad to have read this. Reading this brought me into a head-on collision with nostalgia. This first act is filled with scenes from the Harry Potter series and it both made me both happy and sad reading, reliving those memories again. I reread Harry Potter quite frequently and I've similar feelings while reliving memories then. But this is different, this has a sense of finality to it because I am aware that this is a play written after the original was finished, done. Anyway, I liked the play. I loved the first act so much. I was curious and excited about the next generation of Potters, Weasley-Grangers and Malfoys. I liked Albus Severus and Scorpius very much, though they make stupid decisions, because who wouldn't at their age, Harry and his friends did too, right? But I think they made Ron look too stupid sometimes, his part in the whole plot and play is very weak. I was aggravated at the beginning of the play because of how Draco Malfoy's character was developed, but then I liked it when the writers took his character in the direction I wanted. I liked the story in the beginning but then it slowly went in a direction I did not like. The writing's great and all, but I wish the major plot of the play was something else. The story was all over the place at times. To the writers' credit, this play is similar to Harry Potter series in the sense that it ties off things to the T most of the time like how JKR does. Tying threads from book 1 with something in book 7 and we'd be left awestruck about it all. I almost had tears during Snape's scenes. It was a good play on the whole but I'm sure a major part of my appreciation is due to my preexisting love for Harry Potter universe and what it means me. It is also the source of criticism, I would have liked if the main plot did not rewrite or hope to rewrite what has already happened.

Purely out of curiosity, I'm continuing on with what I feel like is a faint shadow of the Vampire Academy series. In this book, Alex continues on with her training, snarks off even more to Seth/her instructors/everyone in a position of power, despite knowing what's in store for her if she gets in further trouble (mindless servitude to Pures). The plot is also gaping with holes; several important plot points never got resolved in my mind. They were just presented, then seemingly forgotten about through the very end, even if they were a recurring point in the story (the mysterious servants at the New York Covenant, for one). I think my main qualm with this book is not so much that it's a copy of another series. I have no problems with that. Masterpieces are influential; great works of arts often start an entire new movement. I don't see the negativity in imitation as long as the imitation is an amazing one. My main problem with this series is the main character, Alex. Alex is such a bloody hypocrite. She loses her temper easily, she is bitchy (admittedly so to herself). She slut shames (calling a rival a skank? Not cool). She repeatedly makes terrible decisions, suffer bad consequences, and then regrets it in hindsight. And still, STILL, after everything she's done, she repeatedly makes the same mistakes, showing no signs that she has learned from her experiences or has matured in any way. "I didn't think; I just launched my shiny red apple right at her face." Yep. She didn't think. It seems to be the recurrent theme in the book. Alex's personality, actions, and beliefs are all contradictory. She is supposed to be an amazing fighter, killing three daimons on her own, yet she can barely hold her own in class. Romvi was an embarrassment to the male race, but he didn't hear me bitching. Calling your instructor names after he beat your ill-prepared ass to the mat. Real mature, Alex. She hates her uncle and stepfather, and refuses to acknowledge the fact that she really owes much to them. Her peers and instructors accuse her of using her influential guardians and family to get out of trouble, and they're right. With all the stupid shit Alex pulls, having the Headmaster as an uncle and the Minister as a stepfather has gotten her out of trouble countless times. When the school seems to be infiltrated by daimons, Alex rebels against the restrictions placed on her and the other half-bloods, even while knowing that the Pures themselves are placed under similar rules. She chafes against the rules and seeks to break then as much as possible. While visiting the zoo, Alex sees the caged animals and observes "Here the animals are safe. Out in the wild, they'd be killing one another or being poached. I know they've lost their freedom, but sometimes things have to be sacrificed." Uhh...a little contradictory there, Alex? It seems like that's what they're doing at school. Aren't you being a bit of a hypocrite? The list goes on and on. Repeated mistakes, no learning, no maturation. "I should've stayed in my room like I was supposed to. There was a reason why a curfew had been imposed. The sanctuary of the Covenant had been violated once. I'd forgotten that, or I just hadn't thought about it, or cared. I never stopped to think." No shit, Sherlock. Despite everything she fails at doing, despite barely being able to hold her own in class, Alex is still queen of the Mary Sues. Without being even a Sentinel, she single-handedly kills daimons, furies...everything they can throw at her. Yeah, I know she's the Apollyon. There has to be some sort of realism in her development as a fighter. To flunk so badly in practice and in class and then become a superhero in the middle of a real fight? Doesn't work that way. I don't buy it. Another thing that irked me...I don't know if it's my version of the e-book that's got the spelling wrong, but the singular for furies is A FURY, not furie. I think I'm done with this series.

Ally Carter writes the some of the cutest literature. Don't take that the wrong way, it's a compliment. If you need something light-hearted and simple to read curled up somewhere on a rainy day, Ally Carter is your way to go. I'm going to say her Gallagher Girls series didn't start of that well, but it's definitely much better in the later books. However, Heist Society is good throughout the series. The plots are very simple; there's a bad guy, then Kat's adorable family gets involved. They pull the biggest con ever attempted, and they win YAY. It's very suitable for younger kids, (except for when Hale gets drunk). But even then, it's written for a more juvenile audience. If you're looking for a complex. emotional plot, with twists and turns this is not it. BUT, it's still so, so enjoyable. It's fun and adventurous. The names of some of the Heist capers are ridiculous (ex. Three Blind Mice, the Anastasia, Cat in the Cradle, Count of Monte Cristo). It's so much fun imagining all the different cons those could possible refer to! The characters are definitely one of the best aspects of this book. Kat, Hale, Uncle Eddie, Bobby, Gabrielle (who I really love), Angus, Hamish, Simon, Silas Foster, Marcus, Marianne. They're all fantastic and whimsical and hilarious and very, very lovable. And the bad guys are fun to hate too! Hale's entire family is horrible, Garrett was despicable. But it was all so lighthearted. Although, there was a scare towards the end, there is nothing awful that happens in these books. They'll just make you plain old laugh in amusement. The relationships are beautiful. Kat and Hale go through some bumps, but they still love each other. Kat and her Uncle Eddie are always there for each other. Kat and Gabrielle...I adore them and their little cousin bickering. The characters never let each other down though, they are loyal to the end. In these books, family is everything, and it just adds a bright spot to your day. Overall, these books are simple, delightful, and heartwarming. It's just a pleasure to read, and will take your mind off your problems.

It's Worth Listening when THE WHOLE TOWN'S TALKING http://fangswandsandfairydust.com/201... Advanced Reader Copy provided by publisher for review. No remuneration was exchanged and all opinions presented herein are my own except as noted. This is a wonderful story -- about a community I think we would all have loved to grow up in. It is funny, sweet, sad, and even occasionally tragic -- I cried more than one tear listening. There's nothing sexy, nothing risque; but there is plenty of surprise, and even celebrity visits. To be sure, there is a bit of existential uncertainty in the story, but no overt religion. Trust me, I was on the lookout for religious sentiment to slip in. There are a lot of themes, one is innocence and the loss of it. Another is how we can be accepting of other people, despite their backgrounds or abilities, if we all behave decently with each other. The story is beautifully read, I especially loved Lordor's voicing and Katrina's. I adored, the neighbor, Elner and wanted her to come over and cheer me up. Elner, in particular, is the funny neighbor, the loving aunt, the best-hearted, the humble and a sweet woman who knows what you need and offers it without expectation of recompense, character I love. I think THE WHOLE TOWN'S TALKING has a IT'S A WONDERFUL LIFE vibe; filled with characters you'll love. This is the perfect book for a trip, for a gift (especially Mothers Day! I really enjoyed this one -- It's THE "feel-good" novel this spring.

His mother is in a new "relationship" since his father left them shortly after Alyssa disappeared, but the new relationship is full of drugs, booze and abuse, so Johnny's really taking care of himself. I really liked this. There were some unexpected twists, and it was one that I wanted to keep reading. It was told from a few different points of view, and there were times, unexpectedly, that I actually enjoyed reading the detective's point of view more than Johnny's. Overall, though, very good book!

Ugh. Who know that a story about a supernatural serial killer, set in the time of Jack the Ripper's London, could be so godawfully boring? For one, there was no suspense or thriller aspect. It read more like a procedural, of sorts, and not a particularly good one, at that. I mean, there wasn't even any doubt as to who the killer was, because the audience is out and out told, so there's no guessing, no mystery, no suspense. The best thing this story has going for it is the idea of it. A story of murders in the time of the Ripper's reign, the Thames Torso Murders - which I had not been aware of prior - which have a supernatural aspect to them which is actually partially responsible for Jack. I mean, great premise, right? But, no. Most of the time is spent on Dr. Bond's dithering, and his repeated visits to the opium dens (and even that wasn't written in a particularly interesting fashion.) It sort of tried to be From Hell, or even Murder as a Fine Art, and just completely failed in both endeavours. As to the dithering, first it was the whole "but I'm a man of science, I can't believe in the evidence of my own goddamned eyes" thing, and then it was the "oh, but why does this fall to my lot". He even calls attention to it at one point, saying he's as annoying as Hamlet at one point. This does not make it any less annoying. And then that ending. Dear gods. Pages of pages of nothing, and then the final confrontation is over in, like, 2 pages. That's not even much of an exaggeration. And after dithering about killed James, even though the priest wants to... suddenly the priest decides to extricate the Upir instead, and Bond looks into his eyes and is like, "Yeah, you're totally guilty" and stabs him in the throat. The end. And then it literally just ends. I mean, there's an epilogue, of sorts, that's another 2 pages, but there really isn't in the much of wrap up. Apparently this isn't a standalone, because of course it's not. Though I'm not sure why they thought putting the Upir back in the river would stop it, since that's where it came from, and it's not like there's not a choice of hosts in London for it to latch back on to. I've also heard that Kominski and the priest, at least tolerable characters, if underused, aren't even in the sequel. So, yeah, I won't be reading it...

While I liked the first book in this series (also a standalone) I REALLY enjoyed this one. Jeannine Allison portrays real people in real situations that are rife with emotion and depth of character but somehow manages to keep the angst-factor very low. The situations are heavy, dealing with alcoholism, drug addiction, depression, but handled with a deft--not heavy--touch. The realism portrayed in the pages is something I appreciate a lot. For instance, at around the 60% mark the main couple have a discussion/mild argument. It's not resolved immediately but doesn't blow up into something forced. Both characters maturely agree to disagree (for now) and move on. It was a tiny moment but to me, lack of unnecessary angst was a nice touch and added to the sense of these characters being real, full people. I love both characters. Naomi is feisty and smart, not a pushover. She holds her own against Damien who is tough-but-sweetness underneath. I liked the character of Ellie too--Damien's ne'er do well sister who's been a heavy drinker since she was fifteen. The subplot of Ellie's situation was one of the strongest parts of this novel for me, and I think she's due to get her own book. Yay! I love her. It came at me swift, and had I not been sitting down, it surely would have knocked me on my ass. Nothing else could explain this extreme sense of rightness, of fullness. Lots of quotable moments, lots of insightful observations about addiction and the pain of loving someone through it, and the second chance we all have living within us (for the addicted AND those who suffer from the outside) should we only choose to dig deep and grab for it. This author seems to get stronger with every novel she writes and I'm looking forward to the next in this series.

Girl finds herself dead in a void-like place she dubs IS, filled with objects lost during her life. These objects take her back into her life, revisiting the events and even changing them. But what does it mean? What's the point and how did she die? The story overall felt very repetitive. Just a series of life events visited. I understand each event was chosen for some specific relevance, but I found myself getting tired of them anyway. The characters were fairly realistic. Very teenager, if you know what I mean. I did feel for them now and again, but didn't feel connected to any. The ending was... closure. It didn't make me happy or angry, it just ended the story. I put this novel down feeling it was complete, but not altogether satisfying. 2.5 out of 5. Something was just missing for me. A surprisingly lucid and profound take on loneliness even when surrounded with people, racial tension in the late 1930s Southern small towns, and growing up. Some characters could have used a more development (like the angry Dr. Copeland), but I greatly enjoyed the slow studies of their lives and evolutions. It's very light on plot - more a string of relentless, subtle and not-so-subtle bad things happening to people, and the way they weather it all. But this isn't at all a depressing book. "I wasn't sure if I wanted to hear such a big secret. It might not fit in my head and then it would spill out everywhere." A Head Full of Ghosts begins as many horror stories do. The Barrett family is a pretty normal group. Mom, Dad, and sisters Marjorie and Merry live a peaceful life in their suburban home. Things change when older sister Marjorie begins to exhibit odd behavior. The doctors and specialists can't seem to find a medical explanation for her condition. Dad turns to the church and becomes convinced that Marjorie is possessed by a demon. Given their unusual circumstance, the Barrett family does what any American family would do. They cash in on their troubles by allowing a television crew to film their life and attempts at exorcism for a reality show. What ensues is the tragic erosion of a once happy family. The parents don't agree on how to approach treatment for Marjorie, Merry is ignored by the rest of her family, and Marjorie is pushed to physical and emotional limits. Is the girl truly possessed, or is the Barrett family merely enacting a hoax for financial gain? A Head Full of Ghosts is a refreshing addition to the horror genre. Paul Tremblay writes with a self-awareness that gives an original perspective to an otherwise familiar story. Tremblay clearly has an extensive knowledge and appreciation for all things horror. There is nothing overtly shocking or gory about this book. Rather, the story unfolds with a slow build that gives just enough suspense to keep us hanging onto every word. I like my horror stories to make me think and fill with dread. By that mark, A Head Full of Ghosts is an excellent novel that will leave you with an anxious paranoia of every little bump in the night.

Review originally posted on Quinn's Book Nook You guys, this book was totally kick-ass. I had been wanting to read this book since it came into the library last year, but never got around to it. Even though I wasn't in love with Bray's A Great and Terrible Beauty, I still wanted to give Beauty Queens a try. Finally, I decided to go the audiobook route, and I am so glad I did. This book was so much fun, and I often sat in my car for an extra five to ten minutes, just to see what these girls would do next. I will admit that it took me a little bit to get into it. At first I thought it was going to be mainly about Adina, and although I do agree with her opinions, she was so annoying. But this book is actually about almost all the surviving beauty contestants. And by the time I read half the book, I loved all these girls! Libba Bray certainly knows how to create unique personalities for all the different characters, and let me tell you, there are tons of characters to keep track of. But somehow, it isn't as difficult as you would think. And I ended up caring about every single beauty contestant, even Taylor Renee Crystal Hawkins and Adina. Something that I absolutely loved about this book - it shows how women and girls can be great friends with each other. I absolutely hate when people say that women are catty, because that is bullshit. Excuse my language, but seriously! I actually stopped reading a YA book, because the author made that catty girl comment (in an attempt at humor) and although it wasn't a big part of the book, I just couldn't continue with the story. So it was so wonderful to see these girls become so close to one another, and to see them helping each other out. And one cannot comment on Beauty Queens without mentioning the footnotes. Oh my gosh, they were hilarious, and really helped set the ton of the book. And did I mention there are pirates in Beauty Queens! Yeah, pirates! And I absolutely loved the captain. Libba Bray herself narrates the audiobook, and I am often a bit nervous when authors narrate their own books. But man she totally rocked it! She created all these different accents and voices for the girls - it was wonderful. Also, if you listen to the audiobook, at the beginning of every disc one of the girls says "Beauty Queens, Disc X." then she says something hilarious about that number. Too funny! So, basically, if you haven't read this book, you should. Right now! Better yet, listen to the audiobook!

A Separate Peace tells the story of a boy, Gene, who goes to a boarding school called Devon in New England while World War II is going on. He has a few friends, but one of his friends shines above all. Phineas is handsome, athletic, and just an overall good person, and sometimes Gene wonders how he ended up with such a great friend. Even though Gene is more academically inclined than Phineas, who slides through his classes with D's, Gene begins to envy Finny's goodness. This leads to something happening between the two friends that summer that banishes the innocence of both of them. Okay, I literally never thought I would rate a book one star whenever I started goodreads. Things I Liked: 1) Phineas He was literally the only part I liked of this book. The beginning of the book, I was pretty intrigued by because Phineas isn't only likable at Devon, he's a likable book character. He was so sweet and I was hardly surprised when he forgave Gene for all the stuff he put him through. (Even though I highly doubt someone would actually forgive their friend for something like that...) Things I Disliked: 1) Gene I hated Gene. From the very start. I would kill for a friend like Phineas and he just has to go being jealous of him. Like Gene, you could change yourself and be more like Phineas but no, that would be too much work for you. I'll admit, I'm a jealous person. However, I would never do that to someone that treated me as well as Phineas. Here are some example of Phineas being the great person he is: 1) Phineas and Gene were walking back from the beach after they spent the night there. All these girls were staring at Phineas because he was obviously the more handsome guy. Phineas turned to Gene and seriously told him that the girls were staring at him. Uh, no. 2) Phineas broke the 100 yd Freestyle in the Devon pool but he told Gene not to tell anybody. 2) Rambling/Empty This is one of those books where I'll be reading a page, and once I'm finished with that page I'll look up from the book and be like "what was the point of what I just read?" and there were times when I thought to myself, maybe it has a deeper meaning, but mostly I couldn't think of one. Besides the rambling, this book was just so boring and hard to get through. The most exciting parts were the ones with Finny in them, and he was absent from the book for about half. There was nothing to it besides the accident. 3) Unbelievable Although Phineas is the perfect human being, he should have caught onto Gene sooner just because of when he first tried to admit his wrongs, etc. He knew what happened at the er, spot of the accident, and even though he was a straight D student, he would have caught on. And there was like a 10% chance someone would forgive someone for that. Not only the first thing Gene did, but not telling him? Someone else had to make him admit it, and that led to the second thing happened basically. If Phineas was a real person, he would have told Gene to get the hell out of his life because he was the best friend he could have asked for, and he betrayed him. 4) How They Called It An "Accident" Throughout the book (and throughout my packet of questions for school) they called in "the accident" but it obviously wasn't. If it was an accident, Gene would have automatically apologized and said that he just slipped a little. Also, how at the end Gene said "I never killed anybody" and then a few lines later "I killed my enemy." WHY WAS PHINEAS YOUR ENEMY? HE WAS THE BEST FRIEND YOU COULD EVER HAVE. JEALOUS BASTARD. I read that page like 5 times. The last page is usually supposed to make a sad book seem a little better, but it just made me feel worse. Overall... I wouldn't recommend this book to anyone. I doubt I would have read it if I wasn't forced to by my teacher. The description of it on goodreads just sounds lame because you can't make the book sound interesting without spoiling what happens. This book was just overall depressing and I think it had some good overall lessons, but I don't think anyone would be so jealous of their friend that they would do what Gene did to Phineas. Especially when the friend was as good as Finny.

As ecstatic as I was for this books release, I was equally as nervous and already a wreck after the first few pages. Part of me loved the back and forth style from past to present but this story is so intense that it was a real test to not skim or skip chapters entirely to get find out what happens in one of the other aspects. I still cling to Claire's character, some would find the writing style excessive in detail but it made me connect to her more in Consequences and really follow her throughout the entire story. The ups and downs through all three books are intense but the "present" narration really put my mood in a downcast over the entire past, I felt like I wasn't going to be satisfied after everything my emotions had been through. Regardless my emotions will recover as this story will leave its mark and will always be carried with me; I would say the cause is of the excessive detail ... the constant building of varying aspects and perceptions that give you an excited cringe as you approach every new twist and turn. Every situation drops a bomb that either gives you a taste of relief or adds to the weight bulking on your anticipation to just reach the end because somewhere there has to be more relief! Although you always have that hope, the possibility was somewhat drowned with the 'present' narrations. Whatever you want or expect the next page to bring, or the ending to be...my only advice is to not even try to assume where the story is going to take you! So I'm exhausted and have to unwillingly tuck these away until I recover enough to thoroughly enjoy them again aaaand again!

This book is one of the best ever! Oh my gosh. There are no words to describe this book. It is now one of my all time favorites. This is a story of a small town where five young men go off to war and only one returns home, but he has been markedly injured and scarred inside and out. He knows his life will never be the same. There was so much loss. Loss of lives, loss of beauty, and loss of one's identity. There was horrible guilt, as well, because Ambrose is the one who convinced his four friends to join the service with him and they didn't make it home. Ambrose Young was the most beautiful of young men with everything going for him until he was critically injured in war. He was a wrestling star that had the opportunity to go to college on a wrestling scholarship. He had what all young men dream of. It is the tale of one girl's (Fern) love for a broken boy, and a wounded warrior's love for an unremarkable girl. A friendship that overcomes heartache. The Book Description say it like this: Modern tale of Beauty and the Beast, where we discover that there is a little beauty and a little beast in all of us. Fern had loved Ambrose from afar. She knew her appearance: fiery red hair, braces, thick glasses and a very small stature were not appealing to guys and there was no way she could compete against the beautiful, curvy gals in her school. But, our girl Fern, she knew and loved the real Ambrose, the one underneath the beauty and the wrestling. This book was remarkable, the writing excellent, and the storyline gripping. It pulls you in and doesn't let loose until you have read it all...and then I didn't want it to end...ever!!! Amy Harmon is to be commended. Added to this story is a wheelchair bound young man, Bailey, Fern's cousin and best friend. He is an incredible young man with Duchenne muscular dystrophy. He displays great courage and heroism and was so completely lovable. DO NOT MISS THIS BOOK!!!!! I read more than 300 books a year and have for many years and this book ranks in my top 5. Words cannot efficiently describe how wonderful this book was. There is angst; you will cry; you will feel so sad; but you will also rejoice in the power of love!

When I heard Stephanie Perkins had edited another anthology of short stories, I immediately put it on my TBR list. I adored My True Love Sent To Me, and I had high hopes for this one. And I wasn't disappointed. As with any anthology, not every story was a hit. Some were spot-on, most were good and only a couple were only-okay. I don't really read short stories that often, but I think Stephanie Perkins has the knack for collating a great collection. Some of the stories are contemporary and some are fantasy, but each story was so summery, it was so evocative. A breakdown of my ratings for each story..... Head, Scales, Tongue, Tail by Leigh Bardugo - 4 stars The End of Love by Nina LaCour - 4 stars Last Stand at the Cinegor by Libba Bray - 3 stars Sick Pleasures by Francesca Lia Block - 2 stars In Ninety Minutes, Turn North by Stephanie Perkins - 4 stars Souvenirs by Tim Federle - 4 stars Inertia by Veronica Roth - 4.5 stars Love is the Last Resort by Jon Skovron - 2 stars Good Luck and Farewell by Brandy Colbert - 3 stars Brand New Attraction by Cassandra Clare - 5 stars A Thousand Ways This Could All Go Wrong by Jennifer E Smith - 4 stars The Map of Tiny Perfect Things by Lev Grossman - 5 stars My favourite was Brand New Attraction by Cassandra Clare - I think she's one of those authors who I just click with because I've never read anything of hers that I didn't like. Brand New Attraction is the story of a girl who lives in a dark fairground with her dad. They have tons of creepy attractions and the whole fairground is powered by a demon (obviously). Another really good story was The Map of Tiny Perfect Things by Lev Grossman. It's kind of a pastiche of Groundhog Day, but every day is 4th August and the boy it's happening to is pretty content to spend every day for the rest of his existence just sitting reading books, until he goes to the swimming pool one day and meets a girl also stuck in the time loop. It's funny but also really emotional. The only story I couldn't get into was Love Is The Last Resort. It was written in a style that made it feel like it was set in the 1940s; I could imagine Katherine Hepburn and Spencer Tracy were playing the lead roles. There was nothing specifically wrong with it, it just wasn't for me. I'd definitely recommend this for anyone's summer reading list - it's a great book to take to the beach. 4 stars overall

Due to life getting in the way, I was unable to read this book as quickly as I wanted. Once I started I didn't want to stop. It was a fast paced smooth moving story with characters that kept me engaged and a plot that I needed to follow every step of the way. Riley is a raven shifter that is living with a wolf pack. No one knows why she left her previous pack but they are accepting of her nevertheless. Tao is a wolf that doesn't like anyone from outside of his pack. He's highly suspicious of strangers and that includes Riley. I haven't read the previous books in this series so I'm unsure what led up to a drunken hook up between these two. However, once they're together, they ignite the pages of this book with a fierce passion and connection. Tao is an abrasive, tactless, and direct hero that isn't concerned with keeping his thoughts from those around him. Riley is a tough, independent heroine that is comfortable letting her inner strength show in all that she does. Normally, it would seem this couple could not work together. However, as they move forward to solve a mystery related to Riley's past, as well as other danger that is aimed at the wolf pack, it becomes obvious that this pair is perfect for each other. I especially loved the fact that Tao's character didn't change once he began to give into his feelings for Riley. He was still harsh and confrontational and she was completely capable of dealing with him and turning the tables on him at times. I would absolutely recommend this book to anyone who enjoys shifter stories as well as a couple that know how to deal with their issues in a straight up manner without all the push and pull. While I applaud this book for having a character with memory loss NOT caused by amnesia, and while I usually love twin stories, the idea of this absorbed/missing twin suddenly controlling Sasha and her love life was just a tad too woo-woo for me. I'm a Harry Potter fan, but not what I'd call a complete Potterhead -- you know, one who has every single thing from canon memorized -- so I thought I'd give this a shot. The books seem well done and I liked the author's website. Sadly, I'm not very far in and I don't think I can keep reading. Firstly, it's really glaringly not Rowling's voice. I know the author tried hard to keep it in her tone, but boy, those are some big shoes to fill. Secondly, one of James's first adventures when he gets to Hogwarts is to go on a night adventure in which muggle-baiting takes place. James is spelled to look like an alien, and he stumbles out of a space ship of sorts and scares a poor old man half to death, who, by the way is holding a shotgun. I realize this is an attempt to bring in some silly Weasley-twin style fun, but isn't it in book 5 or 6 where Mr. Weasley is dealing with the exploding toilets and explains to Harry that it's not so much the prank itself as the feeling behind it. The idea that wizards are better than muggles -- eg: all that they were fighting with Voldemort's supporters. That's a pretty major canon theme to mess up, yeah? I don't know where else this "Raise the Wocket" club goes, but I don't think I can continue. I do like some of what I've read that makes it seem like James will have a friend in Slytherin, and that maybe some of those old hatchets will be buried. It's probably pretty cute, and maybe my kids will like it, but I'm afraid it's not preserving any of the original magic for me. I do hope the author keeps writing, and love that he has a fan base for this.

He also deals with a haunted veteran father and a brother he never sees. As you read, you see that he's trying to find his other emotions other than the rage that seems to always come first. Dante seems to be more of an intellectual rather than an active person. He understands more of who he is and I think that helped Ari along his own journey. He coaxed answers from Ari, made him think, but still struggles a little with his identity - that of his heritage. They make for an adorable pair at times, willing to protect each other. And I loved the family element in this. That was well done. Deep, complex characters: check! However, the dialogue and writing seemed...stunted at times. Stiff. It didn't flow well, it wasn't a comfortable atmosphere. It jumped oddly. This made for a tough time in connecting with the characters, as well. I can see their problems, understand how they can be problems, but sometimes the writing made it hard to really feel it. My rating from 5:

This book came to me highly reviewed by trusted media, peers and the ever wonderful Emma Watson; however, The Queen of the Tearling fell very short of my expectations. The story is set up in a way that makes readers expect a strong leading lady, but instead we are left with 300+ pages of the novel's 434 wherein men continuously disregard our heroine and make decisions while blatantly ignoring her opinions and wishes. The Queen's Guard justifies this enraging behavior by explaining to Queen Kelsea that she is missing information crucial to making informed decisions, yet they refuse to fill Kelsea in on any of the information she is missing or answer any of her questions. I wanted to like this book. I really, really did. I understand needing to establish setting, characters and plot, but Johansen spends an exorbitant amount of time describing each narrator's current surroundings in painstaking detail, and spends no time answering reader (or our leading lady's) questions. Additionally, Johansen's attempts at defying the "pretty princess" archetype does more body shaming of Queen Kelsea than societal good. Overall, this book was ok. I may continue the series out of curiosity, but really wishing I was able to be emotionally invested instead.

This book has singlehandedly turned my insatiable reading addiction towards the last, yet unexplored area of post-apocalyptic / dystopian writing - namely Zombie Apocalypse. I've bought this book on impulse and this is was definitely one of the best spent money in my life. Actually, although zombies in Newsleflesh trilogy mean the end of the civilization as we know it and are a deadly danger, they are used by humans as a handy tool to fight other humans. The bad guys are not the brainless creatures you have to shoot, slash and cut by the dozen, but the political chosen ones whose motto is, or rather should be "To Serve and Protect". "Feed" is a great thriller taking place in the near future, but touching upon many contemporary themes - freedom of speech, whistle-blowing journalism uncovering dirty secrets, a governmental conspiracy protecting such secrets and treating lesser humans like cannon fodder (in this case quite literally) in their machinations. Finally, this is a great emotional rollercoaster revolving around a blogger Georgia Mason and her brother - Shaun Mason who is Irwin. Being blogger myself, I felt an instant sympathy for the Masons' little motley crew of characters and their dead and serious fight with the unknown enemy, which from the start looked a few sizes to big for them. Don't hesitate, read this book. Don't be put off by YA labels attached to the series. It has YA characters and a few typical features, but it is much more than that. Since the time of "Feed" I've read tons of Zombie stories, but Mira Grant's Newsflesh Trilogy still occupies the top spot in my ranking. I wish I haven't read this book yet ...

Gaia is now the Matrarc of New Sylum and she is leading her people to The Enclave in hopes of giving them a chance to survive. They have no idea what welcome they will receive but it is better than succumbing to certain death in Sylum. The Enclave is not the same place Gaia left a year before. In an effort to wipe out hemophilia there is now a baby factory where designer babies are produced for the wealthiest Enclave inhabitants. Gaia also has something that The Enclave wants, and they will not stop pursuing her until they get it. After being a bit disappointed with Prized, I was a bit tentative approaching this book. My fears were unfounded as this book was the sequel that Birthmarked deserved. The old Gaia is back instead of vacillating, submissive Gaia we had in Prized. She is trying to lead her people and trying to stay one step ahead of The Enclave. She has to make some difficult decisions in this book which she does well. There is a lot of action in the book over the slowness and directionlessness of Prized. The pacing is done very well. I enjoyed catching up with the old characters from Wharfton and The Enclave, as well as meeting some new faces. The last 50 pages are just crazy (in a good way). I think the book ends the series appropriately, though I wished for some sort of epilogue and less of a happy ever after feel. I truly enjoyed this series even with a bit of a bum middle installment. I highly recommend it to fans of Unwind and The Hunger Games. Paranormal Scavenger Hunt: Dagger

4 Stars I received a copy via Netgalley in exchange for an honest review. I actually really quite liked this. It was a really sweet book about coming out of your shell. It was a bit sad but a lot happy and cute. So, the perfect contemporary for me. I will start with one thing that bothered me quickly just to get it out of the way. Manic pixie dream girl, or should I say manic pixie dream boy. I kind of got a jist of that with Esben. It wasn't a huge deal but it seemed a bit like he was created only to bring Allison out of her shell and he was a bit too perfect for me and it just rang manic pixie dream person at me. He was a really pure and genuine person who really unconditionally loved Allison. Like, he took everything with her so well and it all seemed weird to me. He didn't get frustrated or anything, I don't know it was just strange. I think there were about two occasions in the whole book where we saw that side of him. I really liked Allison because I saw a lot of myself in her. At the beginning we see her as quite introverted and she likes to keep to herself. We learn that it's a trust issue because of her past in foster care. I can totally get that, I've always been a little introverted and sometimes simple things can set me back, similarly to how we see Allison go a bit back and forth in the book. I think she had an awesome character development and I loved seeing her open up and 'be brave'. I really loved the phrase 'be brave' throughout the book, it kind of reminded me of a similar thing in The One Memory of Flora Banks. I really loved how Allison took that on. I adored the relationship between Allison and Simon. I always love a good family in YA. I think it's so important. I really liked that she had a really strong father figure, even if he did come later rather than sooner. I really enjoyed seeing their relationship blossom as Allison learnt to open up. I think strong father figures are really important in YA. Simon reminded me so much of my own dad and I really liked him and the role he played in the story. I liked the modern kind of take on things. YA is getting more and more modern and I think it's kind of cool. It's cool to read about social networking and internet personalities. This book has a lot of that so if you think that's as cool as I do, I think you're going to like this one. Also, it has social experiments and I love social experiments so that's something to look forward to. 180 Seconds was a really lovely book. I really liked the meaning behind the title. I grinned almost the whole way through because it really was too cute. Watching Allison bloom was really lovely and kind of inspiring for me, I think I'm going to try to 'be brave' now. Relating to Allison so much was a really strong point for me. I liked all the characters a lot, I think Esben could've used a bit more personality but otherwise, I liked him. It was pretty heart warming and I think it would be worth a try for any contemporary fans. Also, look at that cover. More @ https://brooklynsippingacupoftea.blog...

Historically speaking, his racism in the second book is logical... but at the end of the day... it's a book. And not many people like to have someone they "idolized" in a sense be brought down. I don't know. The entirety of GSAW's publication in the first place was shady enough, but I honestly wonder if Harper Lee held off from publishing it was because she knew her characters had changed when writing TKAM.

13 takes off exactly where Spellbound ended, Waking the Witch, Spellbound and 13 are actually the only books from the Otherworld series that don't have a big time gap in between them. Savannah and Jaime get "arrested" while trying to get away from the lab explosion, they get taken to a police station but don't get booked or anything so conclude that it's a trap. After fighting off a crazed werewolf and and escaped hellhound, they manage to get away from the station with Eve. Eve and Savannah find out that there's an anti-SLM group as well. They plan to infiltrate the SLM to take it down from the inside but the plan fails when the Nast cabal get involved and take Eve and Savannah into custody. After getting away from the Nast cabal, they team up with the rest of the Otherworld crew minus Antonio & Nick (*sad face*) and through some helpful demon Lords in the shape of Eve and Adam's fathers, they manage to find out exactly what's going on and stop it - with a lot of magic and action. So yeah that was a very small recap because so much happens in this book that I'd end up just writing the whole damn story here. Anyone who reads my reviews or knows me personally knows how much I LOVE Kelley's books - it's impossible to not love her writing. For me - and any long time Otherworld fan - this book was a bittersweet read, as much as I couldn't wait to read it I also didn't want to read it 'cos as soon as I did then the series would be over. So some of my favourite bits or my gasp out loud moments ........ ....... Malcolm - yes, Malcolm! He's alive and he's in Nast custody. Karl gets shot - I thought he was dead, luckily he survives - I didn't like that I thought he was dead for a short period. Elena gets in a fight with Malcolm and gets the better of him, she wants to kill him before Jeremy and Clay know he's actually alive but Clay walks in on them and then he fights him, almost kills him too but the Nast cabal intervene. Jeremy reveals he's going to make Elena alpha immediately - OK not that big a shock since it's the last book but still a tingle went through me (yes, I was that happy). Savannah and Adam finally get together properly but agree not to tell Paige and Lucas. Paige and Lucas find out anyway, Paige is fine with it, she's seen it coming for ages apparently, Lucas is most definitely not, he doesn't want Savannah getting hurt. So any of my readers know they aren't going to get an unbiased review from me about a Kelley book - there's no such thing when it comes to Kelley. I freaking loved this book - sad to see the series end but Kelley did it justice. We got to see all of our favourite characters again and she tied off some open storylines while still leaving enough open to warrant novellas at a later date - which Kelley has said will happen. FROM RUSSIA WITH LOVE Is a very short story purely there for the Alpha hand-off storyline. While 13 was happening, the twins and the rest of the pack were in Russia with the Russian pack so when Elena, Clay, Jeremy and Jaime join them, Jeremy officially hands the pack over to Elena. I love the way he did it. Traditionally it would be a challenge so Jeremy challenged Elena to a game of chess. Which was already set up so that Elena would win since it was only a formality, everyone but Elena knew what was happening. Then there's a cool little scene with all the pack playing touch football as Elena watches them - and Jeremy is playing - realising they are her pack. As I said, a tiny short but it was only to serve one purpose. Oh and also let us see Xavier one last time.

GAAAAAH! THE MASTER RETURNS!! I don't care if the cover of this book reminds me of McDonalds, nor am I bothered by the fact that the plot differs completely from Harry Potter, this is J.K. ROWLING we're talking about here! Therefore, I will continue to do the following until the day that this book is released:

Warning: I get positively excitedly sweary when I love a book like I love this book. So, uh, fuck? This book. This fucking book, man. It is amazing on so many levels. I had admittedly forgotten a lot of the nittier grittier details of the first 3 books in the series, because there is admittedly a lot of nitty gritty to remember (The Character List, Glossary, and Appendix of this volume alone was nearly 10% of the entire book, by my kindle's reckoning, if that puts it into perspective). Thankfully, there was a wonderful recap at the beginning. For people like me who are not always inclined to re-read books in a series before a new one is released this is an amazing thing. I don't re-read many books, even if they're favorites, even if I loved them. But if I do a re-read, and it's entirely possible that I will in this particular case, it'll be shotgun-reading this entire quintet until my eyeballs fall out. Parts of this book blew my fucking mind, just as others in the series have done. It happened more than once, and quite often. I remember really liking the Night Angel trilogy, but it doesn't hold a candle to this series for me. This one is on another level, and each book keeps getting better! I wasn't expecting to get all teary-eyed (and by Andross Guile of all fucking people at one point... Mostly Gavin Greyling though *sadface* ), but it happened. Most of all though, this series makes me laugh. I do love me some smart-mouth characters, and so therefore I love Kip the Lip. He uses all kinds of slang that I would totally use (he calls someone a flesh protuberance at one point FFS, lol), and as modern as the language sometimes is, it fits well in the world in which it's presented. The Mighty's banter fits The Mighty. I've always hated Andross, because I think you're just supposed to hate him, but goddamn is he ever a fantastic character. All of the Guiles are, but I especially loved how in this volume, the most exalted holy leader in the Chromeria can just walk into his office and say 'Andross, you motherfucker.' Because, you know... someone's gotta say it. Because he is. He totally is. But, we got to see more than his douchebaggery this time, and I am so fucking down with that. I also appreciated less of Zymun in this one. Because fuck that guy. Something is going to happen there, and I know it, and I know I'm not going to like it.... but fuck that guy. All this shit is the kind of shit that makes me love a book. I love a book where a girl gets her period and it's no big deal, it's just a thing that happens because this shit fucking happens. I don't expect to see this sort of thing, especially from a male author, nor do I expect an actual gynecological condition being woven into the story, which both makes sense and has an actual reasonable function in the plot (and yes, actually exists in real life). I don't expect those things but I appreciate seeing them nonetheless. And lastly, I've gotta say that I've never before wanted a fictional character to get laid so much in my life. Go Kip Go!

I think I got an accidental ARC. A few days ago, I signed up for a free Sacked e-book from Jen Frederick because well, free e-book. And indeed I got it, along with with a Downed ARC. It seems that the Book Gods do favor their faithful servants. I'm not exactly a sports adept. In fact, back in high school I was the girl everyone avoided in P.E. class and with good reason; they wanted to protect their heads and other vital organs from my rogue throws. Even my teachers were scared of me. Hell, I was scared of me. The only time I get really obsessed with sports is when the Greece National basketball team plays. I still recall the glorious semi-final of the 2006 Fiba World Championship, when to everyone's astonishment we beat the United States team 101-95. Setting aside my mediocre knowledge on basketball, I suck at sports. And since Downed was focused on football, you can understand where this long introduction is going. I didn't understand much. But, this doesn't change the fact that I had a wonderful time reading Downed. Jen Frederick could claim that pink unicorns participated in the game and I wouldn't know whether she was joking or not, but Ace and Bryant's story was everything I needed; a sweet, sexy and funny romance of the heart/panties-melting variety that kept me great company! "Ace is an asshole... But he's my asshole." Bad boy meets good girl and together they create fireworks. That's Downed's concept, and Jen Frederick executed it perfectly! Ace is the jerk everyone hates, his team avoids him and treats him like he has the plague because of his bad reputation. Until his coach's daughter, a proper southern lady that can't say "no" to anyone, decides he's her next project and that she'll make a decent human being out of him. Yes, I said project. You see, after a tragedy that marked her, Bryant took it upon her to make happy the entire world, even if that meant putting aside her own desires. But what happens if Ace isn't the one who needs saving after all? "If I date you, I have one rule, too." "What is it?" "You don't hold back on me." Reading on the bus can be difficult for various reasons. You can't cry, laugh or swoon because you have to maintain the image of the proper young lawyer you are. An image that crumbles anyway when the sweet grandpa next to you takes a peak to your e-reader and notices the hot'n'dirty cover. And the content matches this delicious sight. Ace and Bryant were two characters with sizzling chemistry that did funny things to your insides, and their scenes were tastier than sin. But there was also affection and gentleness. Both of them fought their demons and their fears and conquered them, and in this journey they were together. Ace, besides the cocky, filthy-mouthed and bitter bastard that he was, was also vulnerable and insecure, and wanted someone to believe in him. And Bryant did. While I liked her a lot, her compassion and her sweetness, there were some things that didn't sit right with me. She could be such a doormat, always pleasing others, and I could not comprehend her whole project thing. She thought of Ace as a broken toy that needed fixing, while it was clear that she had huge issues to deal with. "Football is a game, but Bryant is my future. And I'll keel fighting for her as long as it takes." In the end, I am glad I got this accidental ARC, because Ace and Bryant's story cured my romance withdrawal. Who knows, maybe Downed can make a sports fan out of me!

This is a cute little book, even if it didn't feel new or different from anything I've read before. Nory lives in a world of magic and she is studying hard to get into the best magic school around - where, coincidentally, her father is headmaster. Unfortunately, Nory's magic is "wonky" and doesn't always work right. So instead of getting into her father's school, he sends her away to live with her aunt and go to a special class for kids with "Upsidedown magic." During her time there Nory learns to accept her magic for what it is and that being different is not only okay, but sometimes a really good thing. Overall it was easy to read and I think the intended audience will enjoy it. The message is a bit heavy-handed and obvious, but of course it's a good message. The characters aren't as well developed as they could be, but in a short book that's not surprising. There were actually a couple of areas where I would have liked to read more about. The world that's been created here, with the different kinds of magic and how they work, is really interesting and seems to be well thought out. I really dislike it when one-off books become series, but in this case I would actually like to see some sequels because I think there's a really good base for a whole magic universe here. One thing that I would have liked to see explored more was Nory's father. He's described as being rather strict but nice enough. However, he not only sends her away to live with her aunt, he refuses to answer the phone when Nory calls. And he in fact forbids her siblings to contact her either, and they have to sneak away to be able to call her. This is such an extreme reaction that I think it really should have been addressed a bit more. Overall I think this is a great option for kids in the 3rd-4th grade age group where we don't often see a lot of quality literature. A very enjoyable little book!

I left the perfect amount of time between re-reads of this book. That translated to everything feeling new again, which meant I enjoyed this book just as much as I did the last time I read it. Perfect amount of sci-fi, perfect amount of angst, perfect amount of humor, perfect amount of emotion. This book has just enough of everything to be engaging without being overdone. Most of my highlighted passages in this book are about the relationship between Brady and Cam. For a cocky little shit from the slums, Brady has a truly romantic heart (just don't let him hear you say that unless you want your nose broken). And Cam, god, Cam, so sweet. You'd think with all the dystopian books flooding the bookstores there wouldn't be too much left to the imagination to make the world building in Dark Space worth mentioning. You would be wrong. The setting of this book is Earth several generations after a devastating sort of hit-and-run alien attack (they attacked, then didn't bother to stick around). Instead of going the futuristic techno babble Star Trek route to the story, the author chose to build a world not too much unlike our own. For me, that mostly-familiar setting made me comfortable...for about two chapters. After that, it served to reinforce just how scary and alien everything really was. It was easy to feel Brady's fear of the Faceless because the writer had already made it easy to feel Brady's homesickness for a world I could easily envision. So yes, world-building worth mentioning. I couldn't write a review for this book the first time I read it mostly because I am awful at writing reviews for books I love. Crazy, I know. I still only shared a sliver of everything I enjoyed about this book but it will have to do for now. Perhaps I'll come back and add more after the next time I read this book. Because there will be a next time.

Actual rating 2.9. A very average collection of very average love stories. Then again, if you're reading a book of summer-themed love stories, it's exactly what you'd expect. There are the bittersweet tales of heartbreak and separation contrasting with hopeful tales of reunion, characters of all sexualities and colours making it a fully representative anthology. I gave a few of the stories 5 stars ('The End of Love' by Nina LaCour, Stephanie Perkins sequel to her short story in 'My True Love Gave To Me', and - surprisingly - 'Inertia', the short story by Veronica Roth) but the rest of them only merited 2/3 stars at best. My least favourite stories (and the two stories that I only awarded 1 star) were 'Love is the Last Resort' by Jon Skovron (which features extremely stilted language that makes the characters the least authentic teenagers I've ever experienced) and 'Sick Pleasure' by Francesca Lia Block (whose characters are only given initials instead of names, making it one of the most unemotional and disconnected short stories I've ever had the displeasure to read). If you enjoyed 'My True Love Gave To Me', you'll probably like this collection, but I kind of wish Stephanie Perkins had left her foray into anthology editing as a one hit wonder.

DNF review. I've enjoyed Ahern's adult books and had high hopes for this, but stopped after about 60 pages. If you're a diehard, will-read-any-dystopian-you-can-get-your-hands-on kind of reader, then definitely check this out. If, like me, you're suffering dystopian fatigue, you might want to try a few pages first. I found the set-up predictable with a side of WTF. After a financial collapse, some Guild (?) decides to throw out anyone in any position of power who is dishonest or unethical. Maybe that could work, but then the book ties its hands by saying that "anyone who made the smallest error in judgment was immediately punished." Um... so who, exactly, is left to run things, given that 92 percent of Americans say they lie regularly? And, if you're in a position of power and say you're in the 8% ... I say you're probably lying. Of course, I'm sure the only reason that the society in the book cracks down on small errors is so that Celestine, our squeaky-clean sixteen year old heroine, can be thrown into peril, rejected by her oh-so-perfect boyfriend, and fall in love with a tattooed bad boy (they tattoo an "F" on anyone who messes up). But I digress. I quit reading because of a) BTDT premise, b) bland main character, and c) a set-up that practically screams love triangle. In 2016, I think a YA dystopian needs to bring something fresh and new to the table, and after a few chapters I didn't see that happening here. Feel free to disagree in comments if you've finished this, though! In a world where being Gifted is punishable by death, the heroine must be silent. She is a hostage for her father in the king's court as a war rages on. I'm so sorry I hated this. It was everything I hate in a YA book. A stupid girl, a poor romance, a dumb plot, and nothing makes sense. (I am really shocked that this book made it on the goodreads Best of 2016 nominees. Maybe I'm reading the wrong book or something...) First of all, the premise is completely ridiculous. When the heroine is taken up as hostage, I literally rolled my eyes and went, wow how dumb. What court would allow a tyrant to randomly pick up the daughter of an ally and make her a hostage without fake courtesies? And there were no repercussions. Does that even make sense?!?! That is not how politics work. And it is a super lame way to make her someone important yet also a hostage. Not believable at all. Court is all about appearance - and yet there are overt threats, no servants for her, no treaty, no talks. Second. The relationship between the king and the heroine. Just wow. So gross. How does this king that is in charge of a kingdom and fighting a war have so much time to just play around with a hostage? Does not make sense. And then every single freaking interaction between them is the king just asking her for help and she's like.... iono... yes, i like being helpful, i think i luv u, i'm not strong and wise and powerful but i'll be queen anyway, yah i have a gift that's super strong that will win us this war. Gifted, powerful but naive, innocent and excited about little things, no faults, accidentally queen. Yeah. Mary Sue much? I feel dumber just by reading this book. One star. But don't take my word for it. There are a ton of other reviews that love this book. Heck, one of my good friends gave it 4 stars. It must be doing something right for a lot of people. Didn't work for me. Read at your own discretion.

The plot is decent and exciting to keep you reading the book, but there's nothing that really sets it apart from other YA dystopian novels. There's very little to explain the world that's been created, The Republic of America, where the United States is a secret that's been erased from history. There's really no explanation why the US broke out to be the Republic and the Colonies, or why they're even at war and what started it. The characters, June and Day, are young and on opposing sides - June working for the Republic and Day a criminal on the streets. Both are 15 and prodigies who scored a perfect score during the Trials. This is an examination conducted on children when they're only 10. The characters strike me as being too young for what they're doing, and could have been aged. Alternating viewpoints can be tough to execute, and unfortunately, the two voices in this book are hard to differentiate. The book formatting changes between the two characters, but there's really no other differentiator to make you feel attached to what the character feels or gives you any sense about their personality. It's not too distracting since the storyline does move the story along and the alternating viewpoints certainly isn't anywhere near as bad as Allegiant. I didn't find myself speeding through this book as much as I do others, but I'll continue reading the trilogy just to see what happens.

You've got to have a certain kind of cold heart in order to kill for hire, and that interfered with my enjoyment of the rest if the story. Then, West becomes 'active,' and has to kill her Alt. But she doesn't. She runs from every opportunity, and continues with the killing for hire. I wasn't okay with this, either. I'm guessing that the author was trying to allude to scary aspects of oneself, how it's easier to face other people's faults than your own, but the killing overshadowed all of that. I give props to the author for tackling such a difficult and strong theme, and I wish it had come across stronger. So, overall, it was okay. This is another one of those books that I've had in my possession before, but something just kept me from reading it. So I finally picked it up again and told myself I'm going to finish it this time! I kind of wish I didn't.... We're introduced to Princess Elisa. She's fat, overshadowed by her (skinnier) sister, and loves food. And she describes herself as having dark skin and dark hair. So a POC overweight main character as our heroine? Sign me up! I was so excited to see this sort of representation in a YA novel, because I just never come across it. I'm just very disappointed in how it played out. Elisa has all these problems, she doesn't believe in herself, her new husband doesn't seem to love her (or notice her at all, to be honest), she can't see herself as a Queen and ruling a country, never mind leading a war, and all of these problems seem to magically vanish when she trudges through the desert for a month and loses weight. She literally looks at her old clothes in disgust. She acts like being overweight is this terrible thing that can be easily be solved by not eating, and that message is just so wrong and such a bad one to put in a YA novel, or any novel really. I'm just so mad with how this was handled and this was my main problem with this book as a whole. All the religious talk bugged me a bit, only because I'm not huge on religion and especially Christianity-esque religion tends to bore me. It's not the authors fault, and it was actually integrated quite well, I just didn't care for the numerous excerpts of religious texts that didn't really seem to fit in so well. It's supposed to be a prophecy, but I don't really see it. I assume it will play out more in later books. It does bother me that a lot of problems seem to be solved by just prayed the trouble away. I'm not ragging on beliefs here, I'm saying if you're writing a book, and your characters get into some sort of predicament, praying the trouble away makes for some very boring writing. I want to see our characters fight their way out, not pray. On that note, in one of the very first chapters, Elisa kills a man. I think she acted very well in this situation, their caravan was ambushed and Elisa's new husband was about to be killed and she jumped in and killed his attacker. That's the kind of action I want instead of praying. And the aftermath of that little skirmish were handled pretty well, too. Elisa seems to have a few flashbacks to that moment, as she should, and it wasn't just written off and forgotten about. However, when Elisa is trapped in an enemy camp, she is faced with the need to kill another man. Stabbing is preferable at first,but she says that's wrong and she hopes to never have to do that again. Okay. Reasonable enough. Except she then proceeds to poison the man unconscious, checks to make sure he's still alive, is relieved he's still alive, and then sets the tent on fire burning the man to death. Now, this man most likely would have killed her. I'm not saying she shouldn't have killed him. It was a pretty reasonable thing to do, given the circumstances. It was her process that confused me. How can you be against killing a man, only to poison him and then set him on fire? You can't have a character being against killing one second, and then literally go and kill someone the next. The "love story" aspect of this book was a bit refreshing for me. I've never been a huge fan of romance, especially when I want more action instead, but I can usually understand why it's in place. It was expected here. We have a young princess being married off to an older king. I expected them to fall in love eventually, and was super happy that they didn't instantly fall in love. It seemed like Elisa had a crush on him when she first saw him, which is fine! But they didn't have that instant connection you find so often in YA novels. I honestly think they could have formed a great relationship, if Elisa hadn't been kidnapped, and if the king wasn't so absentminded. Elisa's relationship with Humberto grew naturally, although awkwardly. I'm still a bit confused as to how and why she became friends with her captors. I mean, they were the only ones to tell her the truth about who she is, which is great, but they kidnapped her. I just think she became BFFs with them a little too easily. I'm also slightly upset that Humberto and Alejandro were both killed. On one hand, it's great that Elisa can go about her duties and doesn't need a man or anything, but I would've liked to see where her relationship with Humberto went. And Alejandro's death was very anti climactic. Can't say he deserved better, he was pretty much an ass, but I would've liked to see something other than "He fell into a coma and never woke up the end". I never really felt connected to any of the characters and didn't even realize it until people started dying and I didn't care. Elisa's Guardian/maid is the most interesting character to me, but we hardly see her at all, barely even speak of her once Elisa is kidnapped. Already, the names are fading. No one was particularly memorable. The idea as a whole is really nice. World building needs work, especially where magic is concerned. I guess it works with blood and prayer? Maybe? Who knows. I'm curious where this series goes, but I don't know if I'm curious enough to continue. This book wasn't awful, but I'm left wondering if three stars was too high of a rating. Maybe if someone tells me the next books definitely get better, I'll check them out. Other than that, I have better things to do.

Check out my full review here! http://www.readsbyamanda.com/2013/12/... Brave New World is the dystopian epic released in the 1930s by Aldous Huxley. Equal parts horrifying and a sharp contrast from the utopian novels being released at the time, this novel has managed to keep readers enthralled over eighty years since it's original release. Now I was beyond excited to read Brave New World since I've heard so much about it and it's concept of human cloning and biological engineering really interested me since this was a novel written at a time when such concepts didn't even exist. In the beginning chapters, we are taken to London's Hatchery and Conditioning Centre where the Director of this building who is named "The Director" (insert clever joke here) is giving a tour to a group of students. This is a great set up since we are being explained everything without one of the character literally explaining everything which takes the reader out the story. In the centre is where human beings are made and raised by the government since concepts such as mothers and family are considered barbaric and no longer used in this society. People are separated by castes: Alpha, Beta, Gammas, Deltas, and Epsilons. Each caste is genetically manipulated and modified according to the attributes of the caste. The lower three castes' eggs are subjected to x-ray radiation and doused in alcohol to near death in order for them to be intellectually stunted and easier to control. They also do this in the fetus stage where you are taken into a dark room with red lighting full of fetuses in jars where the nurses make routine "adjustments" to them. All of this is creepy and unsettling which was Huxley's point. Then you are told everything about this world: The world in general is referred to as the World State, there are ten world controllers who each represent a region. We meet one of them, Mustapha Mond who is the controller of the European sector and personally one of my favorite characters because he was so intelligent and it was hard to make out his true intentions. There is no history, no literature, everyone is encouraged to be promiscuous, including the children who are taught to play erotic games with one another (while being naked by the way) which is horrifying to say the least and everyone takes the popular drug, soma, in order to escape reality and have mandatory orgies with each other. Unfortunately, Brave New World disappointed me. It starts off strong with the introduction of the world but once the story actually starts, it quickly dies off and nothing really happens. There's little to no character development and nothing changes in the end. This is the case when an author has a strong concept but falls flat in its execution. Would I recommend this? Eh, not really? I would recommend reading the first three chapters because the short summary I gave above does no justice to the horror you feel while this world is being laid out to you. It is truly great storytelling but after the world is explained and you start to meet the characters, it gets extremely dull.

This is my fourth book by this author and they just keep delivering. This one has echoes of Stephen King, both IT and Salem's Lot. There's a palpable sense of menace in this small town that's been flooded when "the narrows" spilt its banks. What has been washed up from the toxic depths of the old plastic factory? But I'll go out on a limb here and say this writing is vastly superior to King's. Sure, Stephen King is the master of the horror genre and he can tell a fabulous story. When he's good he's very, very good. But I occasionally try to reread King and find them almost too crass now. They lack the subtlety these Ronald Malfi novels have. Honestly, I can usually find something in a book that I liked. There wasn't much in this one. I finished it with a gut feeling that I had wasted my time and money on the novel. My advice is to not pick this one up. I have no clue why it's a Young Adult book. If anything, I would put it in the children's section (as younger kids are the only ones that might find this interesting). There were elements I really liked, the blue girls in particular, the strong relationship between Mackie and his family but more than left me slightly puzzled. Mostly having poor Mackie so very sick so much of the time forced the story into a somber mode which felt passive. I think Yovanoff has the potential to write some fabulous books in the future. Despite the multiple points of view, the story was tightly focused on the expedition and the humans and dragons that comprised it. In City of Dragons, the focus broadens considerably right from page one. We expand outward to see--among others--the villains who have thus far been distant figures: the Duke of Chalced, his representatives, and Hest, Alise's husband and Sedric's lover. We get their perspectives as well as those of Tintaglia and the Elderlings Reyn, Malta, and Seldon, that she created, met way back in the Liveship Trilogy (okay, I'm almost finished with book 4 of this series, and I'm having a hard time remembering if Reyn and Malta are in this book or don't arrive until the next one, but I think we at least see Selden). The story seemed more exciting and faster-paced than the first two books, as though the series has really found its stride, with the tableau set for everything that is to come in this volume and the next.
