Read this and other reviews Ampersand Read The Sculptor is delightful. You can definitely see that McCloud knows his stuff. The artistic style is really on point. The character's expressions, and the inventive way McCloud utilizes speech bubbles (so skillfully that you forget it's a comic, that it's a speech bubble spouting from someone's head), are impressive, to say the least. And the way plot twists are laid out really gets you turning pages. You really start to feel for the characters, and you ache a little when the story ends. The premise alone sets you up for some heartbreak: this guy is going to die in 200 days, and partway through that, he meets and falls in love with someone (who just happens to be a little damaged too - character flaws are well-rendered here too). But the journey to this deal's end is a long and tangled one. David's success doesn't come as easy as he would hope. In fact, his first exhibition kind of flops. He's crazy awkward around women, he makes misstep after misstep when it comes to his lady love, and he's moody and depressing and somehow, still brilliant. The book had a lot to say about art and commercialism and living in the big NYC. I liked that it was a gritty graphic novel. It dealt with real, complex issues in a way that was visually beautiful. The ending felt a tad clumsy...without spoiling the whole thing, you have to pause at the end to suss out what's real, and how the book really...ended. For such a solid book, it was an ambiguous ending, and I felt the story deserved more (and the sunshine and rainbows half of me wanted it of course to end happily for everyone!) Great art, that has a lot to say about art itself. The ending brought the work down a little, but it's a story that makes you think about it long after you've turned the last page.

"Love is never wrong." Every freaking time KA releases a new book the natural reaction for me is And this time was no exception. However, in the first half of the book, we meet a determined Frankie and more determined Benny. I have not met one who could always say the right things, at the right times, and say it so sweetly, but still be as alpha. (Sorry Luke). Frankie was in many was in many ways a typical KA heroine. But there was still something just plain unique about her. The way she loved is unparalleled in many ways. She loved the Bianchi's though they blamed her for years for the decisions their son had made. She loved Benny though he's rejected her at her lowest moment. She loved her family though they were an insanely fucked up bunch. She loved Uncle Sal, though it was basically his fault her bf had been killed. She loved and loved and loved. And no one ever gave that back. No one until Benny. So the story was great, real normal ever day people, dealing in very every day circumstances. And then... Luke Stark YES LUKE FREAKING STARK!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!! And Luke Stark in the same room with Benito Bianchi... I read that seen 100 times cause lets be honest, those two in the same room, talking, and smiling... that deserves to be engrained into the minds of human females for life. So overall this book was fantastic! Another 5 star read! If this was how it felt to get what you wanted for a lifetime. Have it stretched out beside you. The promise of it there all night so you'd wake up to it in the morning. The promise of it going to work the next day with you knowing it was coming back. A promise that would stay a promise - beautiful, forever there, beckoning, even as minute by minute it was being fulfilled, leaving you taking your last breath on earth knowing you lived a life filled with beauty.

While the book does make you wonder how far you would go to protect family, there FAR too many questions left dangling. The beginning of the book is intriguing. Two brothers and their wives meet for dinner. Everyone knows something and isn't sure who else knows and/or how much they know. By the end of the book, I didn't even care anymore. None of the characters are likable. I didn't care who knew what when and I didn't care how they all ended up. I just wanted the book finished. I personally found the 'I'm not going to tell you the specifics of _______' tactic that was repeated numerous times throughout the book to be incredibly annoying. I can only presume the author thought it cute or clever. It wasn't. Tell me, or don't, but don't say 'there was an illness, but I'm not going to tell you the name of it'. Certainly don't use the same I'm-so-coy tactic over and over about various subjects. That makes me say 'fine, don't tell me, I don't care anyway'. I thought the video was going to be an entirely different secret than it turned out to be. The reveal of the video's subject was a surprise to me. What the video turned out to be was an interesting plot twist. Unfortunately, that was the only interesting twist. The book could have been so good. The premise was good. The execution and conclusion? Not so much.

I don't think I have ever been disappointed in Jodi Picoult's books and am fascinated at the subjects she writes about and how complex and outside of the box her writing is, so I am pleased with my reading of The Pact and look forward to my next Picoult title.

I would have liked to see a little more resolution with Ruth, because it seems like she goes from hating Amelia, as she should as a "ghost hunter/exorcist" to pretty much out of the picture. I think that the main plot line was wrapped up fairly well, although I'd liked more of my questions answered. I know it's a first in a series, but to me, the ending felt rushed. Though with the great story idea and the sweet romance, I still recommend this one!

I picked up this novel expecting an easy to read, contemporary romance with a frustrating love-triangle plot. It could not have been anything more different. I cannot express how this book tore me apart. I loved Lily. I loved Ryle. I loved their development and story. They were an amazing couple and that made me feel the blows to that foundation all the more. I needed them to be together because I am a romantic, even as I knew that Lily deserved more. I loved that neither the love triangle or abuse storylines were overpowering, but that they fed from each other and fired the other on, without ever being too hard-hitting and forced. The only aspect I did not enjoy was Atlas. I felt that Lily's love for him was borne out of shared experience rather than chemistry or attraction. Lily's love for Ryle was palpable and developed, she loved him because he did x, y and z. But with Atlas, he was just her first love, and their relationship - for me - was never any more than re-meeting your first love. The ending was great for Lily and Atlas, because they both got what they thought they wanted, but I had never seen any real evidence that they would work as a couple. Atlas seemed to feel grateful to Lily, and Lily liked Atlas at 15. But did they share interests now? Were they the same people as adults? Who knows, because it was never really developed. Amazing, beautiful and so important. I would not only recommend this book, but I am already adding Hoover's back catalogue to my Christmas List.

I received the first 100 pages of this book as part of the Hugo voters packet, but I only made it to page 46. Harlan Ellison once used the phrase 'obscurantist drivel.' A bit harsh maybe, but that's the phrase that kept occurring to me as I was reading. I don't mind dense writing and detailed worldbuilding - Dune is one of my all-time favorites, after all - but it seems like Stross is dense just to be dense. Like he thinks his world will seem more rich for being incomprehensible. His writing is far too self aware; reading his books (I previously read The Atrocity Archives and had the same problems) I can hear him thinking 'oh this will be funny,' or 'this makes me sound smart.' It's annoying. It's also dull. I cared nothing for the characters or the story by page 46. The world was moderately intriguing but mostly just weird. Stross's fancy words fail to transport; I'm left staring at a fat book instead of traveling in space and time. No vote for Stross, and no more Stross for me.

Jill Shalvis has wowed me in Lucky Harbor again. In this installment we finally explore the combustible chemistry radiating between youngest sister, Chloe, and local sheriff, Sawyer. Chloe's sisters and Lucky Harbor locals refer to her as the "Wild Child". She is a free spirit who longs for others to take her more seriously (especially her sisters) without having to sacrifice the fundamentals of who she is. Sawyer is just about as opposite of Chloe as you can get. Only thing is Sawyer wasn't always such a straight arrow and has spent most of his adult life trying to forget the troubled teen he used to be. These two have more in common than either realizes. I absolutely adored the first two books in this series, but Chloe and Sawyer's story is my favorite. Chloe is a total sweetheart and the sister I feel has changed the most since the inn she inherited from her mother brought her to Lucky Harbor a year earlier. She has such an intoxicating personality and her love of adventure is highly contagious. She also has the ability to love others with such intensity, even if actually speaking those three little words out loud scares the hell out of her. Sawyer is all alpha and serious. He has such a strong need to protect those around him. It is no wonder he became a police officer. The care he shows Chloe over and over when it comes to her debilitating asthma had my heart melting into a puddle of goo. You just don't expect the sweet side of him. He is undeniably sexy for a man of so little words. I usually like my male leads sarcastic and funny, but Sawyer is an exception (possibly the only one) to the rule. I was crushing hard the entire time I read. The romance between Chloe and Sawyer shouldn't work, but it does beautifully. Jill Shalvis has outdone herself with Lucky Harbor's newest love match. Contemporary romance isn't one of my "go to" genres. I do enjoy reading it, but find I usually uncover more misses than hits. Jill Shalvis is an author who I know won't disappoint. She proves romance novels don't have to be cheesy or host to page after page of sappy cliches. She combines witty dialogue, swoon worthy romance, and dramatic elements with expertise. There is also a little action in this one thanks to Sawyer's new side job. The Lucky Harbor series is without a doubt one of my favorites. I can see myself reading these again and again. I'm also thrilled my time in Lucky Harbor won't end with Head Over Heels. Other residents of this adorable little town will have the chance at their HEA too! This is a series that doesn't have to be read in order, but I highly recommend it to get the full backstory on not only Chloe and Sawyer, but the other one of a kind characters you will meet in Lucky Harbor. P.S I'll never be able to paint again without thinking of Chloe and Sawyer. Believe me when I say it is a scene not to be missed :)

The first time the two eat a meal together was just the straw on the camel's back for me; Andrew first describes Colin as chomping away on his roll like a horse, and then later, when they're eating soup, he talks about how Colin uncouthly slurps it from the front of his spoon, so Andrew ever so kindly sips his sedately from the side hoping to set an example for the other man. Like, I can do flawed characters, couples who don't seem to fit at first, etc. but I can't do it if I hate the ever loving guts out of one of the main characters. I could read about someone who did some horrible shit because I could at least enjoy watching them find redemption. This guy, though- he is walking talking privilege. He's the privilege that quietly and solidly believes in its own supremacy, the kind that you can rail against all you want, but that will always, always come out on top. His guts-deep level surety, the complete and utter lack of true empathy- this, to me, is the real and true evil of this world. Even if I know from reading other reviews here that in the end he changes his views, I CANNOT make myself read about this asshole for 300+ pages. There is no redemption here for me, because, no matter how his views might change, unless he wants to burn the system to the mf ground I am not interested.

Fracture opened with an explosive chapter, and it's impossible not to be entranced by the mysterious tale. When Delaney Maxwell falls and traps herself under a newly-frozen lake for 11 minutes, she should be dead. She's alive. Her doctors say she'll remain in coma. She wakes up. The cat scans of her damaged brain show that she should have memory loss, a speech impediment and so much more. She's fine. The catch: Delaney feels a pull towards the dying. Megan surprised me with her uncanny ability to pull my heartstrings at her mercy! We follow Delaney's tough recovery, filled with parents who doubt her sanity, boys who twist her brain wires and strangers who die soon after she predicts. I could embrace Delaney's frustration at not understanding what happened to her, why her and being helpless against death, because Megan put me into Delaney's shoes right from the moment she slipped under the ice. In fact, I was so invested in the characters that I feel like punching someone just because Delaney does! Enter Decker Phillips, heart throb #1 of 2012! His relationship with Delaney is pitch-perfect. Being neighbours since young, their chemistry and emotions boils beneath the surface without them saying a word. Seeing their sweet friendship, their little fights and banter, their highs and lows and in-betweens, and the complicated possibility/impossibility of something more, I feel like screaming at Decker: JUST TELL HER YOU LOVE HER!! Seriously, how more obtuse can this pair get? xD Meanwhile, Troy Varga is out to complicate matters. He is always in shadows, always lurking, always presenting a dark and enigmatic vibe. A typical bad boy? Oh no, Troy frustrated me so much to the point I almost hated him! He feels the same pull as Delaney, but the traumatic ordeals in his life forces him to take death into his own hands... And he wants Delaney to do the same. Should the dying be given death? Fracture is an addicting, haunting novel that will send your emotions spiralling down the same twisting thrill-ride as Delaney's. Trust me when I say that Megan is crafty with her mysteries, they'll make you hungry for answers!

I hadn't even finished reading my last book, when my sister burst into the room, shoved this book into my hands and said, "Read this!" Coming from my reluctant reader of a sister, I thought I'd give it a shot, especially since it made her so excited. But it took me a solid five days to get through compared to her three. In the end, I liked the world-building and the research that went into the story. But I didn't care much for the writing style. Perhaps it was because it was difficult for me to get into the book, so I skimmed over things. Or perhaps the book wasn't written well. I'm not entirely sure. It was probably because the book was just so full of environmentalism that I couldn't get into it. My real issue was with Lily's morals. First off, allow me to clarify. I believe the environment should be treated with more respect and care than it currently is. My family and I recycle to a ridiculous degree, and I like gardening with flowers for the purpose of helping the bee population. Lily is a vegan. I get it. While I, myself, still eat meat, I do not disagree with this kind of lifestyle. What I do disagree with is her refusal to eat meat, but killing the Woven (genetically hybrid monsters, which I understand to an extent) and killing people is suddenly okay. What? Why is the life a squirrel suddenly more valuable than that of a human? And why is nobody else questioning this? When I gave this book 3/5 stars, my sister didn't want to talk to me for the rest of the day. But we're all allowed to have different opinions. Personally, I would not recommend the book, but I'm sure if it were my sister, she would say it's a great read for anybody who enjoys reading about fantasy and parallel dimensions.

** spoiler alert ** Frankly, I'm appalled that this is YA. The gratuitous violence, the submission to rape, the ultimate message that you can commit evil deeds without it marking your soul are, in my view, totally age inappropriate. That aside, the author had no compunction about having the "heroine" make choices that only someone too stupid to breathe on her own would make in order to make the plot work. Emer has been a brutal pirate in the Caribbean for years, yet when she decides to retire, she get rid of the cannons on her flag ship "so she has room for food" to make the transatlantic trip home. Like there's no other pirates in the Carribbean. Or like she has no clue that she has other enemies. How convenient. No really. How conveniently stupid. But necessary if the end of Emer's life is going to happen the way the author has been promising since page 1. (I kid you not. The prologue shows Emer's death. The rest of the book is only necessary to put that scene into context.) On top of that, the romance between Emer and Seanie, while sweet at first, was totally bland when they finally meet again. I couldn't have cared less about them being together. Seanie had become a non-entity by then. A mere plot necessity. In the end, I disliked pretty much every character except the poor, abused dog that so conveniently leads Saffron to the treasure. (Another convenience for the author.) Not recommended unless you really want to know what your kids are reading.

Umm. So. I have really enjoyed how this "series" doesn't constrain itself by trying hard to fit in every fairy tale detail in some contrived way. And each book has gotten better at that, since they're only really inspired by tales, not based on them, and that's nice, because retellings get old. Like this latest one is much more a sequel looking at who the Sisters of the Air might be instead of retelling The Little Mermaid. That said, there's a lot of stuff here that is sooo random. Triplets with magical powers what? And who are we rooting for, Lo or Naida? Because that seems to be inconsistent. Also, this book felt way too much like it was trying to be Lost Voices, and I don't read Jackson Pearce when I need a literary fix, because that's not her thing. And because the writing seemed to be striving for that instead of being like the first two books, it fell short, because it didn't actually work. In the end I didn't care for any of the characters or their problems, because everything about this book was so random, and unlike the first two, which work both together and alone, this one felt much more like I needed a family tree and a timeline to make sense of the greater story at work, and I shouldn't have to do that to read a book. Now I wish I hadn't given people my copies of the first two books, because I won't get those covers back.

This wasn't bad. I probably would have rated it 3 stars if it wasn't for the end. It just didn't do it for me. The premise of this story was definitely out there...unrealistic. But somehow, it didn't bother me all too much. I thought it was well-written. I loved how Jessica Martinez made the ending and beginning of chapters connect. Subtle yet effective. I felt like I could relate to the characters, and for the most part, they seemed very real. For the most part. There were inconsistencies, especially in regarding the plot. My main problem was that Mo let Annie give up her life for him, yet he claims to love her. It just seems like a contradiction. And then Annie, who's supposed to be there for Mo, turns her phone off when he needs her the most. But she loves him, and that part is obvious. This really all goes back to the plot of the story which is just too far-fetched. The beginning was a bit slow. It wasn't a drag, but it didn't pull me in immediately either. My biggest problem with this book, however, was the ending. It seemed very rushed, and I didn't think there was enough build up towards it. And because of that, the result made it feel like the whole story was for nothing. I felt like I read the entire book just to get back to where I started. Overall, not bad at all - a lot better than I expected, actually. There were just a few hiccups along the way.

I wanted to like this book. I really did. But the plain truth is that I didn't. My book-dud rule is if the plot is still unclear by page 50, you are allowed to abandon. But I really wanted to like this book, so I pushed the rule aside and read up to page 150, waiting for some substance. But I finally gave up and closed it. To be fair, there was a plot - a political seat needed to be filled because of a counsillor's death - but waiting for that dull concept to become riveting simply didn't happen. To begin with, there were a lot of characters - so many that I had to write a cheat sheet and refer to it often. Each character seemed to have a complex history with the dead guy and each character had some reason to be angry, jaded or mean-spirited. All of this 'character development' slowed the plot down to a crawl. I mean who really cares about a bunch of whiney townsfolk who have nothing to do but scheme and complain? Aren't there any good running trails nearby? So after Miles or Howard or whoever shreded someone else's election application form for no good reason, I decided that I would close this book for good and go out for a run on my town's fabuous running trails. As for the famous J.K. Rowling, I think I am done with her. I know that I am one of the very, very few people who did not enjoy the first two Harry Potter books and didn't bother completeing the series. I really do not enjoy reading children's lit (for pleasure) and I felt like I was reading it because of peer pressure. But I really thought that her adult book would allow me to enjoy her obvious talent as a storyteller. Sadly, this is not the case.

That, combined with the summary on the back, made me think I was in for Vikings and Norse Mythology...Percy Jackson Style. Next, I realized that the author was Jonathan Stroud author of The Bartimaeus Trilogy. I've heard nothing but good things about the trilogy and bought bargain-priced hardcovers around Christmas last year, but have never gotten around to reading them (though as of now, I've finished the first one and started the second). I was going to order a hard copy to match my other books by him, but changed my mind when I saw that there was an autographed plate inside. All of this, combined with the fact that all four copies were sold the day they came in (I should know; I shelved them myself) convinced me to buy this book and read it right away. That being said, the book wasn't what I was expecting at all. I don't mean that in a bad way, either. I just had my own idea of what the book would be about. I actually like the fact that Stroud placed his characters in their own time period and not present-day better than my initial assumption. I love the fact that the beginning of each chapter starts with a tale about the hero Svein. This addition allowed the text to feel more like a traditional folktale from the days of old. The novel takes place during the time of the Vikings (I kept envisioning the sets/costumes/hair styles from the movie How to Train Your Dragon when reading this novel). As the novel opens, we learn the tale about twelve brave men who heroically died fighting to save their homeland from the evil Trows. The men become heroes and their bodies are buried in the valley to keep the Trows away. The descendents of each hero come from twelve different houses. Our protagonist, Halli Sveinsson, is related to the mighty Svein himself. Halli is a mischievous boy and constantly in trouble for playing pranks on people. One day, he goes too far and sets off a chain of events that will cause him to set off on a journey to the other houses as the truth about everything he thought he knew completely turns inside out. The book starts off slow, but maintains a lush form of storytelling that allows the reader to overlook this. Once it picked up, the book was hard to put down, especially once invested in Halli's plight. Even so, the final climax introduced a new plotline that seemed out of sync with the rest of the work and changed the entire tone of the novel. I never saw it coming and wish the climax had been handled differently. The novel ends on a note where it can stand alone but can also be revisited if Stroud chooses to do so in the future. If he does, it would be interesting to see him deal with the aftermath of the first novel's climax so that it doesn't seem so out there. If I had to choose, I'd say that I like Stroud's Bartimaeus work better, but I've only read the first of the trilogy to date and can't speak for the remaining two novels. At the same time, it's not fair to compare the two because the tone of each novel is so vastly different. I do love the concepts introduced in Heroes of the Valley and admire the style that set's the novel's tone, but the climax and slow start prevented me from enjoying the novel as much as I originally thought I would.

AHHHHHHH, I loved this book! It's been really hard for me to pick through the fantasy genre and find a summary that even interests me enough to comb through reviews, so I was relieved to pick this up due to my friend's recommendation. Actually, she had recommended it to me a while back but another friend of ours also read it and loved it, so I couldn't resist. And I must say, I have found THE fantasy book that just satisfies all these criteria I've built up in my head somewhere (and it most certainly isn't because of reading many well-written fanfics and stuff. Of course not. Nope.) The hardest part, in my opinion, to reading this book was perhaps the first couple of chapters. In no way was it boring or anything especially since it did capture my attention, especially the whole dragons and virgin daughters thing without an actual dragon , but it was a little slow. Not complaining too much considering it was necessary for background information and character introduction along with Agnieszka's initial life in the Tower , but if it weren't for the whole thing that I mentioned in the spoiler tag up there along with the promise of magic, I probably would have taken a lot longer getting through those first chapters instead of reading through them in one sitting. The main character Agnieszka was definitely a likable character who came with her own faults. Perhaps it's because she's younger than me and is a teenager and obviously grew up in a very different environment than my own, I have to admit that I found her to be quite irritating in certain scenes. Not to say that she isn't a lovable character because I found her to be quite humorous and respectable on many occasions, but her immaturity and naivete in certain scenes throughout the book sometimes got on my nerves. Or it might just be because I can relate to the Dragon better than I can to her... It's hard to say. However, I really did love the portrayal of Agnieszka's magic, especially when shown in contrast to Sarkan's magic and when both were used together. It definitely satisfied my magic craving in all the right places! And of course, the Dragon. He was probably the character I enjoyed reading about the most - it helps that he's the character that introduces magic to the readers - and satisfied that secret part of me that likes these types of fictional guy characters, I will admit. I found him to be more relatable probably because he viewed magic sort of like how scientists go about things, only just applied to magic. Not to say that I shared his view towards Agnieszka's magic since both types appealed to me immensely, but his approach was something that I understood and was familiar with due to my own education. There are many different types of characters in this book, but if I had to choose which ones really left an impression on me, aside from Agnieszka and the Dragon, I would have to say Marek and Kasia. Marek definitely left an impression as "the character I wished would die by the end of the book", but that's only covering the surface. He was not a character I immensely liked (in fact, I disliked him), but he had the charisma, the potential, the talent to be something great (one part that really stood out to me is that scene when he's killed and had managed to inspire everyone around him that he was certain that he would win and looked like a king). Funnily enough, that line made me think back to all the times where I felt he wouldn't have made a good king (and I'm sure we can all find them and list them out) and despite Agnieszka's observation that in that moment, he had looked that way, I just couldn't see any other result but his death from all of his actions up to that point. I would have placed Solya as a character that left quite an impression as well, but he sort of ended up fading to the back after a while, so I actually stopped thinking about him (but when he was an active character, I found him to be quite annoying and disliked him as well). Now, Kasia, oh Kasia. She was just an amazing character that balanced out well with Agnieszka. She just seemed to bring out to best in Agnieszka. Despite having gone through so many ordeals, Kasia was such a strong and dependable character. For me, she was a rock because she was constant and powerful in her own way (and in a completely different way from Sarkan yet those words would describe him just as well to me). I loved her and because of that, I could really relate to Agnieszka's love for her as well. However, there was one thing that kind of bugged me when I finished the book and still does even now. It was after the whole"His tower was broken, he'd drunk Spindle-water, and he'd held my hand. So now he was going to run away as quick as he could, and find himself some new stone walls to hide behind. He'd keep himself locked away for ten years this time, until he withered his own roots, and didn't feel the lack of them anymore." Don't get me wrong. I found that part quite interesting and it described him well, but it just bugged me that in the paragraphs afterwards in which we find out what Agnieszka's been up to after quite some time after that scene, she barely mentions anything about that scene aside from her vague summary of her feelings of the ENTIRE day which consisted of being "tired and lonely and angry and sad all at once". Not to say that I was expecting her to spill out her emotions regarding what happened and she did mention her lack of contact with him, but I was sort of expecting a contemplation regarding that day that kind of acknowledged her thoughts in that part I quoted from the book earlier and what her current thoughts were regarding that. Just... something more to build up to the ending where Sarkan returns is what I was looking for, I guess. Not to say that I can't fill in the missing parts myself, but yeah. I did really enjoy the ending with their reunion scene because it just fit them. The two of them are just adorable together. Because really, I ship it! OTP Yes, but seriously, I definitely recommend this book! I haven't read a book that I've enjoyed as much as this one this year and can see myself rereading this again in the near future.

I am incredibly torn as far as how to rate If We Were Villains by M.L. Rio--and, for that matter, quite torn on how much I enjoyed it even without any sort of arbitrary Goodreads rating. I went into the book knowing it was going to be some kind of Shakespeare-related murder mystery, the latter genre I am not quite so fond of, but at the same time I follow the author on Tumblr and was prepared to give her the benefit of the doubt. The trouble is, now that I've read the book, I am unfortunately filled with more doubt than I had hoped for. Perhaps my expectations were too high or my nerddom too lofty, but I was disappointed with the way neither the plot nor the characters seemed to be very fleshed out developed where the inclusion of such heavy themes--Shakespeare, tragedy, death, etc--would make sense. If We Were Villains is the story of a group of conservatory theater students who study Shakespeare every waking hour of the day. They are so caught up in their lives--and dramas and tragedies--surrounding their education and performances that when disaster happens in their friend group, they all have to come to terms with how to deal with it. When they don't, their friend group starts to unravel, as does each individual character, as the pivotal event affects every aspect of their lives, both on- and offstage. The story was quick and entertaining, if predictable. The foreshadowing in the beginning is incredibly strong, that it was nearly impossible for me to be surprised when the ending came--yes, the how of the climax wasn't clear to me, but it was no surprise what generally was going to happen. Because I am a huge fan of Shakespeare, having some of his play's plots come back into play for this story was a bit of a plot-ruiner as well, once it became more obvious which character in If We Were Villains was like which Shakespearean character. In that sense it was an interesting read, and though ti was predictable, it was fun to put the pieces together in a sort of dramatic-irony type of situation. I read the book in one day, in more or less one sitting, since I wanted to know what happened after a certain point. However, the dependence on Shakespeare as a plot device to keep all the action going--whether it was symbolism or parallelism or tragedy arcs--seemed a bit heavy-handed in certain places. Certainly some uses of Shakespeare's works were very effective, which I noted with glee, but others were a bit pretentious in any context and ended up making me roll my eyes. As I said, I love Shakespeare, and I was familiar with almost every single reference Rio included in the book (haven't read Pericles yet), so it is not out of a lack of understanding of Shakespeare's words or themes. No, even for me sometimes it was overdone. Some of the quotes and the parallel structures felt very forced to me, like the author was purposefully inserting them but not really understand how they would connect with the rest of the plot. (The disjointedness between the characters and their actions was hard to look past in some places.) I do understand the effect that pretentiousness had on developing the plot, however, thinking about how all these students are trapped in this classical conservatory world, in which Shakespeare is their life. In that sense it worked, but Rio didn't seem to make it work as well as I would have preferred. I also could not decide if I liked the inclusion of Detective Colborne for this reason: On one hand, he seemed disconnected from the world of the conservatory students and thus out of place; but on the other hand, his detachment from that thespian world may have been for the better, to serve as a reminder that not everything happens the way a bunch of Shakespeare-obsessed college kids think it does. Which, in turn, I suppose, is a good lead-up into the ending, when revelations are made and judgments are formed and shattered. My biggest regret with this book, and probably why I cannot rate it higher than three stars, is because of how poorly the characters were developed. As I was reading, the direct and indirect interactions between everyone started off interesting as I was just discerning who each of the characters was. But after a while, their stories turned into those of an ordinary sitcom, with jealousy and anger and a complete lac of communication. There were zero subplots to make things more complex and interesting and show off different sides of the characters. They were not multi-faceted when it came to each of them dealing with situations that arose in their lives. The ending was the only part that impacted me as far as character connection went, and I won't give away spoilers, but it was only at the end that I really felt the humanity and the sorrows of the characters, like I was finally emotionally invested in them. It took 350 pages to get there, unfortunately. My review of If We Were Villains could be entirely more nit-picky than this, but I will leave it at that. It wasn't a bad book by any means: certainly an entertaining read, and I did want to know for sure what happened next, all the way to the end. But its predictability and pretentiousness outweighed some of the more positive aspects of it. If you like murder mysteries and you like Shakespeare, this one is a fairly fun one, but definitely more a light read that won't make you think too hard.

I certainly wasn't expecting verse! It was a bit distracting, though, which is why I don't usually read verse. I get so focused on the lyrical quality that I don't pay attention to what's happening. Holly Bodger's prose was beautiful, though! I liked that Sudasa's POV was written in verse and 5's was written in regular prose. It made a clear distinction between their voices. I'm afraid I didn't connect to the story quite like I'd hoped. While the idea was interesting, it didn't capture me. And the short length of the story made it seem very abrupt and rushed. I mostly enjoyed it while reading, but it won't stick with me, which is the main reason for the lower rating despite higher ratings on some things in the Overall Assessment category. I did like the concept of 5 to 1 being the ratio of men to women, and men compete for the women because they are a prized commodity. I got a very good feel for the dystopian society that Holly painted. I could feel 5's deep rooted bitterness toward women whenever he spoke of them, and the unfairness of the society. In the beginning, 5 had a very negative opinion of Sudasa. He thought she was a spoiled rich girl, and he thought that she looked down on him. He also thought that she wanted her cousin to win because he was the rich boy. I enjoyed how those opinions changed as he got to know her, and he came to realize that she wanted to get out as much as he did. Also, there was a year!! That's always a plus for me. Overuse of mesarchia (a figure of repetition) mars this otherwise decent modern fantasy novel about someone who wakes up in a different body every day. But I want to say one thing about the prose. I want to tell you this is not good form. I want you to know that using the same beginning to three or four sentences in a row over and over and over throughout a book is really annoying. Imagine a state that ceased to exist. It has been swallowed on the map by hungry neighbours, swept away by winds of history and not even an empty space remains to bear witness to what once was. Things like that have happened before. Take Poland, partitioned by her three neighbours and for 123 years disappearing from the face of the world. But where the state had vanished, the people survived. And so the people of Poland cultivated their language, their arts, their traditions, their culture. They nurtured their collective memory and so the memory made it possible to resurrect the state even three generations later. What if the invaders erased these memories along the physical borders of the state and its landmarks? Would the idea of their country be able to live in the hearts and souls of its people? Now, imagine a different land, a peninsula shaped like a human hand with third and fourth fingers curled. Welcome to the Palm divided into nine proud provinces incessantly engaged in the political dance of alliances, betrayals, wars and conflicts. It is not surprising then that when two powerful sorcerers arrive to the Palm, one from East and one from West, they conquer the divided peninsula without greater problems. Wow, I did not think it was possible to dislike a book that covered two of my personal favorite genres (Space scifi and gaming). In theory this book could have been so awesome, but the execution failed epicly for me. I think the main issue for me was that the entire book seemed aimed at the YA crowd, which I definitely to not relate to. Because of this the book felt really childish and almost hoped to redeem itself with with pop culture references. Sadly the childish nature of the book really detracts from the enjoyment of the book to the point where I wanted to stop reading it because of how annoying the main protagonist was. On a slightly more abstract note, the idea behind the book was pretty decent. Using games as a means to train an army/soldiers has been brought up a few time in the past (the book covers most of them). While there are also issues to this method of training (some of which the book touches on), most importantly the lack of discipline and mental fortitude. Using this concept of training players and then recruiting them could have still been used really well with a slightly grittier tone. This book almost feels like the author read enders game and wanted to do the same thing in his tone/style (which he is entitled to). I should also mention that if you havent read it at this point, the enders game book does a much better jobs of tying gaming and war together (even if its not gaming in the sense of pc/console gaming). The ending of the book was stupidly cheap as well, its really weak when you end a book with "everything is magically fixed", there is some small text in the end that leaves it open for a sequel, but I personally hope that never happens. While I am not a huge fan of Wil as a narrator, I do feel he did a pretty good job in this book. I generally dont listen to fantasy books on an increased speed, but this book was so bad that I had to speed it up so that I could get it over with as soon as possible. Overall I really didnt enjoy this book and mostly on listened to it since I didn't have anything else on hand. Would never recommend this to anyone over the age 17-18 unless you are a huge fan of the author (and then to only if you are really into pop culture and gaming).

Long ago, dragons were hunted to near extinction by the Order of St. George, a legendary society of dragonslayers. Hiding in human form and growing their numbers in secret, the dragons of Talon have become strong and cunning, and they're positioned to take over the world with humans none the wiser. Ember and Dante Hill are the only sister and brother known to dragonkind. Trained to infiltrate society, Ember wants to live the teen experience and enjoy a summer of freedom before taking her destined place in Talon. But destiny is a matter of perspective, and a rogue dragon will soon challenge everything Ember has been taught. As Ember struggles to accept her future, she and her brother are hunted by the Order of St. George. Soldier Garret Xavier Sebastian has a mission to seek and destroy all dragons, and Talon's newest recruits in particular. But he cannot kill unless he is certain he has found his prey--and nothing is certain about Ember Hill. Faced with Ember's bravery, confidence and all-too-human desires, Garret begins to question everything that the Order has ingrained in him--and what he might be willing to give up to find the truth about dragons. 3.5 stars Ok, so I really wanted to like this, and I did eventually, but it took me awhile to do so. I felt like the book took forever to actually get going. I wanted to be interested and invested, but I didn't really start to connect until the second half of the book. For me, it felt like things clicked right after Riley shows up at the house and Wes is announcing that they've lost contact with their safe house. Up until that point, I was there, but there wasn't much of a connection for me . From the start, I was worried that I wouldn't like Ember, she just felt like she was going to be too whiny/bratty. Towards the end when she started to actually show some spunk, rather than just plain bratty/rebelliousness, I started to like her more. I get that her character wanted to experience the whole "teen" thing, but she can't have it both ways--she can't be a regular human and dragon at the same time. Although I will admit that I felt bad for her when she had to deal with Scary Talon Lady who clearly had a secondary agenda going on I was so on to her from the beginning! Why else would she be doing nothing but shooting Ember and forcing her to think as the hunter rather than the hunted? . I also didn't understand why she kept seeing Cobalt as a different person Cobalt and Riley are one and the same. Why should his name change just because his body does? I could see him using one over the other--Riley wasn't known to Talon so it would be harder for them to track him--but Ember didn't need to keep switching his names. She didn't when she learned Lilith's name, she just kept calling her Scary Talon Lady. So what was different/special with Riley? I will admit that I liked Riley, but at first I was a little wary of his character. He showed up and was giving off these strange vibes. It took me a bit to figure out if he was a good rogue or a bad one. I also liked how protective he is of the hatchlings he saves. It seems like he'll do whatever he needs to in order to keep them away from Talon permanently. Garret intrigued me. He was the stereotypical perfect soldier, but at the same time, once he showed up in Crescent Beach, I could sort of see him starting to unravel. As they moved closer to pegging Ember as the sleeper, he was starting to question what he'd known. Ember definitely helped him see that not everything they'd been told was true. I kind of want he and Ember (with some help from Riley) to be the ones who make everyone stop and reevaluate what actually caused the war and maybe find a way to put a stop to it. I didn't like the fact that the love triangle was introduced so late in the book. That was one of those inevitable things, I saw it coming from a mile away, but it still felt like it came into play too late. Dante didn't really surprise me at all. When Ember showed up and told him her plan, he agreed way too readily, even though they're siblings. His attitude did a 180 in that moment and I knew that he wasn't being completely truthful. I do have to wonder what the plan is for him though; Scary Talon Lady hinted at it and that could explain his actions. I still wasn't surprised, but I am left wondering.

Originally Reviewed At: Mother/Gamer/Writer Rating: 5 out of 5 Controllers Review Source: NetGalley/Publisher Reviewer: Heather Each book has gotten better, and the story never seems to end. I never want the world to end, and I fear the day that Kristen Callihan decides to close the book on this series. I have enjoyed reading every book in the series, and I hope that, if you haven't started this series yet, that you will. It isn't your average paranormal romance, and it certainly isn't your average historical romance. From the mythical creatures and those she's invented, readers can find themselves stepping back through time to historical London. From romance to magic to action to sex, it has steam, invention, and uniqueness like no other series. So, on to the book. As I said, I wasn't disappointed at all. From the first time I met Adam, I was curious about his story. GIM--Ghost in the Machine--the name alone is enough to spark interest. And then there's Eliza-May, the woman who seemed to change him. We learned so little about her, but if Adam gave notice, I knew we must too. No, there was something about this unlikely heroine, who probably isn't as prim and proper as she appears. But what I love, and believe me this is present in all of her works, is the dialogue. I have yet to read another author who can have her characters banter while making me laugh and shake my head. It's comical, but it fits the story perfectly, and does what dialogue is supposed to do: entertain and crate tension. Speaking of tension.... The tension between Eliza-May and Adam was unbearably hot. I'm still fanning myself. Ah, and although I'm a purist of sorts, you can read out of order, but for the full effect, start at the beginning. You will not be disappointed.

We begin from her birth and slowly walk through her life in Wallachia with her brothers Mercia and Radu. Then Lada and Radu being used as captives by the Ottomans and the subsequent meeting with Mehmed (the Sultans 3rd son). Lada had very little growth through the books. Rainbow Rowell has to be one of the best authors I have had the good fortune to ever come across. Because she just does it everytime! I absolutely love anything and everything she writes. Completely. And Landline was no exception. A brilliantly written novel dealing with a sort of broken marriage. From the very start, I was in love with this book. This is the story of a couple, Georgie and Neal who have been married to each other for 14 years now, I wouldn't say they don't love each other, they do, a lot in fact, but they are just unhappy. But then Georgie discovers a magic phone in her old childhood room, well just her old landline but sort of magicky which could take her to the past. Not really take her to the past, but rather let her call to the past . Could this be a chance to fix her broken marriage? It might sound a little childish but it wasn't. I loved the concept. I loved everything about it. I don't know but her relationship with Neal felt so real, so damn real. Neal was not your book boyfriend who we could only find in books - All swoony and dayum types. He was a serious, kinda short tempered but a charming, loving husband and father. Their relationship wasn't one that would make you shout Goals! But it was a beautiful thing. Both of them were unpredictable, and even though everything was alright in the end, there is no guarantee that things wouldn't go downhill in the future. Which I suppose would but it was extremely evident how much the characters loved each other and that's all I need to know. That's all they needed to have to make it work. I could read this book again and again and still fall in love with it each time I do so. It was jut awfully sweet. Not in a cheesy way. In realistic way. If that even makes any sense. It had the best ending ever, better than what I could have hoped for. Yes, the flashbacks and that sort-of-time-travel-but-not-really sometimes got a little confusing but nothing major there. Overall, it was an utterly fantastic read. Now I just need to go read all the books by RR, ones which I haven't. (Which are probably only two, one out which is a novella) Because she rocks my life. Truly. Meow.

** spoiler alert ** Ugh this book. It was my first foray into this romance-erotica genre and I believe it's not for me, or at least the typical books in this genre anyway. Like many terrible YA romance books I have read, the "plot" was awful and the whole time it felt like a bland backdrop for the romance (reminded me muchly of "The 100"). And, "romance" I should say. I don't know why I was expecting anything more but this was just as bad as most of the YA insta-love crapfests I've read in the past. The main character Garrett was somewhat funny but you really didn't get a chance to know him on any sort of personal level. I was so annoyed with the author's insistence on calling Cam "Cameron Rushton" (full name) for the first third of the book that by the time he got close enough with Garrett for him to start calling him Cam I was just irritated with him. I didn't get ANY sort of romance/connection between Cam and Garrett. Garrett spent almost the entire book being like "I'm not gay! But I'm so turned on! But I swear I'm not gay! But he's so hot and I can't stop thinking about him! BUT I'M NOT GAY." And then immediately following this up by doing very gay things with Cam. Like, really? I don't know. I guess maybe it's some sort of trope/turn on for some people to have this kind of romance but I didn't get it at all. Is it too much to ask for some sort of actual mental/emotional connection between your characters before they start fucking like rabbits? Feh, I say.

Hmmmm. Still not sure how I feel about this one. It took me a looooong time to start feeling at all invested in the characters (not until the last tenth of the book or so, actually), and even then, I'm not convinced I care about them enough to want to read the second book in the series when it comes out. It's an interesting premise, and I like that a good deal of it is grounded in facts, things that actually did happen. However, something about the writing sometimes made that hard to believe, and I think it's that most of the characters just never felt like real people to me, most especially Hitler. There are also several events that strain credulity a bit too much to me--unlikely coincidences, decisions that don't really make any sense, people just acting in ways that felt fake and forced. Still, the ending is pretty exciting. I don't know. I can see why so many people are loving this one, but I can also see why a number of other people feel frustrated with it. I think I'll just stick with Elizabeth Wien for my WWII fiction for now...

While I normally like Penelope Douglas's books a lot, this one was a little weaker for me. Our heroine is Easton, former professional tennis player, now graduated teacher accepted to her first teaching job at a prestigious high school. She is young, self-sufficient and determined to make a difference in her student's lives. She is not willing to change her attitude toward dealing with her difficult past, tainting her chances for brighter future. She believes she doesn't need anyone, in fact, she believes that needing someone is a weakness and she doesn't want to feel week and out of control one more day in her life. Here comes the hero - Tyler. This man is a definition of determinition. He goes after what he wants not accepting a failure. He does everything neccessary in order to reach his goals. His only problem is defining his priorities. He is a very succesful entrepreneur, upcoming state Senate candidate and not to mention his teenage son, with whom he doesn't have a close relationship. What happens when these two strong willed individuals meet? Is there any chance? Easton and Tyler first meet at a Mardi Gras ball, they share few intense and captivating moments together only to part ways. Six month later and Easton finds herself being introduced to Tyler as a new teacher of his son. They both know that it might be trouble. The beggining of their relationship was a rocky one, Tyler being an incredible asshole and jerk (thank you Penelope!) - seriously, you want to throtle him. He's condecending and patronizing, arrogant and felt entitled to everything he wanted. And even though he exceeds in business word, he fails at prioritizing. How to jugle a demanding carrier building his empire, approaching announcement of his candidacy for state Senate, his long estranged son and a budding relationship? Slowly he opens his eyes to discover what is important the most to him and sometimes a man has to make a sacrifice in order to do the right thing not just for him, but for the people he loves the most. Easton took a journey of her own - she had to learn how to let people in, to trust them and their motives. How to open up to them when she knows that consequences of her actions (direct or indirect) can be catastrophal? And is it a real weakness to need and want and love someone? Overall I liked this book, but it's more of 3,5 read for me. I am used to some gut clenching tension, something more thrilling, just something more. It was supposed to be a taboo read, but it didn't really felt that way. Ok, she was his son's teacher and he was older, but not by too much and I don't really see the "teacher-student's parent" relationship as a taboo. I couldn't really connect to the horror of Easton past - maybe if it was more described, if it got more space and not just those 5-6 sentences in the whole book. Somehow I just couldn't find a real sympathy for her, because I couldn't imagine what she went through, therefore I didn't feel the need for her to close up. There was no real climax, no real danger or plot, mostly it was about the h's and H's struggle with their own problems then battling any outside forces or any forces at all. It just lacked some drama. Easton was good heroine, temperamental, she could be a real bitch (and mostly I don't like that), but she was smart, strong (in her own way), she gave as good as she got, she never withered under Tyler's assholeness (which I applaud! Tyler was a good asshole. I really liked in the beggining that he was different than any other classic heroes with kids. He didn't put Christian as his first priority, which was the reason they didn't get along and he had to find his way to understand that somethings are more important than money and power. It wasn't given for him and his character went through real development. I just wondered what happened with her brother Jack after discovering he was the one screwing with her apartment ? I read Corrupt some time ago and that was more my speed. Penelope Douglas has an amazing ability to write about heroes that are AA - amazing assholes that you hate to love and love to hate and heroines that don't hide from them and give as good as they get. And I really like that.

Book two in Julie Ann Walker's Black Knights Inc series and I'm enjoying. This is a black ops suspense type series, but it is on the lighter side with lots of humor and over the top situations. This is Frank and Becky's story, who we meet in book one. Frank is the top dog at Black Knight Inc, a group of ex-military men who go on super secret assignments. Years ago, Becky's brother suggested to Frank they use Becky's custom motorcycle shop as a front for this secret op group. While Becky obviously knows these men are involved in secret government affairs, she has never been asked to be an operator for the group, nor is she allowed to sit in on their meetings. This frustrates Becky to no end, as she thinks she is just as tough as everyone else involved in this operation. Frank is 12 or 13 years older than Becky and has had a crush on her since the first day he saw her. But being that much older than her and kind of being her boss of sorts, he has stayed away from her. But the sexual tension between them is off the charts. Becky feels the same way about him, and yet his huge, serious demeanor and presence has scared her enough to keep her distance over the years. When this book starts, Becky is on vacation with her friend Eve in the Indian Ocean when their fancy boat is over take by Somalian pirates. Kidnapped and held for ransom, all they can do it wait and hope the Black Knight inc boys can find them and rescue them (which they do of course!). Frank and Becky's brother Billy along with the hottie Angel, come to their rescue. During this event, Frank becomes badly injured, and everyone arrives back in Chicago, all more beat up then when they started. From here, it is just a story of the two of them dancing around each other until one of them finally makes a move. I liked this one a little more than book one. I think the sexual tension is better and the suspense part is more fun to read about. All the characters are very likable and the author does a nice job with bringing in supporting characters to make the world feel very full. They joke around a lot, and I like that all the men are so intense and bad ass. What can I say? I'm a black ops ho. I did have a few disappointments. First, while there is great sexual tension, there is not a great pay off with the sex. There is really only one scene. Fail. I needed more. And I needed the sex to be a little intense and dirtier. I guess you can say the sex scene fit the tone of the book, a little silly. But I don't want that kind of sex. I want hard core sex that only super secret black op military men know how to have damn it! So I really hope books in the future bring that part out more. Second, and I mentioned this is the review of the first book - there is a lot of over the top, slang words used, and in particular slang words for curse words in this book. Frank says 'Keerist' instead of Christ. Becky says 'dill-hole,' and Eve. Oh god Eve. On multiple occasion she says 'cheese and rice' instead of Jesus Christ. Just fucking curse people!! (see what I did there?). Seriously, y'all are bad asses, cuss like one. Please. Otherwise this is a fun book, and I very much look forward to book three. Rating: B

A piece of art I really enjoyed this book and although it wasn't easy, for me it was well worth the read. Heart of Darkness tells the story of a sailor named Marlow, who decides to join a naval company that takes him from London to Africa. There he discovers how different the African continent is. The narrator refers to it as "the darkness". First of all: the racism. Was Conrad a racist? Well, this question is hard to answer. Heart of Darkness is about a man witnessing horror and the same man's struggle to put his experiences into words. In my opinion the way that Marlow told his story was a huge part of the story and therefore it's hard for me to equate Marlow and Conrad. I definitely disagree with Chinua Achebe that this is all automatically Conrad's opinion too plus it's hard to judge something by today's standards when it was written in 1899. Nonetheless, while the main message of the book was that "colonialism is bad" Marlow views the black man as less than him. So, this book is undeniably racist but it is hard to tell where the satire starts and stops. Overall, all I can say is that I'm happy I read this book and while it sure isn't for everyone, I found the language astonishing with lots of thought-provoking imagery.

Review originally posted at Ramblings From This Chick Third Debt is the fourth book in the Indebted Series, and these absolutely have to be read in order. If you haven't read any of the previous books in this series make sure that you start there before reading this book or review. This series gets better with every single book, and I honestly have no idea how Pepper Winters does it! She weaves everything together perfectly, giving us just enough to drive us mad and keep us reading! This installment was honestly the best yet, and it absolutely brought out all the emotions! I have no idea what will happen next, but I can't wait to find out! Nila Weaver and Jethro Hawk are no longer the same people they once were. The debts have changed them, and they find themselves torn between what they have known all their lives, and what has happened since finding one another. With so much on the line, they find themselves facing dangers and punishments far worse than they have ever experienced. Now they must try and prepare themselves for the next debt, and it will test them more than any of the previous debts have. I love these characters so much, and we have honestly seen so much change in them over the course of these four books. Jethro struggles so much with what he is and how Nila affects him, but he also still craves approval from his family. We really see a lot more to him in this book, and finally begin to get some answers about what makes him the way he is. Nila is strong and yet she has also figured out that she has no control over her feelings for Jethro. She loves him and wants to be there for him, but she also struggles with everything that is surrounding them and what he must do. But for me, this book was an eye opener when it came to Kestrel. I have always liked him, but I absolutely fell in love with him in this installment. He is so much more than we have ever seen, and I found myself hoping for more and more of him as the story continued. To me, this installment was the most intense one yet. Things started off a bit slow with the aftermath of the previous book and where we were left after the second debt. But then things started to change and as the third debt approached, I knew we were in for something shocking. I felt so bad for Nila and all that she was going through, because she was completely blindsided by the third debt. She had no idea it was coming, and it was heartbreaking to watch. I have no idea what awaits these characters as they still have the fourth and ultimate debts left, but I know that the ride is far from over. I think that this cliffhanger is by far the worst of the series, and it really might kill me to wait. That ending left me reeling, and I have so many questions. As much as I had hated Cut before, I absolutely loathed him after this installment and I really hope he gets everything he deserves. I need the next book in the worst way, and I know that things are not even close to over. Knowing Pepper Winters, we still have many more dark and twisted things to come before we get to the end. I am still hoping for some kind of HEA, but I know that whatever the ending is it won't come easy and the journey is far from over. **ARC Provided by TRSOR Promotions**

Let's recap briefly: Rainbow Rowell wrote a book (Fangirl) about what it was like to be a Big Name Fan and in order to capture this experience she made up a fictional Harry Potter series, which the protagonist of Fangirl wrote a fanfic about. Then, Rainbow Rowell decided to actually write this fictional Harry Potter series, which is Carry On. Meta'ed out yet? But, honestly, this kind of makes sense, because the Simon Snow snippets were the best part of Fangirl. Rowell is nothing if not wicked clever, and it shines the most in the way that she used the fact that everyone knows and understands Harry Potter to include huge swathes of background in a couple of paragraphs, which gave her inversions and subtle changes context. One of the coolest feats of literatures someone's pulled off in awhile, but I was worried that it was not particularly sustainable in a stand-alone novel. Good news, bad news? The way in which Harry Potter provides a context and background to Carry On is probably the strongest part. The whole book exists in a dialogue with Harry Potter and the two most interesting themes of the novel grow from here: Doesn't it kind of suck to be a mage in a magical/muggle world? The way HP is set up, you can only be a wizard if you're a wizard (you don't get the basic education required to be anything else.) What if you want to be a doctor or a mathematician or a chef in a big restaurant? Suck to be you: wizarding world or bust. But in the HP world, no one discusses this. Rowell actually explores this concept and how much magic destines people. If you're a mage in a magical/muggle hybrid world, and you get to go to magic school, the rest of life is a downhill slog of hiding and never being around your people. Another thing Rowell does great is evoking the culture and community of teenagers and it's really on show here: the sadness of graduation is clear in a way that Rowlings did not succeed at. I love the loyal opposition. That you can be boyhood enemies and play kid games, but if there's going to be a war and its going to be real, how does that change and mature your enmity. Because so much of childhood opposition is the loyal opposition: the person you depend on to antagonize you and play the foil. So, cool. This part is fun. Bad news: The book reads like Harry/Draco fanfiction. Not that I read fanfiction (only pro-singularity propoganda, Harry Potter and the Methods of Rationality.) But still. So still some good news, in that those of us who have spent the last 14 years and 7 books growing to love the Harry Potter characters will be invested off the bat. But on the downside, very little actually happens. Literally, the first 20% of the book is HarrySimon wandering around HogwartsWatford looking for Baz. The majority of the rest is Simon and Baz mooning at each other. Also, it reads to me like Cath actually wrote it, i.e. that it was written by an 18 year old girl: Is falling in love with your sworn enemy actually a thing that happens in real life? Just one minute you're fighting and the next you're swooning and then a second later you're "snogging"? OK... Also, I talk a lot. I think in words. I need to talk to process my thoughts. My friends get sick of hearing me think out loud. Both the thinking and the talking. I get told "most people don't think that much; they just do" a lot. In Rainbow Rowell's world, I am both basically selectively mute and impulsive. Her characters talk about everything always and at length (usually sounding like self-important teenagers in their word choice and punctuation.) I have never in real life met someone who articulates quite so many thoughts, and definitely not a 17 year old boy who does so. Finally, despite having read approximately 20 pages of Baz's thoughts on Simon's hair, I still have no idea why they actually like each other in anyway. (Besides the hair. It seems easier to have your boyfriend wear a wig than to date your sworn enemy because he has nice hair.) So, in conclusion, its a fun romp, with interesting commentary on the world of Harry Potter and school fantasy in general, and it's the only book you'll ever read that's a fictionalized version of a fanfic of a fictional novel, so there's that.

Stephen King book blurb says: "If Summer of the Night isn't the best horror novel of the last five years, it is surely one of the best three - a gorgeous and terrifying story of five boys who come face to face with a monstrous entity during an enchanted Illinois summer thirty years ago. Simmons writes like a hot-rodding angel, loading his American nightmare with scares, suspense, and a sweet, surprising nostalgia. This is one of those rare must-read books, easily surpassing Clive Barker's Books of Blood. I am in awe of Dan Simmons." This book was written in 1991. I have to believe there were many better horror novels around that time, including Stephen King's! I just can't agree with sai King on this one. It wasn't awful, but it certainly wasn't great. I hate to disagree with King cause he's the MAN, but geesh... maybe he was paid A LOT for this blurb? Shaking head in wonder. I can't agree with anyone who has reviewed this book and compared to Stephen King's IT and found this one superior. WHAT? No way, Jose! IT was in all ways superior to Summer of the Night. I think Mr. Simmons was trying to create his own version of IT, but fell short. Now, don't get me wrong; I think Dan Simmons is a great writer and his recent stuff rocks. But this one... well... Ok, let's talk about continuity and repeated text galore! For example he mention's that Dale's basement has flooded 4 times in 4.5 years; several chapters later he says that the basement has flooded 2 times in 4 years. He also mentions that the same basement has no windows two different times. Another time he mentions that Lawrence usually wanted to hold his older brother's hand while falling asleep, but most of the time Dale told him no. He mentions the same thing almost verbatim later in the book. Simmons does this several times... I guess it's nice he wants to remind us of something he told us earlier in the book, but it really annoyed me. Also, there is one boy in the group who sets out to fight the evil in their town that has never actually witnessed a supernatural event. All the other characters have seen stuff and experienced stuff that scares the bejesus out of them, but not Kevin? Why does he even believe his buddies when they share their experiences? His character is very under-developed so you have no idea why he buys into participating in life-threatening plans, when he has no first-hand experience of what has been going on. And why did a key character get killed off early in the book; the most well fleshed-out character of them all? Why take the time to get us so invested in him and then eliminate him? I did find that Dale's and Mike's characters were well-developed, but didn't really buy Kevin's and Jim's. Lawrence was somewhere in between, but why was he often alone in the brothers' shared room when he was sooooo afraid of what is under his bed? No way would he EVER be in that room alone, even in daylight. An HOW could any of these boys experience periods of "normal" boyish moments like searching for a buried cave, playing hours of baseball, etc. when they all knew they were in grave danger at any time of the day and night? I'd be sticking close to home and worrying myself sick! Just too many things didn't work for me with this book. It took me longer to read than my usual fast pace, and it wasn't plausible. It did have some creepy parts and the premise was good, but otherwise I just wouldn't recommend this to others.

I'm not the type of reader to bash classics because I can recognize literary merit without actually enjoying it. I didn't enjoy "Huckleberry Finn" or "A Tale of Two Cities" at all but I don't go around and say that they are terrible, crappy books, because I know that they're classics and there must be a good reason for it. Unfortunately, I feel the same way about "Wuthering Heights", which is a shame, since I very much enjoy other Bronte sister books. The main problem I had with this novel is the fact that there was not one character I really cared about. The novel begins with Mr. Lockwood, a narrative character without any real connection to the story, stopping at Thrushcross Grange, looking for a place to stay. He sees the unpleasant family that lives there- Heathcliff, Hareton, Cathy, and their servants Joseph and Mrs. Dean (Nelly/Ellen), and he is curious about their odd circumstances and connections to each other. Throughout the novel, the story of this strange little family is revealed, and there is much loss, anger, sadness, rivalry, and unhappiness among them, and most of it can be traced back to the forbidden and doomed romance between Heathcliff and Cathy's mother Catherine. My interest just wasn't in this book as I read it. There were so many characters and I had a hard time keeping track of them. I couldn't stand most of them, either! I found Catherine and Cathy to be such awful examples of literary heroines- they are stuck-up, spoiled, immature brats who just make life miserable for the people around them. The men and boys are all either cranky, pompous, or pathetic. The ending was a good ending I thought, and it did emphasize the bleak and dark tone of the novel, but I wasn't sad when it ended. It takes a certain person to like certain books, and I just wasn't a fan of this one. I felt no connection to it.

Princess Snow is missing Her home planet, once known for lush landscapes, is now filled with violence, fear, and corruption at the hands of King Matthias and his new wife as they attempt to punish the princess's captors. The king will stop at nothing to get his beloved daughter back--but that's assuming she wants to return at all. Essie has grown used to being cold. Temperatures on the planet Thanda are always sub-zero, and she fills her days with coding and repairs for the seven loyal drones that run the local mines. When a mysterious young man named Dane crash-lands near her home, Essie agrees to help the pilot repair his ship. But soon she realizes that Dane's arrival was far from accidental, and she's pulled into a war she's risked everything to avoid. Actual rating: 3.5 stars Ok, so I liked this book, but there were a few things that just felt...off to me. Let me explain. There are definitely aspects that I liked. The idea that Snow White is actually in hiding has been done (take a look at Snow White and the Huntsman, Mirror, Mirror. Granted those are movies, but they've got the same idea--Snow White's alive and hiding, and doing what she has to in order to take back her kingdom), but this time around, she's a really bad-ass fighter/brawler and essentially a hacker. This is also one of the times where she actually doesn't want to take back her kingdom. That was one thing I wasn't to sure about though. Obviously, she knew her father and stepmother were no good, so why wouldn't she do what she could to dethrone them? Yes, she mentions something to the effect of being scared, but still...I think she should have at least been doing something to try and interfere--hacking into the networks and giving false movement orders, changing supply runs, things like that. Moving on. In the beginning, I wasn't all that fond of Essie. Granted, she didn't want to draw attention to herself, but really, why would she try to sabotage Dane's ship MID FLIGHT! What was she thinking? Aside from the fact that they both could have likely died, that was definitely a red flag that would draw attention. I'm just saying . As she started to become more of the rebel and less of the scared girl, I started liking her more. I really liked the drones! Especially Dimwit. They were great comic relief and it was an interesting take on the dwarves. Dane was great. I actually really liked him. From the beginning, it was clear his "treasure" was more than he'd claimed but I was surprised that he was able to figure out where Essie was likely hiding . I thought he'd been way to impulsive when he showed up on Thanda. But, he started seeing things a little clearer once he was actually spending time with Essie so I'm glad he changed his mind. Obviously Matthias used Essie's disappearance as a way to gain the control he'd always wanted. Olivia too. However, some of the things that went on, I have to wonder how much Olivia did without Matthias' knowledge. And how much he actually sanctioned. I mean, obviously he wouldn't have been happy to know she'd tried to kill Essie but I wonder if he was 100% aware of her "gifts". Or how loyal her Midnight Blade was... Overall, nice retelling. Not my favorite, but I'm glad I gave it a chance
