Originally published at yAdult Review. Ah, this one. I heard so many good things from reader friends I trust, but GoodReads reviews scared me a little. We start off learning the history of Russalka, how it was colonized and the wars that followed. Katya is nearly sixteen, living in a world ruled by martial law, when she is granted an apprenticeship on her uncle's ship as a navigator. Things go horribly wrong, however, and that's when the real story begins. The first quarter gets pretty technical about submarines and how they work, which was interesting, if a little confounding. Kane is very intriguing, and I really wanted to know more about the war with the Terrans. We get more information in bits and pieces throughout the book, and really, Kane was probably my favorite character next to Tasya, a war criminal. I don't know if my brain is twisted, but these people are supposed to be the villains in the story. Shows how well Howard writes to make them so sympathetic. I also liked the world: a sea-based world with just a smattering of land and sea mountains. However, I didn't much like Katya. You know my biases about male authors writing women and girls, though I don't know that this was the problem this time. Katya was just irrational for the first half of the book, or maybe I just liked Kane too much to see her try and torture him. That Katya realizes she is being irrational made no difference to me. When we finally find out what the Leviathan is, the things she said to Kane made me put the book down. Maybe my bleeding liberal heart is too soft. In fact, by the halfway mark, I pretty much hated Katya. How many times was she going to get angry about something she didn't understand only to be schooled and made to feel stupid later? It's like she never learned that maybe she didn't know everything. Despite hating the FMA, she was still a government shill, believing everything they said to the detriment of everyone around her. I delivered many incensed diatribes to my boyfriend about this (he read the book too and liked it more than I did). And, honestly, I'm used to disliking protags in YA, just not ones who could kill people with their temper and stupidity. I was ready to flounce at the 2/3 mark and toss my Kindle against the wall, but I was assured Kayta is prevented from doing the stupidest thing she has ever thought of, and that's saying something, because I can think of no less than six times when she does something dumb. Katya has no characterization beyond being sanctimonious and stupid. This is a problem with all hard sci-fi in my opinion: it tends to be plot-driven, and the characters suffer. And that's fine if that's your thing (it's my boyfriend's thing, for sure), but I wanted her to be more fleshed out. The submarine terms become tiresome after awhile too. I didn't much care about how the ships worked or what depths they were at or how Katya navigated. I wanted to know about the Leviathan, about the war, about Kane's family and his relationship with Tasya. So, this one just did not work for me. I hate to give such a negative review for anything; three paragraphs on what I didn't like isn't fun for me to write, but my problems with the book seem to be somewhat universal, at least on GoodReads. I will tell you what I did like: no romance. Zero. Katya is in no way attracted to anyone, and just thank you for that, Howard. And that's about all I can say about that.

I have heard it said that every author has that book that they keep under the bed. Their first attempt at writing, so shameful in comparison to their later works that they hide it from daylight and the eyes of the world. From what I've been told, this was originally one of those books. In my opinion, it should have stayed under the bed. This book is poorly polished, hastily edited, and in places very confusing to read. It is also, in my opinion, unfinished--leaving the reader to wonder how much of this was the original writing of Harper Lee and how much was the editor's agenda inserted for the sake of selling a book and making a buck. Okay. I know that there is an election coming up. And I know that there is a lot of racial tension flaring up in parts of the United States that seems relevant to the subtly-disguised manifesto in this book, but are we really supposed to believe that everything political said within these pages was what Harper Lee thought about the matter fifty years ago when she first penned this manuscript? It seems more likely to me that somebody in the publishing world felt that they could make some more money off Mrs. Lee's name by hastily pushing this manuscript through the editing process and onto the shelves. Either the goal was money, similar to J.R.R Tolkien's post-humus works, or it was to wade into the politically charged atmosphere of this election year with yet another rant about race. On a positive note, we are allowed more glimpses of our dear Scout's childhood--this time her adventures take her from tween-age to young adult. Unfortunately, they all come by way of flashbacks, which come at odd times throughout the story and often without clear indication as to whether what is being said, done, or thought is in the past or the present. I'm pretty sure there was a flashback inside of a flashback, and at one point there was what I can only describe as a flash-sideways (sorry, Funny Farm). These flashbacks were the best part of the book, and I have to wonder if they were actually the original writing and the politically-intense, present-tense narrative was added later to tie them together. In many places, the wording within conversation took on an air of college political essay, and at times I felt like an editor must have accidentally deleted the paragraph somewhere towards the chapter's beginning that explained exactly what it was they were talking about. Did it ever say what year this was? What Supreme Court decision? What bus? Did I miss that page? I mean, I can make reasonable assumptions based on my knowledge of history, but the average reader--especially a reader twenty or thirty years from now--isn't going to have a clue what was going on in the mid-fifties in that particular, forgotten corner of the world. (Don't believe me? Then I dare you to find an older-edition of Trivia Pursuit and see how well you do with those questions.) Towards the end, as the conversations just become philosophical dialogues so long that I wondered if I was reading Plato or Daniel Defoe, it became hard to tell who was speaking in each particular paragraph. The author (or authors) seemed to have spent more effort getting their rant out than putting quotations and speech indicators in their long-winded paragraphs. I found at least one missing quotation mark that those big-city editors ought to have caught, and the whole thing just felt...unfinished. It just plain did not flow the way a well-polished manuscript usually does in its later drafts. Overall, the experience was akin to reading an indie book that I paid way too much for and heard way too much acclaim for to not be disappointed with what it really was: just another poorly polished, hastily edited cash cow for the political agendas and publishing demigods of New England.

My thoughts on The Hard Count by Ginger Scott: I don't want you all to just look at the 3 star rating and think this is a meh book. Because, it's definitely not a meh book. It's a book with a heart, and an important message, and characters to fall in love with. A book with a family to shake your head over but then watch proudly as they grow and develop. The Good! I really enjoyed the emotional intensity and the family dynamics. There is a theme of racism and lots of private school politics which I loved to hate. Reagan is the coach's daughter, and twin sister to the team star player. Nico is her biggest rival in class, they love to debate and score points. There is a delicious chemistry underlining their connections. Even more so when he proves he is as talented on the field as he is in the classroom. And stirs up a hornets nest as he is not from the right side of town, not from money and not a legacy player. I thoroughly appreciate diversity in books and I loved this theme. The Bad! But the football...yawn! That's just me, I don't get football. I still have no idea why it's called the hard count. I think it's some kind of a football play, if that's even the right terminology. Don't ask me! Because I was skimming all the football stuff to get back to the bits I love. The swoons, the toxic school old-boys-club politics, and did I mention the swoons! I also prefer sports themed books where the GIRL is the sporty one. I loved that Reagan loved photography and making videos and had her own interests. But I personally love books where the female character is out there being all athletic. As it inspires me and sends out such a positive message. Overall: If you love football, sweet romances, and more football; then I think you'd love this so much more than I did. Basically for me it was like a sandwich where I preferred the filling and left the bread behind! Who should read The Hard Count by Ginger Scott? I'd recommend this to you if you like YA romances with a sports theme, or if you like seeing the underdog battle his way to the top. And it's probably best if you love football as there is a lot of that here. Fans of Ginger's previous books like On The Sidelines should also enjoy this. I'd also recommend it if you like authors such as Rachel Harris or Michelle Kemper Brownlow. Thanks to Ginger Scott for sending me a copy of this book. A review was not requested, but as always I am happy to give an honest, unbiased one.

The filthy lying dust jacket! The "praise" on the back of the book quotes Lisa Dierbeck, "This is classic, cinematic suspense. I read it with sweaty palms and a racing heart... The taut pacing evokes Hitchcock." Liar! Whatever was she reading it was not this book. It had a bit of suspense (or more appropriately drama), but is far from making me perspire and elevating my heart rate. I love Hitchcock, and I'm deeply offended this would be compared to him. This is a 1 (maybe 1.5) only because of the quality of the descriptive writing, which generally is really well done. But the content/substance of story is horrible. How do you have a story with the description from the dust jacket which just draws you in and then never address what happened to that story? Instead we have to wade through the slow drawn out sub-story of the current day murder. They are not linked in anyway except for the fact they happen in the same place (and that same place is meaningful to the narrator). Why do that to me? I feel offended and taken in. I like the writing style. It really shines especially in the interview scenes. You feel like you are in the room as it is going on, the subtle movements, the idiosyncrasies of the characters, etc. I really liked how French uses the narration for the "interrupted" thoughts. They just interrupt you like they would the narrator and that is really well done. The story is too long. It is essentially a catalog of dead-ends. The narrator is unlikable. He is a terrible detective - he makes huge mistakes and jeopardizes his career, his relationships, his work, and the current day case from a simple birthdate calculation. There's nothing likable about him other than you feel some pity for him due to the incident of the abduction of his friends from his youth, but even in that you miss out since neither him or we know what happened. He lies to everyone and gets duped by a fraud, and his temper and poor judgment lead him astray all the time. As an aside (and this may come off as sexist which is is not) and I know no other way to say this: but I felt like I was reading a novel about a man written by a woman. I cannot explain it very well, but as a man I felt like I was reading something that was not masculinely right, if I can say that. The content of his head was not the way a man would think or something. It is a very subtle issue, but overarches the whole story for me. If I didn't know the gender of the author before I started, I could have told you 20 pages in. I have never really encountered that in a novel that I know of, so it was fairly unique. And quite honestly a knock on the book. I could see through Rosalind the psychopath throughout the story. The narrator bargains for your sympathy since he was taken in by her and presumes you were as well. You could tell from the initial meeting with her in the victim's house something was off about her so the appeal for sympathy is lost. I have a problem with the slow crumbling of the narrator. I just do not like anti-hero stories. However, I could have dealt with it if there was some type of redemption involved (which I guess would imply it is not an anti-hero story). But there isn't. He loses out on what could have been the love of his life, for no reason I could really see other than his own internal tensions which are selfish and poorly rationalized. He blows the case against the prime antagonist in Rosalind by messing up her birthdate, and worst of all as he loses pretty much everything else in his life, he (and we) get no resolution to the childhood kidnapping incident. I do not mind things dying off in a story; I just want something to rise from the dead three days later to make it worthwhile.

I'd heard lots of amazing things about this book. It was about time I picked it up. While this inside jacket is captivating, it does little to sum up the plot line, so I'll do so here. Daisy is fifteen. She flies off to England to stay with her cousins in the remote countryside. While she is there and her aunt is traveling, a war breaks out. The story follows the children as they are left to fend for themselves amongst a crumbling society. The books is told in first person, from Daisy's point of view. Her narration rambles and is very stream-of-consciousness-like and the sentences seem to go on and on much like this one, but there is something so magical in the way that Rosoff does it, that as a reader you're just sort of like, Wow, I think I might actually dig this. It does take some getting used to though. There are no dialog tags and every thought just sort of flows into the next. I was trying to decide, when I first picked this book up, if I thought Rosoff's style of writing was beautiful or annoying. It took me only twenty pages to decide. It's beautiful. And amazing. I read this one line and knew, without a doubt, that I was going to love the book and every single word that followed: Then Edmond and Piper cam and lay down on the blanket, one on either side of me with Piper holding my hand as usual and Isaac still standing in the water looking peaceful and they started arguing about what flies trout liked best in a quiet lazy sort of way, and Edmond blew smoke rings in the air and I closed my eyes and wished they were mine. Is it possible to fall in love with a book from just one line? It must be, because it happened to me with that one. Getting back on topic... The story takes place today, or maybe in a very near future, but because the war unfolds in such a familiar setting, the story itself becomes terribly disturbing. At first the children thought of it as an adventure, being stranded without parents. Things were originally fun, and maybe just a tad inconvenient. They were so far removed from the bombings that began the war, that the threat didn't seem real and sometimes Daisy even feels guilty about enjoying her life. I enjoyed this. It felt realistic. Of course, that all light-hearted adventure business changed rather quickly. As things go from inconvenient, to suspicious, to full on frightening, the book because an experience you can't put down. By the time you reach the end, you feel like Daisy, so changed by the whole affair that you can barely remember the person you were as you started reading the novel. Just as Daisy discovers that so much can change so quickly and one must learn what they value in life and what they hold dear, the reader will find themselves asking similar questions. Another amazing thing about this story is that it touches on about a hundred different topics but somehow does it in a way that doesn't overwhelm you. It's a story about love and hate and anorexia and incest and war and perseverance and recovery and death and HOPE. The ending was so moving I literally had to shoo my husband away so I could frantically cling to the book and read those last few pages in peaceful solitude. Gosh, I'm still trying to recover from this experience. In a good way. If you haven't read this book, you should. Unless of course the idea of cousins being sexually involved makes you squeamish. In that case, it might not be for you. But even still, that's just a fraction of this powerful story and you should still give it a try. Right now. Originally reviewed here

Oh, John Green. I think you're a nice guy who really believes he's delving into some super deep issues with his novels, like depression and isolation and having a terminal illness. But you're not. You're glorifying sadness and you're glorifying illness, and it makes me sick. Oh, wait, I AM sick. That's right, I have cancer. I was eighteen when my abdomen turned into a puffer fish and I almost died in the course of a week. I underwent several procedures to remove the liquid from my abdomen and began chemo immediately. I've had a picc line, MRI's, CT scans, blood draws, hair loss, mucositis, debilitating nausea, and an endless line of pills to take. The experience is hellish, and I did not see it in The Fault in Our Stars. So I can legitimately say I'm not poo poo-ing cancer because "I don't understand." This is not a book about cancer, not really. It's John Green using cancer as a way to make his relatively vapid characters seem tragic. Hazel is the Mary Sue of Mary Sues. Her name, her attitude, her book - they're all incredibly pretentious, so I can't sympathize with her or identify with her, even though we're both in the cancer boat. Hazel is white, seemingly well-off, and narrates in purple prose. Shockingly, Augustus is all of those things as well. John Green seems incapable of writing about any other types of people. And this is not John Green hating - his Civil War videos helped me pass my IB history test. He just doesn't get what he's doing; at least, I hope he doesn't get it, because whether it's making Alaska's depression irresistibly attractive or making Hazel into a special snowflake, Green glorifies illness. It's gross. Cancer does not mean spouting metaphors, finding your soulmate, and taking vacations to foreign countries. Cancer is having your hair fall out in clumps. Puking at 3 in the morning. Not being able to get out of bed to see your grandparents. Yes, I know Hazel isn't getting chemo anymore, but this is awfully convenient for the plot and for making out. Frankly, I find it offensive to write about cancer in a way that is so obviously not about cancer. I'll be generous and say that Green is exploring the idea of impermanence and how people deal with death, and that he legitimately thought cancer was a good way to do that. Why didn't he write about the ACTUAL EXPERIENCE THEN? What about writing about being in the hospital, or the wonderful people you meet along the way, or acknowledging how good it feels after the effects of chemo have worn off? It takes a few conversations and a bit of research to figure out the basics. There were no scenes that truly showed common cancer experiences like radiation, surgery, or chemo. You know, the old burn, cut, or poison. You were lazy, Mr. Green, and for the sake of all the children who have cancer, I find this unforgivable. I could discuss how contrived the romance is, how ungrateful Hazel is towards her parents (I know how taxing it is on mine, so I find her attitude unpleasant, especially since so many people consider her wise), how flat both of the characters are, how silly their dialogue is, how the jibe at the support group probably hurt people who've found a lot of comfort in those, how the track and field jibe about the hurdles really pissed me off, and how the ending is incredibly bothersome. Luckily, many other people have done so incredibly eloquently, and my two cents really has more to do with Green's portrayal of cancer. I've been touched by the cancer stories I've witnessed and by the grace with which people tackle a sad, painful, and difficult disease. So why miss an opportunity to make this real, Green? Why not have Hazel and Augustus struggle with the betrayal of their bodies and the journey it takes to forgive those bodies? In fact, why not take out Augustus entirely, and make it a story about finding yourself in the midst of a confusing and inevitably tragic journey. I would have read that. Stop making illness so beautifully tragic to advance a theme that doesn't have much substance anyway, because it's been done before. We all contemplate our demise, terminal illness or not, so next time don't use cancer as your crutch. Maybe you'll finally write a book that proves me wrong about you, but I think you'll flaunt your vocabulary and ability to create pretentious quotes for the rest of your writing career, and continue to use illness and sadness as a way to legitimize it.

Binti swept through my friend's list last year, and everyone loved it! I ended up reading (and disliking) Okorafor's Who Fears Death? before I got to this novella, and given my experiences with that novel, I had some reservations picking up another by this author. However, in the end, Binti was quite enjoyable, though I wasn't quite as enamored with it as others. Okorafor excels at crafting protagonists who aren't just white North Americans in future clothing. Her characters are usually of African descent (well, future African, or at least, future person from that particular area of the world, whatever it is referred to at the time), and they read quite differently from what one usually gets in North American SF. Culture is often important in Okorafor's stories, and Binti is an excellent example. Our young protagonist is from a fairly insular community, and she defies norms to go study at the best university in the universe. She is the first of her people to leave in such a way, and much of the story deals with her feelings of isolation and discrimination. The story takes a dark shift when the ship carrying Binti and her future classmates is attacked by hostile aliens, leaving Binti the only survivor. She is saved by a strange device she picked up in the desert, and she negotiates with the aliens and agrees to help them get an important artefact back from the university. Binti's time on the ship that has been taken over is eerie and full of tension. The aliens are quite alien, and one is never quite sure whether Binti is going to live. Fortunately, she does, forging some interesting relationships along the way. A few other reviewers have mentioned that the science fiction aspect of this story is weak. While I don't think that authors need to go full hard SF to prove their mettle in the genre, there are things I look for when reading SF. In particular, the social dynamics need to reflect the way the universe has been structured. I have no issue believing that Earth is still mired in racism. Humans are dicks. Us not changing over the course of a few thousand years isn't terribly surprising to me. What threw me, however, was the way racism/speciesm/classism was treated in the greater universe. At one point, Binti thinks that the university professors are mocking her for her adherence to cultural norms (namely the clay that her people use to clean themselves). I buy that class is at issue on this university planet, and that Binti is seen as less advanced (re: intelligent) than the other people at the school because she comes from an insular community. However, given the fact that the university has a dorm room for students who need a specific gas filled environment so that they can float properly, and the leader of the professors is a spider-like creature, the fact that she uses clay on her skin isn't actually something I think would standout as weird. This, I think, is why people thought the SF was weak. The universe isn't fully fleshed out yet (which, admittedly, is to be expected in a novella), and this means there are little things that can easily draw the reader out of the story. Okorafor gives us weird aliens, but she doesn't shift the social dynamics to take advantage of this much. I am often fascinated with how SF authors deal with discrimination in different contexts, so I was disappointed that this novella didn't think through its own implications more. The novella also starts quite strongly, but meanders to the end. The tension of Binti's time on the spaceship leaves readers quite breatheless at points, but things slow down quite substantially at the university, even though the stakes are so high. Not to say that I disapprove of a story that takes a less explosive approach to negotiations, but the pacing was off. All in all, Binti is definitely worth a read, and I am excited for the second installment in the series. However, it had some lofty aspirations that it didn't quite manage to meet. (To those that really liked this, I also suggest Rochita Loenen-Ruiz's "Dancing in the Shadow of the Once" a gut-punching story of the terrible bargains made between colonised and coloniser that occurs in a much vaster universe than our own currently is.)

TL;DR Maxon is precious and I love him. America is one of the most infuriating MCs I have ever forced myself to put up with. Alright ya'll strap in because this one was a rough read. When I started reading this series a friend of mine (@ashleybbooks) told me that I was going to end up hating America. And at the end of the first one I was like "I don't know hate is kind of a strong word. She's different I kinda like her." Then I read this one. And the further I read the more I understood. Spoiler free, this is the entire plot of this book: "I might like Maxon." "But oh my god Aspen." "No. No definitely choose Maxon." "I HATE MAXON I'LL NEVER SPEAK TO HIM AGAIN." "But I still kinda like him.." "But also Aspen.." My face through this entire book: This is the type of series that you force yourself through because you know how it ends and you want to see how it gets there, even though the MC is so freaking infuriating. Like I said in my review of The Selection, I absolutely loved Maxon, and mostly kept reading the series because I wanted to see his happily ever after. So every time America made a stupid decision (which is like every decision), instead of sympathizing with America's inner conflict- which I think is what I was supposed to do- I was just like "STOP WHAT ARE YOU DOING TO HIM OH MY GOD JUST LET HIM BE HAPPY" My frustration with her grew gradually until the very end when she royally effs up everything at which point I officially disowned her ass. Like. God she's so stupid. I don't remember the last time I was as angry with an MC as I was with her. I get she's immature and impulsive and confused, but I just could not with her anymore. I also, again, felt like the rebels should have been more important to this book. It is so obvious the whole time that they are going to play a pivotal roll, and yeah they are introduced more in this one, but still. The story going on in the background was just so much more interesting than America whining and making dumb choices. I just feel like it was super unnecessary for this to be a trilogy. It felt like the author just kept adding in new conflicts to pull Maxon and America apart for the sole purpose of extending the length of the story. Like, honestly, she easily could have just written one book that was a bit longer instead of writing three. Maybe if I had read this book when I was 13 I would have liked it better. I would recommend it for younger readers, but I just don't think this is a YA book that works as well for older audiences as some do. But maybe that's just me. *shrugs*

Well, this year was not very prolific, in terms of reading. I blame James Joyce, largely, for his excellent Ulysses. While not my favorite read of the year, it was mostly engaging and brilliant in long stretches. I think I'm good for one big, difficult read a year, and that's about it. I need to tackle Proust sometime in the near future, probably next year. Probably. As far as "best of", I don't have a lot to choose from, but here goes: Best Novel: Experimental Film by Gemma Files. Best Graphic Novel: Space Riders, Volumen Uno: Vengeful Universe by Fabian Rangel and Alexis Ziritt. Best Non-fiction: Spring Chicken: Stay Young Forever. Best Short Fiction (collection or anthology): Burnt Black Suns by Simon Strantzas. Now, I must admit that my interactions on Goodreads have been minimal this past year. I've been working on a non-fiction book and self-published a role-playing game supplement, so that's curtailed some of my social media time, not to mention my reading time. Again, though, I can't overemphasize how much of my time was taken up by Joyce. That will free up some hours to read more - thank goodness!

Oh, my. I can't believe I'm saying this, but To Taste Temptation was just extremely disappointing. It was almost excruciating in its slowness, and half the time I was just wondering if something even remotely interesting would happen soon. There were so many unnecessary scenes that, if cut from the story, would have made it slightly better. But noooooo, we had to hear about Emeline doing this, or Sam doing that, or Emeline's son saying whatnot. I also had a few issues about the characters. Up to a certain portion of the story--at around the 30-40% marker, I think--I found out that Emeline was actually engaged. What? She never gave any indication that she was engaged. You would think that a betrothed woman would be more disciplined in her thoughts or actions, especially towards other men. But Emeline just acted as though she was free for the taking. Yes, it wasn't a love match, but still, what she did and how she thought about Sam were practically cheating (at least by my definition of cheating). Others may feel differently about this but I, for one, felt really betrayed. What's worse, the man she was betrothed to was the one her best friend loved. Yes, I might as well go on and reveal it. I'm talking about Jasper and Melisande, the primary characters in the next book in the series. This just felt wrong in so many levels. Call me a prude, but my personal code of honor dictates that "one must not covet thy best friend's lover under any circumstances." Under any circumstances. I absolutely hate, hate, hate it when a woman falls for her best friend's man. I don't give a damn if it was under weird circumstances or whatever, I just hate it. Oh, it didn't help that Emeline was such a stuck up aristocratic bitch who busied herself by looking down on Sam from under her nose. He's a colonial. He's an American. He came from the New World. He battled wild Indians. OKAY, OKAY, WE GET IT, WOMAN. YOU DON'T NEED TO MENTION THAT EVERY DAMN CHAPTER. Ugh. I am so done with this shit. I'm just hoping that Melisande and Jasper's book would soothe my angered soul.

In all honesty, I did not care much for this book. Reading the description of the story, I had high hopes for Romancing the Nerd. However, the hopes feel flat. The story felt very similar to movies and books I have read before. And though I love stories that follow the premise of the plot, I didn't feel that way with this book. The major problem I had with the story was the writing. This book featured outdated fads that weren't relatable to me. In my opinion, I feel like the author should have used fewer fads. Instead, I think she should have created fake apps, brands, and other things so they didn't end up seeming outdated to the author's audience. Also, the author used terms like "drama-ramma" which personally, I didn't particularly enjoy. If the author used the word "drama" in the text, I feel like the book would have been a better read. Terms like "drama-ramma" felt somewhat cheesy. Another problem that I had was Zelda. I admit, I am stubborn and at times, I do overreact. However, that girl was crazy. Yes, Dan did ditch you once and ACCIDENTALLY hit you in the face with a basketball. Yes, it sucked but to go to the extent where you create a fake account to catfish him to the point of embarrassment is extremely bitchy. Zelda is somewhat crazy and petty. Finally, the last problem that I had was the whole scheme that Zelda initiated. The plan is used frequently in books and movies. I did not feel that this story complemented the plot. Also, (spoiler) why would Dan end up with her after he realizes her crazy scheme?! I would be running as fast as I could to get away from her (spoiler end). The book was easy and fun to read. I did not have difficulties getting into the story. Most characters are fun to read about. Also, they have great depth to them. Overall, the book was not something that I enjoyed but it could just be me.

DNF @105 pages I read this first book in this series last summer. Although I REALLY enjoyed it and get it a 4.5/5stars, at the time I had said I really didn't know whether or not to continue, because I really didn't like where the story was going. Recently I was convinced to pick up the second book and give it a chance this summer - but, unfortunately, I was right and should have stuck to my gut instinct and knowing myself and what type of story I like. I remember the first book being written much better. I remember it being much more adult rather than the cliche, typical YA fantasy that this was. I remember much stronger characters. And, again, I don't remember the writing being so incredibly juvenile. It might have been because I did read the first book so long ago, and therefore have read many amazing adult fantasy novels since, but this book was just bad. The second Yelena shows up at her family's home/clan/thing, without ANY proof that she's actually their daughter, they immediately take her in and treat her like their family - and the whole situation was just VERY convenient and unbelievable. The dialogue was also so incredibly juvenile I was honestly shocked. It sounded like something a brand new writer or very young teenage writer would do. It was very cut and choppy and perfect grammar and every single person sounded exactly the same. The writing also just wasn't at all gripping or nicely written like how I remembered it being. The brother's hatred for Yelena was also just a very convenient plot point since he really had NO reason for being angry but hey, it made conflict. Also the whole IMMEDIATE capture or whatever thing was just stupid. Needless to say I won't be continuing this series. I still will say I REALLY enjoyed the first book, and I'm perfectly content with just leaving it as a standalone.

I tried really hard to like this book. I really wanted to, but just couldn't get into it. The premise behind it is great, which is why I picked it up despite reading some not so great reviews, which I usually avoid before reading a book. The whole idea of creating serial killers from actual serial killer's DNA is horribly frightening, which is why I thought "that's gonna be a great book with a main character who will have a terrible struggle with his own identity", but while I got the struggle, I just didn't like the way it was presented. When we start the book, everything has already happened to the main character so we get this story of events with interjections like "little did I know what would happen next" or "if I had only known at the time". Drove me crazy! Then there's the whole preaching issue. Jeff has never heard of any of these serial killers and is actually pretty naive for someone bred to be a killer so we have to learn all these statistics and facts about real serial killers and the governments involvement in wars and secret projects. Which is cool, but again, not in the way it is presented. The facts are just interjected and stops the whole flow of the story. Instead of being pulled into the story and feeling like you are next to Jeff, we are simply being talked to or rather, at and it's very hard to like any of the characters, especially Jeff (the main character we are suppose to feel sympathy for). His struggle with "what's bred in the blood will come out in the flesh (pg 80)" is second fiddle to the author's clear disdain of America's obsession with all things murder and mayhem. It made me ashamed that I watch shows like CSI and Criminal Minds and like them. Not because of the murder, but because the bad people are punished. I'm not cheering for the killer or think their murders are "cool". I'm sure there are people out there who do, but it felt like the author was saying our obsession with death is morbid and should be put to an end. Death is a fact of life. The whole book just felt like social commentary. I'd watch Fox news more if I wanted that. Again, the premise was fantastic, but the execution left much to be desired.

I am an emotional wreck. Much like when I first read The Sisterhood of the Traveling Pants a few years ago, I was not prepared for all the emotions this book brought up. You strike again, Ann Brashares! Everything in this book probably affected me more than the previous ones because I'm the same age Tibby, Carmen, Lena, and Bridget are now. And at this point in our lives, the friends we have are those we've chosen to have for the rest of our lives, so the loss of any one of them (for whatever reason) is devastating. It means you've lost a part of your future as well as your present and your past. I didn't even know this book was being planned until the day it was published so I remained spoiler-free, which is good because had I known, I may have chosen to skip this book. I'm still recovering from Sweet Valley Confidential and the carnage Francine Pascal did to my memories of Sweet Valley High. I was afraid Brashares was pulling a Pascal after the first few chapters of Sisterhood Everlasting, but she came through. Tibby, Carmen, Lena, and Bridget are in different places (literally and figuratively) and ten years have passed since Forever In Blue but unlike the characters in Sweet Valley Confidential, they're still recognizable. I still felt an emotional connection to the characters even though I hadn't read the books in years and didn't particularly feel the need to read a 5th book. At times it felt like an extended epilogue, but it was still a pleasant reunion -- one I hadn't planned but still came away feeling positive about -- with characters I once loved.

From my blog Auntie Spinelli Reads DNF **WARNING: SPOILERS AHEAD** I usually hate to include spoilers in any review, but the reason I put this down is based off of a spoiler, so that's most of what this review will entail. I think my hopes for this one were much too high before I picked it up. The story was decent. The originality was great. The characters...eh. I love the premise, really I do. A flower that can make people immortal and a perfect being with impenetrable skin is awesome. There was a lot of science involved (although most of it didn't really make a lot of sense, but oh well) and I like science. And Pia's friend is a jaguar. So cool. The romance = instaluv. I understand that Pia has never seen a boy before, and OMGSH Eio's abs are just, like, soo sexy, but damn. Within a mere week of meeting they're all, 'I love you, you are my heart, I'd die without you' and it was just a little much for me. The L word could really have waited until the end, moving a little slower to let the romance truly develop. But whatever. The whole Evil Scientist spiel was...interesting, but perhaps a little overdone. Rooms with chairs that have shackles on them, lies and cover ups, putting birds inside a cage with electrified bars to see how long they can stay in flight, keeping a nest of man-eating ants for examination, killing a kitten to pass a test of 'perfection'...Why? Because they're scientists and they only care about a means to an end? Let's get to the real reason I marked this as DNF. Killing kittens in the name of science. I bawled. Ugly cry does not even cover it. Not because the writing is good, or because the author is talented, but because the idea of someone purposely killing a kitten is just so horrific to me (I am a crazed cat fanatic) that I think a little piece of my soul died just reading about it. I will never understand for the life of me why an author feels the need to put something like this into their novel. To get a rise out of the reader? To make an emotional connection? To create controversy? Unless the book is focused on animal abuse, there should be absolutely NO reason for it. Especially in fantasy/sci-fi novels. And with this particular reader, an appearance of said abuse is more likely to make me get angry, throw the book, and never pick it back up again than to make me give kudos for being ballsy enough to face such a controversial topic. Sorry, that's just my opinion. Actually no, I'm not sorry. I hate it when authors kill kittens fictionally, no matter what the reason. I am a cat lover, and any abuse or murder of a cat is enough to condemn any book in my eyes. I don't care if anyone thinks I'm overreacting. That's just the way it is for me. If a two-week-old kitten getting stabbed with a syringe full of poison and then thrown on the ground doesn't bother you, then give this book a go; you'll probably like it. The issue here is that it just wasn't for me. I made it through more than 250 pages before the kitten murder. I was mostly enjoying the book, sure, but it wasn't anything particularly spectacular....not so engaging that I feel the need to finish it. I can part ways with it without feeling any loss. I read the last few pages and I know what happens ultimately, so I could really care less about that 100 pages in between. I just can't bring myself to continue. I can't. Favorite character: Little Sneeze, the two week old ocelot kitten. OH WAIT, HE WAS BRUTALLY INJECTED WITH POISON AND DIED. ASSESSMENT Plot: 3.5/5 Writing style: -- I can't rate this because the cat killing destroys my ability to be objective. Originality: 5/5 Characters: 3/5 World-building: 3/5 Pace: 3.5/5 Cover: 5/5 NOT recommended for cat lovers.

--DISCLAIMER: THIS REVIEW IS KIND OF SPOILER-Y! SORRY :)-- Mackenzie (Mac) Dobson was part of a tight knit group of friends living in the town of Hemlock, until one of them died. Amy was killed by a werewolf, and the rest of the group--Mac, Kyle, and Amy's boyfriend Jason--are still reeling from her loss even months later. After all, it makes it impossible to forget about how she was killed, when werewolf Trackers are in your town and school. When Mac starts to unravel the mystery surrounding Amy's death, she uncovers a myriad of secrets. It almost seems no one in her life was telling her the truth. But once she finds out what the truth is, will she be able to handle what comes with knowing? Well...I had a couple of issues with this book. Mac wasn't likable, but I didn't hate her either. I really didn't have strong feelings for her either way. But one thing she was, was weak. Someone was always coming to her rescue...and I don't love that in a female protagonist. I actually really didn't get a sense of Mac's personality at all...which is why I'm so confused about how both guys in her life ended up in love with her. The love triangle in this book bothered me a great deal. Jason was in love with Mac but dating Amy...and Kyle was in love with Mac but dating Heather. I dunno if this is just me and my adult perspective (both boys and Mac are in high school), but why continue dating someone else when you are in love with another person? In Kyle's case, when he finally kisses Mac, he said he had been waiting to do that for two years. So, for TWO YEARS he suffered through dating another girl when he was really "in love" with Mac. I don't get it. The author also didn't explain at all how Jason ended up in love with her while he was already dating her best friend. So, I know the story was supposed to be about werewolves, but on a slightly deeper level it's about prejudice and being afraid of people who are different. The motives behind the main villain's actions are sick and twisted...and frankly I can't believe the police in the town let him get away with as much as he did. If you are reading Hemlock expecting an awesome supernatural story, you will be sorely disappointed. There are so many lies and drama filled conversations, the werewolf aspect is pretty much secondary. The book wasn't bad, per se, it just left me with a kind of "eh" feeling. I'm really not sure where the next book could even go...but I think it will be more Teen Drama than Teen Wolf.

"You might not remember me, but --" "Travis Stephenson," she interrupts, her words like a roadblock. "Welcome home. Now leave me alone." It's always nice to come across a book that has a little bit of everything. Something Like Normal definitely covered its bases in the emotion department. If there was an emotion left to be discovered, I couldn't tell you what it was. Everything from fear, anger, joy, sorrow, caution and anticipation was explored. This particular (male) narrative was somewhat different because his story revolves around living life while continuing to suffer from Post Traumatic Stress Disorder due to his lingering pain and recollections of what happened during his time spent on tour in Afghanistan. "I left everything the way it was," she says as I drop my bag on the floor. "So it would feel familiar. Like home." I don't tell her that it doesn't feel like home at all. The voice of Travis sounds like the voice of a guy you might know. When he's not suffering from reliving the harsh reality of his life through nightmares, he's drinking and fighting and screwing just like any other guy. I appreciated the balance in his tough guy persona as he explored a missed opportunity of being with the girl he'd always had his eye on. Harper comes up alongside me, all green eyes and tousled hair. I could probably look at her forever and not get tired of that face. She's a good kisser. So good I want to beat the hell out of whoever taught her. She beams at me and it's almost enough to make up for the fact that I'm harder than trigonometry right now. Okay, so maybe those lines bordered on cheesy but they made me smile. It's always nice to see a bit of sweetness or humor interjected into a serious subject. There was a diner scene which happened to be quite funny. It's not quite as good as another famous diner scene from another book but I still had a big grin on my face while reading it. It was also nice to see the bond between male friends who have been to hell and back through war, yet can still joke around with each other. "I still have my half of the necklace, and last night I wrote in my diary, 'Dear Diary, Kenneth is my BFF. I hope he gets laid, because it's a special night when a man loses his virginity and contracts a sexually transmitted disease at the same time.'" I thought I was safe from the crying thing because for whatever reason, the flashback scenes sort of played out in my head as an old black and white movie and didn't seem to completely move me. Then the last couple of chapters happened and a lone tear fell from my eye (cue sad music). Don't worry though. The book has plenty of hope to go around. I thought the author did a great job of showing the rough road of healing that was ahead for our main character. If I had to mention one of my favorite things about Travis it's that he was not without flaws, yet he still managed to recognize and take responsibility for the bad things he had done to the one girl who had every right not to forgive him. Watching the relationship develop between Travis and Harper was sweet to witness. Neither one was able to guarantee the other much more than what they could give in the moment and I liked that. Realistic relationships for young people = my stamp of approval. I can't make that kind of promise when I'm only nineteen and owe the Marine Corps three more years of active duty. Anything could happen. If I had to come up with any complaint it would be that there were a few moments which made me feel uncomfortable as Travis described the enemy. I do understand though that this is the "trained" mentality of war. War forces you into an us vs. them, regardless of who you're fighting. This was a sweet book with a realistic love story. War is not pretty, nor are the aftereffects, but it was nice to see that hope does have a chance of winning out with the right support system around you, whether it be friends, family, or a special loved one. I don't know if my life will ever be completely normal again, but something like normal is a good start.

And my marathon of Mielville continues! Again so different than PSS and Embassytown, I'm impressed. Finito. Actually a few days ago. While reading Mielville I have so many thoughts, I even plan some sentences in my head for my GR review. But usually these thoughts are nowhere in sight when I sit and write! Especially with this book, because I'm still deliberating over the end. It's one of those ambivalent endings, what REALLY happened, there are various other possibilities. Which is really the point. Still, I like knowing what happens, but in some rare instances these endings work - similar to Labyrinth, and oh shoot, another book a group of mine was just discussing but I can't remember, and I'm not going to fret about it, I will NOT, argh. The reason this doesn't get a 5 is because I was removed from the main character, I'm still not sure I like her that much, even tho I can relate. The city here is remarkable - a floating compendium of many many ships of many types. There are ridings - ie counties within the whole, and each have their own politics. All are ruled by the Lovers - we never do learn their names, and really I don't think of them as individuals even at the end. There are many scars - the Lovers, 2 of the main characters, and the planet itself which has a rift in time and space and dimensions wherein others arrived and had a 500 year empire. One of the things I love about Mielville is his universe, or universes. Basically I really love how he does time and space! Ya know, the whole space/time continuum! Which is one of the things I love most about sf. The possibilities! And now I need a break from Mielville. His books are just packed with ideas, but also some terror. I need to relax and get away from horror. I don't do horror, yet for some reason his books are OK. But still, enough anxiety. Feel free to comment on what you think happened at the end!

Originally seen on Emily Reads Everything Endings are bittersweet. It's hard to say goodbye to characters that you have fallen in love with. It's hard to know that you can't read a series again for the first time. Endings are something that all book lovers struggle with. At the same time, endings are beautiful. Endings provide a finality and closure that readers both expect and hope for. Endings can end with Happily Ever After. Crystal Crowned is no different. I have been eagerly awaiting this book. I couldn't wait to read it. At the same time, though, I dreaded having to pick up this book and I didn't want to start it. I was absolutely terrified. Elise Kova doesn't write books that are easy to read and she doesn't make it easy to be a fan of hers. She doesn't shy away from dark decisions and character struggles. No one in Air Awakens is safe, ever. After the emotional roller coaster of the first four books in this series, I wasn't sure how Crystal Crowned would measure up. I was concerned that it would be difficult to wrap the series up in a satisfying and meaningful manner in just one more book. I was especially concerned because I had issues with Water's Wrath. I was worried about that happening again. I didn't want this series ending to disappoint. I was wrong. Crystal Crowned is just as fast paced as the rest of the series. I'm always shocked by the sheer amount of story that happens in each and every one of these books. Aldrick and Vhalla have a lot of ground to cover if they are going to save the world. Best of all, my favorite characters returned. This wasn't an ensemble book but the other characters are mentioned. I especially loved learning more about Jax and Elecia. This finale will not disappoint you!

Orson Scott Card correctly mentioned that much of contemporary "literary" fiction indulges in super-sensitive protagonists who have a gift to see the world in a way no one else does (thereby not-so-subtly suggesting that the author is a superior being). Rachel is a hopeless alcoholic divorcee. Despite losing her job, she still takes the train into London every day, passing the house Tom, her ex, lives in with his new wife, Anna, and their kid - a child she couldn't give him herself. Then Rachel sees their married neighbour, Megan Hipwell, from the train window kissing a man who turns out to be her therapist. When Megan goes missing, the secrets of her life reveal a startling link to Rachel's own... I couldn't finish this so-called "thriller". It's not a long book either at just over 300 pages but, some two weeks of picking it up, reading a few miserable pages, and quickly putting it down again, I'm ready to admit defeat at the 180 page mark. Paula Hawkins' novel is full of seedy, unlikeable people in a "plot" that reads like an overlong episode of Eastenders. Rachel's ex Tom and his missus Anna argue with Rachel in the street while Megan's cheating on her husband Scott who argue at home and Cathy, Rachel's housemate, wants her to get help, and blah blah blaaaaah who finds this interesting! No real story appears until well over the halfway mark and even then it's really only the hint of one. Most of the time it's this soap-opera dogshit as the dimwits bicker like the dreary suburbanites like they are about dull nonsense. Paula Hawkins' writing is pedestrian at best, rendering it all in flat, un-evocative prose. Quite why The Girl on the Train is such a runaway hit, I have no idea. It's tedious claptrap of the lowest order. Then again Eastenders is incredibly popular too so there's probably a crossover between those audiences. Don't listen to anyone who compares this crap to Gone Girl, they are nothing alike and at least Gillian Flynn can write. Exhausting and boring, The Girl on the Train is a total waste of time.

My mother-in-law had this book sitting on her shelf for the longest time. In some ways, she's a lot like me - she collects books and takes her time reading them. In her case though, I think she really just enjoys buying books and letting them sit. I knew she wasn't really going to miss this so when I was looking for something interesting to read, I snagged this off her shelf and scurried away to the bedroom to escape the world for a while. This was one of those books that really ended up surprising me by all its twists and turns and unexpected moments. Cora's ability with being able to see other people's auras around her fascinated me. I used to be intrigued by the notion of being able to see auras and sometimes like to pretend that I can see them myself (though maybe, not as strongly as this character can). I was fully prepared for this book to end up being one of those types of reads where a character struggles with her ability to see something others can't, then meets the one person who maybe understands her and loves her despite it and romance ensues and happily ever after, yadda yadda yadda ... But such wasn't the case. She meets a boy, yes - but he turns out to be someone completely unexpected. Her ability to see auras ended up being something else that she hadn't expected and is still coming to terms with. Somewhere in the middle of the book, it takes a turn for the interesting - where a mystery opens itself up to her. She ends up traveling to Ireland to find her answers and in turn, end up meeting the boy who 'got away', and meeting another who actually does understand her. There were a few heartstopping moments, frustrating ones, confusing ones - turning the pages was something of a roller coaster. I liked it. This book, while not an intensely unique one, has its own unique attributes. It's a page-turner and I felt like the author did a great job with sucking the reader in (namely me) to its story. That cliff-hanger ending, as usual, drove me crazy - but I have the second book sitting on my shelf, waiting for me to pick it up as soon as I'm done reading the book I have now. So yay!

** spoiler alert ** I didn't expect to like this book once I read the back cover, and in the end, I was right. I've noticed that a lot of the reviewers here have already covered how disturbing Travis' behavior can be. Additionally, Abby is sometimes likable, sometimes ridiculous - I would respect her when she recognized Travis' behavior as childish, and then toss the book aside in frustration when she made a decision that was completely unrealistic and obviously meant to keep the drama in the book going for another fifty pages (the most obvious example would be when she decides that having sex with Travis will be a great way to get him to fall out of love with her). Throughout all of this, the author can't seem to decide whether or not she's a feminist - first, before they're even in a relationship, Abby changes her clothes when Travis tells her that what she's wearing is too revealing, and then, later on, she tells Travis he'll have to get over the fact that she's attractive and other guys are going to check her out when they go to bars. Oh, and then the whole matter of the "Mrs. Maddox" tattoo. But, at the same time, if I COULD give the book no stars, I would still give it one. And that's because personally, as I read it, there were parts that I found entertaining. Abby has some great conversations with her friends and even with Travis. Also, the whole poker twist to the story was melodramatic but a lot more interesting than Travis describing how he broke his phone to keep from calling Abby on New Year's Eve. I know that some people will read this and maybe, as other reviewers were arguing, it will lead them to look for Travis-type guys in real life - and those guys may very well be dangerous. But as for me, I just saw their relationship as a fantasy, and an occasionally fun fantasy to read, at that.

Kirkus Review Mari Baroja is found dead at the Durant Home for Assisted Living. Her demise isn't too surprising, since the Basque woman was well over 70. Her neighbor, Lucian Connally, however, insists she's been murdered, and he ought to know. He retired as sheriff of Wyoming's Absaroka County, and convinces his protege, Sheriff Walt Longmire, to investigate. With some timely help from his foul-mouthed deputy Vic, Cheyenne barman Henry Standing Bear and new recruit Santiago Saizarbitoria, Walt finally unravels the tragic love story of Mari and Lucien and the violent ruckus her last will and testament has unleashed. Tiring Every single woman wants to climb into bed with Walt. Setting Tbe book begins three weeks after The Cold Dish, the first book in the series. The conclusion of that story is discussed early in this book. Durant is the town, in fictional Absaroka County, Wyoming. Modern times. Characters ~Sheriff Walt Longmire, widowed about 4 years. His wife died of cancer just after they assembled a log home. As the book opens Walt is clearly depressed and is not taking care of himself or finishing the work on his home. The home needs extensive work. He drinks a lot. His internal monologue is funny, insightful, and kind. Walt is a college graduate, Vietnam War veteran, and has been the Absaroka County Sheriff around 25 years. He plays the piano. ~Henry Standing Bear, Cheyenne, Walt's pal since childhood. He owns Red Pony tavern, Vietnam veteran, Native American. Gourmet cook. Supports Indians with groceries, cash, and more. ~Victoria "Vic" Moretti: a sheriff's deputy and a former Philadelphia Police Department homicide detective. Vic was hired as a deputy few years ago by Walt who plans to have her be sheriff when he retires. Sheriff is an elected position so it will take time for the community to support her. She relocated with her husband to Absaroka County because of his work. Her husband is working in Alaska now and she's not wearing her wedding ring. She curses a lot and is grumpy. ~Santiago Saizarbitoria, has come to interview for deputy job. The past two years he workd as a guard at the state's maximum-security prison. Rancho is a nickname. I absolutely cannot stand 1st person narration, very little makes me want to pull my hair out more. Predictable, at best, this novel is all telling and no showing. Characters are unrealistic as are the sudden changes they undergo when the plot demands it. The writing is sub-par and the plot, while having potential to be interesting, falls drastically short of the mark. It's some of the most unimaginative writing I've read in the YA category. The bad guys are straw-men, and are all men who want nothing more than power and control over everyone around them. There's nothing deeper than that. The conflict of the story is a pretense for the romance of the story, and even that is entirely unbelievable, though the writing will pound you over the head with the romance's inevitability. But the romance isn't the reason for the low rating -- there are just too many moments where allegedly intelligent characters act stupidly just to drag out the plot. Some of the examples - At the feast: Yelena falls asleep, has a notably bizarre dream, wakes up to find a character with a known shady past smirking at her, and Valek says that he detected magic being used at that exact moment. Yet Yelena doesn't think to connect the dots and at least raise the possibility that maybe the sinister guy maybe was the source of the magic? Like, not even to investigate him more? - When meeting Irys: Irys asks, "Do you know why the king is acting so totally weird?" What Yelena said: "I couldn't tell you." What Yelena should have said: "I'm not really sure but I caught a creepy sinister guy with the Commander and the Commander had a totally vacant stare. Dunno if it is related or not but figured I'd mention it just in case." - Valek: "I'm suspicious of this new dessert. You should stop eating it, Commander, while we investigate it." Commander: "You're my chief of security but I am going to overrule you because this dessert is really good." Also: Are you really trying to tell me that Valek couldn't command two soldiers to guard Yelena day and night? The only option was for her to move in with him? Really? Also, again: in a world where the Rules of Behaviour are so iron-clad and ruthless it is amazing that the repeated "attempted kidnap and murder of the King's Poison Taster" is continually swept under the rug with no repercussions.
7/10: Good solid read, something to get your teeth into.

The Darkest Kiss is the second book in Gena Showalter's Lords of the Underworld series about a group of immortal warriors being forced to house demons inside their bodies as punishment from the Greek Gods for opening Pandora's Box thousands of years ago. Lucien, keeper of Death, is covered in mysterious scars all over his face and body. Despite his constant control and composure, he's a very tortured soul. He considers himself unlovable and is glad that women are repulsed by his appearance. Plus, he's got more important things to think about other than women such as the Titans who have escaped from Tartatus and taken control from the Greek Gods. Anya, Goddess of Anarchy, is a smart, mischievous, bold and full of attitude. She's not one to be pushed around or take no for an answer. She always gets what she wants, and what she wants right now is Lucien. She's incredibly attracted to him, scars and all. Unfortunately, Lucien resists her advances, and she finds this unacceptable. Anya decides to accompany Lucien and the lords on their trip to explore one of two ancient temples that have emerged from the sea since the Titans gained power, even though she wasn't exactly invited. That's when things start to heat up between Lucien and Anya ... Lucien is a compelling character. Right from the start, the reader probes his mind, learns about his past, and comes to understand why he is so withdrawn and cold. He's an easy character to sympathize with and get attached to. Anya on the other hand had me laughing almost right away. She's spunky and aggressive. She has a whole different feel to her than the heroine from The Darkest Night, Ashlyn, but like Ashlyn, she too has a secret. A few of the other lords, Paris and Reyes, have their own subplots that break off from Lucien and Anya's story. The Greek mythology that is worked into this series is so refreshing when compared to the vampire mythology that is so common in paranormal novels these days. The Darkest Kiss briefly explores the history between the Titans and the Greeks which adds nicely to the back-story of the novel. A lot of events remain unconcluded or open creating plenty of suspense for the next installment of the series. One of my favorite aspects of the novel is how both Lucien and Anya faced decisions with seemingly no "right" choice. Gena Showalter is brilliant at creating sexual tension and intensity between the characters. There were moments when I had to take a deep breath because of how steamy it was getting. I highly recommend this series to paranormal romance fans. The steam factor is high and so is the suspense. I cannot wait to get my hands on the next book, The Darkest Pleasure.

You can also read this review on my blog. This review applies to the entire Series of Unfortunate Events. Never has such a miserable tale of the depressing disasters that follow the lives of three unfortunate orphans been so charmingly absurd and enjoyable to read. Though the books are intended for an MG audience, the satirical humour spouted by narrator Lemony Snicket and more mature themes of moral complexity in the later books can be appreciated by an older audience. The books are incredibly formulaic and repetitive (essentially the orphans are passed off to a new guardian each book, Count Olaf shows up in a new disguise and attempts to steal the Baudelaire fortune, and the orphans use their smarts and talents to get away from him), but the repetitiveness had a more familial and calming effect on me rather than boring me. I read the series in its entirety via audiobook, narrated by inimitable Tim Curry (except for books 3-5 which are narrated by Lemony Snicket himself). And I can't think of two people more suited to the narration of the gothic tones combined with the general absurdity of the stories presented in A Series of Unfortunate Events. If you're looking to try out the series for yourself or want to do a reread but don't feel like you have the time to fit all 13 books into your reading lineup, I would highly recommend checking out the series on audio. Finally, let's talk about the Netflix TV Show. I can't speak about the movie adaptation starring Jim Carrey that was released in 2004 as I never saw it, but I understand it was not at all well received. However, I have seen the first season of the Netflix adaptation, starring Neil Patrick Harris and covering the first four books, and I am happy to report that it is most excellently done. It took me a few episodes to get into the rhythm of the story and characters, but once it hits its stride the show captures the gothic tone and absurdist themes of the books perfectly and is pretty faithful. Once again, this is proof positive that having the original author of the books (Lemony Snicket/Daniel Handler) handle the script of the movie/TV show is the best way of ensuring that the adaptation is a good one.

2.5 stars. Despite my rating, I did like this book. While the story is set in a very typical fantasy world without much to make it stand out, the characters are solid, and I found myself rooting for Celaena on more than one occasion. She's much more confident and even cocky than some of the YA heroines I've encountered in recent memory, and while it seems this turned some people off, I loved it. The girl's beautiful, and she knows it. She's also strong, and she knows it. She still has believable moments of self-doubt, and she struggles through that and comes out on the other side, flexing her biceps for the crowd. You go girl. Chaol and Dorian were also enjoyable, though I'd be lying if I said Dorian didn't feel like a familiar character. He's far from the first Bad Boy with a Heart of Gold in a novel with a significant romantic plot, and at first I found his scenes painfully annoying. By the end, I liked him more. It's interesting to see the parts of him that shine through as he falls in love, though I prefer to think that the changes were not REAL changes, but simply a reflection of him growing up. He acknowledges that the women he hooks up with before meeting Celaena are using him as much as he's using them, and Maas does a good job of showing us his evolution as he decides that those relationships aren't what he wants for himself forever. But I'm intrigued to see if she'll take him right back there in the next book, now that Celaena has hung him out to dry. Chaol is...well, he's the best friend. Another cliche, yes, but that's the cliche I prefer, so I give him an unfair advantage. I took less of an issue with his relationship with Celaena and more of an issue with his strange incompetence. When he brings Celaena to look at one of the murder victims, she makes observations that -- in my mind -- a person of Chaol's position should've also made. I think many people probably looked at that scene and got annoyed with Celaena for being a know-it-all, but for me, it's Chaol who deserves the criticism here. How am I supposed to believe he's the Captain of the Guard if he doesn't pay attention to details like that, despite being the head investigator? And how the hell does he examine every crime scene and not give the Wyrdmarks a second thought? Sure, maybe he wouldn't have been able to examine them openly because of the ban on magic, but he didn't even NOTICE them? I have a hard time buying that. It seems like this was a matter of Maas trying very hard to make the plot work around the characters. After all, if Chaol had noticed the marks, that would've added a whole new dimension to Celaena's investigation. And that wasn't the only plot point that took me out of Maas' world. I'm always bothered when I see a world that worships a female goddess and yet has the same patriarchal system we're used to seeing in high fantasy novels and fairy tales. Does not compute. If everyone worshipped a woman, and if even the priestesses are women, how are women not given more power in society? I have practice overlooking this while reading other books, so it didn't spoil the story for me, but it's worth thinking about. And lastly, why do we have a heroine who suspects her closest friend of attacking champions when the true identity of the attacker is painfully obvious? This was a real weak point in the arc of the story. I still enjoyed this book, and I wasn't going into it expecting to be thrown off by a plot twist, so this wasn't particularly upsetting. But once again, this seemed like Maas making her characters fit uncomfortably into the Plot Box when letting them be themselves would've made for a more believable reveal moment, even if it wasn't such a big reveal. I've heard the series gets better as it goes on, and I definitely like the characters enough to invest more time in them, so I'm planning on continuing with the next book.

On the plus side, this book has made me really want to read Carry On!

I really enjoyed turning over many of the questions this book raises about spirituality and about humanity's place in the universe, and the exploration of unintended consequences. There is a lot of good food for thought here and many different perspectives. I like that this book does not take sides between belief and unbelief, between the goodness of God and the chaos of the universe. That said, I had some problems with this story. It was a little dated, having been written about 20 years ago and taking place in a future only a couple of years from now, but that was not a huge obstacle. What really struck me as odd was the way in which the characters went off on a mission of first contact without giving much thought to the effect of their presence on an alien race. In a different fictional universe it would be easy to cry, "but what about the prime directive?" Even in The Sparrow's universe, however, it is surprising that trained missionaries and anthropologists don't seem to consider this question very deeply. I also found that the treatment given to Father Emilio on his return didn't really ring true. Not to say that there aren't judgmental people in the world or even in the church, but I found it surprising that so few were interested in his side of the story, or even considered the possibility that there was another side of the story to be heard. In the end, it was this kind of broad assumption throughout the book, this type of unquestioned premise that prevents me from giving 5 stars.

The family that was hosting turned out to be on the Silver-Bloods side, and they were murdering the Conclave by the masses. It turns out that Mimi's suspicions about Kingsley were false, that he was not a traitor as she thought. Meanwhile, a giant force is stirring. It turns out that in Rio de Janeiro , under Christ the Redeemer's statue, a Silver-Blood called Leviathan is attempting to break out of his prison. Lawrence, Oliver, Schuyler, and Bliss try to stop a Silver-Blood. Schuyler takes her sword and tries to stab it, but misses. Lawrence kills it, but ends up getting killed himself. The Silver-Blood that is killed turns out to be Dylan, but it was an illusion to get Dylan killed. He was only being controlled by Silver-Bloods. The real Silver-Blood turns out to be Bliss, and she was the one that killed Aggie and the Conclave and set their house on fire, and much more, which is why she was getting black-outs. She thinks that the man in the white-suit is probably Lucifer, telling her what to do

** spoiler alert ** I enjoyed this book. It dragged once or twice but mostly kept me engaged until the end. It is very much "hard" science fiction in the classic vein whereby the science is the star, not the characters. And there are some really great ideas and scenes here, such as the nature of the "lock" that will stop all human technological progress, and the destruction of the ship. Unfortunately I had a few issues that keep it from being a truly great example of the genre in my mind. The biggest by far is the presentation of the "Three Body" video game that takes up much of the middle portion of the book. This whole section made little sense to me. Sometimes it's implied that the other players in the game are NPCs, and in a contradictory fashion sometimes it's implied they are actual humans, but they don't really behave like either. Moreso, it's not really clear to me why this game would be considered so challenging or mind-blowing, since the main "mystery" behind it is pretty simple and there didn't seem to be anything required of the player after this mystery is solved in order to progress (GameFAQs would have a field day with it). Likewise, there's a lot of pages both within the game and without devoted to various methods of solving the three body problem, but as is clearly explained later, this is all completely irrelevant because the Trisolarians have to leave because their planet is going to be destroyed someday by one of its suns no matter what. So why does the scientist who is going to solve the problem (which they've also claimed to have proved is unsolvable) need to be killed? I don't get it. Finally, the international publication of this book was somewhat botched as the editor chose to include a spoiler in the back cover copy. I don't know if this blurb was originally in the Chinese edition, but either way it's clear from the way the text is written that the fact that aliens are involved in the narrative is not meant to be revealed until nearly the second half of the book. It's debatable how necessary this is or to what extent it ruins the book as a whole, but in my mind knowing something I'm not supposed to for a full half of the story definitely counts as subtracting from it.
