This and other reviews can be found at herbookstacks. This is seriously a long time coming. And I can't believe I am actually saying that this is my review for THE BECOMING OF NOAH SHAW. That it is possible that there is a sequel to the Mara Dyer Trilogy. I find the idea of it absolutely ridiculous but I can't stop my hands from typing out about this because this is seriously insane. Okay, enough rambling. Let's get down to business here and get into it already. Can I talk about how beautiful this cover is? I was an enormous fan of design behind Mara Dyer, but I kind of love this aesthetic even more. I'm not sure what it is about it that I love - but I think it's embers. It's got this great color contrast and really pops off the cover. Plus, I love that it has a different spirit and tone that the Mara Dyer books had. And when I think about it, I feel as though those books were colder and dissonant (like Mara!) and this cover is warm and fierce and like a crashing crescendo of stringed instruments roaring against the large open spaces of the orchestra halls. It's just pretty beautiful. This book is dark. It is super dark and intense and vicious and visceral and all of these things that I was blown away by - Michelle Hodkin is a brilliant storyteller. There is no doubt about that. I felt like I was beig twisted and thrown about - feeling one emotion after another. But I can guarantee that felt shocked and awed through much of the book and xouldnnot believe when things were happening. I will say that I have read other people's thoughts about this book and have heard them say that nothing really happens in this book. I think a lot does. Just because something isn't FIGURED OUT and there are no real answers to ease a reader into the ending of it doesn't mean that nothing has happened. Sure, nothing is solved, but do not be mistaken that that book has a lot going on. I didn't think that Michelle Hodkin could DO MORE with world. At least not much more but she continues where she left off with RETRIBUTION and it is a wild ride. Also, I think Hodkin has always been one of those authors that has straddled the line between young and new adult. There are some rather racy scenes that happen. Even before thirty and I was fanning my face. I am a huge sucker for those sort of scenes and you obviously know that it's gotta do with Mara and Noah and those two are like two sticks rubbing on kindle to start a fire and once it starts, it burns. I am a fan of those sort of scenes and I know that there is definitely sexual undertones to the entire story, especially when it comes to Noah talking about Mara. It won't be everyone's cup of tea and I'm sure people will think it's inappropriate, but I think Michelle does a great job in finessing those undertones in. I will say that everyone is insanely suspicious to me as a character. Something begins happening to other carriers and everyone seems like a suspect, especially Mara. I think that the one issue I had with the POV being Noah's was that the autonomy of other characters, like Mara, suffered. I was suddenly asking who the heck she was and where the girl from the Mara Dyer trilogy was. I became suspicious with her and if she was behind things that were happening. I started distrusting Jamie because of his own motives and Noah's suspicions regarding him. And then I started to dislike Jamie. I was not a huge fan of his in the original trilogy and I feel like the only reason I liked him was that was he a support system for Mara. There are definitely some new characters to meet. And some old ones come back. I love that Michelle Hodkin has expanded to more characters because it just means more characters to like, but then it also means more characters to hate and no one wants that. I mean, there were some characters that I was really, really disliking (LEO!). I was delighted to see Daniel again in the story and I wish that there was even more of him. He is such a great character. It's hard to imagine regularity when the story is saturated with these uniquely-powered characters. And I love that Daniel is the character that grounds the rest of the story to the real world. And even more, I love that he is a rather loyal confidant to Noah, who I think really needs one. I would have loved to see more of him, but he does go through betrayal in this book and it HURTS. Oh, does it hurt. To be quite honest, as I'm writing this, I really feel like The Shaw Confessions are giving me ORPHAN BLACK vibes. It's sultry, dangerous, high-adrenaline, intense, mystery. You know. It's kind of crazy. I will say that the ending - I did not expect that ending. It kind of blew me out of the water because it was NOT what I saw coming at all. I knew that there would not be any clean and tied up ends. It would be messy and sad and visceral and AHHHH. But oh my gosh. I really don't want to spoil it, but let us just say that Noah meets someone from the past - someone that we have all met before and wondered about since she was introduced into the books... And guys, I am not ready for The Shaw Confessions #2. I am not.

Sickly sweet; attempts to pander to the "strong female protagonist of middle-grade fiction" genre and bugged the heck out of me. Sooooooo booooooooring and predictable. I would've personally killed some of the characters in order to read an amusing scene or two.

I love how the story is told from the past the present. I can see the Nell transform from a young, innocent girl into woman. With Kyle, she learn to fall in love and explore everything for the first time but when Kyle died, Nell blame herself for what happened to Kyle. During Kyle's funeral, Nell met Colton, Kyle's older brother for the first time and felt something between them which she denies because she feels guilty of what happened to Kyle. Two years later, both Nell and Colton met again in New York. That's when Colton helped Nell to let herself be hurt and broken so she'll let go of the past. I really wished Kyle didn't die. I'm a sucker for first love stories...especially if they started out from best friend. I really thought Nell and Kyle were match-made in heaven with the birthday two days apart, same age, same birth hospital, neighbors and best friend. So when Kyle died, my heart shattered just like Nell's. When Colton appears, I was thinking..."There's no way I'm gonna like this older brother taking over love thing with Nell! ", but hey....I was wrong. I love how Colton break the walls around Nell's heart, make her try letting go of her guilt and make her believe whatever happened isn't her fault. Colton knows this because he went through something similar before. The relationship between Colton and Nell is way more mature than what Nell and Kyle had though.
The plot is expected, but this is probably the best Karina Halle's contemporary I've ever read.

DNF @ 56% Slow. That is the one word I have for this book. I kept reading it on and off for a period of four months in hoping that maybe the pace will actually pick up. However, I just can't do it anymore. I'm not wasting any more time in putting in an effort to read this book. I really did want to love it-- I love Cassandra Clare's Infernal Devices Trilogy, and I love reading books set in Victorian and Regency period England in general, but I am positive that comparisons and general setting interest will not get me to finish this. Slow Pacing. It takes forever for anything to actually happen in the book. It takes about a third of the book for our main character, Helen, to start diving into the shadows of London that the premise promises. Heck, it takes 70 pages for her "debut presentation to the royal court of George III" to even take place, and the premise states that the story launches on the eve of it. Slow Writing. Okay, I really want to continue on with using the word slow here, and slow writing just sounds like another way to say slow pacing, but allow me to elaborate. Mrs. Goodman's writing just does not allow me to feel anything. I do not feel any romantic tension between Helen and Lord Carlton (which I think I was supposed to be swooning for). I did not feel concerned that the maid does go missing. I did not feel a thrill at, well, really anything. If something actually happens it is all explained so plainly I feel as if I am reading an encyclopedia. And I'm pretty sure we can all say that the task of reading an encyclopedia would be not be thrilling. Needless to say I am not going to slowly force myself through this book anymore.
I'd be hard pressed to come up with anything I liked about this. I'm really tired of fat as a metaphor for insulated and unhappy.

For the full review, click here Thank you to Macmillan- Tor/Forge for sending me an advance copy of The Nightmare Affair through NetGalley. In no way did this affect my opinion of the book. NOTE: Quotations were taken from the ARC and may not be the same in the final published copy. A fresh take on the genre of young adult paranormal fantasy, I must say that I enjoyed the fact that the novel focused on the lesser known mythical creatures, e.g. Sirens and Nightmares, rather than the cliched vampire or werewolf. With no build up, from the start of the novel, we're plunged straight into the action, with Dusty attempting to dream-feed off of her former classmate, Eli Booker. Within his dream, she finds herself looking at the dead body of one of her classmates. And when the classmate actually does turn up dead, Dusty is told that she is a dream-seer- a Nightmare who can predict the future by entering the dreams of a certain partner (in this case, Eli). One aspect of the book that I really enjoyed was all the lore backing up the main story, i.e. the background to Nightmares, the Keepers, the Will- it was obviously well thought out and well written, with all the questions that I would have had about these things being fully explored. I also quite enjoyed the light humour scattered throughout the novel. Some examples from early in the book: Some stories said that Nightmares were demons (not true), while others said they were "hags", as in scary old women who lived in the forest and abducted lost kids to cook for supper (more true, although I didn't recommend saying so to my mother). "I didn't do anything wrong. I swear." He grunted. "Liked I've never heard that before. Funny, but I expected a little more originality from Moira's daughter." "Yeah, well, the dog ate my notebook with all my good excuses." Sidenote: I love how so many books these days take a dig at Twilight&Co. Magickind started rumors about themselves in the ordinary world all the time, the latest example being the ordinary pop culture obsession with vampires as misunderstood victims who'd rather kiss a human than kill one. So not true. All the characters were well developed by Arnett, particularly Dusty (really interesting nickname by the way). Both love interests, Eli and Paul, were relatively well developed, and I could see Dusty connecting to both characters rather than the superficial instalove many novels include. One thing I didn't enjoy so much was Eli dating the bitch of the book- why does this happen so often in Young Adult? A minor issue that I had was that some sections were a bit cliched, and the writing style at times seemed as if it would better suit a younger audience, but it wasn't so much so that I found it annoying or boring. The scene at the climax of the novel was pretty damn epic- action packed and dramatic, it was exactly the sort of scene needed after the skillful build-up of suspense and tension throughout the book. Unfortunately, I do have to say that I predicted some of the "big twist", but some parts were completely unexpected, so, well played, Arnett, well played. The Nightmare Affair is definitely an impressive start to the author's career. For more reviews, check out my blog: http://lookingforthepanacea.blogspot....

As I walked to my car, I said good-bye to Emi, the girl who begrudgingly went to frat parties and football games; the girl who pretended like everything was always okay while unenthusiastically teaching Intro to Writing classes; the girl with no past; the girl who wasn't real and didn't exist. Trigger Warning: Abuse Swear on This Life was not my favorite New Adult novel, and even though I was expecting to like it, I had lots of problems with it. The only reason why I bought it was because my friend Amber wrote a positive and wonderful review about it, giving me high hopes and expectations of it, while my friend Mikee didn't enjoy it as much. I was hoping I would like it, since I normally enjoy reading NA novels I always decide to pick up, surprisingly. I was also in the mood for a sweet and fast-paced contemporary, so I was hoping this was it. It was fast-paced, sweet and cute at times, depressing and sad other times, but it wasn't the best. I haven't read Renee's other books, so I'm not very fond with her writing and familiar with her taste, but that didn't change much from the way I looked at this book. Now, I wish I read her previous books before. I always do. For some reason I haven't been enjoying the recent contemporaries I've bought or checked out, and this one was no different. Swear on This Life is pretty much a novel about a novel. Emiline, the protagonist in this novel, is a writer who graduated and got her masters degree in creative writing, going to a University in San Diego and trying to full-fill her dreams. The problem she has is that she isn't able to find her voice and see what the problem is, trying to write something and accomplish it. It's like she never was made to become a writer before and can't figure out what to write of, getting her friends and professors ideas but not taking them for granted. One day, her friend Cara, who is a successful writer and gave Emiline an idea that wasn't taken, lets her borrow a book that she fell in love with immediately. It's a bestselling debut novel that has become one of the best and most gifted literary works out there, being sold to many people and leaving them shocked as to how this story fit in. Emiline has never heard of this book called All the Roads Between, but as soon as Cara lets her borrow the novel and Emiline reads the first line, finishing the first and second paragraph, Emiline is shocked and notices there isn't something right about this. The reason she is so drawn into this novel and knows what it is about is because the novel is about her, about her past and how she had to suffer with her unloving mother, abusive father, and first lover that somehow faded away from her life and left her alone. As she is reading this, she realizes this book was written by her first love; the boy that left her alone and promised to stay with her even when he didn't; the boy she fell in love with; her childhood friend; the boy that became her first and best friend; the boy she told everything to, Jason Colbertson. He doesn't go by that name for some reason, now going by and being known as J. Colby, but he's still the same Jason, the same Jase Emiline grew up with. Now, what Emilie wants is to finish this book and see where it ends to, and find Jase and see why he wrote this novel about her past, and in her perspective. Even with her past being the main key, J. Colby even added more details and changes a lot of the scenes, making them more dramatic and realistic. And as Emiline is reading this novel as time passes, she realizes there is a reason Jase wrote it in her perspective, and realizes the message it was supposed to carry and deliver. Like I said, Swear on This Life wasn't a big hit for me. Emiline is Emerson, Emerson is Emiline. Emerson is the fictional name of Emiline in All the Roads Between, making Jase Jackson, and Jackson Jase. Even though this whole story is about the novel Jase wrote, I felt like there was no point in it. I really didn't understand the whole reason for writing a book about a childhood friend's past after he left her, alone. I enjoyed the beginning of it, but then I was annoyed with the fact that the whole story is about Emiline's past and I couldn't even figure out what the whole story was really about. I mean, I know what it's about, I mean I didn't get the point of it. I didn't understand why this wasn't all about Emiline and her current and future life, but instead about her past and bringing back past and horrible memories. I also didn't understand why Emiline decided to even read the book after crying when she finished the first page. Emiline is our protagonist, but so is Emerson. They felt like different people, even when both are the same. My problem was how Em acted as she was growing up. Even as she was growing up and becoming a woman, I hated how she took it really far and didn't even bother acting like a child anymore. I also hated how she took all this adult life to a whole other level and didn't even want to consider hanging out with Jax anymore as "playing." I don't get it, you're only 13 and you're already freaking out because your breasts are growing, your period started, your hips are getting wider, and your crush is getting cuter. Well, according to the novel and to Jason's writing, that's how it went. It really bugged me how she was changing so much and sometimes she would want to be with Jase but other times she would push him away. Also, what was she doing being 15 years old and already having her first love touching her and running his thumb over her nipple? Wait, it is 2016 so I guess that's normal.... She was strong in both, the past and present, but she wasn't my favorite. She cried a lot, but I understood that because of her past. The reason they were different to me was because I was able to know more about Emerson than Emiline. The fictional characters had more details to explain that the realistic ones, not knowing anything about them except for where they are and what they were doing. As to our other character, Jase, I didn't swoon over him. Sure, he was sweet and caring, but sometimes I didn't understand him and/or his personality and attitude. He went from caring about Em to trying to push her away because of the things that were happening in his life, but sometimes I wished he didn't do that because she was the only one who understood him and was available to help him. I hated some of his decisions and I hated the way Jason wrote the book in Em's point of view, leaving a lot of specific details out and changing everything. Jason and Jackson were different people as well, in the past and present life. Even though I couldn't relate to any of the characters and can't see this in my life, I could see Em having trouble with her mother and stepping up to her mother after all those years. She even was able to forgive both of them after everything that happened, and I was actually glad and proud. I did cry when her father punched her, yanked her hair, kicked her, and slapped her, even when he called her a slut because like dude, I can only imagine that. I felt really bad for her but I was glad Jax came and literally saved her so that was good. I admit, I liked their relationship more than reading only about Em, but again, I wasn't feeling any OTP feels or swooning over them, crying and rooting for them. In the past, their relationship started off as kids hating each other. Suddenly, Jax is that loving and cute kid who apologizes to the girl he called medusa because of her horrifying hair, and suddenly growing up with her and becoming her best friend. As time passed, they both turned 15 and things changed. Ever since Jax's brother, Brian, died, Jax wasn't the same. He was growing and becoming the man he was made to be, growing and becoming stronger. He was still sweet, but still different than the young boy he was. People change, I know that, so I was okay with the change he made, but then at the same time I hated it. He had his own past to deal with, including an unloving father that left his brother and him with his mother, and an alcoholic mother who became a bitch to him after Brian died. His past was similar to Em's, except her mother left and his father became the abusive, unloving, rude, and alcoholic father that calls his daughter a slut and whore and blames her mother for it. Because of that, they both had their similarities and were able to trust each other, tell each other everything and be open about it. The relationship and romance wasn't my favorite thing about this. Nothing really was. It didn't feel real, only because they were kids who fell in love as they were growing up and nothing felt real. I didn't feel connected to them and didn't feel any romance between, not even in the end. Even though they loved each other, they were only high school sweethearts having sex. It's New Adult, but it's not at the same time. When both are adults, they don't have any sweet moments. All they do is talk and make up, but as they're teenagers, they're having sex and hiding. It felt like they didn't know what love meant at a young age, and after the end of All the Roads Between, it finally felt like something. There was finally something shown between both and I wished there were more moments of them being together when they were old and adults, but Jase had to change it all up and end it with them being 50 and over. Now when we come to discussing Emiline and Jason, there really isn't much to talk and discuss. They hadn't seen each other for 12 years, and suddenly they see each other and they start hanging out, communicating, and even start a relationship. I didn't get it, and I didn't like it. I hated how Em still loved him even when he left her and was the reason for her therapy sessions. She was trying to get over him and bringing past memories in her therapy while he was writing a novel about her novel and not giving her credit. Other than that, he was with other girls and even when he didn't feel the word "love" in them and didn't feel like he was in love with them, I still hated him for what he did without even getting her permission. I also hated her for forgiving him so quickly and not being so pissed off about it. Their past was more enjoyable and a lot better to read from, since they had an actual relationship, whereas their present relationship or whatever they had didn't feel real. Another thing I did not like was the whole Trevor and love-triangle thing. I wished she wasn't into Jax and didn't admit it to him after dating him for 7 years. First off, they have been dating for 7 years. After all those 7 years, the sad thing is that they both don't know much, anything really, about each other and have never been open to each other. Even with that, they have never said I love you to each other which was even more sad to read about. A 7-year relationship where secrets were kept and truths were hidden, nothing felt real between them, even more fake and boring than Jason and Emiline. They didn't feel like a happy couple and I wished they broke up in the beginning. I'm not only blaming Trevor, Emiline was the bitchy girlfriend as well. She would ask for his advice and wanted to know what he thought of her work, and even asked for his honesty. As he gave her his honesty and personal thoughts about her work, she got mad and decided to go for a run because she was all mad and hated him for saying that. Well, if you didn't want him to be honest and instead lie about it, why didn't you just ask? I hated their relationship more and I wished there was more background between them. Also, I couldn't believe she would always say "I love you" to him right after she said she still had feeling for Jase, and then suddenly had to say she would think about their relationship and see what she thinks about it. Oh boy. Overall, this wasn't much of a disappointment but it's my first NA novel that I did not enjoy thoroughly. I hated the past and present times and I wished it was only told either in the past of present, finding a way to make up for the way Em found out. If that didn't make sense, I just wished there was a better way of writing the relationship between Emerson (Emiline) and Jax (Jason). It upsets me to not like this one because I really did enjoy the beginning of it, and most of the middle, but then it got to the part where Em reunited with Jase, feeling things because she still felt in love with him and would pretend she wouldn't want to kiss him when he wanted to kiss her because she had a boyfriend. I'll probably still pick up Renee's other works and future novels, but it upsets me knowing this one was a drag. It's always new novels that are disappointing and it's so upsetting because you can go from loving an author and considering them your favorite, to not knowing what to think about them and questioning yourself why you enjoyed their previous work.

I received this advance copy from NetGalley in exchange for an honest review. Yes! Thank you David Shafer for keeping me up all night. The last book that caused me to lose a night of sleep was Dave Egger's The Circle. Like The Circle, Whiskey Tango Foxtrot contains an interesting fight against a conspiracy to own the internet and take over the world. Sound a little far fetched? What makes this book so enjoyable it the utter plausibility of it. You can't have a conspiracy to take over the world with the information super highway without a dysfunctional group of characters that do all they can to stop it. The group is comprised of old school buddies Mark, Leila and Leo. I feel in love instantly with Leila, a sharp witted do-good-er who works for the nonprofit entity "Helping Hands". Mark and Leo are also engaging interesting characters who are stressed out and hyper intelligent. I wanted to join forces with them to take down The Committee, the super-force comprised of industry and media leaders who has plans to privatize the news, the publishing industry, and all other social media. This book is the intelligent person's thriller which makes you think without having to think too hard. The characters are deeply realized and the central espionage plot is current and believable. The only thing that could have made this book better for me would have been some gaming and pop culture references.

How many people with similar names can you tolerate in a story? Well, I get totally lost whenever I pick this book. Every time a character is mentioned, I have to stop for a minute to figure out who exactly he is and why he is doing whatever he is doing. Do you, my dear reader, wonder why?? Because they all have same names. Its a story of many generations of the strangest of families living in a town called Macondo in "the world that was so recent that many things lacked names, and in order to indicate them it was necessary to point." So this family got hold of just two names Arcadio and Aureliano and let them suffice for generations to come. And the children came from so many various sources that it becomes really hard to keep track. Likewise, so many events keep occurring in such abrupt fashion in it that its mind-boggling to remember the sequence. About the story: it is interesting and funny and strange. It's my first encounter with Magic Realism, a genre where magic elements are a natural part in an otherwise mundane, realistic environment. Things are just going the normal way, well as normal as this strange family can manage, and then suddenly things start flying, people come back from death, at one time, the whole town suffers from insomnia and when they have been awake for months or may be years and have started losing their memory, suddenly they come back to normal. So I am still reading it, rather slowly. But honestly, I cannot make any sense of events and cannot tell whether the Arcadio and Aureliano being mentioned are son or grandson or great-grandson of the original Arcadio.

You know who would like this book? Lit majors who went to a fancy private university in Paris. ;) Lookn' right at'cha, Caite Dolan-Leach. (I'm just guessing she's a lit major, the way this book reads.) I guess I can't be overly critical, because she did do a good job painting her picture. But the writing style is so off-putting, and the story so uninteresting that I can't muster more than two stars for this novel. Generally, I really enjoy word play and having fun with language. I was hoping for a more clever use of this based on the promise of the book's title, blurb on the back, and general set-up in the beginning of the book. There's a lot of alliteration, a kinda half-baked promise of a word game that seems conveniently placed throughout the whole "mystery" aspect... I don't know. It just didn't come together for me. I didn't find the word play interesting enough. It didn't tie in seamlessly with the suspense portion of the novel. It was a gimmick. Something that author clearly found interesting and did her best to build a story around. The author spent a whole ton of time on thesaurus.com, but that doesn't make for clever wordplay. It makes for writing that reads unnaturally, as you trip over uncommon terms and phrases every other sentence for no reason whatsoever. Speaking of tripping over stuff, I found many Dolan-Leache's references unclear and ill-placed in a novel that's supposed to be a suspense. Again, the story read like it was written for a specific audience. Am I the only one who didn't know what Oulipo is? Is "constrained writing" a common term among casual readers who didn't specifically study literature and literary devices? Maybe I'm just a moron, but I had to stop and take some time to look both of these up. And then, after presenting all this, the flippin' author didn't even follow any interesting constraints in her own writing! I mean, yeah, there's the stupid word game that was baaaarely interesting nor did it have any meaningful place in this story other than to give the illusion of clever writing. There was so much missed opportunity for creating all sorts of word games throughout the novel. Maybe I missed them? IDK. I went back and read through all the letters and noticed just the alliteration. The important chapters followed an alphabetical order. What else was there? I wish there were more fun linguistic puzzles for the reader to solve. Maybe they're there and if I missed them please someone point them out to me. Other than the annoying writing style, there wasn't much else I really noticed about this book. The characters are all horrible people. Including the protagonist. They lead miserable lives and have shallow, unhappy relationships with each other. They never grow, they never develop, they're all petulant, immature, uninteresting people. I have no idea why Wyatt loves Ava, because she's awful. But he does. It's just stated like, "Yep, he's always been in love with her. Whatever. Accept it. This is the love story of the book, so you gotta believe this feelings part of it." There's no complexity to the characters or any of their interpersonal relationships. I don't really get the driving force behind why a common reader would enjoy this book. But it's got a lot of good reviews so far. It's pretty new though, so it may all be downhill from here. I suggest you skip this one.

Flow, and the full story, Grip, are standalones featuring two characters that are present in Kennedy Ryan's Soul Series. Sometimes sparks catch and an inferno builds rapidly, and there's nothing we can do about it except watch it and feel the heat. 3.5 stars I was given a copy of Delicate Monsters in exchange for an honest review. Many thanks to St Martins Griffin and Netgalley. A copy of this review is also on my blog: www.bookblogbird.weebly.com This was not a comfortable read. Bizarre and compelling, but definitely not comfortable. Delicate Monsters is written from three perspectives: those of Sadie, Emerson and Miles, three disturbed teenagers whose lives intersect and whose fates seem intertwined. Sadie Su has just been kicked out of boarding school for almost killing a fellow student. She returns to her family's vineyard in Sonoma and enrolls at the local high school where she meets Emerson, a boy she used to know as a child, and his brother Miles. Sadie is a psychopath. Completely emotionally detached from those around her, she doesn't care what people think about her, she has no empathy whatsoever, she almost killed a fellow student at her old school, she has no trouble lying to get what she wants and doesn't feel remorse, shame or guilt. Sadie wandered out to the main road and waited for cars to pass so that she could throw rocks at them. She does have some small redemption at the end, but other than this she is terrifying and her emotional vacuum meant that I didn't connect with her as a character. I was always curious to see what she'd do next, but ultimately she could have lived or died and I wouldn't have cared either way. Actually, scrub that: I just wanted her to die so that the world could be rid of such a horrible person! Emerson displays very disturbing tendencies as well. Arguably, his behaviour resulted in some part from the death of his father but not every child who loses a parent does the kinds of things he did. When he was ten, he cut the legs off a frog and masturbated as he watched it die on the ground. As an older teen, he gets the girl he is seeing to lay on the floor and pretend to be dead so he can do the same thing. He drink drives, he's racist and he doesn't care that his brother is being beaten by the school's homophobic bullies. Like Sadie, I was torn between not caring what happened to him and wanting him to meet a sticky end. Delicate Monsters left me wondering if the author has something against the townspeople of Sonoma. Seriously, there's only one person in the whole book who seems to have any redeeming features - May - and at times it just seems like she's there to act as a foil to the unpleasantness of all the other characters! Even poor Miles, who suffers under the weight of the visions he sees and is bullied mercilessly, saw visions of the Boston marathon bombing and the Japanese tsunami and let it all play out without attempting to warn anyone. People kept dying and people kept suffering, even when he knew about it ahead of time. Delicate Monsters plays out kind of like a soap opera, or The Jeremy Kyle Show. The writing is more graceful, but you still get the sense of watching awful people doing horrible things and you can't quite bring yourself to look away. It's completely compelling and leaves you wanting to take a shower afterwards. I have to say, I didn't enjoy reading Delicate Monsters (and I have a feeling that was the author's intention) but I didn't seem to be able to put it down either. I'd recommend this book for anyone who likes their YA very dark indeed.

A weird read, not quite sure what to make of it. Big Machine has a brilliant set up: a group of black Americans, all older and with pretty awful pasts, are ?randomly? brought to work in a strange library, where it slowly becomes apparent that they are to become paranormal investigators. Only, this is a literary novel using genre set up so nothing goes anything like you might expect (which is a bit of a shame for this genre reader as I liked the way it looked to be going, and we abandoned the group of interesting women very quickly to focus on the sole bloke). It becomes mostly a book about faith and doubt (doubt is the big machine of the title) where the supernatural elements are in play with human atrocities: religious murder cult, serial killer torturing a woman to death, domestic terrorism, as well as cats that eat your soul and weird devil thingies. In particular the handling of race in this book is brutal and we're left in no doubt about the pervasiveness of US racism and the effects on black lives. As is the way with literary novels a lot of it is kind of shifting and uncertain and the ending is kind of open. Which is I suppose fair enough for a book about doubt, and doubtless (haha) intentional. But I felt like LaValle's recent The Ballad of Black Tom, a much more straightforward embracing of Lovecraftian fantasy, actually handled a lot of these themes much more deftly and subtly while delivering a more satisfying whole at novella length. Then again the author's had the best part of a decade to hone his craft since then. An intriguing read and very well written, if not entirely satisfying to me, but that probably had a fair bit to do with my expectations anyway, she says doubtfully.

Still, I liked Watts' voice so much that I would give the next book a read.

I've been in a reading slump lately. The only books I've been reading are the ones that have been assigned in my English classes. It's been like this for the past six months. And it kind of sucks, but at the same time I had accepted it. However, I got this book in a giveaway that I entered mostly for the promise of makeup. It sat on my bookshelf for the longest time, taunting me with its pretty cover. So, during finals, when I should have been studying but didn't, I picked up The Wangs vs. The World, hoping that maybe I could get out of my book slump. You know what? That was a horrendous idea. Because this book...well. I'll tell you about this book just a bit later. Still, it got me to actually write a review, which may be a greater feat in itself. The crux of the issue with The Wangs vs. the World is that all the characters...ALL the characters...are completely horrible people. And yes, there are some plots where this manages to work. I root for Frank Underwood even when he's murdering innocent people to further his political agenda. Daenerys is going on a bit of a power trip in GoT, but I will cheer for her the whole time. However, the Wangs being poor little rich folks who have to learn to be NORMAL while complaining the whole time is not a group of characters I can appreciate. Enough with the whining already! Grace complaining about every little thing is enough to drive me mad. Barbra too. And of course, Charles can't stop going over his failures time and time again. We get it. You made poor choices. Live with them. It seems at every point the characters have to bring up something that they hate about being Poor. They have to eat hotdogs now. The travesty. They sleep with sheets that aren't fully cotton. Dios mio. Enough with the casual racism! (Yes! It's pretty freaking bad, and it comes from the main character Charles Wang himself, so that's just great.) This is something I just didn't have a tolerance for. When a book has a whole paragraph dedicated to the ugliness of 'mixed' babies, then it's usually not a book worth reading. And the way that this racism from the characters is played off in the books definitely rubbed me the wrong way. Any remark of the sort is seen as a way to get the know the characters better. See their innermost thoughts. Show their flaws. Instead of doing that, it just made me uncomfortable while reading. Enough with the cheating and lying to your significant other! Looking at you, Saina, who cheats on her loving boyfriend with some jackass who previously cheated on her and then got the girl pregnant, causing him to leave Saina. I mean. Why. WHy. WHY. After the jackass leaves her, she gets back with loving boyfriend by lying to him. Of all the questionable decisions these characters made, this is the one that I really hated the most, because YOU SEE THE STUPIDITY PLAY OUT RIGHT ON THE PAGE. Not only that, there's never any resolution to this soap-worthy plotline. Loving Boyfriend never finds out that Saina lied to him; maybe the author didn't see it as a significant part of their relationship. However, I was cringing. Honorable mentions of wtf? moments in characterization: Andrew masturbating using ketchup (is this actually a thing? Please don't let this be a thing), Saina believing it was a good idea to photoshop pics of war refugees so that they look like magazine models, (and then not understanding why people were getting upset? ), Grace just being a grade-A brat for most of the book, Andrew throwing a hissy fit in college and yelling at his professor, and Charles being glad his wife died in a plane crash because that meant he didn't have to go through the trouble of divorcing her. Another problem was writing. It was meant to be very eloquent, a bit flowery at times. Once, I would have praised it because at a glance it seems like very intellectual and adult writing, and as a young teenager it would have intimidated me. It doesn't any more, though, and so I can admit I hated the writing style. The book's writing just seemed to take itself too seriously. Made it seem like a Very Deep Book when the book. Just. Isn't. I don't need the characters to wax philosophical while they pack their suitcases, or put on moisturizer. The high brow language was simply unnecessary at most times, and a bit boring as well. I read another review of this book saying the humor wasn't funny, and at first I disagreed. Not because this book was at any point funny, but because I honestly didn't recognize that some things that happened in this book were supposed to be jokes. It wasn't until I pondered over some of the weirder plot points in the book that I realized, yeah, some things were played for humor and just fell completely flat. For God's sake, there's at least three standup routines in this book, and even they aren't funny. There's a lot of crude humor. Aforementioned ketchup scene was, I think, supposed to give me a chuckle, but it just made me grossed out. Charles Wang talking about making his makeup empire with urea (urine) just made me side-eye my makeup cabinet a bit. There was nothing humorous in this book, try as it might. Finally, I got to the last page, and the book just...ended. It stopped without wrapping up certain plot points that very certainly could have and should have been resolved. Obviously, this should have annoyed me; but honestly, I didn't care anymore. I had spent too much time being bored to care that the ending was so lackluster. And maybe that's all I need to say to show you that this book just isn't worth your time.

This book was picked out for me by my significant other from a pile of romance novels. "Which one should I read next?" I said. "This one's about an earl," he said. "You've been reading a lot about dukes lately. Maybe an earl would be a nice change?" Thus far the only difference noted is that the earl has a younger half-brother who is a duke, so presumably another (the next?) book in the series can be about a duke. Anyway, this book is what it is and you know what you are going to get once you read the back cover. If you don't, you figure it out pretty quickly when you open the book and find yourself reading a sex scene. Between the hero and his mistress. He hies back to his house, musing on his Sad, Sad Story as he goes, and discovers his estranged wife (the heroine) waiting for him. We quickly learn that they are estranged because he discovered her in bed with his younger brother (not the duke, a different one) on their wedding night, which she agreed to only because the brother told her that this was the only way the earl wouldn't insist on consummating their marriage too soon, but he would totally chill out after he was mad for a bit so it would be fine. This struck her as a good idea. At this point, you probably have a pretty good idea of how the novel is going to go. Where has she been for the last couple of years? Well, running his estates wisely, of course. Why is she back in London? To save her beloved younger sister from marriage to an elderly roue, of course. The hero angsts over his inability to love - of course. We get a scene of the hero's mom in bed with an artist fifteen years her junior and musing on the fact that she's been in love with another man throughout her last two marriages, which made me want to read HER novel instead. That said, why one star? Because I just couldn't finish this thing. I kept getting distracted by other books and annoyed by minor details, and the authorial meddling was just too obvious - the hero kept ping-ponging between being wildly attracted to his wife and asking her for a divorce so he could marry his mistress, although he wasn't actually in love with the mistress. The villain of the book is, in fact, the mistress, who turns out to be totally insane and obsessively in love with the hero; I just can't deal with that plotline. For me to believe in a Happily Ever After, there would have to be an insane amount of groveling from the hero, which there wasn't (hey, guys, the mistress was really good at hiding her insanity, so how could he know?). Additionally, I really hate it when most/all of the prominent female characters in a romance besides the heroine are Evil with a capital E. Have the courage to believe that the heroine's awesomeness is sufficient in and of itself without needing comparators to demonstrate that she's "better" than them. I skimmed through the last few chapters, was thoroughly irritated by them, and did not force myself to read the rest of the book more thoroughly.

I think I also tried on Kindle before the last time and again, to no avail. But this last time, something changed. Once I got through some of the rougher parts, I was racing through the book and even finished it in record personal time. One thing that I did not enjoy about the Kindle version was that it hindered my enjoyment and visuals of the more visual things in this book. I didn't figure out how to zoom until the last 30% of the book and before them, had to squint and guess as to what they said or find a copy in a store and check them out. Anyways, back to my thoughts on the actual book. Like I previously said, the beginning to this one is a little rough. I wasn't too into the interviews and was unused to the style. But, I quickly eased into it and I think I most enjoyed the chats and pages that involved text woven within an image. This one was a step out of my reader comfort zone that I am so glad I took. Science fiction at its best! Beggars in Spain is set in the near future (year 2008, but it's written in 1992), where genetic engineering has advanced so much that it is now possible to genetically altered fetuses to possess certain qualities, including sleeplessness. Leisha, is one such genetically altered child, a Sleepless. As it so happens, her twin sister, Alice, is a Sleeper or a normal human child. What would happen in a family with two very distinct children growing up together. What would happen if you find out that you're a special child. Or that you and a select few of other Sleepless children have more brain power and more time to learn and accomplish things than other children, or even adult human beings? How would the other "normal" human beings react to this disruptive force in their daily lives, especially if they see that their economic abilities are being threatened by the Sleepless? On the other hand, what would Sleepless do? Do they try to integrate themselves better? Or do they think it's better for them to seclude themselves? The cast of characters are also very believable, especially, I believe, the main antagonists. I've read a few comments that argue the antagonists are unbelievably too extreme in their "badness". But, I would argue that if you narrow down the relationships that you have with like-minded individuals, then more likely than not, you would start to lean towards fundamentalism and/or extremism, because you live in a self-fulfilling bubble. One main reason why I don't give this book a 5-star rating, is because the way to story is being told. I believe in many places, the book feels flat to me. A lot of the events that occur in the book are told after the fact, through some other character telling the main characters of what had just happened. In other words, a lot of telling and not enough showing. However, it's still a very very good example of what science fiction can give to the world: several important questions to ponder on the subject of what it means to be human. I find it especially interesting that Nancy Kress decided to write this book based on economic and political points of view. I believe an analogy of what happens in the book, is currently happening in our real world. Does an economic principles of "from each according to his ability, to each according to his need" work best for all humanity? Or does a more socialism system (everything for the community) work better? The book tries to depict these two opposing economic systems as being unreasonable. For example, the Sleepless under Jennifer Sharifi tries to create a perfect Randian economic system, where only those who can contribute to the community is welcome. However, this leads to the question of what happens if one member of the community, for some reason, ceases to be able to contribute? On the other hand, the United States has set up a perverted, in my opinion, system of social democracy. In this system, 80% of the population are "livers", who get to enjoy the perks of being alive with free everything (free food, free "brainies" drugs, free parties). All they gotta do is vote to get the money. The remaining 20% are called the "donkeys". They are the ones who keep the economy and the government running. They do business. They do legal administration. They are the elected officials who are slightly more intelligent and wealthier than the "livers". However, one thing that I find it strange is that the "donkeys" seem content to want to run things for the "livers". I would argue than the "donkeys" would want to create a separate system of economy from the "livers". Another important issue discussed in this book is the issue of tolerance. How should we tolerate another group that is significantly different than the rest of us, especially if that group is also significantly better, more intelligent, and is more successful than us? Furthermore, this book also warns of the danger of fundamentalism, which echoes what's been going on in our real world very recently. Jennifer Sharifi, in her single-minded focus to protect "her community" from intolerance of the outside worlds, has, inadvertently, created an intolerant community herself. One last, but not least, key point of the book is the ideas that there is no perfect community, and that to affect change one must attempt small changes bit by bit. I would argue that in this book Ms. Kress argues that there's no perfect economic, judicial and political system that guarantees equality and personal freedom to all. Like when Leisha realizes that the Yagaiist economic system isn't broad enough to accommodate all people on earth, because there will still be "beggars in Spain" (interestingly, why choose a relatively developed country in Europe? Why not some random third-world country?). But, at the same time Ms. Kress also argues that complete social democratic system is prone to manipulation without strong check from the populace. This is ironically shown by Jennifer Sharifi herself. In her attempt to create the perfect Randian economic system, she inadvertently creates a community that values sameness. There's no details in the book, but I think the way it works for the Sleepless community is that each individual works on certain projects that can be sold or traded with the outside world. The money from these transactions is then pooled into a fund to be distributed back to the community. However, this system doesn't work, because Jennifer Sharifi tries to control the entire thing. Therefore, to prevent gross abuse of power, there needs to be strong check from the rest of the community members, which requires differences to arise, which means inequality. Thus, there is no perfect system, because humans change.

The second Xanth book is obviously a sequal 24 September 2011 This book doesn't actually seem to be much at all. It is a sequel to Spell for Cameleon and the second in the Xanth series. It appears that the Xanth series probably should be read in order because, unlike Discworld, it appears that it moves around the same characters (though considering that this is only the second book in the series that is probably a pretty tough call). In this book Bink has discovered his magical power, which is deflecting spells targetted at him. This is probably why it appeared that Bink did not have any magical ability. However, it seems that Anthony really didn't have an idea of a plot for this book as Bink is sent on a quest to discover the source of Xanth's magic so that he can be protected from any attacks on his life. Really, it does not seem to have any point at all, but then this is a series that is generally aimed at a younger audience (and indeed I did read it as a teenager, and I am unlikely to read it again, since there are a lot of other books out there that I would rather read). He does discover the source (after many varied encounters), and it is a demon with a strange name that is read as 'Xanth'. However the catch is that the demon is imprisoned against his will, and that Bink is thrown into a moral dilemma: keep the demon imprisoned and keep the magic in Xanth, or free the demon and destroy the magic. I guess this is something that we all face: do we act selfishly and hurt others, or do we act for the benefit of others and hurt ourselves. Bink decides on the second choice, however ends up convincing the demon to remain and keep the magic in Xanth. Things generally don't work out that way in life, but I guess all American (okay, most) books have to end with everything working out for everybody.

This book was like a combination of cheese wiz, marshmallows and ketchup. Not that those foods are never appetizing... but they are mostly empty calories and pretty unappetizing when consumed together. Plot summary: girl goes into fairy real to rescue stolen little brother and winds up uncovering frightening changes in the fairy world caused by the modern technologically-oriented society that is losing it's dreams/imagination. Basically this is a Labyrinth/Neverending story rip-off but without David Bowie or an awesome flying dog thing. Instead, we have a brooding Puck who makes half-hearted attempts at mischief (a totally missed opportunity for a cool character, in my opinion), an even more brooding fairy prince and an obnoxious half-human fairy princess, Meghan, who is inexplicably attractive to both brooding fairy men. She does have a couple of talents and those would be: never listening to what anyone tells her and repeatedly making bad deals with fairy creatures. The whole romance was lame with our brooding prince going from broodingly aloof to broodingly smitten in maybe 10 pages. Our heroine's heartstrings meanwhile seem to flutter for any character described as "gorgeous" that shows the remotest amount of interest in her. And seriously, if you have to specifically tell the reader the character is gorgeous (multiple times) you have done a poor job of characterization... Show, don't tell, people! Poor characterization is a big problem in this book -- all the characters are either completely flat or else come off feeling cartoonish in an unsuccessful attempt to differentiate them. I also found the pacing off. The story is almost episodic moving from one confrontation to another. The problem is since each event is written with the same intensity, they blend together so that after a while it's hard to care about what's coming next. And any moment that might possible have held some introspection/reflection/poignancy is quickly destroyed by the next adventure crashing in in the form of some new creature/fairy monster. And the bad guys -- the iron fey -- iron fairies reflecting, hmm, could it be, modern technology? Oh you mean fey=creativity/dreams and iron fey = industry/modern age? And we are killing creativity with modernity? I feel like I've read/watched this before... (Like 100 times.) Well, if anything might prove that creativity is dying in the modern world it would be this book. I literally made it over 3/4th through and could not read any more. To sum up, this book is shallow, unoriginal and boring. Not recommended.

Who named this book? Seriously, who? It has nothing to do with the storyline. At all. The same goes for the cover. It's like someone just picked it at random. Ignoring the weird title and cover, this book turned out to be rather excellent. It was completely different than I assumed it would be. I can't think of another time that Enoch has created a heroine quite like this. I loved it. Diane was an awesome heroine. I think some readers might not like her because of how cold and manipulative she could seem, but I loved her. She was a woman who had been knocked down in life, only to pull herself up and take control. I loved that we weren't just told how capable she was, we saw it in every page. No matter what was thrown at her, she took it in stride. It drove Oliver mad how rarely he was able to come out on top in their battles. If he tried to embarrass her or manipulate her, she was always ready to turn the tables on him and come out on top in the situation. At times she came off as a little too bitter but I was too caught up in watching Oliver and Diane's relationship power struggle to care. I thought Oliver was a great match for Diane. They were both willing to do whatever it took to win and had no qualms about walking over other people on their way to success. This is not a rare quality in an Enoch hero, but I can't think of when I've ever seen her do such a like pairing with the heroine. The mercenary natures of the characters could have grated if left in less capable hands. The author always keeps us firmly on the side of the protagonists, even when we're fully aware of the wrongs they are committing. Case in point being the way Diane acquired Adam House. Oliver and Diane had a past together that didn't end well. Diane and Oliver have both changed from the people they were at that time, but it's hard for both of them to forgive and forget that time. "I am sorry," he said, trying to keep his voice low and measured. "You were looking for hope, and I was looking for a bit of fun, and when I realized I'd began to care for you far more than I was willing to acknowledge, I ran. Like a scalded dog, I believe you said. I apologize. It's not nearly enough to say the words, or to confess that leaving you in Vienna stands as the greatest regret of my life, but there you have it." That's pretty much their past in a nutshell. Oliver hightailed it out of there with no word and Diane was left to face the financial mess her husband had left her in. Only now she had to deal with a broken heart on top of it. There was no excuse for his actions, but Enoch did an excellent job of showing us his mindset, so it was easy to see why he felt he needed to run. Diane doesn't make it easy for him to prove himself to her, but he's nothing if not determined. Even Diane eventually can't deny how much he's changed. He was right in saying he would have been a crap husband to her if they had married then. He just hadn't grown enough. Despite the different tone to this book, Enoch's characteristic writing style is still there. The dialogue is snappy and you can feel the tension between the two leads. Unlikely situations occasionally crop up but, as with all other Enoch books, the characters approach them straight on and keep the book from veering toward the silly end of things. We were introduced to quite a few intriguing side characters who always managed to steer clear of the dreaded sequel bait role. I'm particularly interested in Greaves and Jenny. If this is what I can expect from the other books in this new series, I'll be on them like white on rice. I can't wait to see what the next book brings. Favorite Quote: "It's not about what I owe you, Diane. It's about what you're worth to me now."

I've completely (well, almost completely*) done with the romance part of these books. I just don't fall in love with her main characters anymore. I don't get a tingly feeling when they hook up for the first time. I don't feel any kind of urgency that they have a HEA. i just don't care about the romance in these books anymore. (*I still care about Qhuinn and Blay and I am very much looking forward to their book. After which I am probably done with this series.) I think Ward did as good a job as she could have done with Tohr's story, given how attached people were to him and Wellsie. But it just fell flat for me. There was absolutely nothing about Autumn that made her interesting as a heroine. No reason for me to give a shit about her, no reason for me to understand why Tohr fell for her (frankly, no reason for me to believe that he did fall in love with her), no reason for me to root for them other than to end Tohr's misery. It's not that I disliked Autumn. I just didn't care. And that's been a problem with most of Ward's heroines, with the exception of Xhex, and maybe a few others. (I liked Mary and Bella, and Ehlena was kinda cool.) So I am not reading these books for the romance anymore, which is kind of disappointing since I will never again experience from these books what I experienced originally when I read Dark Lover 4.5 years ago, and read feverishly day and night until I finished Lover Unbound with a huge sigh about a week later. That urgency, that feeling of being completely immersed in a fantastic story with a steaming hot romance, and having to fan myself periodically, is gone. So why still read? 50% because there are still characters in the series that I find interesting, and 50% peer pressure. That's the truth. It actually might be more like 30%/70%. So I think because I don't feel anywhere near as wrapped up in these books as I used to is probably why I don't really care about this Layla drama that everyone else is freaking out about. I know that Qhuinn and Blay will be together and it will be fine. (Until it's not, but I don't plan on reading that far so it's okay.) I liked the John and Xhex stuff. I would have liked the Xcor/Layla stuff if I gave a shit about Layla. She doesn't annoy me the way she seems to annoy everyone else, but like the rest of Ward's heroines I find her completely drab and devoid of personality. How can Ward create these steaming hot male characters and just continue to pair them with cardboard cutouts? Why is she sooooo bad at writing compelling female characters? Ironically, I guess this is what makes me have faith that the next book (Qhuay!!) will actually be good. No vapid females to ruin it. (I know, I know. Layla's still around, but at least I won't be asked to believe that one of our charismatic, super hot guys is actually in love with her.) So this book. Much better than Lover Unleashed. Still not as good as Lover Mine. Thank GOD Qhuay is next.

Summary: * SS agent is in a car crash, stranded in a small town. I won't get into to many details, because I don't want to spoil anything. I read this right after finishing the original Dracula, and I found myself both liking and disliking the sequel. I wasn't thrilled with the way they altered the original to suit their needs. I didn't mind the changed timeline to fit into 1912, but to turn the original novel into the Francis Ford Coppola Dracula film was a tad unnecessary. Also, changing the basic character of Dracula (and therefore changing the entire plot of the original story) was over the top. In the age of the romantic vampire figure, it would have been nice to leave Dracula as pure evil. I get that there was some ambiguity in the original novel, but in reading it, I never once thought that maybe Dracula could be a good guy. And without getting into spoilers, I was downright shocked at what they did to Van Helsing. I found it totally out of character. I was often quite annoyed with the lack of conversation between characters. It seems as if much of the plot was carried on because characters wrongly assumed things about each other. Everyone wanted to hold onto their information to the detriment of everyone else. I found myself constantly yelling "maybe you should stop and have a freaking conversation to hash this out before you do something stupid!!" more than once. Ok, now for the things that I liked. I enjoyed the character of Elizabeth Bathory--I've always found the historical Bathory to be fascinating, so to find her in this story was fun. It was nice to have a purely evil vampire. You rarely see that anymore. The Jack the Ripper storyline was an interesting twist as well. I was pleasantly surprised to see Bram Stoker show up in the novel and I liked how they tried to keep things historically accurate. The book reads like a movie--in fact, I had the movie playing in my head as I was reading. I imagine that was done on purpose, as Holt is a screenwriter. I wonder though, if they'll bother since the book received such a bad reception. I actually think I would have liked this novel a lot more had it not been a sequel to the original. If you change the names of the characters, and make this a stand alone book, I think it would have been a really good story.

I like Pratchett's witty writing style in the Discworld series, but it seems slightly out of place in this book geared towards kids. (Original review posted on my livejournal account: http://intoyourlungs.livejournal.com/...) Why I Read It: Now that I think about it, I'm really not sure why this book caught my eye. I remember coming across it at work back when it first came out and thinking "Whoa, that sounds kind of intense" but never got around to buying it. Then we got some new Bargain books in and this was going for $5.99 for the hardcover (not counting my 30% off employee discount) so I impulsively bought it. I seriously wish I had reigned in my impulsiveness when I bought this book. It ultimately ended up feeling like a waste of time and I wish I had just put it down and marked it as a DNF (something I really need to learn to do). Thankfully it wasn't a very long book. I think what bugged me the most was that I never felt ANYTHING for these characters. I never got the sense that they were depressed and suicidal: they just felt like teens who were suffering from normal teenage angst and were kind of mad at the world (which is FINE but that does not equate to suicidal for me). It also didn't help that we got little to no insight into the characters' minds; we don't get to see how they deal with the horrible feelings of being suicidal. I wouldn't have minded if they didn't have reasons for feeling depressed/suicidal (depression is not always circumstantial) but we get so little from them. Actually, all the characters seemed to be defined by one dominant trait: the asian girl was a lesbian, the driver guy was an alcoholic wannabe athlete, Alice was a compulsive liar and the narrator just cried a lot. I never cared about any of them and I honestly wasn't invested in whether they actually offed themselves in the end or not (though it's pretty obvious that they WON'T -- what kind of message would that send?) Oh yeah, and there's "romance" in this book (I use that term very lightly) between the narrator and one of the girls on the trip (the one who isn't a lesbian). The problem is that the girl was a very unlikable character, and not just because she was a liar -- she was just annoying as all get out. Yeah, she may act like a typical angry teenager, but unfortunately, most angry teenagers are irritating and aren't fun to read about it. She had NO redeeming qualities, and while she obviously has very real and serious problems (she's obviously neglected which is why she feels the need to lie and be an all around annoying brat) it's just skimmed over and never really addressed, which made it impossible for me to feel an ounce of sympathy for her. Big spoilery-bit ahead concerning the ending here: And then we actually get to the ending of the book. What a freakin' cop-out. So the narrator starts freaking out and pulls out a gun that one of the other people brought and shoots it at a grave, has a bullet ricochet and then graze his head. This near-brush with death has made him realize that he wants to LIVE. How does that even make sense? It's been stated that the kid has tried to kill himself before and he's never had this epiphany. I suppose this time was supposed to be different because he's made some friends along the way, but his change of heart still felt incredibly abrupt. And then BAM the book ends. That's it. I'm sorry, but depression and feeling suicidal DO NOT go away that easily. It's a long healing process and the flippant attitude (whether intentional or not) grated on me immensely. Final Verdict: I did not like this book. At all. This could have been a heart-wrenching, potentially edge-of-your-seat read (will they do it or not?) if the characters had actually been developed or been people I could actually bring myself to care about. Unfortunately though, we're stuck in the POV of a character who was boring, and thus we're given very little insight into the other characters' minds (who could have potentially been interesting, maybe). There's a little bit of romance in the novel that's laughable, and the ending made me angry at how abrupt it was, and I'd argue flippant as well. I never got the sense that these characters were actually SUICIDAL -- it almost felt like it was tacked on to the characters as an after-thought even though it's supposed to be a huge part of their predicament. It's the driving force of the story!! Anyway, I'm going to end this rant here. I obviously don't recommend this, but if you're looking for something "edgy", or are interested in reading about this kind of thing, maybe you'll enjoy it more than I did.

I read a few reviews about Belzhar before I began reading it. It generally received average reviews and a few people stated that they were bored while reading it. That was not the case for me. I was intrigued the entire time, especially when we got to learn the back stories of every character and why they were at this special school for highly intelligent and fragile teenagers. The ending is where my four stars come from. Although I was surprised by the twist ending, I wish it went a bit differently. Throughout the whole book, we know that Jam was sent to this school because she was deeply depressed about her boyfriend Reeve dying. The ending was a shock because we find out that Reeve didn't actually love her, he wasn't even interested in her but her mind fooled her into thinking he liked her and she became obsessed. That part I liked and was very reminiscent of the French movie "He Loves Me, He Loves Me Not" which is a fantastic film everyone should watch. What threw me off was the fact that Reeve didn't actually die. When Jam starts describing the moment that she found Reeve making out with another girl (a girl who has been bullying Jam for quite a while) it made it seem like maybe she would snap and accidentally hurt or kill Reeve. When it turns out that she just killed him in her mind I felt kind of let down. Not that I wanted her specifically to kill him, just I wish there was more to it than that. Something small was just missing there for me. All in all, I did enjoy this book more than the average reviewer and I would recommend to at least give it a chance. P.S. I know you aren't supposed to judge a book by it's cover, but I thought this cover was beautiful.

Mild spoilers ahead, I will warn you in each line before giving them. I'm going to ignore all the hub-bub the negative reviews give about this being a Twilight rip-off because A/ all YA paranormal fantasy I've heard about since Twilight's release is as well (note those I've heard about, not every single one) B/I don't beleive it intentional because to be honest you pick any two books in the same genre and you can come across similarities eg, 'The Wheel of Time' vs 'The Belgariad' both have farm boys forced to leave their farms by dark forces only to discover their own magical power, and also feature a woman from back home who has incredible magical power and a red-headed princess as a possible love interest. See what I did there? And that was with only five minutes thought on books I last read years ago. So to sum up, not paying attention to it because I DON'T CARE. Now onto the actual book review. I read this book based on a four star review from a book blog I like/respect. That and the cover art caught me. I became even more enamoured when I heard the writer was discovered online. The dreamer in me desires that so I felt obliged to get the book despite having already spent my book alowance on manga. I enjoyed the fact that the book was set in Ireland and really loved that there were Celtic myths woven in. However I would have liked some more mythos personally or to see the realtionship more closely bound to a myth, but that's personal taste. I loved the fact the school system in Ireland seems to be very similar to the Australian system and it made me nostalgic for those good old school days. I like that the author pointed out these differences to show Megan (the protagonist) was American in a foreign country. What makes it impossible for me to give this book anything more than three stars is the relationship between Megan and Adam. Yes you saw it coming, I had no problem with that, what I struggled with was the fact I couldn't connect with their romance. I thrive on romance in a book. A good couple in a book/tv show/ movie will keep me watching/reading even when other plot points are falling apart because as much as I may deny it I LIVE for romance. Megan and Adam were not that couple for me. I couldn't feel the love. At all. Normally I'll enjoy a giddy feeling at the moment of confession and anticipation for the first kiss and if it goes further well I'm not complaining ;p However very quickly I got bored with the PDA's all over the place and even the private expressions bored me. Yes, bored me. I skipped paragraphs wasted on what should have been passion. I skim read some pages to avoid getting bogged down in it. I gave a few pieces a try to see if I could catch the spark but the last page (literally) was the only page I liked the romance on. Perhaps it's because I'm nearly thirty and reading a book aimed at teens and maybe teen romance doesn't thrill me anymore and I'm happy if you think that and want to give the book a try. The end felt a bit rushed, like she realised she needed some action to end the book with and I hate that she leads us into the book with a snippet of said action but when you get to the action it only lasts a few pages. Then again I hate when books lead you in with a snippet of the action near the end of the book regardless of the book. Start your book in medias res a different way people! /rant, sorry. I will give Fallon props that Megan has appropriate injuries after the action with (mild spoilers) a puffy swollen face, stitches and burns on her hands. I hate it when characters come out of danger unscathed and she obliged me by wounding her heroine. Overall I feel the book lacked the romance needed to pull off a paranormal romance. Their love felt farcical to me. However I did like the writing itself and the ideas of (SPOILERS AGAIN) people being bred like animals to propagate a line of people able to carry the magic and linking genetics with magic. I think teens would better connect with the romance and thus this book in general.

Thoughts.. It is really difficult to love dogs and read dog books. I think that probably many of us have a different notion of what a dog thinks and feels about its' surroundings and humans. This book didn't quite capture that for me. I mean, I knew this wasn't going to be great literature. I don't think there is any piece of great literature with a talking/thinking dog. I'm not entirely sure if this is because that would be impossible or if it just hasn't been accomplished yet. The book uses fairly simplistic language as it is supposed to be communicated by a dog. Though, I don't find that this particularly detracts from the story. The big detractor for me is the reliance throughout the book on extreme situations for emotional effect. The life cycle of a dog has enough reason for emotion without that sort of exploitation. I did like the overall voice of the dog, his joy in simple pleasures which I found to be in keeping with what I think of when I imagine a dog's thoughts. The complete converse is "The Art of Racing in the Rain" where the dog's voice is complex and you get the feeling that simple dog pleasures are beneath him. Honestly, my imagined dog voice is somewhere between these two, neither one is completely satisfying. There are just times when dog people need to read a dog book whether these are entirely satisfying or not. So, read this if you just need to read a dog book, expect the shortcomings common to all books with a talking/thinking dog as the main character.

The Goddess Test was a very unique read with an interesting take on Greek mythology. The way Greek mythology was incorporated into this book was different and didn't overpower the story. You don't have to really know Greek mythology to understand the idea behind it. I felt that there wasn't really a climax in this story. Some exciting things happened at the beginning of the book but none of Kate's tests were huge events so the story moved at one level. This fantasy story, which should be fast paced, moved along like it was realistic fiction. Another thing that I think would have helped the book would be seeing Henry's point of view. I know sometimes I complain about books having too many POVs or praised authors for writing in first person but The Goddess Test could have used another point of view. I think Aimee Carter would have done a fabulous job voicing Henry's side and another POV wouldn't have been a problem. One thing about The Goddess Test that was really interesting was that it only focussed on the story of Persephone and Hades with a twist. For most people I am sure that when they think of a fiction series inspired by Greek mythology, Rick Riordan's Percy Jackson books come to mind. In those books, there are all sort of Greek myths coming to life and even some Roman ones later on in The Heroes of Olympus series. It was nice to just focus on one myth and have it be the centre of attention. With the myth being about the underworld it provided a new take on death and afterlife. The Goddess Test was a solid read and I recommend it if you are looking for a book that's not super crazy and over the top. It can definitely be categorized as a "cool down" read. www.justonemorechapter.ca
