I'm really conflicted about this book because I want to give it a higher rating, but I just can't. There are certain aspects of this that I absolutely LOVED -- as in had me jumping up from my bed in excitement type of love -- but it wasn't enough to push it up there with my favorites. What I LOVED: The plot twists! Boy, does this book have it's plot twists! I can honestly say I did not expect the majority of those, and I enjoyed being mindblown during those instances. The characters were great, for the most part -- not likable per se (some not at all), but they were intriguing to read about. The villain was especially twisted and sick, I thought, and I loved to hate her. The writing was great. Even when I was frustrated that the story was going nowhere, I still enjoyed the reading experience (if that makes sense?). Melinda does a fantastic job with ambiance, and I thoroughly enjoyed her writing in that sense. What I...didn't...love: I mentioned it previously, but I found myself a bit frustrated with the first half of the book. I feel like not much happened in the first half. High fantasy novels obviously need to set up a whole new world, but compared to everything that happened in the second half, I don't know if there was enough of a setup in the beginning for all of the twists and turns at the end. This leads me to my next point: It feels like this was trying to tackle and include too many elements in such a relatively short novel. The fact that she's supposed to have these powers, but no, wait, she doesn't. So there's no magic in this world? No wait, yes there is! Remember that medallion mentioned really briefly 150 pages ago? Yeah, that's super important now! That fairy tale you thought was merely symbolic and random, turns out it's very literal! And the guy she (and I as a reader) fell in love with is really a total d**k, but you only find that out in the last 10pages! Ugh! I really, really wish that this was a longer novel. There were just too many things going on and I wish some of them were better developed. That being said, I think I will read the next book. I was invested enough in the story (and some of those twists) to want to know how the story continues -- especially with this new discovered threat, and I really want to see Twylla develop further. I wanted her to be a lot more badass than she was. I'm definitely keeping my fingers crossed for the next one!

Disclaimer: I'll be honest - I was a little hesitant before reading this because I was worried that it was going to be a total redux of Jonathan Strange & Mr Norrel. On paper these books sound super similar, and it's only just over a year since I read the latter and LOVED it. And while there are strong similarities between the books, it feels pretty unfair to write about Zen Cho's book only in comparison to JS&MN. So I'm going to acknowledge the similarities exist, but honestly, in the end it didn't end up mattering to me in the slightest. Because this book is so charming. Set in the regency era, it follows the beleaguered fortunes of Zacharias Wythe, a former slave who has now reached the exalted office of Sorcerer Royal. He has a whole host of problems: mutinous magicians who refuse to believe a black man could be their leader; a decline in the flow of magic from Fairy to Britain; and the debilitating after effects of the pact he made that led to him taking office in the first place. Into this mess wanders Prunella Gentleman - headstrong, rash, and insanely gifted with magic. The moral codes of the time forbid women from practising magic - but that's not likely to stop Prunella. And Zacharias, reticent and particular as he seems, has a passion for reform, leading him to secretly take on Prunella as an apprentice. The book is witty, adventurous, and immensely readable. There's a real lightness of touch to Cho's writing - she evokes the period, but it never gets too far into hamminess (unless for comedic effect.) But despite the comedy of manners feel of much of the book, Cho doesn't shy away from big issues: the book is an intricate study in the the intersections of race, gender and class. What I love is that Zen Cho has Zacharias and Prunella (who is mixed race) take on the overwhelming conventions and beliefs of their day, and come out the other side. These are characters you will really spend your time cheering for.

I'm not going to rate this one, as it would be such a jumbled, 'but-on-the-other-hand', still not sure what I felt kind of rating, it's not worth anything. So, on the one hand... I really kind of liked Stark, who was - most of the time - an 'anti-hero' with enough basic decency to carry sympathy for some of the things he did, which weren't -- gentle remonstrances of those with whom he had grievances. Actually, it was kind of creatively nasty sometimes, and there was a lot of humour for a book about someone escaped from Hell to create some hell of his own. On the other hand... I get really quite anxious when the protagonist is told that there's a strong possibility the world is going to end (literally), and it's his fault. At least when nothing could have told him that taking a seemingly sensible - like you'd be brain-dead NOT to if you could - action was somewhere down the line going to end the world. It's worse because the person who makes the accusation should be 'good', and worse again because Stark just wants to save his friends and let the others get on with saving all of humanity, and ... yeah, just anxious. And then there's the God stuff. I'd suggest looking away now if you are going to be offended by language - though seriously, avoid this book if so. I might have a small bit of detail wrong here, but the important bit is that the creation of humans is acknowledged by angels fallen *and* unfallen to have been a major fuck-up by God because He got too distracted playing with cosmic stuff to notice He'd made earth and all. I've no problem reading books with a god, heaven, hell and a (what's the collective noun for angels, I wonder?) bunch of angels that are different enough to treat as fantasy religion, but this gave me pause. It might well be addressed later in the books, but I don't quite get what makes such a big kid God. And back to the first hand .. Stark uses 'best first date ever' in the best way ever, and for that alone I was happy to have read this. I'm not planning to read on at the moment, but that could change as I see GR friends loving later books in the series...

I haven't loved each and every Flavia de Luce book equally. I definitely enjoy Flavia as a character and narrator even though I can't always relate to her all the time. In this sixth mystery, Flavia's focus is NOT on a current murder mystery. Far from it, even though a murder occurs practically in front of her (at the train station), she can't really be bothered. Why? Well, her mother is coming home...at last. For Flavia, the one de Luce child who CANNOT remember her mother at all, this is just confusing and bittersweet. Is she glad her mother's body has been found? That the body is being returned so it can be properly buried? In a way, perhaps. But. The homecoming is just as bitter as it is sweet. It upsets the family so much, brings so many emotions out in the open where they cannot be ignored. The situation is forcing Flavia outside her comfort zone. If the novel does NOT focus on the current dead body, what does it focus on?! Well, it focuses on the past; it focuses on the years leading up to World War II. It provides context for her mother's life...and death. For Flavia solving this mystery of who her mother was, who she really was, her worth and value, means EVERYTHING. There were quite a few uncomfortable scenes in this one for me. I found the scenes where Flavia is trying to scientifically bring her mother back from the dead (after ten years) to be a bit creepy--she's trying to acquire the right chemicals to resurrect the dead. Just like the previous book, this one closes with change on the way for Flavia.

It took me a long time to get into this book. This book was written before dystopia really caught hold of the young adult genre so I'm sure it paved the way for many dystopian books but it just isn't that gripping itself in my opinion. It didn't have a striking, capturing element to it in the beginning like most dystopian books have now and the conflict of the book didn't even occur until about a third of the way into it which left me feeling bored the majority of the time reading it. I think it might be the concept of the book too that just puts me off a bit. I don't understand why a society would take hold based on the idea of making everybody "pretty." Of course, the "pretty" operation is partly a cover-up of a more sinister motive to keep everybody under control, but I just think it's a bit strange and illogical. The plot was slow for me up until Tally arrived at the Smoke. I finally became interested in it by that point. I loved the glimpses into their world that we were given and how they foraged a lifestyle in the wilderness away from the cities and their pretty operations. I wish that the book had focused more on Tally's time there and had extended her time in the Smoke. I also liked the characters that Tally met there, especially David of course. I also wish that the book had explored a bit more of the rift between Tally and Shay that developed. There was a lot of focus on the big picture of the book rather than any actual character situations or character development. I will read the next two books simply because my friend has lent them to me and wanted me to read them but I don't think I would finish this series otherwise. I think there are a lot better dystopian books out there with similar storylines and characters. Likes: The Smoke. David. Tally. Shay. The dystopian world was built well. Dislikes: Boring. The concept of a society being built simply on being "pretty" is a little ridiculous to me. Too much emphasis on boring details like Tally learning how to hoverboard. The entire beginning of the book is just that in itself with bits of Shay in it to attempt to break up the monotony. Also, random, but Tally is said to have dark eyes in the book yet her picture on the cover has blue eyes so who missed that in the publishing world?? Overall: Recommend? No. Reading the Next One? Yes since my friend lent the first three to me and wants me to read them. Otherwise I wouldn't continue the series on my own.

It's interesting how much more readable this book was than Oryx And Crake, which I suppose makes sense once you realize (as I hadn't till I read the header on this page) that The Year Of The Flood is the second part of the trilogy. That said, I think it also read more easily because Margaret Atwood always seems more at ease when writing from the point of view of a woman. I don't mean for that to sound like a slur, but I think she makes it easier for us to sympathize with her flawed female narrators than with her flawed male narrators. Crake and Snowman from the first book felt like constructs, whereas Ren and Toby (especially Toby) in this book feel like real people. Overall, once I got over the book's The End Is Nigh, Be More Eco-Conscious nagginess of tone (and don't get me wrong: I reuse, recycle and try to be environmentally friendly in my day-to-day living, so it's not like I don't fundamentally agree with the premise,) I began to really enjoy it. I tore through this book in about a day, and am really looking forward to seeing where it ends. It reminded me a lot of (though, tbh, paled in comparison to) David Mitchell's Cloud Atlas. There was only one thing about this book that made me start to question Ms Atwood's writing techniques, and that is the ubiquitous presence of the distant-artist-female-maybe-friend stand-in. I'm kinda tired of her showing up in almost every single book Ms Atwood writes, even if I thought that at least her embodiment in this novel was pretty badass. I'm hoping Book 3 proves as much better than TYOTF as TYOTF did OAC.

BEWARE YA NOVELS WITH PRETTY DRESSES ON THE COVER. B.E.W.A.R.E. I have yet to read one that doesn't fantastically suck in one way or another. Now, I do feel bad about giving this one star, when it is clearly superior to Kate's "Fallen" (which is an insult to the intelligence) and Fitzpatrick's revolting "Hush, Hush" (which is an insult to common decency.) But anything that turns the act of reading into such a soul-crushing chore should get one star from me. This is the dystopian novel Henry James would write if he were obliged to write for today's publicists. It is fraught with sudden cuts to the history of the clothes Narrator is wearing. But DeStefano is not nearly a good enough writer to make such rambling drivel worth reading. The premise of this novel: A war explodes the world, (except for North America, WHEE!) but hark! Science discovers a way to make the next generation uber-mensch out of us all. Everyone, without regard to race, creed, religion or socio-economic status has this procedure done. (Alright... well, I suspend disbelief as this is a premise I would probably have come up with when I was fourteen.) Unfortunately, no one in the whole world could have forseen the Dread Consequences-- that the children born to said uber-mensch now Explode and Die when they hit 20 years old (25 for males.) It is always this exact year, regardless of how well or poorly the child has lived. In answer to this, the wealthy elite go around kidnapping young girls, with the intent of marrying them against their will. Very much like in "Pirates of Penzance" only it's polygamist marriages. The wealthy elite want a new generation of Soon to Explode and Die people, and will get this via conservative polygamist marriages. Not orgies or attacking women with turkey basters, or Massive Multi-Player Polygamy. They are somehow socially obligated to have no more than seven wives, and no less than three. (Eh?) Also, they kidnap huge numbers of girls and then sell off as prostitutes or outright murder anyone they decide not to marry. This does not lead to revolt or anything. Everyone seems kind of okay with this. Also also, although it is not really a part of this book, there is a new war going on. It is a war between the scientists, who are trying to find a cure, and "naturalists" who are basically terrorists out to kill anyone who is looking for a cure. Because, you know, humanity deserves to die for coming up with the whole uber-mensch thing and exploding the world. (I'm sorry, what?) So... yeah. And, alas, the further I go along, the stupider and more insulting the whole thing becomes. Halfway through, Narrator abruptly and for no stated reason, abandons her escape "plan" (which is more of a nebulous escape "wish" that she acts on exactly never) in favor of throwing herself out a window in the middle of a category four hurricane. Her previous escape plan involved 1)becoming his favorite wife 2)get invited to a glamorous high-security party 3)escape high-security party because it will obviously be easier to escape there than from the grounds where you are allowed to walk unsupervised. Except... 1) she doesn't do ANYTHING to try to become his favorite wife. 2) When she does get invited to a glamorous party, she doesn't spend any time looking for an escape route. 3) When an escape route jumps up and bashes her in the face, she is suddenly too much the devoted wife to actually leave. She never makes any alternative plan or does any ACTUAL PRACTICAL PLANNING. 3/4ths of the way through, when Narrator has been "trapped" and dreaming of escape for over a year (and bear in mind her hourglass is running out) she suddenly realizes that her limp noodle "captor" is unaware of the fact that she might want to leave. Because, you know, she's never mentioned it. Also, why the FRICK is it such a big deal that everyone in the manor gets autopsied? There is a disease that is killing off EVERYONE IN THE WORLD... and she, even though she has to kill and dump bodies off her front porch, has NIGHTMARES about autopsies? That another horrible thing about this book. Nearly every chapter has a dream sequence. It's more like the dream journal of a whiny, do-nothing side character than an actual book wherin stuff happens. It's not just that the stated goals are a little questionable and obstacles facing the people in this book make no sense, it's that nothing that they do seems designed to further those goals. Much has been written about how nonsensical this world is, how the polygamy makes no psychological or practical sense and the author obviously isn't trying to be realistic in her portrayal. (Dude, no one likes polygamy. Not even guys.) I just want to talk for a minute about how boring it is. Let me give you an example of what I'm talking about: Chapter 8 -servants are rushing around to attend on Whiny Pedo-Bait (from here on to be known as Nymphette) who has fainted. -Servant who Narrator is Trying to Have an Affair With comes in. He (*dun DUNN! *) CLOSES the door behind him! Narrator (*dun DUNN! *) HUGS him! She cries on his shoulder because of the EPIC TRAGEDY THAT IS HER LIFE! Servant is jealous of her husband and shocked that they might be sleeping together! Narrator thinks of taking him with her when she Makes her Desperate Escape! They BOND like the soul mates they obviously are. (Now, I know this sounds like some relationship development and buildup for action. Don't be deceived! These SAME EXACT POINTS are brought up OVER AND OVER AGAIN in EVERY CHAPTER.) -Nymphette is going to have a baby! [cut scene] -Narrator talks to Servant about the exact geography of her hometown complete with all the names of all the districts. Narrator (*dun DUNN! *) SITS ON THE BED with Servant. She OBLIQUELY INVITES HIM TO ESCAPE WITH HER! Again! -Nymphette INTERRUPTS this Not-Affair! Narrator panics and draws more attention to her infidelity by trying to hurriedly Act Natural. -Nymphette, who apparently suspects nothing, and who has shown exactly no signs of not being a cardboard cut-out of a character, spends another TWO PAGES grousing and being pregnant child-bride-zilla. AAAAND DRAMATIC FADE TO BLACK. There are 26 more chapters of this, folks. Things that could have made this book better: - Servant Love Interest could have been a eunuch. At least 50% more interesting. - This story could be told from a dog's perspective. This would explain why the narrator has such difficulty finding the escape route. And also why Governor Linden is not having sex with her. -It could be a re-telling of 'Antigone' which would explain the narrator's aversion to autopsies.

EVERLOST by Neal Shusterman is one of my favorite books, so when I found out it was part of a trilogy, I had to get the second one right away. I never thought the genius of EVERLOST could be outdone or even matched, but I was pleasantly surprised by EVERWILD. It was even BETTER than the original. I should start off by saying that I don't think the impact of EVERWILD will be as powerful if you didn't read EVERLOST first. EVERLOST introduces the world of Everlost and the primary characters (Nick, Allie, and Mary). Seeing them develop from the beginning of EVERLOST to the end of EVERWILD is a journey that you must start from the beginning of the first book if you want the most out of it. Nick has become the Chocolate Ogre, Allie has become Allie the Outcast, and Mary is now deemed Mary the Sky Witch. The way Shusterman follows these three characters and tells each of their stories individually but weaves them all together at the end is genius. There are new characters as well, who fit perfectly into the story. Neal Shusterman's writing is brilliant. I have never read a book by another author who can describe things as well as he can, which is why he's my favorite author. The way he brings the world of Everlost to life is astounding. EVERWILD is engrossing, suspenseful, and grim at parts, but it is also beautiful in so many ways. The different elements Neal Shusterman brings in have such depth and meaning that I can't even explain what I'm talking about in words. The character I feel the most for personally is Mikey McGill, and he very well may be my favorite character. When you read the book, you will understand why. I can't wait for EVERFOUND. The Skinjacker triology is one you mustn't miss.

** spoiler alert ** Every time I think of this book, it always remind me of another "Angel Story" so I decided to reread it and give it some justice. And justice I have. I didn't appreciate it much when I first read it (based on my previous review) nut now I do. Yes, it's a typical story about an ordinary girl who found out she's supernatural (in this case, part angel) but the story is supported by a very strong background about angels, bible stories and facts turned into a non fiction story. Violet has been secretly in love with his friend Lincoln for a very long time. On her 17th birthday, she decided that it's the right time for Lincoln to know how she feels, but then, she found out Lincoln's secret that could change her life forever. It turns out that she's a Grigori, a human blessed by an angel's essence, just like Lincoln. Feeling betrayed and confused, Violet turned to a new friend, Phoenix. Which happened to be an exile -- a former angel who chose to remain on earth and the enemy of the Grigori. It's the Grigoris' mission to return the exiles where they belong, as exiles are not meant to be on earth wreaking havoc and all. But even with the betrayal and anger she's feelint, Violet can't deny the fact that she'll still do anything for Lincoln, even if it means giving up her own life. I find Violet an ordinary hero, very strong but still has her weakness. She's imperfect and that's what I like about her. Her friendship with Steph keeps her on the ground with all the craziness around her. Lincoln on the other hand is very closed. Mysterious in a way. I haven't understood him much, maybe because it's on Vi's POV but I could sum him up as the handsome protective partner that's also in love with Violet. And Phoenix? I actually liked him more. Sadly, I am seeing a dark future ahead of him. But I'm not losing my hope for him. In my opinion, he turned out the way he was because of Violet. Violet used him to forget, to get over Lincoln. I felt Violet being inconsiderate with Phoenix and part of me hated her for that. It's a catchy story. One that won't let you stop until you read the rest. It's a well planned out story with all the foundations being set up clearly.

So I'm going to buy it when it's the paperback it was sold to loyal readers as. Not because I can't afford $11.99. I've got plenty of money. It's just that I don't like being taken for granted by authors and their publishers. So my protest will include me spending the money I might have spent on Blood Vow on something else. I'm gifting some of my favorite books to some friends. First up: Melody -- tonight she received: Grace Draven's "Entreat Me" ($3.99, full novel) Grace Draven's "The Undying King" ($1.99, long novella) Ilona Andrews' "Clean Sweep" ($4.99, full novel) Why these books? Because I loved them, they're independently published, and these two (technically three) authors never seem to forget that their fans are more than dollar signs. Total cost to me for three books: $10.97. Wow. What a bargain. True -- pro published books are more expensive. So it behooves the author to give what she or he promised the readers. Because ... see ... we're the ones on the other end of the transaction. The ones with the money. If you sold a series as paperback, then give us a reasonably priced paperback instead of greedily bumping it up to HC on the second book because you know we're loyal and you can squeeze a little more out of us. That kind of stink doesn't just go away. Some people might think I need a waaaambulance and it's really not all that important. But some of us are just plain tired of being played for chumps and something that might seem like just a few bucks give or take ... well there's that one last straw that breaks the camel's back. Frankly, it's insulting, and my money goes where I want it to go. Because while authors may not be their readers' bitches (thank you Neil Gaiman for that one), readers are not authors' bitches either. ETA: the giveaway goes on. Look I know what the problem is here. Other authors have attempted this trick. Sometimes it works others, not so much. The ones that work find the beauty in the intersection of the previous story and the wonders of the new ongoing one. Just by using a different perspective doesn't make it awesome. There has to be new content but what may not be as obvious is there needs to be old stuff in there too to fluff the entire tale out.

For a novel about cadavers, this book was very lively! Okay, terrible puns aside. I headed into Stiff with uncertain expectations. I was interested in learning, but was not sure that the author could deliver. However, I was not disappointed! Roach provides entertainment, jokes and information rolled into one, providing the dignity that the subject requires while not boring or goring the audience too much. She is free with her tangents which follow similar paths to her thinking and her discovery about the subject, which I appreciated immensely because it allowed me to learn about things that weren't necessarily cadaver related and also helped the reader "step out" of the icky-sticky stuff sometimes. I felt it was a good mix of staying on task and exploring all the avenues that her investigation offered. As for the less pleasant elements of the book--by this I merely mean the necessary descriptions of bodies rotting or baking, or whatever process they happen to be going through at the time. For the weak stomached, I would skip the section that describes the rotting process and the cremation process (which I believe is "How to know when you are dead" but don't quote me on that). While reading this section made me think about my rotting corpse, which I really didn't want to do, I'm glad she included it because if not the book would have felt like it was cheating the reader. I was really impressed with how well she handled this topic; she offers the reader a lot to think about in regards to death, the positives of donating your body to science and, in the end, whether you should or not, including her own personal decision (and the reasoning behind it). This book is human in its handling of death and has a cast of great characters who entertain and warm the heart. Although it makes me wish to avoid death all the more, bravo!

this could have been so good. i don't rightly know how to rate this because it had some real strong moments which were alas mixed with very disappointing authorial choices. very strong beginning, interesting characters. love owen. i really appreciate characters who grapple with serious issues, and i like personal growth and happy endings for people with a lot stacked against them. loved nick's sister june; what a force of nature, and what a wonderful way to open a door for owen to come out of his own, sad, self-limited life. there was some really good stuff in there about disability, and how difficult it can be to handle sensibly even for people of good will. it looked like a great 5-star story. but then nick dropped his bomb shell. and my opinion of him went through the floor. not because of the bomb itself, but because of the timing. sorry; not negotiable. this is something you talk about before getting intimate. and completely unnecessary to the plot. because nick's fears? make sense. even though we now know a lot more than we did in the 80s (though i wonder whether marie sexton does; there was some weird conflation going on). it stretches believability because nick's a vet and has medical knowledge, but sure, his irrational mind might still not have caught up with his reason. but then what the hell is he doing with owen? one of the tropes i do not ever buy in romance is that we're slaves to our overwhelming sex drives. no. we're not. if we were, that would be a great excuse for rape and all sorts of other atrocities. we can damn well control ourselves. if nick really cared about owen, he would have controlled himself. he would have talked instead of getting physical and then blowing cold all the time. so in one swell foop marie sexton made me dislike one of the main characters in a romance. that's a death knell. everything from then on was a mess. and it overshadowed how much i liked owen and june. owen's mother -- there's a tough thing to assess in a short romance. to the people who thought her unbelievable per se: oh, i wish. that's my mother right there. and my father (minus the same back story). contrary to owen i dumped the lot of them at 17, but i know too many people who put up with utterly cruel and despicable parents all their lives, so i can't blame owen for not manning up sooner. if you've never met someone like that, consider yourself lucky, but also sheltered. yet in the context of this romance, i agree she was probably too much. it wasn't necessary to paint her this black; she could have crippled owen's self-esteem without being so relentless. i generally don't like pure good/evil characters; they're just not very interesting. the ending -- what the heck? was that supposed to be a pun? dear marie, did you want me to dislike owen as well? what did regina ever do to him? she didn't ask to star in his -- wholly inappropriate and misguided -- fantasies. did he ever even correct her when she got his name wrong? no, that ending was a total miss. usually such solid writers who i basically had on auto-buy, but this series is not making me happy. after reading 6 of the books in this series i am thinking riptide needs a much stronger editor. yeah, i know, none of these small publishing houses can actually afford a good editor, one of those cranky, chain-smoking, NYC types with a massive red pen and an unerring nose for turning the so-so into something shiny.

I suppose that a major charm of Stiefvater's stories is that in the end you have only understood half of the novel. Or you're missing some kind of details. Because that's how I always feel at the end of Raven Cycle's books. Blue Lily, Lily Blue is full of this confusing magic and tha the same time is one of my favorite novel of the series. So, as always, the author use the particulars of "strange and bizarre", making thing up, complicating the events, and yet at the same time it focus so much on the characters that I had the constant feel, especially at the end, that something was missing. The plot develop in something really delicate, that I feel how is almost impossible to talk about it without doing a little bit of spoilers. For many times Stiefvater depicts a little fact, a word, or a phrase that seem useless at the start but in the end they all compose a good system of events. And it also leads to new characters! I had a bit of hard times with decisions made by some minor characters, just like Maura's path during the novel, but I definitely fell in love with some new people - that hoped to see more in The Raven King but it never happened. Cry with me, please. In that case I don't feel like my connection with the Raven Boys made a big progress, but I definitely fell in love with Blue. But I should totally note that the mechanic between the crew was great to read about. Everyone complete everyone, even if I think that would have been nice to see more interaction between Ronan and Blue. Okay, talking about the girl, there's a reason why his book is named after her. I couldn't have been more happy discovering how this novel started to move around her and also the discovery of something really important about her family. For reasons, some more close some more afar, I really related to Blue on various levels. How she fights for her future, how she defended herself against bullies - even if it wasn't directly showed - and how she decided to start move towards the truth. I would have loved to have her same strength and same occasion. I also loved the low-toned magic, yet incredibly dreamy, and how it mixed perfectly with the story and the whole character driven plot. Also, Sitefvater's managed to mix that magic with new characters, as I cited above, and one in particular made me really happy... even if he had such little pages. In the end, I think that Blue Lily, Lily Blue is one of my favorite and more complete novel of the cycle after The Dream Thieves, and also the novel where things start to become heavy and serious. Definitely the book you should read if you're not s interested in the series or thinking to drop it.

See more of my reviews on my blog the Book Deviant Why even have a summary? One thing I hate the most is when the summary promises something, and the book doesn't deliver. Intrigue? Nope. Mystery? Aha, what mystery? "Bloody events"? Unless you count the decapitated mouse head, then no. This book was a huge disappointment. Besides skipping over everything that was promised in the summary, I found nothing at all interesting or new. Nothing original-just another retelling of Alice in Wonderland, taking the oh-so-unique idea of delving into the Queen of Hearts's past. I have to admit, this is the first one I actually read, but after this one, I don't think I'll be reading another. Instead of mystery, we get constant complaining from Dinah. Instead of "bloody events", we get a severed mouse's head and more complaining. That's literally all this book was. Dinah complaining about one thing or another, whining, whining, and, yes, more whining. I don't even know what the mystery was supposed to be. There was one thing that pointed to there being a problem, and Dinah used her 'super-sense': "I can't explain it, but I need to find her. Faina. This note wasn't sent in malice, I can feel it." One-sided characters None of the characters were interesting. None of the characters were reminiscent of the White Rabbit or the Mad Hatter-in fact, the character that was called the Mad Hatter was basically a small child. He was described as small, and acted like a child, and I don't see how that can be considered 'mad'. The romance between Wardley and Dinah was just so awkward. Dinah was obsessed with him, while he just 'wanted to be friends'. Not only did I have to read through her unwanted advances towards him, but I also had to read how she kept doing it over and over again. And don't even get me started on her father and Cheshire. one and a half stars - Overall? This book was a huge disappointment. I found a few things interesting, but of what I did find interesting, they were brushed aside within a paragraph. The writing was somewhat decent, but that's all I could really stand about this book. The characters were just cardboard cut-outs, some of which were obviously put in place only to get killed. Would I Recommend? Probably not. This was my first Alice in Wonderland retelling that I've read, and I was ultimately, hugely, disappointed. Overall, it's completely up to you whether or whether not you read this book. But, in my opinion, find a different retelling.

I received this free from the publishers via NetGalley WE COME APART tells the story of a working class girl called Jess and a Romanian boy named Nicu whose path cross when taking part in a Reparation scheme after both get caught for theft. Nicu struggles to find his place in his new home - a country where he faces prejudice and racism. Jess faces abuse in her home life, and wishes to escape. Both find comfort in each other and bond over their pain and their friendship turns to romance and they see hope in each other. WE COME APART is a free verse novel, which therefore made it a quick read. I can't say I enjoyed it as much as Sarah Crossan's other free verse novel ONE, but it was an okay read. I felt that the characterisation was lacking is places, perhaps due to it being such a sort read, so I felt that the characters and the romance were not as fleshed out as they could have been. Nicu is Romani, originally from Romania. I can't speak for this representation, but I was uncomfortable with how often the g**** slur was used, even when considering the context it was used in, as racism against Romani people is rife in Britain. The book featured this slur to highlight this racism - especially prevalent in a post-Brexit Britain - and while it was sometimes called out in the text, I still feel like it could be harmful to some readers. I liked the fact that Jess was a working class British girl, something we don't see very often in UKYA, but I didn't enjoy this book as much as I hoped, especially considering how much I loved Sarah Crossan's other novel.

Final Review (also appears at Once Upon a Prologue) Grave Mercy was one of the books I fangirled over the most in 2012; it was just beautiful, macabre, and unlike anything I'd ever read. I don't read much YA historical fiction but when I do, I tend to fall in love with whatever book I choose in that genre. I loved Ismae and Duval in Grave Mercy, and waited forever, and EVER for Dark Triumph. The publisher was generous enough to allow me to read an e-galley but as much as it pains me to say, I wasn't quite as enamored with Dark Triumph as I was with Grave Mercy. Dark Triumph picks up hot on the heels of Grave Mercy, and we see so many characters - good AND bad - and familiar events from the first book through Sybella's eyes. I think part of my problem is, although I loved Sybella, and wanted to hug her and protect her, because we only saw her from Ismae's point of view in Grave Mercy, I think I expected something MORE from her. She's a very sympathetic character, but she was built up so much in Grave Mercy, so for me she fell a little short of the mark in Dark Triumph. Maybe I was expecting her to still be "half mad from grief," as the synopsis alluded, but whatever was missing, I wrestled with my conflicting emotions about Sybella throughout Dark Triumph. That said, I DID like her - she's very fierce, and very loyal to those she cares about, which earned her lots of points with me. Dark Triumph was one of those books that I read slowly, because despite not clicking with Sybella as much as I wished, I was once again drawn right into Robin LaFever's gorgeous, heady writing, and brilliantly alive descriptions of Brittany, and various historical figures. My heart went out to so many characters - Beast, Duchess Anne, Sybella, Julian, and more. Dark Triumph hit me hard, and kept beating up my heart-strings. Plot-wise, Dark Triumph is a stellar read. The pacing is spot-on as in Grave Mercy, and never feels hurried; at the same time, I was never bored while reading Dark Triumph. Anne's perilous hold on her power has never been in more danger, and although a large portion of Ms Lafever's novel focuses on Sybella trying to survive in her father's household, there was still the over-reaching plot of Duchess Anne's struggles, which tied everyone together. We also learn more about Mortain, and the old religions, and what the convent's true purpose is. *cue sinister music* My heart went out to Sybella, seeing how she lived. A cossetted noblewoman on the surface, this facade hides Sybella's tortured childhood, her escape to the convent of Saint Mortain, and her return as an implant for the convent in her father's house. D'Albret is a monster, and I despaired, as did Sybella, if Mortain would ever marque him for the death he deserved. Robin LaFevers knows how to write her villains, her heroes, and her flawed characters. Amidst everything else going on, including Sybella questioning Mortain's purpose for her, there's a beautiful undercurrent of self-acceptance and romance in Dark Triumph. We're reunited with one of my favorite characters, Beast of Waroch. Beast is just unfettered, and wild, and I adored him. It was very lovely, seeing him come to care for Sybella, although I preferred the slow-burning affection between Ismae and Gabriel in Grave Mercy. Best and Sybella developed feelings for one another so quickly I could *almost* call it insta-love, which frankly, irritated me. But at the heart, what's between them was genuine, so I did like the romance. I have to mention Julian. Oh Julian. Right away I knew I was either going to love him or hate him, but I ended up getting so invested in him. He did terrible things, but dammit all to hell if I didn't end up tearing up a few times over him. Maybe it's because I read several books as a teen that showed character under intense duress where incest happened in a way I could support *only in the book, never in real life* or maybe it was just how tormented Julian was, but I couldn't help but believe he DID love Sybella. Oh, my heart though. It BROKE for Julian, especially as he finally started to see things from Sybella's point of view. Her memories of him as her protector throughout childhood contrasted with his love for her just killed me. They were so tragically beautiful. Dark Triumph wasn't quite the sequel the Grave Mercy I hoped it would be, but it was still a lovely read that I really did enjoy. And I have no doubts that I'll be adding a physical copy to my collection soon, while I wait - impatiently - for the third and final book!

3.5 stars, which ends up rounding up to 4 stars. I went into this book not really knowing what to expect, as it hadn't been recommended by anyone. I liked the idea of family relationships and secrets, hoping it would be something like The Nest. It was similar, though it didn't draw me in quite as much as The Nest. I still enjoyed it, though, as the characters were interesting and the writing style was wry and entertaining. I liked the sister relationships. I think Laurel was a very interesting character. I also liked the role that music played in this novel. The fact that the author didn't get into any overly mushy descriptions of the music was great-- it was a part of their life and its importance came through through the characters' behaviour, rather than saying something silly like "feeling the music pulsing through my veins" or something. This book was great on audio. Gretchen Mol was an excellent narrator. I think I would recommend this book to people who enjoyed reading The Nest by Cynthia D'aprix Sweeney, due to the similar feeling. This is not a book that I find myself ranting and raving about, but it was a nice simple diversion which is what I needed now. I was a bit confused by Sally's bipolar disorder. I didn't find that it really showed the classic symptoms, as there was more emphasis on the delusions about others and less delusions of grandeur, impulsive behaviour, and such. I suppose the symptoms may have been different than textbook cases due to the fact that she was on mood stabilizers... also, this was not a medical book but a fictional novel so perhaps I'm overanalyzing it. I really appreciate when books accurately represent medical conditions, though, especially mental illnesses. Overall, my skepticism of Sally's symptoms did not take away from my enjoyment of the book. Another spoiler: It was so creepy when Laurel's lies were unveiled! Ohhh yikes! I was worried she was going to kill the narrator or something but I suppose she was a scam artist, no necessarily a killer psychopath. I was surprised Mr. Clean turned out to be the random senile man, which was funny and a nice red herring from the author. I really thought it would be Laurel.

I don't really know what to think. I was really enjoying reading this until things started to pop up and become more and more apparent, and then my enjoyment went down hill. I don't want to rate this poorly because I did get some enjoyment out of it, but a lot of times there was moments that made me dislike the book, especially towards the end. This is not a spoiler free review. The gist of it: Branded is about this post apocalyptic/dystopian/corrupt world where a man only known as The Commander rules all and those who commit a sin (seven deadly sins; Sloth, gluttony, greed, pride, lust, wrath, and envy) are to be branded with a corresponding color collar and sent to a place called The Hole where they work according to a complex system that involves their sin. Lexi has been accused of the sin lust and is sent to The Hole where she is put to work in a hospital and for some reason has a guard named Cole assigned to her. To start off, it was really interesting. But then little things started to irk me, or pull me out of the story because it was stupid or just didn't make any sense. Lexi is branded with the collar color for lust and it seems like the guards and every other male only go to her to try to rape her because she's the most beautiful person in The Hole. This irked me and picked away at me the more it was made known that Lexi is THE most beautiful woman ever, but of course shes unaware of her beauty. Every story has to have that one girl. You know the girl, she's that cheerleader that for some reason picks on the protagonist, who bullies her and is mean to her for no reason, tries to steal the heroine's boy and is a colossal bitch. That girl who was only created to be hated. For Branded that girl was Amber, a nurse in the hospital who was flirtatious and was mean to Lexi for no other reason that I could see other than because Lexi's personal guard was Cole. Now, because Cole and Lexi are intended to be together we the readers must hate Amber because she's throwing a wrench in between them and is whispering seeds of doubt about Cole to Lexi and how she wouldn't satisfy him nor be able to keep his interest anyway. This girl in every book is the girl I end up rooting for because the protagonist does stupid things. Likewise, I hated how Lexi had this holier than thou type chip on her shoulder when it came to Amber. that because Amber was the way she was and Lexi was somehow more clean than her, purer, that she was better and a person who should judge Amber for just trying to survive in a world that fucks you over and laughs cruelly in your face when asked to take it easy. I hate slut shaming. This book's main thing is lust and slut shaming. Other sins and collars are mentioned but the main focus is on lust and slut shaming. How if you have premarital sex you're a slut, if you sleep with many people you're a slut. This lessened my enjoyment immensely. The world building. I don't know if it's me but I just couldn't imagine this world they are forced to live in. What is 'The Hole'? Where is it? what does it look like besides having nondescript alleys and buildings? Everything was so focused on Lexi, Cole, and the hospital that I had a hard time imagining what everything else looked like. I also don't understand why things are the way they are in the book. I'd have to reread some parts to really get an understanding. Speaking of the characters, They felt very flat. I didn't understand why the characters were the way they were, why everyone clicked so easily and was very trusting in such hard times. By the end Cole and Lexi quickly felt like cartoon versions of themselves. I didn't care for any of the characters except Keegan and Amber. Nothing that happened made me care for them, everything happened so fast with little explanation and time passed by so fast that it was hard to care. I really didn't care for Lexi. It seemed like the only thing she could do was vomit a lot and had to have everyone carry her places a lot of the times. It irritated me that she could never stand on her own two feet and had to be carried to places by these few guards who are miraculously well-meaning out of the many guards in this corrupt place. On the topic of them, why were they in love? I can't pin point a moment in the story where I could say that was the point where their feelings started to grow for one another. Their feelings for one another came out of no where and quickly made the story very sappy, which I feel is bad for the type of book this is. This book feels more like a romance story using the excuse of it being a dystopian setting to put Lexi and Cole together and that their romance was more of an important plot than what was happening to the world around them. I didn't even get the pleasure of being able to see their relationship evolve from a hostile,tense, and untrusting one to a forbidden and loving one. It was just there suddenly and for very little to no reason. SPOILER ALERT: a later plot device in the form of a long lost brother comes in and seems to be the second voice of reason, aside from Amber. Everything quickly got sugar coated with the two's quickly budding relationship and Keegan pointed out that they didn't love each other, of which I agree. As the story progressed to the end of the book everything felt immature, very puppy love like and high school love-ish. Keegan is very much the voice of reason and no one takes what he says seriously. Their love is be all end all and can't be deterred by silly things like corrupt politics and the very real threat of dying when/if their forbidden love is found out. Towards the end the story just got very over dramatic and it wasn't even about the corrupt world or anything like that, but instead it was over their relationship being questioned. There was some WTF moments, like when a man comes into Alyssa's (dying child Lexi befriends in the hospital) room for morphine, Lexi throws the chair out the window instead of hitting him with it. That literally made me pause from reading to just ponder, "What the fuck? Why?" Another one was when Lexi was assaulted by a group of four men and she blacks out. Cole and his dog Zeus save her, a Dr. named Sutton performs a rape kit on her and it determined that no only was she not raped, but that she was a virgin because it proved that she didn't have sex before, consented or otherwise. Not only would this not work because whatever assault that may or may not have happened to Lexi have happened too long ago, but that's not how rape kits work and I can't quiet suspend my disbelief that far when we're told very little about the world around them to believe that it's very technologically advanced that rape kits work this way, but they don't know what is causing people to die. Speaking of, I also didn't like how this bloodborne virus was never explained nor hinted at, it was just something that was there and killed Alyssa. Will it be explained in the next book? I don't know. Also, little things nagged at me, like using the word is when it should've been replaced with are, but that was very minor. Like I said, besides the things I couldn't quiet tolerate I really enjoyed this book and can't rate it poorly, even when the characters devolved to high schoolers fighting over if their love is real or not. I am unsure if I'll read the next book, but that's not because of the things mentioned, I just really suck at reading series to completion.

Main character, Philip Kent, finds himself in America working in a Boston print shop. Though he is a bastard son of British royalty, he must choose sides when he finds himself confronted with The Boston Tea Party and his personal dilemmas.

Have you ever felt betrayed by a writer before? It feels awful, right? It feels god damn awful. You can't believe in anything you read. If you want to know about the life of Lili Elbe, the wonderful, courageous woman - the first one ever to undergo a physical sex change, as she was born a male - then leave this book, leave it FAR behind, and run. Run to a reliable source and never turn your head around again. Do not read this book. If you, however, want to read a book that's barely loosely inspired by the story of Lili Elbe and is an encomium to the United States - then read this book. But then please do me a favour and never talk to me again. I'm so upset you have no idea. Now that it's out of the way, here's my review. I am going to be honest with you, and I am probably going to spoil you a thing or two, but I just want to make my point. I adored the story of Lili Elbe, I really did. I read into her actual story before starting this book, and then quit and then only continued to read Ebershoffs book because I wanted to compare the two stories afterward. The story could have been told in such a heart-wrenching way, could have brought tears to so many eyes, but it was so cold, reserved and distanced in a way that troubled me a lot. I know it is fiction, but with changing so many things from the real story (read below to find out), Ebershoff could have at least made up some dialogues between Lili and Gerda. He could have showed some intimate dialogues, some despair, some hope, some love - but he didn't. Ninety percent of the dialogue was utter rubbish and absolutely unnecessary for the plot. Or the characters. And God did Ebershoff fail to portray the characters. Lili Elbe was very courageous. Born as Einar Wegener, she lived the longest part of her life as a male. Einar Wegener married a danish - not american, goddamnit - girl named Gerda, and they lived on married for a long, long while, before Lilis transition into a female. Now, here's what bothered me most about Ebershoffs description of Gerda - Greta, as he called her. Gerda was Danish, and he made her American, with a complex backstory about some other man she married before Einar, and even a child she had with said American dude before he died, and made 'Greta' return from glorious, glooorious America to the ever-so-boring Denmark. Really, all Ebershoff seemed to care about was writing about the US. The US and I have never gotten along too well, so it was twice as much of a bother to me. There was so much more to Gerda than being an american woman that had married before, and now returned to Einar because well, what would a woman other do than run after men? Right? Ehw. Gerda loved Einar, and Gerda loved Lili. Isn't it just... the most wonderful thing you could think of? Loving a person no matter whether male or female - especially when the situation is really as extreme as it was for Lili and Gerda? Isn't this just provoking goosebumps on your arms? Was Gerda a lesbian? Was she bisexual? Did Gerda simply love Einar/Lili as the person they were? Who was Gerda? Who was she? Gerda was devastated when Lili died, and she only then decided to marry again, not before Lilis death, as the book stated. Some say she only got together with Einar because he was quite effeminate back then. I would have loved to learn more about the actual Gerda, about her erotic paintings, about her identity. And I hated that she was a flat, cut-out american stereotypical woman in the book, supporting Lili, but never showing the love she actually did as a real person. And I never complain about women being to flat, so mind that. Also, the ending. If you don't want me to spoil your reading pleasure (hah! A good joke, right) then quit right here. - When I read the ending, I knew that Lili must have died in real life. The ending is an open one, sort of - but it's also deceiving in a way I wouldn't have thought possible. All in all, the book sucks. The real story behind it is incredibly moving, brought tears to my eyes, and this book is just a travesty of it. I can't even bring myself to give it more than one star although the writing was good. You know, the words. But that was it.

You know those reviews that say, "If I could give it zero stars I would"? Yeah, this is gonna be one of them. So, we finally get all the answers we wanted - and nothing else. For me, a good story should leave the reader with questions. Not about the plot or the characters, but about the overall meaning and theme. For example, JK Rowling never does answer if Snape is a good person. She tells us he's a brave person through the words of one of her characters, but not if he's morally correct or not. That's left up to the readers. This book doesn't do that. Tris and Tobias were frustratingly preachy. Every chapter is filled with some sort of "wisdom" about the humanity. The thing is, all the preachy quips are obviously just the author's own opinions about the world. None of it fits the characters and it really pulled me out of the story. For example: "And now that you're out? How does the world seem to you?" "Mostly the same, people are just divided by different things, fighting different wars." This would have been wise, if the author had bothered for it to be in character, for it to fit the present situation, and if it was brought up later for the sake of something like consistency. But we didn't just get answers about 'what it means to be human' oh no we also got answers about 'what it means to be divergent'. Let me tell you something, if it was possible to murder books, I would have murdered this one on the basis of poor research and world building alone. This paragraph is where things get a little spoilery, not by much, just a little warning. At one point we're told about "murder genes" and how they're the cause of human aggression. Not long after that we're told that if you take away someone's low intelligience you take away their compassion as well. Yes, you read that right, apparently in order for someone to be nice they have to be dumb. Smart people are evil, I guess. This is the part that made me have to turn off my kindle and pace for about half an hour. This is such crap. Compassion, or treating people with understanding and kindness, comes from empathy. Empathy comes from you being able to relate to someone, to see things from their point of view. Do you think that if someone wasn't smart they would be able to do that? When the research is actually truthful, it's high school level. At some point we learn about the difference between memories of personal experience and memories of how to do things. The difference between remembering what the weather was on the first day of school and how to ride a book. We learn that those two types of memories are stored in difference types of the brain. This is passed off as very science-y and advanced and all I could think about was "I literally learned this in high school psychology class" I'm getting worked up again, so we're going to move onto the characters, or lack thereof. When I read Divergent, I saw that the characters could be dimensional, but there were two more books so I figured that they would develop into more complex people later on. Nope. As you probably know by now, this book is in both Tris and Tobias point of view. Every time the POV switched to Tobias I had a hard time remembering he wasn't Tris. The author obviously didn't know how to write this character beyond "badass boyfriend". For most of the book all we get out of Tobias is that he pities himself because of something revealed about his genetics. There is a giant ton of fake man-pain going on in this book. I was rolling my eyes so much I thought they were going to fall out. When he finally gets a grip on himself, he becomes so bland I almost wanted to the brooding man-child back. Almost. Then we have Tris who has somehow changed into a full on not-gonna-take-any-shit-from-nobody-cause-I'm-tough badass woman. I didn't believe any of it for a second. The author's idea of what makes a 'strong' character seems more to be of what makes a 'cool' character. Tris is trying too hard to prove to the reader that she's strong and I got sick of it real fast. There's really nothing to her beyond that. She's strong. That's it. Apparently she's smart too, but none of the scenes where she's supposed to be showing off her 'intelligence' convinced me because all of it was freaking obvious. Then we have the side characters. They all had exactly one personality trait and that was it, just like the first book. Nothing about them has changed. Characters like Cara, Christina and Uriah are just the smart one, the best friend, and the funny one. Characters like Peter and Evelyn make character changes that are so forced and fast I had whiplash. One paragraph they're one thing, and then the next they're another with no organic development. Remember how at the first book the conflict was about the factions all against each other? Then at the second book it was the factionless against the factions? We sort of get an answer to that conflict, but it happens off screen. Yes, that's right, what this entire trilogy has been building up to be was quickly tied up in a bow when we weren't looking. We find out more about Tris' mom and once again I didn't care. We find out more about the world outside the city and I didn't care. Tris at point thinks her parents would be ashamed of her, and I didn't care. Quite a few people die, and I didn't care. Character complexity and development needs to be the most important thing for a writer. If you don't give me a reason to like these characters beyond "This one is cool, this one has a tortured past, this one is sassy, this one is funny" I'm not going to like them. I'm definitely not going to care about what or who they do. TLDR: This book is full of the author's preachy opinions forced on us as 'wisdom', absolutely no character development, some of the worst worldbuilding I've ever seen, research that was done so poorly I had to stop reading to calm myself done, and an ending that is forced and overly-melodramatic. Don't read it. It will ruin the entire trilogy for you. I'm sure there's at least one fanfiction AU online, go read that. I'm sure it's written much better.

Well done Catherine; I'm convinced this is your best book yet! I had a fantastic time reading this story; the book is written in such an easy, readable manner, yet the story is a complex web of suspense, emotion, and deceit. The amount of effort behind such a flawless execution must have been immensely time consuming and brain melting; however, anyone who follows McKenzie knows how insanely brilliant and talented she is, resulting in pulling off a book that few could accomplish. Fractured is one of those books that doesn't easily fit in one genre; yes it is a mysterious and suspenseful tale to boot, but it is equal parts domestic fiction brimming with emotion and appeal to all genders. The mystery aspect had me completely fooled. I thought I knew where it was going and that I had it figured out but I was wrong. There's no greater pleasure for me in reading a mystery than when I've been duped and this gave me those feelings galore. At last count I've read 214 books in 2016, and I'd say about 70% of those would fall in the mystery/thriller/suspense category. This is in the maybe 10% that I didn't have figured out before the big reveal. I think this alone proves that McKenzie is a seasoned writer who knows how to fool her readers, even those who are proficient in the genre and become wary of books claiming to give the reader a good twist but utterly disappoint in the end. I also really enjoyed the layers and depth the author gave to her characters. The sole focus of the book isn't on any one aspect, so for me I found reading about the personal, dramatic relationships between characters just as enjoyable as the suspenseful scenes revolving around the mystery. My only complaint (and one only based on personal tastes, not quality of writing) was that I felt a few sections could have been shaved down a bit. If the page count had been lowered by 30-40 pages, I think this would have been a full 5 star read for me. Overall, I would highly recommend this book to mystery and fiction lovers alike. This is a rare instance where you find a compelling mystery and fleshed out characters in one book! I find it rare that a writer doesn't sacrifice one or the other in their tales, but Catherine has managed to include both, making this one of my favorite winter reads. Get your hands on this one; you don't want to miss out! As if she wasn't enough of a winner, the author has also published a companion novel as mentioned in the details above from the perspective of her main character Julie; this book is "the book" discussed in Fractured and I can't wait to pick it up as well to complete my reading experience! *I'd like to thank the author and publisher for my copy; it was a pleasure to provide an honest review in return.

In the dustbowl depression of 1930s America, the Joad family from Oklahoma move to California out of desperation, lured by the promise of a mythical land of endless food and well paid work that doesn't exist. For the first half of this book, I loved it. Steinbeck alternates each chapter between the Joads and a bigger picture of half the country on the move, hungry for work and hungrier for food. The travels along Route 66 were full of drama and tension and the characters well developed. It was a delight to travel along with them, poor and desperate as they were, dignified in their poverty, hoping as they did that they would find what they were looking for...but knowing that they wouldn't, hoping at least for some resolution for them. Some of the writing was beautifully poetic, especially in the wider-world chapters. It was when they arrived in California that the story crumbled and stalled. There were long passages that went like this: Tom pushed open the matchbox and took out a match. He struck the match against a piece of sandpaper and took the flame carefully to the lantern, and lit the lantern with the fragile yellow dancing flame. The lantern lit with a mellow dancing light against the walls of the shack. Tom sat back and warmed his hands on the feeble heat coming from the lantern. How about we try this, Mr Steinbeck...? Tom lit the lantern from a match and sat back, warming his hands on the feeble heat coming from it, the light dancing on the walls. ...and then we can get on with the story. How would that be? No? Okay then, I'll sit through the same drawn out descriptions every time someone does something, no matter how minor. When that happened throughout the last third of the book, it really dragged it down. Steinbeck also decided that he only really needed two characters (Ma and Tom), and the rest drop into the background and become two dimensional and superfluous. He might as well have killed the rest on the journey to California for the impact they have in the story. And the ending. Well, it just...ends. There are no conclusions, and we never find out what happens to the family. It's like Steinbeck died halfway through and didn't finish the story. In fact, I just checked online to see if my copy was missing a dozen pages. Nope. Here's how sucky the ending is (Skip it if you don't want spoilers): The Joad's are flooded out of their shack of the week, and they come across a barn. Rose of Sharon (huh? ), who has just undergone a still-birth, gives an un-named starving man her breast milk. The End. WTF was THAT? After four hundred pages, some of the most wonderful and poetic language, that's IT? Do the family starve? Do they drown? Do they go back to their shack after it dries out? Would it have killed him to write an epilogue? At that point I was glad to finish the damn thing and be done with it. No more Steinbeck for me. After the flat characters of "Of Mice and Men" and making me care about a desperate family and then leaving me hanging, he's had his chance.

I have never been this unimpressed with a Margaret Atwood novel. MaddAddam is a tedious slog through the events of Oryx and Crake - again. While this technique worked incredibly well in The Year of the Flood, providing context for much of the events and letting the female characters flip Jimmy's story on its head, MaddAddam totally fails to provide anything new or interesting in its backstory. (My 'reading' was done via audiobook, and the actor's voices, nuances, and inflections did nothing to keep me interested.) You might think that, now that all of the characters have met up after the end of the world, there would be some forward momentum in the present-day. You would be wrong. If you're interested in what happens to Jimmy, the erstwhile protagonist of the first novel, or any of the characters from the second novel - Toby, Ren, or Amanda - then you are going to be sorely disappointed. Toby's arc during this book is particularly terrible, but Ren and Amanda only escape this fate because they spend most of their time offscreen. Jimmy spends most of the novel in a coma. In fact, the entire plot of the present-day revolves around the Crakers and the Maddaddamites defending themselves from two rogue Painballers. It's just as boring as it sounds. Even if you're reading MaddAddam to be further immersed in the dystopian world that Margaret Atwood created in Oryx and Crake, you'll probably still be disappointed. 75% of this novel takes place in the past, rehashing Zeb's life in the pleeblands and his relationship with Adam One. There are a few interesting new additions to the world, but the vast majority of Zeb's activities are tied to the other books' plot lines; his story just retells what you already know. Finally, the writing in this book is just plain bad. There are a couple moments where the prose recalls the first two books, but they are few and far between. The metaphors have all been done before. The characters are flat and static. The Craker story sections are beyond painful. The pacing is puzzling. It's just one big mess. I don't recommend it, unless you absolutely need to read it, and cannot go without the closure.... I was plain bored of Zeb's 1940's-style of speaking, endless jobs that have nothing to do with furthering his character, and Toby's endless jealousy, and worrying about losing Zeb.

Some Girls Bite is "a breath of fresh air" UF with bits of "isn't that always the case" romantic situations. Eight months ago the vampires of Chicago announced their existence to the world. "The Chicagoland Vampires" are made up of three houses: Navarre (the oldest house), Cadogan and Grey. Only the master of each house has the privilege of turning new vampires. There are twelve houses in the US; Cadogan is the fourth-oldest among them. Merit, a 27 year old college student, was attacked by a vampire on campus one night. Ethan Sullivan, the 394 year old master of the Cadogan house, found her and chose to "save" her by turning her. Merit's none to pleased about this. Her best friend and roommate, Mallory, however, is excited. Mal has always had a passion for all things supernatural, a true "Fang Hag". All organized like, the house makes her family and roomie aware of her attack and let's them know that she is recuperating and will be home soon. Merit is the daughter of the wealthy and famous Joshua Merit. He's always treated Merit as nothing but a disappointment. Her new vampiric status doesn't help matters at all. The fact that she has lost everything she's worked so hard for and that she now has to swear allegiance to the vampire that "took it away" is too much for Merit. It takes her a bit to adjust to "Merit 2.0". During the days leading up to her initiation ceremony, she meets "Darth Sullivan" and realizes hating him is going to be a problem. She reconnects with her grandfather, the only person in her family that truly cares for her. Along the way we are introduced to the arrogant, sarcastic sorcerer, Catcher and adorable shifter, Jeff. She also meets another vampire, Morgan, who, over drinks and dancing at a local club, makes it clear that she's not the only one feeling the connection between them. All the while, other humans are being attacked and killed. Each one being blamed on one of the vamp houses. The group tries to find out who is killing the innocents while trying to keep the fact that rogues exist, let alone might responsible for the killings, out of the press. I loved this book and am anxious to move onto book 2! The chapter names were a hoot. Ex: "Fangs mean never having to say you're sorry" and "There's not much wrong that chunky monkey can't fix". Favorite Quotes: "...Shifters are happy. They're people; then they're animals; then they're people again. What's not to be happy about? They live with their friends. They drink. They ride their Harleys. They party in Alaska. They have hot shifter sex." "I'm going to worm my way into your life, Merit" "Uh-huh. Let me know how that works out for you." "Hey, you're missing out. I've got mad skills."

TWD runs like a bad soap, predictable in the sense that every time they find somewhere "safe", guess what? ZOMBEH TIME. Or typical idiot redneck time, I'd actually say the zombies were much better. It certainly has enough sex, annoying drama and cheating to make this a soap, just with zombies and extra dying. I'm bashing this a lot, but I'm rather disappointed with how it turned out, I honestly thought it would be amazing, not just drama with zombies. TWD is at the best mediocre, if this was a novel I wonder whether it would've gotten published or not. (Probably would have actually...) And I know others have mentioned this, but the art is so different between chapter 1 and chapter 2... (original artist left the project) and it got worse. Charlie Adlard's drawing just look so... thick; I'm tempted to try blurring and darkening it in photoshop to see if it can get even more heavy-handed. It is post zombie apocalypse, so maybe the darkness was intentional, I just wish it would lighten up sometimes in the happier scenes. An okay read, wouldn't recommend buying it since it's so expensive, just borrow it to read yet another work of popular culture.

Wtf was up with this hero? Don't get me wrong, I loved how flawed and three dimensional he was. He felt like a fleshed out character and I fully enjoyed following his story as he tried to deal with his abuse and the effect on his life it had. But dear god what COULDN'T he do? He was a rock star, a UFL fighter, an adrenaline junky, and he could paint VERY WELL. There was just too much that he excelled at and it was fucking annoying. I wouldn't be surprised if it turned out he was also a god damn fire fighter/doctor/hockey player/Olympic gold medalist. I get having a hobby or two but people don't usually excels so well at them that they're considered PROFESSIONALS. Mainly because the things he's "so very good at" take a lot of time and dedication if you want to be good let alone be recognized: being in a band takes up a LOT of someone time (promoting your band, gigs, practice, composing music, recording music if you get to that level or fame, etc), being a PROFESSIONAL fighter takes up a lot of someone's time (training, working out, diet, promoting, etc). You can't be both of those things, be good at both of those things, and have time for friends/family/outside shit other than sleeping. And he seemed to have an abundance of time to agonize over his past and fawn over Mac despite his double profession. To top it all off he was mentally not in a good position to be as successful as he was. He just wasn't. It made what was a really good story on it's own come off unbelievable. There was just NO need for the hero to be a professional fighter, it could have been a hobby or vise versa when it came to him being in a band. But no. He's not only amazing at both those things he's a WELL PAID PROFESSIONAL in both of them as well. Every time they were brought up I wanted to roll my eyes right out of my skull. It was like the author wanted to shove as much interesting things onto Rex to overcompensate for his less than savory background and the things he struggled with: "He's broken but hey look at least he's also a rockstar/UFL fighter!!!!" I didn't need that. The character and the story were interesting enough without the try hard double profession. It was unnecessary. But then that's just me.

I have no idea how to rate this! While it's certainly important to have read "To Kill a Mockingbird," this is a much different book. It's not a inspirational tale of grand rightings-of-wrongs; in fact, there's not much of a plot at all. It's really a story of homecoming, of seeing a familiar place and familiar people with newly adult eyes, of seeing the humanity behind the childhood saints. At the same time it's intensely rooted in a certain time and place and political setting, the post Brown v. Board era in the South. The conversations between Scout and Atticus are dense, rambly and sometimes really troubling. In fact, "really troubling" is sort of a recurring theme here as Scout observes her hometown and interacts with long-familiar people, finding so much disturbing in what she took for granted. Like Scout, I'm really not sure how I feel about any of it, and probably like Scout, I'm not even sure how I feel about the uneasy understanding she comes to in the end. Maybe that's the real profound statement of the novel, the uneasy understandings we come to as adults about issues that seemed so clear-cut in childhood. Vague not-really-a-spoiler about things I hope transpired after the end of the book: I hope and suspect that she returned to NYC at the end of her sojourn and even more than that, really hope she didn't end up marrying Cal. Because no.
