Buddy read with fellow Sanderson fans Robin, Athena and Alexa. This is easily one of the best novellas I have read in a long time. Despite its length I actually felt as though I was reading a full length novel. In so few pages I felt as though I really came to know Shai and Gaotona. There was also surprising depth to the magic system, which as usual intrigued me very much. The gist of it is that certain people, Forgers, can create near perfect copies of an object through rewriting its history. Shai has been imprisoned in the palace for her crimes, awaiting her inevitable execution but then an unexpected opportunity arises. The Emperor barely survived an assassination attempt. Unfortunately while his wounds healed, his mind was damaged irreparably. The Arbiters who rule in the Emperor's stead decide to comission Shai to recreate the Emperor's soul, filling his empty shell with a copy, a fake. An impossible task, considering it is practically unheard of but Shai rarely backs away from a challenge. I really enjoyed Shai's quick witted nature and cleverness. I've noticed that Brandon Sanderson has a tendancy to write strong, witty females but it never gets old. Hoid is also mentioned in passing in this novella. If you read the deleted scene it all becomes clear. I admit that I was quite pleased to spot him on my own for once! If you haven't come across Sanderson's work before this could easily be a great place to start. It's short with a compelling magic system and a fantastic read. Whilst it is set in the same world as Elantris, the two stories share almost nothing in common. Neither will spoil the other. I am once again very much impressed with Sanderson's ingenious storytelling.

** spoiler alert ** Things I liked: Zombies. I like zombies. In our age of obsessive vampire-worshiping when bloodsuckers tread freely through the pages of horror stories and mushy teenage girl's romances, zombies are quite refreshing. There is nothing even remotely sexual about zombies. In fact, they are everything we fear about death. Death not as just the beginning of another great adventure, but death as the end, the end in its most unseemly irrevocable sense. Death as the absence of conscience; death as slowly decomposing, rotting away until nothing is left of you or your loved ones; death as a realization that the corpses of those close to you are just that - corpses - and not a trace of people you treasured can be found, though the resemblance is uncanny. Death as being sworn into muteness, trapped in the body that is gradually falling apart, deaf and blind to anything, but this terrible ever-present need, craving. For brains life. Carry Ryan does a good job painting a realistic end of the world scenario. As long as we are open-minded enough to consider zombies realistic, of course. Small groups of survivors are forced to live behind the fences while those supposed to lie 6 feet under walk the earth with their eyes half-rotten. At first, there might have been a communication system - a web of intricate fenced pathways - between humanity's few last strongholds, but as the numbers of the undead grew, such system must have become difficult to maintain and then the day came when the benefits of sustaining these already threadbare connections were no longer worth the risk. Perhaps, there was a falling out between habitants of different communes - a quarrel over supplies or weapons or resources, there might have been plenty of reasons - and the connections were cut. It's not hard to imagine that one of the strongholds was taken down - fences breached, people infected. It must have been hard to those still on the right side of the fences to watch their neighbors turn or die, but there is no cure and nothing they can or could do, but watch with the gates closed. One way or other, the strongholds were separated and left on their own they slowly began to degrade. There was no time to preserve the knowledge and techniques of old; no time and no use for science brought no reassurance, no remedy. Moreover, it might have been th science that caused the Return. And so people turned to faith, to religion. Because there was nothing left but to hope and to believe. It took three generations of survivors for humanity to return to a christianized version of matriarchy. Things I disliked: The fact that realistic end of the world scenario is as much Carry Ryan's as it is mine. Every so often I needed to stop reading and try to come up with an explanation as to why things are the way they are. There are too many gaps and not enough details. I appreciate when the author makes readers work, makes them pay attention and keeps them guessing to the very end, but there is a limit after which a story stops being a story and turns into a writing exercise. Love triangles. I don't know what is wrong with YA fiction, but this particular routine is always the same. One girl and two boys instantly in love with her. It's hard to say why they are in love with her though, for she is selfish, needy, infantile, obsessed and mostly useless all through the book. And since the story is told from the first person point of view, the reader is forced to sit through her endless whining which pretty much sums up to: "I love Travis and Travis loves me, but I'm forced to marry Harry and - surprise,surprise! - Harry loves me too!" It's never explained why she loves Travis. As far as I'm concerned she lusts after him, of that there is solid evidence, plenty of it all through the book, but love? Not really. It's hard to love somebody who has no personality whatsoever. To tell the truth, most of the characters seem to suffer from no-personality syndrome. General lack of the plot. Technically, there is a plot, but... let's put it this way: there is a girl who lives in a small world with rigid borders and strict rules, she feels unfulfilled and miserable and a little rebellious and often finds herself wishing for something different, something otherworldly. What do you think will happen? Eventually, she will get out. Well, unless you are reading Kafka and in that case I pity the girl because she is stuck with the castle forever. I think that Carry Ryan didn't explore all these plot-lines she had set. Too many questions left unanswered and too many issues just glazed upon, but never resolved.

I really, really enjoyed this book. There are critiques I could make about the writing (there was a lot of telling and some fuzzy head-hopping), and there were some annoying structural parallels to Twilight in the beginning (shy, unassuming girl gets dragged into the center of a super-powered family, has romance with beautiful boy who must resist touching her). Those aside, though, the story is engrossing. I loved the way Greek mythology was threaded through everything; it made me want to pull out Hamilton's Mythology and read through everything again (also oh my god, I just realized, what if she named Helen after Edith Hamilton?! Brilliant!). Helen felt like a very real heroine, one who despite being freakishly strong is also fundamentally peaceful, and I really liked that juxtaposition. Angelini juggles a large cast of characters well, and the pacing! This is a long book, nearly five hundred pages, but the ups and downs are masterfully crafted, and plot action is balanced well with family and romantic drama. And speaking of romantic drama--if you've read about my editing loves over on the B&BD blog, you know that Lucas and Helen's forbidden, hands-off romance is right. up. my. alley. On a more serious note, this book is also very frank about teenage sexual desire in a really nice, non-judgmental way, and I appreciated it very much. In fact, the line "We're talking about you and Lucas and the importance of condoms" had me laughing out loud for at least a minute, which is a very long time to be laughing out loud. I'm late to the party on this book, since it was published almost three years ago, but better late than never! I liked it a lot, and I recommend it highly.

I received this book in a Goodreads Giveaway. Which may or may not have affected my enjoyment of it. Remembering how I won this book has also prompted me to enter a million book giveaways on Goodreads in the hopes of getting lucky once again. I received this book about two years ago, so it's about time that I read and reviewed it. I think part of why it took me so long to read this book is that I don't really read romance books (and it is definitely a romance book...more on that later). But I entered the giveaway because the image of a pie on the cover and the description on the back sucked me in. I love the show Pushing Daisies and the movie Waitress, and I love pie in general, so I figured this could be right up my alley. Delectable definitely had the cuteness and quaintness I was expecting, along with the fun addition of a Montana cowboy/cowgirl feel. I liked the length of the book, and I liked the gimmick of having the main characters bake a pie and then including the recipe at the end. I also liked that the story focused around healing a broken marriage. BUT. I didn't like how the author chose to fix the broken marriage. Instead of focusing on communication and changing behaviors, the focus was on the physical attraction between the main characters. The ending was unsatisfying because the characters had realized their flaws, but seemed destined to repeat their mistakes. Perhaps the ending is a more realistic one, but does anyone read romance novels for their realism? Also, I wasn't expecting it, but this book also had the most romance book-ish scene. I won't describe it because I want to keep this review appropriate for all ages, but is every romance book obligated to have one of those? I couldn't get the image of the author's face out of my mind while reading it, which really grossed me out. In the end, though, I still mostly liked this book. I'm not really sure why, considering how I feel about the resolution of the story. I might have been won over by the idea of pie, or by the fact that I won it. Regardless, I think this book would be good for someone who likes romance novels and wants something short and sweet to read on a plane trip (you could finish it by the time you landed). The author set things up for the sequels in a great way, but I won't be reading them. I don't think romance is my genre.

I love Neil Gaiman's Sandman so much that I am desperate to love the rest of his work, but I can't do much more than like it because it's mostly only okay. He deals with all the stuff I love -- mythology, the occult, death, dreams, the urban fantastic -- but he's too tongue-in-cheek. When I read one of his novels, I feel like I'm reading the Nick Hornby of fantasy. Too clever, too hip and too cool for his own good. It's not that I don't like his prose work. I do. And I even love some of it (like Wolves in the Walls, if that counts, and Stardust), but when I get to what should be the meat of his oeuvre, American Gods and its sequel, i can't help feeling let down. It's not that I don't like his characters. Mr. Nancy, Spider and Fat Charlie are pretty groovy; the book reads fast and is entertaining; I even dig the ending, but somehow none of that is enough. I want more from Neil. I want to be dazzled, and he teases me with bedazzlement constantly, but I've only been dazzled by Dreams -- nothing else has come close. And maybe that's my problem right there: having found Gaiman through Sandman, everything that's followed pales in comparison. I am always looking for greatness, and all I get is pretty good. So if you read this review, Neil, just know that I love you, and I will always read you, and I am constantly looking for that drug-like hit I had the first time I bought a Sandman comic (and yes I am that old) and was blown away by your storytelling. You are a victim of your own best work. Please, please, please blow me away again.

If I Stay is a beautifully written book. That goes without saying. I hate describing why I like a book, because it seems that my pitiful description can never come close to the real thing. So I won't try here, because lord knows that so many others have already written glowing reviews about this novel. But despite the fantastic writing I have to give this only 3 stars, possibly 2.5. Yes, the story is heartbreaking and powerful at times. Unfortunately I was unable to fully believe or relate to Mia. As we know from the synopsis, this story revolves around high school senior Mia as she hangs out in limbo, trying to decide whether she should fight to stay in this life, or leave for the next one. The reader is given a brief glimpse of Mia and her family before a terrible car accident. After the accident, Mia's spirit hovers near her real life body and flashes back and forth between what is really happening and memories about her family, friends and life. Forman's writing is so good and so captivating that it took me nearly midway through the book to realize what a truly blessed life Mia has. She comes from a long line of loving, supportive family members who not only embrace individuality and rebellion but encourage it. Mia's parents are so cool, so supportive... she has a great relationship with her little brother... an amazing best friend... an even more amazing boyfriend....and is loaded with musical talent. Her life is certainly charmed, and I have to credit Forman for not making it glaringly obvious or sticky sweet. It's not something that is really evident at the beginning of the story. Rather, as the story continues the reader is aware of how rare and magical Mia's life is. And it is hard to see why Mia wouldn't stay. The girl has had a life free of conflict. Her hardest times stem from personal insecurities, rather than outside influences. Her only real conflict (up until the time of the accident) was deciding between a scholarship to Julliard, or to remain in Oregon so she is closer to her soon-to-be-a-punk-rock-star boyfriend. Oh, the choices! Yeah ~ it is tough to choose between personal goals and love... especially intense, hormone driven teen love. But even here, Mia's parents tell her they will support her decision either way and don't even try to influence her one way or the other. Initially, I simply didn't understand Mia's battle between fighting to live or letting go. My life isn't half as charmed as hers and I can't imagine giving up. Even when Mia is in a coma in ICU, her friends and family tell her it is ok if she wants to "go" This girl has been supported, coddled and loved by everyone her whole life. Perhaps that is why it is so hard for her to deal with a real issue? Regardless, the one flaw in If I Stay was its lack of flaws. In writing such a perfect world, family and friends Forman made it too difficult for me to identify with her protagonist.

I loved Kell and Rhy's development as it was great to see more complexity added to the characters, especially in Rhy's case - I'm thankful that Schwab has moved him away from the stereotypical flirty, party prince and given him more depth. But then again, it's not surprising as Schwab is fantastic when it comes to writing complex characters. But now on to the bad, which unfortunately for me was almost the entire plot. Apart from a few twists and turns that I genuinely saw coming, the plot to 'A Gathering of Shadows' is extremely slow and boring. The whole novel felt like filler. I never thought I'd see the day when I called a magic tournament dull but in this book it was. Schwab used this event as the main setting for the novel and plot but yet rushed through every scene involving the fights themselves. As a result the whole story felt slow, and off putting. I suppose I enjoyed it, but not as much as I should have. It did however have those moments of brilliance - Lila's flashbacks to her magic lessons, the emotion in every scene with Kell and the King, the drama in 'White London' - which were its saving grace in a way and cause me to rate it much higher than it really deserves. I will be reading 'A Conjuring of Light' but my hopes have been dashed for the greatness of this series to be honest.

EVERNEATH is a young adult fiction based on Greek Mythology, about the life of seventeen year old Nikki Beckett. Last spring she disappeared, leaving behind a father, brother and Jack the quarterback best friend/'love of her life'. After a hundred years in the 'everneath' glued to the body of a very hot eternal boy called Cole (who drains her of her life force), she returns to her home where only months have passed. She is given six months to say goodbye before she will be once again sucked into the underworld, but this time a much darker pit of hell awaits her. So...I didn't hate this book and I didn't love it. I read it in one sitting and skipped very little of it, which means it wasn't totally terrible. But there where too many incongruities with the character choices and world building that left me unconvinced. The things I loved where: Jack and his relationship with Nikki. Their love was convincing and touching, it was built up over a long time and based on friendship, rather than the usual angsty instalove. The things that left me feeling rankled: First of all I actually find the whole concept unconvincing. The idea that there is this whole underworld where immortals take people and suck of their souls for a hundred years to then live for another hundred years is a bit odd. I think with these bizzarro concepts you can go as crazy as you like so long as I could see them conceivably happening...like in the Matrix when the computers take over and use us as an energy source, well the reason it was so popular was because it was conceivable. Just lightly using some old Greek Myths was not enough for me. Cole, well he was a bad boy biker/rocker with no feelings...but he is supposed to be in love with Nikki. I was totally unconvinced. I felt like his personality was not fluid or developed and he didn't act like an immortal. NIKKI BECKETT HAD NO PERSONALITY. Well she was just a very average teenager riddled with self doubt and her main trait seemed to be never ending selflessness! Well I know that selflessness is good, but only up to a certain point...eventually the reader is unable to relate. Because everyone has a desire to live life a little and feel like they deserve some happiness! But no, not our Nikki, she forsakes all her own happiness and I find this BORING. The story line about the 'Daughters of Persephone' along with the Meredith story and the other side characters like their teacher and the professor all seemed like they where just added to beef out the story and make it a bit more than just a love story. In reality the only good part of this book is the love story between the quarter back and his best friend Nikki. The memories of when he first saw her, Nikki's shyness and their eventual relationship was sweet in a very very conventional sort of way.

1.5 stars I didn't like the first of the series and wouldn't have continued it on my own, but my book club wanted to read this one too--I'm not that much of a masochist. Although I have been known to enjoy an occasional hate-read, 1000+ pages in less than a month is more than I would think to subject myself to. This book is better than the first volume in some ways and worse in others. It is more boring than the first in the series; however, it contains fewer overt and glamorizing mentions of controlling and abusive relationships. In my book, this alone means that it is better and that is why there is an increase in ratings. However it does still have some awful awfulness: For instance, when Matthew tells Diana about the non-consensual sex he had with his first wife? (To be clear, he is the initiator.) And Diana's reaction is basically "I don't believe you because your mom told me you LOVED each other"? And then Matthew's like, "She [my ex] was BROKEN and HAD NO WILL." Wow okay rude. Or how about the time when Matthew's like "YOU HAVE SECRETS" and then Diana's like, "No I don't!!" And Matthew lets it drop that if he drinks blood from her heart vein then he would know all her secrets, so she's like "I don't have any secrets Matthew, drink my heart vein blood even if it means you might lose control and kill me! I trust you with my literal life even though you don't trust me to tell you what happened today!!" It's kind of like how controlling boyfriends get really jealous to the point where their partner is just like "Nothing is going on with my male friends and to prove it to you I will never see them again!" because that's easier to deal with than the glowers and moods and tempers. (Note: People who aren't boys/men can engage in that behavior too.) And actually on the heels of recounting that I'm going to bump its rating down a half star. The writing is still...sorely in need of an editor. It's true that certain things that bugged me in the first book--descriptions of every glass of wine, piece of cheese, change of clothing--have been left out. In fact, I do believe that Diana's lock of stray hair, my third favorite character (after Ysabeau, who is pretty cool, and Juliette, who in the first book tried to kill Matthew), wasn't allowed a single appearance in this volume :'( Instead, we get a different kind of "too much." There are ninety-three named characters in this book. Ninety-three. I know I'm in danger of coming off as a dick here, but Deborah? You're out of control. You cannot manage ninety-three named characters. Few could, which is why it's ridiculous that you attempted it. A minor character is introduced; you don't mention her for hundreds of pages; and then in the middle of an off-hand sentence it's just, "blah blah blah, lavender [or whatever] for Susanna blah prattle blah." Wait who? I'm a careful reader and I have a good memory but the book is awfully, awfully padded with all kinds of irrelevant people, conversations, and happenings. Subplots are born and play out and die and we get nothing of substance from any of it, nothing is added to the plot. It's a very simple story but Harkness tries to trick the reader into thinking it's complex by just dumping this kind of stuff on them. So much of what happens in this book is not related to the plot and in many cases is not even historical (which, to me, would make it excusable). As in the first book, the good stuff--the weaving and the spells and the witchy learnings--is left almost entirely to our imagination even though it's supposedly the whole point of this book's let's-visit-Elizabethan-England plot. We learn very little about magic or the intrigue and the bad guys' motives; we lack an understanding of the lore and world-building type stuff that's supposed to undergird the whole thing. The characters also lack any sense of urgency or danger, which I find really odd considering the circumstances. It's very underwhelming. All the characters are static. Hardly anything important happens and what does is contrived and forced. Moments of actual import that a good writer would milk for tension are left wanting or written out completely. For instance, when Matthew breaks into Rudolf's castle and steals the book and Diana is at home waiting to see how it goes?? That would be some intense stuff! Instead, we get the conversation before Matthew leaves the house and then it cuts straight to: "'You got it!' I cried. Annie and I were waiting on the first floor. We had small bags packed with traveling essentials." Um...wut? Before they left everyone was like, o no where will it even be, is it even possible, I don't know this is really dangerous guys. It's skipped entirely and here's Matthew sauntering through the door and talk about luggage and servants. No worry and anxiety ramping up, no wondering about the safety of the child involved in the heist, no fretting and agitation, no hugging or thanking fortune/fate/superhuman speed for the favorable outcome--it's all just so flat. Instead we get rambunctious street urchins and overactive dogs! Forever discovering your hiding places and running around noisily! Haha, kids, they tease each other and have nightmares and none of this is connected to anything important, they're just vehicles to show us how thoughtful Diana is or how sweet Matthew can be. We have to be explicitly told this stuff because it's really not obvious from the way they interact with each other. Anyway... I didn't mean to, but I also wound up ranting about the awful subplot at the end with Christopher Marlowe and Louisa trying to kill Diana (and almost succeeding) and then her "forgiving" them "because as long as Matthew blames you for what happened to me, a part of him remains with you. Forever." Okay, 1) Forgiving someone after they do what "Kit" and Louisa did is not necessary and may not be healthy, especially so soon after the fact. 2) Why would Diana forgiving them cause Matthew to stop blaming them? They are actually different people, and even though they are unhealthily attached, Diana deciding to forgive does not actually oblige or force Matthew to feel the same way. 3) Matthew should blame them for what happened as it is actually kinda their fault. Diana never explains why it isn't, either. 4) That "logic" is really stupid in any case. Why would a "part of [Matthew] remain with [Kit]. Forever" if he blames him for something? Parts of us remain with everyone forever because we have memories and our experiences affect us. Like, that incident and Kit are probably going to remain with Matthew regardless of where or if he places the blame. This is a cultural myth about "forgiveness" that really gets under my skin: that to move on from something harmful, you must forgive someone; it is the only way forward. Or that it's the compassionate and wise thing to do. I don't buy into it. Forgiveness can be great and wise and healing, and refusing forgiveness can be too. There's also a difference between forgiving someone (which is not always necessary or desirable) and simply not letting their actions control you or become a point of obsession (which I do think is necessary for the most part). Compulsory forgiveness can be potentially more controlling and damaging than just not ever forgiving someone . All right, I think that hits most of my low points! As for high points: The book is readable. It's almost 600 pages and I finished it in about four days, which means something must have been pushing me on besides pure obligation. Sometimes I really crave brain candy--you know, "guilty pleasure" stuff--and this would fit that bill except I don't find any pleasure in Matthew and Diana's relationship, which is what the entire series is unfortunately focused on. And then my irritation at that starts tainting everything else. I can definitely see the appeal of it but we're just not well matched.

I bought this book in December 2014 in a book fair. I bought it because everyone kept talking about it and it was big and I love big books (and I cannot lie LOL). For months, it just sat there, on my shelf, between Love in a Headscarf and Scarlett, staring at me, collecting dust, taunting me to read it, mocking me because somehow I couldn't bring myself to go through with it. Occasionally, it will disappear into some friends' place who'll return it not long after, reluctant to part with the book and vowing to get a copy of their own because, dammit, this book deserves to be on everyone's shelves. But still, I couldn't bring myself to start with it. I wanted to, believe me, I did. But I didn't. Basically, for months, my mind split into two and went like this: Me #1: Read it. Go on! All your friends are saying what an amazing read it is! Me #2: I will. Me #1: Now! Me #2: I'll read Scarlett first. Me #1: Now that you're done, read The Book Thief, dammit! Me #2: Wait, there's I've Got Your Number. Me #1: NOW you can read it. Me #2: But...but... I have to watch Hugh Laurie pop pills and save lives! Me #1: EVERYONE SAYS IT'S SUCH A GREAT BOOK SO WHY DON'T YOU READ IT YOU PIECE OF SHIT?!?!!!!!!!one!!! Me #2: Jeez. Don't get your panties in a twist! I said I'd read it, didn't I? Me #1: *breathes heavily* And this of course continues on for six whole months, with me reading so many other books and binge watching rom-coms, Boys over Flowers, House MD and Game of Thrones, staring at the wall and basically being a huge-ass procrastinator. Come summer 2015 and finally, finally! I pull down The Book Thief from my shelf, crack open the spine and start my journey with death (who's the narrator, BTW), ready to be mind-blown. Except I don't. Get mind-blown, I mean. Don't get me wrong, I liked the writing style. And I especially loved the descriptions of everything, the imagery that the author used. The descriptions of the colours of the sky were the best. The narrator is somewhat of a rambler. Well, kind of. A lot of insignificant details were included and this would have been somewhat adorable had the book been short (or a poem, even). Instead, halfway through the book in and I'm still waiting for something to happen. Enters the Jew and things finally starts to look up. No longer do I have to wake up every morning and force myself to read a page or two of the book before I can do other interesting stuff because that's what happened for the first few days. I manage to finish reading the book in no less than a month, and by the time the story ends, I'm absolutely in love with Max and Papa and Leisel. Maybe it's because I've been with the characters a long time (with the book being long and my reading being slow). Or maybe it was just the writing style of the author. Or maybe it was both. Whatever it was, when everybody dies (well, nearly), and the book ends, I cried like I've never cried before. And then I sat there staring into space for an hour straight. And then, at night, I spent hours on the bed. Mourning. Reflecting. Reliving. Aching. All the while being overwhelmed. Overwhelmed in all senses of the word with feelings I can't even give name to. The characters' impact o me can be aptly described by this beautiful quote. Sort of: "There are certain people who come into your life and leave a mark. I'm talking about the ones who, for whatever reason, are as much a part of you as your own soul. Their place in your heart is tender, like a bruise of longing, a pulse of unfinished business. Just hearing their names pushes and pulls at you in a hundred ways, and when you try to define those hundred ways describe them even to yourself, words are useless. If you had a lifetime to talk, there would still be things left unsaid." - Sweetheart. Worth mentioning: Also, I fell for a certain almost-goofy 14 year old with hair the colour of lemons.

Even though I could already figure out what the mystery was behind Serena's death, it was interesting seeing it all play out, despite the mess I had to read through to get to the meat of the story. Left Me Wanting More: I didn't care for any of the characters. Final Verdict: I was hoping for a bit more gore and horror, but I got more annoying characters and random moments. 3.5 stars Not what I was expecting. I didn't love it as much as I did the first book, but it was still enjoyable. Review originally posted at http://fictionvixen.com/review-hearta... Eddie Molina and Jimmy Rafferty have worked alongside each other for years at the J-Bar Ranch. Close friends and work partners who pretty much spend all their time together and know everything about the other. Or so they thought. When their boss, Malloy, falls in love with the new hand and decides to live his life out and proud all of a sudden everything at the ranch starts to change. Now Eddie's come out alongside his boss as a gay man and Jimmy falls off his rocker, getting drunk everyday, making terrible comments to his friends and offending nearly everyone in sight. That's when Eddie and Malloy decide it's time for an intervention. In order to sober Jimmy up and get his life back on track Eddie takes him to a friend's cabin in the middle of nowhere. Detox is bad enough, but now Jimmy has to confront the feelings he's been denying for years. Feelings that tell him that Eddie is more than just his best friend, he just might be the love of his life. Throw in Eddie's close friend who is along for the ride and this becomes a very unconventional romance. I didn't care for Jimmy Rafferty very much when I read book one, My Cowboy Heart. He's rude, crude, disrespectful and full of crap. He talks trash and calls people names, he pretty much hurts and offends everyone around him. Especially the people closest to him. But I loved Eddie. I wanted Eddie to find love and get his happily ever after. I went into this thinking I would get a angsty romance between two tough cowboys, but was a little surprised when this book went in a few directions I didn't expect. Right from the beginning there's not just alcohol and confusing sexual feelings between these two, but another man. Don is Eddie's long time friend and sometime sex partner. Someone Jimmy had no idea existed. As much as he thought he knew his best friend, Eddie seems to have lived a whole other life completely separate from his friends at the J-Bar Ranch. Don is older, a successful doctor and married. Throw him into the mix with these two confused cowboys and I wasn't sure what was going on or how it would all end up. If you've ever known anyone with an alcohol addiction, you can follow along easily as Jimmy makes his transformation and confronts his demons. It's painful to read at times, but I thought the author did a good job showing the ups and downs associated with an alcoholic admitting they have a problem and resolving to overcome it. That's one aspect of the story, the other is all the sexual and romantic feelings that start to finally rise to the surface. Don is the bridge that allows Jimmy and Eddie to finally fall into bed with each other. His character becomes the third in their relationship and is there for all the sexual encounters between them. At first I wasn't sure how I felt about this. The sexy times are smoking hot and as a menage these men work well together, but.... It's clear there are deep feelings between Eddie and Jimmy. Every time they fall into each others eyes while having sex I wanted this to be the time they kicked Don out and decided to only be with each other. I'm not sure why exactly I felt this way, I just know I spent most of my time wanting Don to go away and leave my cowboys to themselves. After awhile I came to understand Don and how he fit in with this couple. I grew to respect him and what he had to offer these two as far as friendship, support and knowledge. There is a lot more than alcohol and hurt feelings that these cowboys have to work to overcome to find their way to each other. Each one has painful pasts that must be talked about and understood. Lots and lots of angst and sexy times, flirting and misunderstandings, but by the end I thought their romance and happily ever after worked. It may not have been what I was expecting, but for this couple it was believable. Final Grade- B Favorite Quote: "Home is Ed. Can't lose that, not now when I finally know what that means."

I asked HarperCollins International for the chance to review Exile because I thought the cover was cute. Was a bit unsure about the summary, but thought I could enjoy it. But I was wrong. I was so, so wrong. I really, truly hated this book. I'm so sorry. But I did. So, be warned. This review will not be nice. As I have a lot of bad/honest things to say about the book. Sigh. I really wanted to like Exile. But I knew from the moment that I started reading it that I would not like it. I didn't like the writing. At all. And there were way too much information about things I didn't care about at all. A bunch of boring things that I feel like no one thinking about. Ever. Sigh. At least not me. There was just so, so much I did not like about this book. I had so many issues with this book. And even thinking about them is making me angry. I wish it wasn't so, but it was. Exile was not for me. I could say that maybe it had been for me, if I had cared more for bands or whatever. But the truth is that I don't think I would have ever liked this book. Because I do like music. But I couldn't connect at all to those parts in this book. It was just a bit boring for me. And way too much drama. The book is all about drama. There is this music school they go to, I suppose. But we never read more about it. It obviously didn't matter in this book. The book is told from the point of view of Summer. Or Catherine. Or whatever. She was two people. One with her parents, one with others. Seriously? Not cool. I didn't like her much. How she lied and never talked to her parents. You don't do that. And she just.. she was not a good person. Well, in some ways. Mostly I didn't connect with her. I'm not going to mention all the things I didn't like in this book. Would take forever. But I'm going to mention some. As I said, I did not like the main character. Probably because we never got to know anything about her. AT ALL. We get to know that she used to be manager for a band that left her, and she dated the guy for years. And that's it. She compares him a little to the new guy, but then we barely hear about them at all. No mentions about what she did back then. No mention about who she was. The whole book was like that. We don't get to know anything about anything. Okay, a few things. But it wasn't enough. Mostly focus on inside her head about things I have no clue what was supposed to mean. Didn't make any sense. Sigh. Oh, then there is the boy, Caleb. Who is dreamy and hot and blah blah blah. They meet. Then an hour later they are kissing. SERIOUSLY. Very bad case of insta-love. She knew NOTHING about him. Just that he was hot. And could sing. I hated the way the romance was written. Sigh. There was just so much I hated in this book. The band parts. I didn't care. Not even a little bit. There's supposed to be this mystery, but I couldn't find it in me to be excited at all. It was just boring and truly not that exciting at all. We meet more characters. Whom we yet again know nothing about. Then in comes Val. And Summer is oh so jealous. And Caleb is saying it's nothing. And it is awful. I hated it. No love triangle. Summer learns about her past, and she is full of guilt. Seriously? Not real. Then there is that ending. It just ended. With the plot half-way there. We didn't get to know anything about what happened with.. you know, THE WHOLE PLOT. The reason for the book. We never got to see what happened. Not that I care, because I don't, but seriously. Not a good ending. Sigh. I'm sorry. There was just a lot of things that I did not like in this book. And I've only mentioned some of it. But I'm not going to say more now. I don't want to. I just want to forget about this book as soon as possible. But huge thank you to HarperCollins International for the review copy of Exile. <3 I'm so sorry that I didn't like it. At all. But I'm still thankful that I got to read it. <3 And I must admit that my review copy looks all kinds of gorgeous, as I do still love the cover. It's pretty. I'm not sure I can recommend this book to others, though. As I'm not sure anyone would like it. Sigh. But I also know that some will love it. But it wasn't for me. But if you do read it, I do hope you like it more than me. Kind of. Probably :)

I was enthralled with this story from the very beginning. Not only did Leah Cypess pull me in with her writing, but she also delivered a fantastic story. The mystery of Mistwood will leave you guessing until the very end. Isabel wakes up in the forest of the Mistwood and is taken back to the castle to protect Prince Rokan. She is the Shifter and that is what she does. She isn't human, she is a creature of mist and wind that can shift forms at the drop of a hat, and it is her duty to protect the king and his family. Only problem... Isabel has no memories of her past before Prince Rokan found her in the Mistwood. She goes on instinct alone, but that will only get her so far. Especially since she can't shift anymore. And with everyone keeping secrets from her, Isabel has to work through them to uncover the truth, a truth she not want to know. What happened to her since the last time she served the king? Why can't she remember? Just like Isabel, the reader is figuring out what happened right along with her. And it's a mystery that is slowly unraveled until the very end. You won't see what's coming. I found myself wanting more when I reached the last page. Leah did a tremendous job in creating this world and showing the struggle Isabel went through as she learned more about her past and her new charge. Things aren't always as they seem and for a creature that works off of instinct and right and wrong, that's not always easy to see. I'm definitely crossing my fingers for more. And in a couple of months a companion novel, Nightspell, should be coming out! Thank you Leah.

The blurb on the back says that All She Was Worth is an "artful blending of puzzle-solving and social commentary," and I suppose it does blend those two, but I'm not sure about how artfully it was done. The social commentary part was pretty heavy-handed, with more than one long-winded description of the evils of the credit industry. The thing is, those descriptions weren't even really necessary; the story got that message through without them. There were a couple parts I didn't really understand, and I don't know whether they are weaknesses in Miyabe's work, or in the translation. One was how it was said at one point that the police wouldn't get involved in Kyoko's problems with the Yakuza, as long as they didn't physically harm her. But if selling her (and her mother) into prostitution isn't physical harm, I don't know what is. So it seems like her legal options for protecting herself were not exhausted before she resorted to murder. The next part that I didn't get was how her husband left her because he overheard her mumbling that she wished her father was dead. Somehow, it made him think she was evil. But he knew what she was facing, so I don't get how he could have ended up at that conclusion, particularly given that he was so in love with her that he was willing to go against his family's wishes to marry her. Aside from that, the characterization was kind of formal and sedate; I never felt like I got in close to anyone, even though I wanted to. I didn't really understand the relevance of some sub-stories, like the one about Blockhead. And the ending felt like Miyabe was tired of telling the story. So overall, I liked the concept and the plot, but there were just too many problems for me to recommend All She Was Worth.

Video review here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YXD8R... - I quite like Kaz's characterisation. I do. At first, with Six of Crows, I didn't quite get the fuss. Eventually, With his backstory and his "affliction" and no, I'm not talking about his limp, i started to find him a lot more interesting, because he was who he was, no excuses, no attempts at "heroics". Basically, I really appreciated that Leigh Bardugo didn't try to pull an uncharacteristic act to make him seem more like the romantic hero in any way. He stay perfectly flawed until the very end. There were no magical cures, nothing convenient about him in any way. So I found myself really rooting for him. If anything, the fact that he didn't have a magical character change and only subtle little changes is what ultimately made me really love the character. - Friendships developed. It wasn't just about a group of people who embarked on an impossible heist together, it was about a group of very different people who embarked on a heist together and somehow, against all odds, ended up caring for one another and being friends. The chemistry between the characters was really great and each of them started to get close on a deeper level and find common ground that was beyond the fact that they all-pulled-the-impossible-and-survived. It also offered some great humor among the characters and I found myself laughing a lot. Mostly at Nina's shenanigans and the fact that Matthias cannot comprehend sarcasm. - I liked that this book focus on the action, the world-building, the setting, the heist, the characters and not so much on the romance. It wasn't romance-heavy. There was some romance, obviously, but unlike other YA fantasy book, the focus didn't veer off from the main events only to giving readers their sailing "ships". It would give the romance it's due, and then move on. - The action itself and the plotting was really great in this book. I honestly just read through it without thinking and trying to guess what would happen next. I just allowed myself to be taken on the ride somehow trusting that Kaz Brekker knew what he was doing even when all else seemed impossible. - Van Eck was a great villain. Absolutely marvelous. Despicable through and through, but I would have liked to have seen a bit more two-dimensionality to his character, because every time you think you see the bit of good in him, it's staunched by finding out that it was merely an act on his part and I would have liked, at the very least, that some of his concern for his young wife and his unborn child was real beyond his build for a legacy. On the other hand though, Pekka Rollins was magnificent because he gave me what Van Eck didn't. His concern and love for his son went beyond anything in the world: his riches, his legacy, his life. And gosh-dern-it! I actually really liked him in his two final scenes (the first with his showdown against Kaz and the second during his last chapter). So I thought it was really interesting seeing those two put side by side and seeing how each one of them reacted differently to their family vs. their legacy in jeopardy and the choices they made. Pekka man. He was the biggest surprise. - I loved the ending as it was. I love that it left the reader wanting more, that it allowed the reader the space to imagine a bit what-could-have-been and what-could-be. There was some happy and there was some sad. - This may sound awful but I appreciated Matthias's death. Maybe not the way he died (although I can also appreciate the cause he died for) but the fact that he did. The fact that not everyone gets their happy ending. The fact that not everyone came out of the battle unscathed and alive and well. No mourners, no funerals.

** spoiler alert ** So I'm not going to write about all my favourite books this year, because I've got a Favourites shelf for that which can be sorted by date read. Instead, I'm going to write about how much reading means to me, and how books helped me get my life back on track. The latter half of 2015 had my life spiralling out of my control. There were too many changes that I couldn't deal with. And I found myself completely and utterly alone. My friends weren't there when I needed them the most. Either they didn't understand or they didn't care. I went through months of crying myself to sleep and being unable to concentrate on anything. I tried journaling, and that helped a bit sometimes. Other times, it unearthed a whole lot of other stuff that I wasn't yet ready to deal with and left me feeling even worse than before. Then in December I was getting home from work and I saw this makeshift stall on the street selling used books. I used to be an avid reader in highschool, but I hadn't properly read a book since my life became super hectic in 2008. I wasn't even sure I knew how to read anymore, if I'd have the patience to sit through an entire book, if I'd be able to even concentrate long enough to bring myself to care. But I decided that it was worth a shot. One book couldn't really hurt my pocket, even if I ended up not reading it. I returned home with six. It took me a while to get into it, but once I did there was no turning back. I spent December with a book on my person, no matter where I went. Every spare minute I had, I'd spend reading. I read during meals and my bedside table perpetually had a comforting stack of books to keep me company. I took a book to bed every night, refusing to give myself even a second to think and let my brain fill up with depressing thoughts. I slept only in those rare moments when I passed out from sheer exhaustion and the book fell flat on my face. In my head, my life was happening in the breaks I took between reading. It was addicting, having this alternate universe that I could excape to, where my problems seemed trivial, and where I knew that everything would eventually be okay. I read the entire Shopaholic series that month, and it made me feel stupid for making such a big deal of my problems, when Rebecca's life was clearly a bigger mess. It also made me feel that if ditzy Rebecca could figure out her problems, I could definitely deal with mine. 2016 has been a year of healing. Books were my escape, they were there for me constantly, non-judgementally, and occasionally offering surprising little nuggets of advice, until I was ready to deal with reality again. And now, I feel okay. Normal. I'm standing on my own two feet again, still alone but not lonely, and I'm happy. I'm also really proud of myself for getting this far. There were a lot of ways my life could have gone from there, and a lot of people would have chosen to drown their sorrows in things other than books. I think as far as coping mechanisms go, I really couldn't have picked a better one. "It's just weird being here again. Being here, and not feeling afraid. It's a big difference from the last time I was here." - Cinder, Something Old, Something New (Stars Above) I joined Goodreads under a pseudonym because I wanted book recommendations, but I didn't want people I knew to find me. Sharing your booklist with someone is like letting them peek into your soul. It's too personal. So I really didn't expect to make any friends here. But I have. There are very few things in life that are better than having friends who read and love the same books as you do. Thank you all for being there. Thank you for reading this long long post. And no matter how this year went for you, I hope everyone has an amazing 2017. We all deserve it.

The Blade Itself is Joe Abercrombie's first novel. I picked it up after finishing his fourth, Best Served Cold. The difference in his writing style from his first book to his fourth is so marked that if I hadn't known better, I would have assumed two different people had written the books. When compared to Best Served Cold, The Blade Itself suffers in essentially every way, but that doesn't make it a bad book so much as one that was obviously written by a novice. That said, this isn't a review of Best Served Cold, so I'm going to do my best to judge The Blade Itself in a vacuum and on its own merits. The first thing that struck me was the prose, which was surprisingly unsophisticated. I didn't care for the way the characters spoke--they often giggled or squealed, and when they were in pain or floundering for words, said things like, "Arrgh," and "Er...". It was the sort of thing that I'd expect to find in a run of the mill fan fiction, not in a professionally published novel. I didn't like it at all. The plot was fine, if nothing groundbreaking, but I found the characters to be fairly shallow and trite, especially considering the amount of praise I've seen for Abercrombie's characterization in this series. One exception to this is Collem West, who goes from a seemingly responsible and honorable commoner-turned-officer to a wrathful woman-beater in the space of a chapter. Abercrombie then revealed the heretofore unknown information that West's father had abused him and his younger sister Ardee (the very person West himself had just beaten) when they were children, presumably as a partial explanation of West's sudden rage issues (the other part being the frustration of working with asinine soldiers during wartime). It's a reprehensible facet to add to West's character, but I'm interested to see what Abercrombie does going forward, and whether there will be some sort of redemption for West and reconciliation with his sister. One thing I was pleased by was getting some explanation of a few things that had confused me or not been fully fleshed out in Best Served Cold. I now know that the character of Shenkt is an Eater who must formerly have been in service to the emperor of Gurkhul, and that the Cripple is probably Inquisitor Sand dan Glokta . In sum, this novel was okay, but nothing particularly compelling. I'm glad that Best Served Cold was the first Abercrombie novel I read, because if I had picked this first up instead, I probably wouldn't have bothered with any of his other books.

This review can also be found on Book Girl of Mur-y-Castell-blog. Zach is on his way to LA and as far away as he can get from London. He only has six more weeks to go, but first, he's asked to edit one more manuscript. The catch is, the novel is an erotica written by Nora Sutherlin. That same novel means more to Nora than anything else she's written and she wants to get it right. She's desperate enough to give Zach total control over it. The blurb promises gruelling, draining, and shockingly arousing writing sessions, which are notably absent from the book. There is writing, there are sessions, there are shredded scenes, and there are excerpts from the book within the book--something I particularly disliked mostly because of the dip in quality--none of which were the reason for my rating. The word I'm stumbling over is the last one in the list--arousing. Once again, I'm the odd man out; I don't get the appeal. Reisz can write well and there were certain things I enjoyed reading. I mostly liked the banter between characters and the characterisations. I liked the fact that none of them were boring or insufferably honourable and good. I liked that they were flawed. I adored Wes. He was used to mirror Nora's relationship with Soren and I kept thinking he was better than that, that he deserved to get away. As good a guy as he was, as vanilla, he never came across as sanctimonious. Quite the opposite, he knew his flaws, just like he recognised Nora's flaws and accepted them. He was honest with himself. Unlike Zach. The Jewish--a very important fact that--Zachary or Zechariah Easton had to quite literally have the truth beaten out of him. That certainly didn't add to his nonexistent appeal, but I'm glad someone found him appealing if it takes him far away from the story. Zach also earned the label too stupid to live for not figuring out or at least suspecting what Nora's day job was. Soren, Nora's old Dom, let's just say that I liked him much more with the robes on than off and that I didn't understand why he'd care for Nora on any level. Although, I wouldn't mind reading more about his flavour of mind-fuckery as long as it was kept out of the dungeon-hell. As a turn on, Soren fails. J.P., Kingsley, and Mary, were among the supporting cast I'd like to know more about, but not as much as I was left wanting layers for the office villain. He was an example of a lazy characterisation and especially disappointing compared to the effort put into the main cast. And then there was Nora Sutherlin, the author and pseudonym for Eleanor Schreiber. The woman, the Switch, who's not afraid of her sexuality or playing the game. In fact, I think that might be the only thing she's not afraid of, the game. Nora only ever came close to being honest with herself and facing her own feelings when she was with Wes. I'd go as far as to call her a coward that's how busy running from herself she was. And all I have for a coward is pity. No, Nora isn't a likeable main character, but being a user and a bitch doesn't make her strong either. It simply makes her interesting and that's where the strength of this novel is--in the characters. But. There's more. Or rather, there isn't. The Siren is an erotica but very unerotic at that. I'm not a fan of pain and I don't particularly get excited by the forbidden aspect of sex--hazards of having been born a Finn with a mother who never shut up about the human reproduction when I was growing up and living in a sauna culture where the most natural state of man is in the nude. The closest I came to finding anything erotic in this book was when Nora was with Wes, Michael, or Sheridan. That's when she let little bit of her armour slip away, emotions trickle out and almost show intimacy. At this point, I feel like I'm repeating myself, because I've written it so often lately. I could list a spoilery list of events--which include hints of blood play, a sex scene with an underaged boy, a f/f BDSM scene, multiple occasions of beatings leading to face injuries, casual dismissal of the law enforcement, a rape, an unrealistic office fight, bringing religion into sexuality, infidelity saving a marriage --and not see a plot in it. A lot of Greek myths were used to explain natural phenomena in the world. Like sin. And Pandora's Box was DEFINITELY trying to explain naturally occurring sin. Pandora opened the box the gods gave her with all of the demons of vice inside and released sin into the entire world. This translates very awkwardly into this novel. London...1812. Prinny has been regent for one year. England is still at war with France, and on the brink of with with America. And Lady Helen Wrexhall is finding out that she possesses a special power that can help rid the world of demons. Welcome to The Dark Days Club Lady Helen has been brought up to be a proper young lady. She knows that all she can hope for from life is to marry well, set up her own household, and have children. But when Lord Carlston appears, and explains to Lady Helen that she has a special gift that will help England, and possible the world, can she really give up everything she knows and wants out of life to become a demon hunter? One of the best things about this book is that Lady Helen has a choice. She can choose to join Lord Carlston and the Dark Days Club, or she can choose to remain a society lady, marry a Duke, and live the life that she has been preparing for. In most other books, when a power or destiny is revealed to a MC, that MC has no choice, but to except that power/destiny. In this book, Lady Helen always had a choice...right until the very end...it was always her choice. The other great thing about this book is the secondary characters. They are all well thought out and written true to the Regency era. Lady Helens' aunt is only concerned with making sure that Helen makes a good match in her marriage (preferably to the Duke of Selburn) and, of course, the latest fashions and what balls and dinner parties she can wear them to. Helens' uncle thinks that a woman should be seen and not heard, and can't wait for the day that Helen gets married and becomes another mans problem. Darby, Helens' maid, turns out to be a very good friend. At first I thought that she could not be trusted, but she turned out to only ever have Lady Helens' best intrest at heart. Lord Carlston is arrogant, handsome, rich, and extremely frustrating all at once...which makes him the perfect "I hate you, but I really kind of like you" guy for Lady Helen. All in all this was a great book and I cannot wait to read the next book!

The Druid Stone is the third strikingly intense urban fantasy I've read from this very talented writing duo currently making a name in m/m for dark, beautifully written fiction that defies description. As with Cruce de Caminos and Hawaiian Gothic, we get a blend between (1) the realism of contemporary gay romance + (2) the supernatural. It's hard for me to pin down what I mean by supernatural with these authors, but it's addictive. There is too much depth and world building to label their fiction as a mere paranormal. There is too much compassion and emotional warmth to label it as horror. Probably urban fantasy is the best description. If you love Irish mythology, you just can't miss this. And if Irish mythology is your least favorite thing, you may still find yourself seduced by the authors' beautiful writing, wild imagery, and deeply endearing characters (e.g., Sean). As a reader, I'm the antithesis of the "plastic Paddy" mentioned early on by Cormac. Too much high fantasy when I was younger has left me completely oversaturated with, and allergic to, all things Celtic. Now, I can't even read high fantasy, and Irish folklore makes me recoil - but, I was willing to try The Druid Stone because I trust the authors. And, once again, they gave me a gripping story. Here are some of the highlights for me: * Sean. He's such a great character. Innocent, funny, resilient, with a deep core of integrity. I'd be willing to read anything with him in it. He is the source of the humor in this novel, and several of his reactions made me laugh (e.g., humming "Hotel California," thinking upon his first glimpse of Finnbheara, "he's really into the seventies.") :D * The way time behaves in the supernatural realm. It flows back and forth and bends in upon itself. Everything involving traveling through the triple spiral, seeing the life-threads that lead to the people they need to find, the angles of light that Cormac uses to find the inter-dimensional portals - all that was breathtaking and very believable. * The Irish folklore. I know it's not my favorite thing in fiction, but here it's done very well and in perfect consistency with everything I've ever heard about. I enjoyed how Cormac is so well versed in the various rules (e.g., iron, hospitality) that he can manipulate them to control the supernatural types. I liked how well-spoken he is in the Irish folkloric sense of being a kind of lawyer-diplomat who can negotiate his way out of trouble with powerful entities, and how those skills are valued by the entities. * The contrast between Finnbheara, who is kind of like a rock star and true to the usual daoine sidhe we fantasy readers know (while having a delightful and original irreverent streak), and Sreng who is more bestial and subterranean. * The concept of Cormac trying to make his living as a druid in the modern world intrigues me. At one point, he contemplates working with magic in the new world (i.e., it doesn't have to be in Ireland) and that REALLY intrigues me. I enjoyed The Druid Stone and found the middle part of it (the journeys through the supernatural realms) especially fast-paced and compelling. And the sex scenes are hot! A note for other readers about the three-page prolog, which shows you the torture scene that haunts Sean's dreams. If, like me, you're a lightweight when it comes to violence, the prolog may make you want to DNF right there. Don't do it! Skim or skip the prolog, but don't let it scare you off from the rest of the book, which is suspenseful, but not violent. This engaging and memorable read makes me eager to see the next fiction that these authors have planned for us. Recommended!

"That was part of being a girl--you were resigned to whatever feedback you'd get. If you got mad, you were crazy, and if you didn't react, you were a bitch. The only thing you could do was smile from the corner they'd backed you into. Implicate yourself in the joke even if the joke was always on you." It has been a long time since I read a book that made me so uncomfortable. From Russel's to the girls' behaviour, from the cold distance with which the narrator tells the story, and from the inevitable end that you know to be terrible from the start. Some chapters I almost had the instincts to close my eyes, read faster, or close the book. Just to pretend that what happened didn't. This book tells the story of Evie's childhood, when she met Suzanne and her 'friends' who are all living in a ranch with an older man named Russel. She suffers from a severe lack of attention from her parents and spend more and more times with this group all the while not realising what it really is, or voluntarily ignoring it. The book explores in depths the need for attention and for someone or something to belong to, even more as a teenager, and what this yearning can lead someone to do. I think it perfectly described Evie's naivety, longing and loneliness. It tackles a lot of cliche representation of women and the expectations that are thrown upon us concerning our behaviour towards men. The book explores in depths the relationships between women, mother and daughter, friends, strangers, as well as between men and women. The book was a bit slow at times though, or rather I think the ending that we were all waiting for should have been more spread out and some parts of it are not very clear.

I love historical fiction and was incredibly excited to read this book. I mean, 1920s New York? A girl who is supposed to be Houdini's illegitimate daughter? In the end, there were things I enjoyed about Born of Illusion, and other things that struck me as somewhat less than magical. My favorite part of the book was Anna's relationship with her mother, which was ... complicated. Anna's mother is a spiritualist and Anna resents the way that her mother uses trickery and manipulation to make people think she can talk to the dead. Anna, on the other hand, has the ability to "read" people by touching them but wants to be a magician. So Anna has psychic ability but wants to do magic tricks, while her mother uses magic tricks to make people think she has psychic abilities. Their relationship was pretty dysfunctional -- they almost seemed more like competitive sisters than a mother and daughter. I also liked the mystery surrounding the identity of Anna's father. Anna's mother tells her that she's Houdini's daughter, but the book definitely raises some doubts about that. This ambiguity was interesting -- Anna's mother is clearly a person who has no qualms about telling people what they want to hear. I also wish the romance had either been ramped up or left out altogether. I didn't find either of the guy in the book's quasi love triangle particularly compelling and there was little suspense over who one she'd choose. While I don't always go into a historical novel expecting a fast-paced, action-packed read, the plot dragged until the very end. The book was always hinting that something interesting was going to happen, but it wasn't until the last few chapters that anything dramatic transpired. Even then it was a black moment I've seen in many romantic supense novels. Given the magic themes and the paranormal elements and the amount of time I had to wait, I was expecting an ending with more ... oomph. Recommended for fans of magic and historical fiction; readers who liked this book should also try In the Shadow of Blackbirds by Cat Winters.

I love Edwardian pulp, but... I do love it. I love Golden Age pre-WWI Britain, with well-dressed gentlemen and dastardly foreigners, stiff upper lips and country-house parties, derring-do and plots and amateur spies. John Buchan, Edgar Wallace, E Phillips Oppenheim, and the other wonderful writers of a time when to be a straight white English gentleman was to be at the pinnacle of human civilisation. Obviously, if you weren't white, or upper class, or Christian, or male, or straight, it wasn't quite so much fun. The fiction of the time is shocking to modern readers with its casual prejudices - in particular the anti-Semitism with which the era is so foully infected. But there's also the almost automatic villainy of queer people and sexually aware women; the restrictive class structure; the assumed inferiority of non-white and non-British. I love the balls-to-the-wall plotting and milieu of Edwardian pulp, but the prejudices make it a guilty pleasure. So I wrote my own Edwardian pulp, my way. Think of England features British officer and gentleman Archie Curtis, tackling a dastardly plot in a country house. Because Archie needed shaking up, I gave him decadent Jewish poet Daniel da Silva to spar with: not English, not white, not a gentleman and very definitely not straight. And then I sat back to see how long it would take Daniel to turn Archie's life upside down. I had immense fun with this book; I hope you enjoy it!

This review originally posted at More Than Just Magic I'm one of those weird people who is fascinated by serial killers. I used to read all the true crime novels our tiny book store had, I love Criminal Minds and so on. So when I heard about Project Cain I was excited. Serial killer clones? A chance to really examine the debate of nature vs nurture? It sounded like an intense, action packed read and I couldn't wait to get my hands on it. Unfortunately it didn't work out quite as well as I hoped. The style of this book is very straightforward. Which is great for the parts where the reader is learning about the different serial killers and their histories. Sometimes there's a lot of horrible information to get out and Girard doesn't tip toe around it. He spells in right out for the reader, which I appreciated. That straightforward writing style, however, also contributed to a very action light book. Maybe it's my fault for expecting a lot of action, but you would think a story about clones of the world's most notorious serial killers on the run would be more action heavy. Instead, however, Project Cain takes place primarily in a hotel room. Jeff Jacobson (our protagonist) is a clone of Jeffrey Dahmer and is terrified by the revelation that he shares the exact same DNA as a serial killer, so he runs. He attaches himself to a FBI detective - Castllio - and together they begin searching for the other escaped clones. And this is pretty much where the excitement ends. As soon as Jeff teams up with Castllio he spends all his time in one of two places - a car or a hotel room. There's a lot of talking, a lot of reflecting about why his adopted father would have initiated such a project and a lot of staring at a cell phone trying to guess where some guys he knows nothing about would have run to. I understand the investigation parts are necessary but I thought they could have been broken up by some more action or drama. Something to really get your pulse pounding. I was also disappointed by the missed opportunity for discussion. Project Cain was in a perfect position to examine the discussion of nature versus nurture. The very thing the government was curious about when they started their top-secret experiments in the book. But despite Jeff's constant fear that he may turn into his namesake, it's pretty clear from very early on that he's not going to. This book leans heavily on the nurture side. So heavily that there is never a moment, in my opinion, where I thought it might swing the other way. That's fine if that's what the author believes but I think there was a possibility here to a) build suspense and b) facilitate discussion but that just didn't happen. Overall Project Cain wasn't a bad book, it just wasn't the book I wanted it to be. The book I thought it could be. There's an adult companion novel told from the detective's point of view (Cain's Blood), which might be more thrilling as the detective leaves the hotel room more often and in Project Cain we don't know where he goes. I'll have to check it out and see if it's more my style. Recommendation: If you're looking for a book for the teenage boy in your life, Project Cain might work but I think there are better options out there.

** spoiler alert ** Okay, I believe I have calmed down somewhat. Now before I write out my thoughts about this book, let me just say that my reading experience as an Indian woman who is well versed in "Bollywood culture" is probably different than any reader whose life experiences are different from my own. Reading is subjective but damnit, some things ought to be called out upon instead of being accepted as the norm because if women don't make statements and speak out about things they don't agree with then who will. To say I had issues with this novel would be saying a hurricane is windy: a massive understatement. I almost liked Mili, almost but she is almost of no consequence when compared to the hero of the novel, Samir. I loathed Samir. I loathe Samir. I will forever loathe Samir. If you've read or studied British lit you may have come across the "rake" character or as he (though rarely, the rake is she) or they are also called Libertines. Historical novels delight in this stereotypical character: the rake who is redeemed by the love of one true woman. Samir is presented initially as that rake. He doesn't respect women. He fucks them and then he expects them to engage in the same physical relationship with equal aplomb and coolness. He stereotypes Indian women as those who, after intimacy, expect some kind of emotional reciprocation. His dick is as much a character as he is in the novel, referred to affectionately as "Little Sam." Because Samir has a traumatic past, readers are supposed to give him a green card where present and future ass hattery are concerned. But alas, this reader knows that a douche bag is a douche bag and asshole-ishness isn't excused by past mommy issues. Then there's Mili. Sheltered, exploited Mili who was a child bride. Who has spent her entire life waiting for a husband who has forgotten her. Who wasn't even aware of her existence until a letter reached him and he had that proverbial "oh shit" moment. I almost liked her because I figured she had no choice in the matter. She seemed intelligent until she became completely stupid. Mili is reduced to being a damsel in distress the entirely of the time Samir spends with her: she fractures her wrist and ankle and is dependent on his help where moving is concerned. She has no money for groceries until he buys food for her. He picks her up and drops her off in his yellow corvette every day and she lets him. Even though she knows nothing about this man and has no reason to trust him beyond what he has told her. But what ticked me off the most is when she attacks another woman who shows her a magazine that has an article alleging Samir beat up his ex-gf. Granted, he didn't but once again, she has known him at this point for only 2 weeks. She even attacks her best friend who Samir oh gallantly called "horse woman" because apparently Samir cannot respect anyone who he is either not related to or doesn't want to fuck, that is, Mili. Mili's blind devotion to Samir made me gag. Especially since at the time he is deceiving her about who he is and why he is there. Mili is sexualized almost from the get-go. She is "tiny" with small hands compared to the big buff man. She has a "pert little nose" that, I don't know about you, sounds as condescending as anything I've ever heard. She doesn't just eat food, she has sex with it. Oohing and aahing her pleasure, I'd presume while Little Sam convulses in agony at the sight. Samir goes through Mili's things, betraying her in the worst possible ways (wait, not yet, he can do worse) for the marriage certificate. Then he takes her virginity while she's pushed up against a tree and then we are told he didn't realized it was her first time. Right, right, she has told you she is married, you know she is the traditional type and you think she'd be experienced sexually why? The excuse given? He lost his mind. Right. And it killed me that SHE apologises afterward. When shit finally hits the fan and Mili finds out his true purpose and identity, I thought we'd see some true growth and see Samir growing as well. But no. His solution to absolve the guilt he feels? Give the haveli (palace) to Mili and assuage his sore feelings. When she predictably turns up at his house to say no thank you, all conflicts and hostility are somehow magically swept away in the face of family drama and a baby being born. Mili and Samir end up together never mind the fact that the man didn't once apologise sincerely. This? Is not romance no matter how much the book may want to sell you on that. If by A Bollywood Affair, you mean a shallow, superficial romance set against the backdrop of Bollywood thumka, a romance that doesn't consider too closely the emotional consequences of a betrayal that deep, that shoves logic and character growth aside for a quick and easy ever after, then yep, you've got that. But the true essence of Bollywood, the whole layla majnu deal, none of that here. Sadly.

If a book leaves me unmoved I don't even know what to say in a review. No, this wasn't terrible but it contains nothing exceptional. It is a long story and only covers about twenty years of the main character's life. It is a coming-of-age story about an orphan with a clubfoot in Britain at the turn of the century. By the end he has figured out how he wants to live his life. Let me put it this way - appreciate the small ordinary things in life. Philip, the main character, is terribly naive and he had no help from any parent so I ought to have felt more compassion for him - but I didn't. He makes such stupid choices. He seems totally blind in seeing the real character of people, and he cannot pick girls. The book goes on and on and on until he finally wakes up. The end I guessed half way through. It's cute. Don't get me wrong. I agree with what is being said but there is little to ponder and the message is so unremarkable. Here are the topics covered: faith, art, bullying, boarding-schools, love, travel and choosing one's occupation. There is a lot about art, but it has the tone of art criticism. I personally don't want art dissected or analyzed to pieces. I want it to move me; if it does that I am satisfied. Only the discussion of the Spanish artist El Greco did I find a teeny bit interesting. Maybe you enjoy art criticism.... Numerous artists and authors are discussed. Why? Because Philip had a hard time choosing his occupation so he tries several - the clergy, accountant, artist, doctor. Guess where he ends up. His father had been a doctor. This I found a bit too simplistic. Steven Crossley narrated the audiobook. The women all sound the same. This can be excused by their all sharing a Kent dialect? The story's narrator and the men were fine, but extremely British. They are supposed to sound British so what can you expect?! No, I didn't love the narration, but it was OK, just as the book was OK. Not bad, but in no way exceptional. Some interesting lines, but that is about it. How am I supposed to write a moving review if the book leaves me lukewarm?
