This review can also be seen on my shared blog, Boricuan Bookworms. In a society where women are worthless, Serena knows that any wrong move could destroy her life. Burdened by her father's actions to sell her off to the highest bidder, she knows her freedom is going to get even more compromised. But, when her ownership is transferred to the hands of a barbaric Envadi, she discovers a whole new world; a world where woman don't have to follow a certain set of guidelines and where they can be free. This book was fantastic! It was really difficult to put down. The world-building was great! The society was crafted masterfully and brilliantly. I could actually start feeling myself (as a female) as suppressed and restricted as Serena felt. I was sucked into the story immediately and found it difficult to put down. I loved the way the author created the characters. Serena is the protagonist, and she's an outspoken, independent woman. Problem is, with the amount of magic in her blood, she's too valuable; and so, her father wants to sell her off to the highest bidder. The way Serena reacted to everything life threw at her was completely reasonable and relatable. "What do I really want? I don't know, but not this. Something different. Something that won't require me to constantly submit myself to another's will." Something that I really enjoyed about this book was the contrast between the Chardonian people and the Envadi. While the Chardonian people are a sexist society that subjects women to corporal punishment if they don't behave, the Envadi are a people who believe that everyone has rights and treat women as individuals. I liked the Tarnished concept as well, because it kept up with the magical aspect of this story, and it really did represent a threat to Serena, as well as every other woman in that society. This book really engrossed me with the romance. It was slow building, but steady and without a doubt, swoon-worthy. I loved Zade so much! He was hilarious, awkward and completely honest and I loved everything about him! This story was amazing and completely unputdownable. I can't wait to see what happens in the rest of the books! I could keep mentioning everything I liked about this book, but I'd just waste your time. Just, please, read this book, like immediately. 5 stars eBook copy provided by author via Making Connections YA Edition in Goodreads.com

"Man cannot be freed by the same injustice that enslaved it." I didn't know alot about this book before i read it, did i miss the reviews or what? I did look at a few before i started it mainly because i was stuck between choosing two books and seeing that it was compared to the Hunger Games, Ender's Game and Game of Thrones, i was down to read it asap. Do i think its the best dystopian novel ever? Probably not but for me it was captivating and well thought-out and i will be continuing on with the series. Darrow is a red, and all his life and many generations before them their purpose is to work as hard as possible to make the surface of Mars livable. Being the lowest colour in the colour-coded society they live in, acts deemed as treason or anarchy type behaviour is punishable by death- Something Darrow has had to see his loved ones face. What the Red's dont know is they have been lied too. Mars has been habitable for generations and great cities have already been built on the surface, and ruled by the Gold- the highest colour in their society. While the Reds slave and dream to make life easier for their future generations, the Golds are living it up on the surface, ruling over everyone and deciding which live and which die. With everything to lose and an anger for justice rising inside him, Darrow with the help of some friends will make the transformation from a Red to a Gold in order to infiltrate the Institute and bring down those who have oppressed his people for so long. First goal, change everything about himself; from the bones in his body, to his eyes, his hair and how he speaks- everything must change in order to become a Gold. Second task, pass the tests and obstacles before him so he can become a highGold and bring down the Institute from within. In a story about life and death, loss, lies, great conquests/battles , epic friendships and a troubled colour-coded class system, Darrow will stop at nothing for the justice, and vengeance he seeks for his people and those he loves. But will he be able to manage the life of a Gold, and the cruel tasks set before him or will death come knocking sooner than he thinks? "I would have lived in peace. But my enemies brought me war." I think the world building was well done for it being such a BIG world. The writing wasn't anything too complex, though descriptive it wasn't over bearing, the fighting scenes were epic and something i looked forward too whilst reading, the characters were well written and thoughout, although there was alot of them and that at times became confusing and had me like "Who the fuck is this guy now?". Something that also confused me was the new terms that would sometimes appear in the world, maybe i needed a glossary or something but it just lost me at some points. Some parts were a little slow, and then it would speed up for awhile then slow down again, i would have liked a more consistent pace, because i think it would have made it even better. "I'm a sheep wearing wolves' clothing in a pack of wolves." Darrow isn't the most heartwarming likable character, but his mission to help his people and the sacrifices he makes in order for this to happen, make him likeable. For most of the book he has to play a character he doesn't like, he has to act and behave as the Gold do in order to go undetected in their world, in hopes that he alone can bring down their rein of power and oppression. Being the HellDiver for the Reds in the mines, means that he is not only good with his hands, but super fast with them as well. Racing against the Grays Helldiver for the Laurel (extra food and supplies for their families) Darrow works as hard as possible to gain whatever he can for those he loves and his fellow Reds, little does he know that that as well is rigged. I think what makes the reader really feel for Darrow is Eo, and her part in this story. She warmed his heart, but also made it go stone cold. Through her strength and sacrifice, Darrow developes into someone she would have been proud of, the person she wanted him to be all along; the person who could change it all. "I live for the dream that my children will be born free. That they will be what they like. That they will own the land their father gave them.' 'I live for you,' I say sadly. She kisses my cheek. 'Then you must live for more." In all this was a great book, not the best dystopian novel i've read but the added in space concept was pretty cool. I liked the characters, i liked the world. There are a few things that could have been alittle tweaked but overall nothing that affected my reading experience to the point i couldn't continue on or felt like i was bored. Now, usually fratire (and I would lump it in with that genre) is also very homophobic and misogynist, and, to be fair, the homophobia of Zeus is limited to one throwaway line, and its misogyny seems mostly pro-forma. * Even if that were any kind of praise, though, the pig ignorant racism and condescending attitude more than balance it out, though neither really hits it stride until O'Brien lumps three West African myths from two separate traditions together and just calls that chapter ``African''+ (something he repeats for ``Native American''++). My Reaction in a Nutshell: Overall, the most anticlimactic book of the three. The Long Version: This book was much slower than the first two which really surprised me. The Forever Song begins with Jackal, Kanin, and Allie on the hunt for Sarren. Allie, distraught from the loss of Zeke, begins to ignore her humanity she so desperately clung to in the first two books. Rather than grieving, she starts to give in to her inner demon, the monster she fought for so long. She kills without remorse, calls humans bloodbags, and hides all painful memories of Zeke. This book started off great. I kind of secretly love it when the good guys turn into villains, so I loved reading about Allie's moral dilemma. This book, like the previous two, did not gloss over the messier details of vamp life. But that being said, I could predict every "plot twist" in the book. Nothing surprised me. It made the whole story anticlimactic. Just a general (but super spoilery) question: After Zeke broke Sarren's compulsion, why did he never ask about his cross? He wore it every day in the previous two books and Allie left it at the graveyard outside of Chicago, but Zeke never asked Allie if she knew where it was. Kind of feel like that's a loose end that needs to be cleared up. The writing was more reflective in this book than the previous two. Allie has longer inner-monologues and there is less action. Overall the plot moved slowly. I liked the first half of the book better than the second. This book falls somewhere between a 3-3.5 star rating for me. I didn't like how predictable it was and the extra focus on romance. It followed a lot of similar tropes of YA which disappointed me. Similarly to the last book of the Angelfall trilogy, Kagawa had a slow plot with a mediocre ending. Plus this book had more dramatic speeches (which I don't like) than the previous two. But that being said, I still enjoyed the book. I love Jackal. I could never tell if he was good or bad or a little bit of both. He provided excellent comedic relief. I want a whole book only about Jackal. Overall, this is still a great vampire series even if the last book wasn't the best. ***TRIGGER WARNINGS: mind control, terminal illness, threat of implied R, kidnapping, PTSD, suicide, death, murder, torture

When Randi Rhodes moves from adventurous New York City to Deer Creek, she doesn't expect to stumble across any mysteries worthy of her ninja detective skills. Yet it isn't long before Deer Creek's Time Capsule goes missing at a crucial point that could mean a terrible loss for the town if it isn't recovered in time. Determined to solve the case, Randi leaps into action with the aide of her new friend, D.C., to discover the perpetrator and bring them to justice. There's something hidden in the history of Deer Creek and Randi won't stop until she finds out just what it is. Randi Rhodes is a head-strong protagonist who can be stubborn to a fault. She can also be very considerate, especially when it comes to her new friend D.C. She makes for a likeable character that you can really root for and want to continue reading about. I liked that there was a dynamic cast of characters. Randi and D.C. are particularly compelling and come across as likeable and realistic. They aren't without their troubles or conflicts but they are also passionate about their interests - such as martial arts and detective work - which is the magnetism that brings their friendship together. Pudge, an allusive character that always showed up when Randi was investigating, instilled a definite curiousity. The relationship between Randi and her father was an interesting one. I liked that there was juxtaposition between how he could infuriate her and yet how he also inspired her. It made for a conflicting dynamic between the two of them. The novel was well-paced and there was never a lull. Randi may think the town is dull at first but the fact that I rarely put this book down was enough to prove her wrong. The mystery of the capsule was intriguing and not one that was simple for me to figure out. There was a great balance of plot and character development. I liked the ninja tasks included in the appendix. I particularly found the one about plastering a footprint very interesting. It added an extra layer to the novel and made Randi's antics all the more plausible to the reader. Randi Rhodes is the real deal. She is inquisitive, intuitive and driven. I look forward to reading more about her, D.C. and Pudge in future and would be quick to recommend it to anyone seeking a children's novel with great character and mystery. I'd rate this closer to 2.5 stars. After finishing Graceling I really looked forward to the other two books of the series/universe. I do still look forward to Bitterblue even though I didn't enjoy Fire nearly as much as Graceling. Pros: -The Prologue. For those who have read Graceling this is a great bit of back-story for a character we met there originally. It gives some book background for that character, and I think Cashore chose a good way to tie the two novels together. The way the prologue leads into events later in the story was done well. Small spoiler: After Brigan's remarks about exploring the western mountains to spy on the neighboring lands there, I hope to see more cross-over between the lands, either with characters we already know, or new ones, whichever. I haven't read Bitterblue yet so I don't know if it happens there or not. -I like that Cashore doesn't shy away from including sexuality in her books, and I like the more blunt mentions that LGBT people exist. Even though the author says on her site that she won't answer if Raffin and Bann were a couple in Graceling, I feel like the text leads readers to that conclusion, but there are not any definite mentions that same-sex couples exist. Although we do not see any same-sex couples in Fire, Fire herself tells us that LGBT people are there. Though I'm glad Cashore brings up issues about bodily autonomy (such as choosing sexual partners, birth control and safe sex, abortion, and hints of slut-shaming and possessiveness), I wish she'd been more inclusive about LGBT people and not leaving these characters simply mentioned as existing. -Non-traditional families! Spoiler: I really enjoyed reading a happy bond growing between Fire and Hanna which becomes a sort of stepmother and stepdaughter dynamic. I'm not clear if it's implied Fire and Brigan marry or not, though the text certainly tells us they're planning to be a committed couple and Fire points out that the royal family is rather flexible. Cons: -As with Graceling, I didn't really feel romantic love between any of the characters who later become a couple. In fact, my appreciation for Cashore's inclusion of sexual issues got to be too much here, to the point where I felt it was melodramatic. I simultaneously liked that Cashore pointed out the double-standard between men having many sexual partners versus woman doing the same, and men being jealous and possessive over women over the same issues, but also grew tired and felt like the story was becoming a soap opera with its relationships, rather than showing it's okay to have sexual relationships with different people, it's okay to love more than one person, and that love has many aspects to it. -The writing style sometimes pulls me out of the story. At least once a page a sentence starts with "And." This happens frequently enough that I get distracted by it and other grammatical choices. Cashore is a talented writer, and her description and dialogue are great, but too often I'm thrown out of the story by grammar. This bothered me in Graceling as well, but I hoped to see less of it here. It's a style choice, and everyone has their quirks. For me, this one is distracting to read. -Another similar issue for me between Fire and Graceling was the way Cashore writes children. Bitterblue, who was ten in Graceling I believe, didn't sound much like a ten-year-old. Maybe that had something to do with growing up a princess, and the language of the land, but she still sounded more like a teenager. I felt similarly about Hanna in Fire, who is six and yet her dialogue sounded far more mature than her age. Those are the major things that come to mind. I still want to read Bitterblue because I like the world and the characters themselves. Although I like the characters involved in romantic plots, I feel like in both books the dynamics suddenly shift from flirting and getting to know each other to "in love" which happens in both Graceling and Fire. I'm curious if this will also pop up in Bitterblue, along with a few other themes that she seems to use and tweak, such as couples who end up spending a lot of time traveling apart and go extended periods of time without seeing each other, being able to communicate without speaking aloud, and female characters not wanting marriage and/or children for themselves. I do like how those three things are approached differently in Graceling and Fire since Katsa and Fire are two quite different young women, so I wonder if this will appear in Bitterblue as well.

Excerpt from my full review at http://seattlebooks.tumblr.com: What if you were given the opportunity to find out why a loved one had died - and what part you played in their demise? Would you listen to their accusations? And what would you do with that knowledge if you did? In Jay Asher's Thirteen Reasons Why, high-schooler Clay Jensen is given an extraordinary task when a box full of cassette tapes appears on his doorstep. The tapes contain the last confessions of Hannah Baker, a classmate who overdosed on pills and left her community grasping for answers. The instructions are simple: listen to each tape, find your part in the story, then pass it along to the next person. As you might imagine, this hits Clay pretty hard. Not only was Hannah his classmate, but she was his friend and secret crush. It's difficult to say what devastates Clay more - Hannah's death or the secrets revealed on her tapes. Not only do the tapes expose Hannah's true character, but they unearth a lot of flaws in his friends and fellow students as well. I wanted to like this book. I don't often read young adult fiction, but this premise was unique and moving and the presentation was inventive. Throughout the novel, the narration skips from Hannah's taped messages to Clay's thoughts, memories, and reactions, allowing us to get a fuller picture of the events that transpired. The more I "listened" to the tapes, however, the more frustrated I grew with the characters. Clay is well-meaning and sensitive, the stereotypical "nice guy" who is always lurking around the corner, waiting for the girl of his dreams to notice him, yet never putting in the effort to get to know her. He builds up unrealistic expectations of Hannah in his mind, and is so convinced of who she should be that when he meets her, he is terrified that the Hannah of his dreams might not match up with the Hannah of reality. "What if I got to know you and you turned out to be just like they said?" he frets. "What if you weren't the person I hoped you were? That, more than anything, would have hurt the most." Clay's reactions fluctuate, understandably, between anger and sympathy as he listens to Hannah's confessions. He doesn't understand why Hannah wouldn't accept his help, especially when he was so willing to offer it, and he struggles to shake the feeling that he and he alone could've prevented Hannah's suicide. On the flip side, he blames her for being the target of multiple sexual advances by other high school boys, in a way that is particularly disturbing. These are just a few of his reactions to her confessions: "Whoa. Slow down, Hannah." "She should have asked him to leave. No, she should have wanted him to leave." "You knew what you were getting into, Hannah." Let's get one thing clear here: In no universe, fictional or real, does a girl owe anything to a boy - not a "clean" romantic and sexual history, not an untarnished reputation, not a mutual interest or attraction. Not standing up for someone who is the target of unwanted sexual advances or blaming them after the fact is a very damaging thing to do. This does not make Clay a "nice guy," and it certainly did not make me mourn for his tragic unrequited love story. Hannah, like Clay, is not perfect, either. Some of the accusations on her tapes are very petty. She is quick to judge her peers and slow to forgive perceived slights. Her confessions, while illuminating, might also be described as vindictive and cruel. Unlike Clay's misogynistic views, though, Hannah's flaws strengthened the novel. It was refreshing to read a complex, unlikeable character who could also evoke sympathy. As I said earlier, I appreciate what Asher tried to do with this novel. On many levels, I could relate to the guilt and grief that Clay experienced. A few years ago, I found out that a young boy I went to high school with had killed himself. He had a girlfriend, a close circle of friends, and a loving family. Hundreds of people showed up for his memorial service, and even years later, his friends leave messages on his Facebook feed asking, "Why?" I wish I had the gift of Clay's tapes to find out what made him hurt that badly, and how I could better recognize the signs of distress in those who are still around me. If you take anything away from this book, let it be the reminder that we all impact each other's lives in small and big ways.

"The Invention of Hugo Cabret" by Brian Selznick is the perfect union of art and literature. It represents an entirely new way of reading, and therefore an entirely new way of understanding a story. This is something I've never seen before - and something I'll never see again. I'm not quite sure of what I love most about this book. I can't really decide whether it's the form that keeps fascinating me, or perhaps the beautifully intertwined storylines that left me breathless. Maybe it is both. It probably is. The form of the book, the use of illustrations as a replacement for words, is truly brilliant. It's what makes this books so special and groundbreaking for me. That the author is actually capable of stopping in the middle of a sentence and replace the letters with drawings, without slowing or ruining the plot, and keep moving the story forward, is really something worth a little admiration. However the plot itself is also worthy of some admiring words. The story has so many layers and angles, and so many possibilities for interpretation. On one side it is a story of a lonely boy, who finds consolation, friendship and love. On the other hand it is a story which praises art and inspiration in its many and various forms. But it is also a way of looking at life, a beautiful idea of life itself as a mechanic system - a clockwork waiting for the time to run out, like minutes and seconds ticking away with every heartbeat. I wish I could turn back my clock, and read this book again for the very first time. However that is not possible - which is the lesson we all have to learn.

Actual rating: 2.5 Back in the day, before I discovered amazing YA contemporaries, I always thought many of them would be typical everyday life to really enthrall me the way that fantasies and paranormal books do. That's why it took me so long to read Pushing the Limits, a generic romance between a bad boy and an emotionally scarred girl. Unfortunately, the typical romance within the book was exactly what I got here - with the disappointment being self inflicted as it never really promised to be anything else. Perhaps it's because bad boys aren't really my thing, with Noah as a pot smoker who has been in and out of foster homes. He's rude, dangerous, and has a reputation for being a player, which doesn't really interest me at all. He mostly notices Echo because she's so attractive 'with a rocking body' and most of his thoughts about her turn to how much he wants to get into her pants. As for the relationship itself, I didn't really feel connected to it. Echo is so emotionally and physically scarred that when Noah didn't judge her in the way most people would - she fell for him. She's the typical damsel in distress and he's someone who enjoys a challenge. It was great to see that these two respected each other though, unfortunately I found nothing much really happens within the book. There wasn't really much complexity or depth to the relationship, other than the various problems the two are dealing with in their lives. "Liar....Because the only way anyone will ever be okay with me is if they love me. Really love me enough to not care that I'm damaged. You don't love people. You have sex with them. So how could you want to be with me?" - Echo The guidance counsellor here was an interesting character who played a big part in shaping and supporting both Noah and Echo's future direction, her methods were a bit intrusive at times, but ended up being effective. I was disappointed with the big mystery behind Echo's repressed memories and it was an anticlimax pushing through the book's more mundane moments just to reach that conclusion. Pushing the Limits is your 'bad boy falls in love and turns good' story, which promotes the story that two damaged people being together makes them better because love conquers all. I probably didn't enjoy it much because of my belief you should focus on looking after yourself before you look at being with someone else, especially one who is more damaged. If you like bad boys though, you'd probably love the story here. I've heard Dare You To is better though, so I'll still give it a shot.

Is it possible for a book with a pink and turquoise cover and an author named Rainbow to offer something profound? Maybe not "profound" in the Proust kind of way, but here, offering the sort that's subtle and relatable, where words begin to look and sound like real life. As long as Ms. Rainbow keeps writing books, I'll keep reading them, because she writes real people into the pages of real worlds. No apocalypse needed. No sleepy southern town requiring a tragedy to propel its plot. No gimmicks. Just people, here named Cath and Wren; Reagan and Levi, struggling to find a place/make sense of things within the bracket of college years. Cath can't stop writing Simon Snow fanfiction. She can't bring herself to be socially cool as a cucumber. She can't forgive her twin sister for leaving her to navigate freshman year alone. And she absolutely can't give her estranged mother another chance. But give her a year in a new place with a few people to challenge her and help in their own ways--the straight-talking roommate, the push-you-further creative writing prof, or the 60-watt-smile-farmer-boy, for instance--and Cath will begin to evolve in the way one does when college happens. And while every evolution runs a different course, Cath's story will reveal the bits of familiar its readers can nod their heads to. We begin to recognize the things we held on to, the things we needed to let go, the people who helped all of it make more sense. And Rainbow's characters embody the full spectrum of believability. The dialogue sounds right and while the romance factor can elicit a few groans, it's still entirely goodness, this should not stop. Although Fangirl felt at times to be lacking a few somethings--(Eleanor & Park still takes the cake in my book)--I appreciate how Rainbow's writing is just its own thing. It's cozy like a Saturday morning and familiar like an inside joke. And her characters aren't glamorous; they're people. In this case, fairly nerdy people: hence the fanfic. But what I liked about Cath's Simon Snow obsession (think HP) was how it's still encompassing in its specificity--what is the part of our past we want to take with us? In one lens, Simon Snow is youth--the nostalgia that comes from realizing young was easy. And coming into the brink of now what? There's only forward. And so the profound part is not a cliffhanger or a climax but an observation of where I was/where I am now. It's the subtleties of being a person and the way the story keeps telling.

** spoiler alert ** Don't read this review if you haven't read the book yet, because there will be spoilers. The book was recommended to me by another fellow book dragon, but with deferred explanations, a blunt refusal to describe it to me beyond "It's good", and quietly murmured "Just trust me" and "You have to try it" comments. Turns out the books is about ..... (HUGE SPOILER ALERT) ...zombies. I am not a big fan of the genre because it is usually the same story over and over......and yet... and yet... this book hooked me. It is not your usual zombie story, at ALL. Melanie is, in the first part of the book, a student at a strange school where she is strapped to a chair with her head in a clenching vise, unable to even turn and look at the other students who are likewise controlled. And yet she does not mind this at all. She adores school and is willing to undergo the physical constraints. Her teacher, the best-beloved all-glorious dispenser of fascinating facts, mythical tales, and deep thoughts, Miss Justineau, seems a likable sort. Other adults in Melanie's life, not so much. But as the book develops, and the reader is allowed to see a bit more of the world around the strange school, you begin to understand those other adults more, and sympathize with them to some extent. As they set out on a life and death journey together, something NONE of them wants to do, you begin to see inside each person, learn what makes them see this terrifyingly broken world the way they do. And you are grateful it is just a book. Carey, as always, writes well, a flowing dialogue, both internally and externally. The events are sometimes surprising, but at no point did I ever feel manipulated or annoyed, with that "Oh come on, that could never happen" feeling that you sometimes get when reading an adventure tale. Magnificent details, vivid and compellingly believable reasons for the zombie apocalypse, and an ending with a real twist. Recommended, because the world building is ASTONISHINGLY well done, and the characters are never flat or one sided, but I cannot say this is a book for children. Older, more mature 8th graders and up, but not if they are prone to nightmares.

This review is going to be a bit odd for one main reason - this is a graphic novel but I listened to the audiobook version of it. It's odd to me that they even make graphic novels into audiobooks - the artwork seems so important to telling the story. But not only is Nimona an audiobook, it won an Odyssey honor award given to the best audiobooks in children's or YA literature. I figured that meant it had to be pretty great so I gave it a listen. Nimona is a teenage girl who desperately wants to work with the biggest villain in the kingdom, Ballister Blackheart. She ultimately becomes his sidekick, but sometimes it's hard to tell who's the real villain. Because it turns out Nimona is a shapeshifter, and she seems to be a little more ruthless than Blackheart cares for. They go against the corrupt institution to try and bring it down - but things get more complicated when Blackheart's nemesis (and formerly his good friend/lover) Goldenloin gets involved. Let me first address the pros and cons of the audiobook before I get into the story itself. The positives are that the performers are very good. It's an ensemble cast which works well. In order to assist with the story there are a lot of sound effects included. Unfortunately, I feel that listening to it on audio rather than reading it was probably more of a hindrance than a good thing. A lot of the action is supplemented with sound effects or added in narration, but it definitely feels like it's kind of forced in. Imagine watching an action movie but the screen doesn't work and you can only hear it. That's what this felt like. Especially during battle scenes there would be a lot of "ugh!" "pow!" sort of things, and I got the idea that people were fighting, but I didn't know exactly what was happening. As a result of this I also had a little trouble following the plot at times. That aside, the actual story: in the beginning it felt rather cliche. The villain against the institute, but it turns out that he's not actually much of a villain - he has a good moral compass an the institute is the one doing bad things. Things got a little more interesting as the story progressed. We find out more about Nimona as it goes on. The ending left me a little confused/unsure of what I was supposed to be taking away from it. Am I supposed to feel sympathy for Nimona? Because I didn't, not really. Blackheart was an interesting character - he's clearly conflicted about his role as the villain. And his relationship with Goldenloin is complex and interesting as well. I would have liked to know more about that. Nimona, to me, just came off as a whiny sort of teenager. I found her to be rather annoying and kind of wished she'd get out of the picture so we could learn more about Blackheart and Goldenloin. Obviously I can't comment on the artwork. Is a graphic novel still a graphic novel if you can't see any of the pictures?

Vampire Academy, anyone? Where do I even begin? I started this book without reading any reviews or even the blurb (yeah, I'm that reckless), just saw the high rating and decided to jump in on a whim. And it would have been a good story, except that this turned out to be a twin of Vampire Academy, and all the similarities really pissed me off. You see, that is the exact reason I refused to read the Half-Blood series, I hate rip-offs. If I'm a fan of VA, it doesn't mean I want to read the same story again and again. I want the original, not the copycats. There are people who are able to overlook such things and enjoy the story all the same, but I'm just not one of them. The main character of this book, Kendra Irisavie, is like Rose and Lissa rolled into one. She's got Rose's attitude and fighting skills, but her magic gift is very unique and rare (she's an Empath, able to see people's feelings and emotions) and she belongs to a "royal" family. Then we have a selkie prince and guardian gardinel Tristan Belikov Belicoux, who is practically a carbon copy/ lookalike of Dimitri. The first time he is introduced in the story, he wears a long leather jacket, too, I kid you not. Also, he has this weird penchant for country cello music. Then there is Adrian Ivashkov Julian LeVeq. The first time he meets Rose, oops, I mean, Kendra, it is basically the same scene from Frostbite. There is also a Mason, an Eddie, a Jesse Zeklos, a Mia Rinaldi, and I'm sure I'd encounter many more familiar characters if I decided to continue. Aquidae demons play the part of evil Strigoi. People can be turned Aquidae the same way they can be turned Strigoi - "Aquidae were humans or elementals who were turned, either by force or by choice. Once injected with the dark essence of the Shadow, their mortal lives were extinguished. They existed as an empty shell, a vessel for the demonic liquid." I don't completely get the purpose of Aquidae, except that they are soulless evil creatures of Darkness who get off violence, chaos and destruction and want to annihilate all ondines ... why? According to the lore, ondines are responsible for protection and maintenance of water. What does that mean, exactly? There is also mention of some other elementals (Fire), but they were never explained. I really would have liked to know more how the magic world functions *sigh*. Maybe there were more explanations later in the book. By the way, Aquidae can be killed only with a silver stake kouperet (obviously, some kind of knife), infused with the magic of all four water elementals. I think the supernatural world was very poorly rendered. It was all over the place, and at 30% into the story I still didn't know for sure who was who and what role they played in the society. So, they are all Water Elementals. I guess ondines are all females, while selkies are all males, and demillirs are like dhampirs in VA, half-bloods. There is also a mention of dessondines ? ?, who are both ancestors of ondines and demillirs, and they supposedly exist in the present too, but I never met one during the 30% of the story I've read. All the groups of elementals are not immortal, but they normally live long and healthy lives (about 150 years). Only ondines are at risk, it seems. And here's why it sucks to be an ondine - if her husband cheats on her, she will get sick and die. She will also age prematurely, get sick and die if any of her children dies. WHAT THE FUCK? Nothing of the kind happens to males, though. I wonder why ondines even want to get married and have children at all? Redavi are obviously like Moroi royalty, all stuck-up and useless, and completely opposed to learning how to defend themselves against Aquidae, leaving that "privilege" to selkie gardinels and demillir chevaliers. OMG, I'm completely lost in the definitions of all society members. The place is called Lumiere Academy, and is protected with magic wards. There are also many more similarities, but I already got tired of listing them, so I will stop at that.

I finish this book feeling very torn about the rating. On the one hand, it has the terrific character-building and writing characteristic of David Mitchell. On the other hand, it's very repetitive - both within itself, and in the way the book relates to some of Mitchell's other book. I'd probably actually give it 3.5 stars, but feel much more comfortable rounding it down to 3 rather than up to 4. Slade House the book is about Slade House the house. In a dinky alley, a door appears once every 9 years. A series of people enter this door and never come out. First they are charmed by the atmosphere of Slade House, but then they are snatched and devoured by the regular occupants. And... that's pretty much all the happens in the story. Each chapter covers a different person who enters the house. The people are really the strength of this book. I so admire the way David Mitchell can write characters. He writes each chapter in first-person, and it just felt ridiculously believable and engaging. I felt particularly strongly for Nathan, a boy who seems to be a bit autistic (he struggles to read other people's expressions and gets made fun of at school for being weird), and Sally, a college girl who is sensitive and overweight. They both felt very vulnerable to me in a way that I found very relatable. By its nature, the story is repetitive. In each chapter, the main character gets lured into Slade House, then gets bewitched for a bit, then can't leave. After the first story, you know the pattern, and the subsequent stories feel dull because of that repetition. Further, the bewitching is all an illusion, so, for at least half of each chapter, you know that all the stuff that you're reading about isn't real. That's pretty frustrating. So much of the book is "oh, it turns out it was all a dream!" Because of that, a lot of the book felt like a waste of time. Then, the actually substance of the story is super similar to The Bone Clocks, another David Mitchell book. I don't know how I would have felt if I hadn't already read The Bone Clocks, but I was numbed by that repetition as well. The part I probably feel most torn about was the horror feel of the book. Despite some of the dullness/repetition, there is a pervasive and growing sense of dread in each chapter. It was really uncomfortable. On the one hand, writing that can be that evocative is wonderful. But, on the other hand, it was such an uncomfortable feeling that I did not enjoy the experience of reading Slade House. But that's pretty subjective - if you enjoy the feeling of horror stories more, you might really enjoy Slade House. For me, though, it was an ok, but overall disappointing, book.

When I first started reading this book, I thought it had promise. Given that most fantasy books these days feature vampires, werewolves, or fairies, a grim reaper is certainly different. That, and the fact that the book had a decent ending is the only thing that saved this from being a 1 star. The writing itself is mediocre with sentence fragments galore. Since the story was told from a first person POV and frequently narrated the protagonist's thoughts, that could be excused. After all, few people think in grammatically correct sentences all the time. However, the writing went downhill from there. My main problem with this book was that Jones just tried too hard. In attempting to make Charley (the protagonist) funny, Jones over did it. Nearly every other sentence was a one-liner; poorly conceived analogies peppered her writing. Instead of sounding sassy, Charley came across as annoying and ditzy. The book very nearly turned into a parody of itself, to the point where the "drama" was ridiculous. The grand mystery of the book revolved around some mysterious presence Charley is obsessed with, along with some teenager that once threatened to rape her. What a charmer; truly, I can see why she seems to be madly in love with him. Nearly the entire work features Charley moaning about how much it sucks to be her. I could understand lamenting her inability to confide in anyone or being snubbed by her family, but that isn't what Charley complains about. No, her father, her uncle, and her best friend all believe her. Instead, she whines about waking up early, about someone she doesn't even like being skeptical, and about the questions people her ask her. She tells someone she's the grim reaper, and expects him to take it at face value and not ask a single question. And even when a man she had been interested in did the very thing she wanted him to, she blew him off for mysterious entity that scared her shitless. Additionally, the plot itself is murky. Jones clearly attempted to be cryptic, to inspire the reader's curiosity and provoke wonder about what the ultimate conclusion was. The result was several different story lines only roughly stitched together. In attempting to be mysterious, Jones just didn't dispense enough information. Either she was blatantly obvious with her clues and gave everything away, or she was so vague nothing made sense. Basically, this book was a disappointment. The ending was interesting. Again, I give Jones credit for coming up with something different, but that was the only good thing about this book.

This is one of the most riveting non-fiction books I've ever read. I actually carried it around with me everywhere and read it every spare moment. Besides the fascinating medical history, there's a lot of grappling with medical ethics, and the medical ethics of sixty years ago, and how they intersect with race, poverty, and education (or the lack of it). Through all these issues, Skloot maintains a sharp focus on the human side of the story in Henrietta and her family, especially her daughter. In Skloot's hands, all the big issues boil down to a family who is deeply bereft, and then kept in the dark about their loved one's legacy by the medical establishment. I really admire how Skloot opens herself so much to the Lacks family, how deeply she allows herself to empathize and how much she takes their story to heart, while still managing to portray the doctors in a balanced, even sympathetic way.

It's hard for me to rate this book because its timely subject matter is well discussed, but I really didn't like it as a book. The writing style is faux-poetic and the side characters are cliched caricatures. Everything is in past-tense, which might be intentional for creating a distant/impartial narrative, but did not work at all for me. This book reminded me a lot of The Underground Railroad, in that the premise was fascinating, but I couldn't stand the writing. Similarly, the re-imagining of allegorical movement (migration) as a literal phenomenon worked very well as a way to refresh the discussion of s a nebulous subject (in Exit West, actual doors transport you to different parts of the world), and the story was centered around the emotional and physical journey of the protagonists. I love how the protagonists' relationship progresses, and the tension from two people of the same country with different political, religious, cultural views. I also love the general fade of their relationship, and am so happy that the ending wasn't spic and span. In summary, I didn't like the book but I appreciated it, and I would recommend it to others if they enjoyed The Underground Railroad.

THIS BOOK!!!! FANTASTIC! Thank you to Impulse and Netgalley for providing me with an eARC in exchange of a honest review. This book is such a pleasant surprise. It is very reminiscent of Katie McGarry's Pushing the Limits series, especially Crash Into You (which is my favorite book) and I love it! The story of two teens who come from different worlds finding a special connection with each other is one of my favorite stories and this was perfectly done. The story surrounds Frankie Devereux after she witnessed her boyfriend Noah's death right before her eyes. Suffering from PTSD, Frankie becomes a little reckless and has to move into a less "privileged" part of town with her father and enter a public school where she meets the sexy, passionate, and bad boy Marco Leone. The second Frankie meets Marco, an intense attraction begins and it's all you need to realize that you need Marco as your next book boyfriend. I know I did. Frankie is one of my favorite characters. She suffers from PTSD and flashbacks from the night when Noah died. She is desperately trying to remember who killed Noah and she lets this haunt her for majority of the book. I just felt so much sympathy for her. She is lost. She doesn't feel like she belongs anywhere anymore. She has to move into her Dad's place where she hasn't had that great of a relationship with in quite some time as a result of his job. Her mother is distant and pays more attention to her new husband and making Frankie who she wants Frankie to be rather than get to know her daughter. On top of all this, Frankie is trying to forget everything that is connected to Noah because it hurts her too much. That means trying to distant herself for her oldest friends. While I didn't agree with Frankie's decisions, I understood them. I loved Frankie's development in this novel because it showed just how strong she is. She had to fight a hard battle trying to piece together what happened as well as save herself and learn who she now is. She took some risks and it was always for those she loved. She just wanted to do the right thing for the right reason. Oh Marco, Marco, Marco. I was gushing so much over this beautiful soul. My heart broke a million times because of his story and the cards life dealt him, but you have to love his heart. His connection with Frankie is beautiful and the way he cares for his sister will make you love him. I dare you not to fall in love with him. He is so protective of those he cares about and will do everything to protect them and it hurts because he won't fight for himself. He feels just as lost as Frankie does, if not more. He thinks so poorly of himself that it's heartbreaking! "Marco will fight for his sister, for his friends, and I'm willing to bet hed fight to the ends of the earth for you. But he won't fight for himself. He only sees one door, Frankie. He needs someone to show him the others ones." What I really liked about this book besides the intense relationship between Frankie and Marco was the friendships Frankie formed. This book wasn't only about a love story. As a matter of fact, it wasn't even really instalove (not really), but Frankie first developed a friendships with a girl from her class, Cruz and her new reconnected friendships with her older friends, Lex and Abel which was more important. She needed to know that she had people supporting her who can help her see the "other doors." Overall, this book is fantastic and quickly became one of my favorite contemporaries. It's sexy, fast-paced, thrilling, and never a dull moment. I never cry while reading contemporaries, but this book made me bawl my eyes out. I felt so connected to these characters and so invested in their journeys. Thank you, Kami Garcia for writing such a beautiful, heartfelt story. It will stay in my heart forever.

When Graeme Montgomery receives word from the king that he is to marry the daughter of the clan that murdered his father, he is furious. How could the king ask this of him? Especially as the girl is rumored to be daft and unable to have a normal marriage. With the prospect of passing on his heritage through his own blood gone, he still reluctantly accepts his duty as to refuse would be treason and would end up in his death. Graeme gathers his two brothers and his men and heads off to his rival Armstrongs clan, prepared for the worst and willing to accept his duty. When he lays eyes on the lovely Eveline he is blown away by her beauty and also her easy acceptance of him. He makes a vow to himself that he will protect her at all costs but is stunned when his clam refuses to accept her and treats her badly. How can he help his clam understand that they can not punish the daughter for the sins of the father when in his own mind he still wants to destroy the Armstongs? Eveline Armstrong is very secure and protected in her clan, especially after a terrible fall from a horse made her lose her hearing, though no one is aware of this. Circumstances prevented her from speaking as well and to protect herself, she let the charade of her being daft keep going. When she sees Graeme for the first time she actually feels his voice vibrations and she is instantly taken with him and knows he will protect her. But upon arriving at his home and experiencing the hatred and ridicule towards her, she is distraught and wants to leave even though her feelings for Graeme have deepened. The time comes when she must face her past and in the process, she just may lose more than her heart to the rival laird. Sigh....such a romantic, sexy, heart warming, tear inducing story!! I loved it! Eveline was so strong and courageous and faced her demons with a spunk I wish I had. She taught herself to read lips, even though she can not read or write, and was able to hide the fact she could not hear for three years. I loved watching her and Graeme interact, with her trying to explain herself without talking. I admire her courage and what it took to admit the truth about her voice and I admired her even more when an accident occurs and she tells the truth as to what she saw. And Graeme, swoon. I really enjoyed the fact that he was not a womanizer, that he was going to stay true to his wife even if the marriage was not going to be everything he hoped for. Thankfully, our couple is able to express their passion for each other and Graeme's tenderness with Eveline was lovely. We get to meet the extended families of both, each with two brothers and Graeme with a sister as well. I adored Graeme for his understanding of taking away a father and mothers only daughter and I thought the resolution near the end for the rival clans was done very well. There was not much that bothered me about this book expect the fact that Eveline was able to hide the fact she could speak but not hear for so long and one small part that involved Graeme's sister and the women of the clan. Overall, an absolutely wonderful romance book that any romance fan will not want to miss! It made me smile, sigh, laugh, cheer and get angry and had me tearing up. I am so eager for more books from the lovely Maya Banks in this delicious series! 4 1/2 stars Thank you so much to Random House for providing me with this eARC!

HOW I FELT ALL THROUGH OUT: Okay, so how should I describe this book... I just can't find anything that will suit it best aside from: IT IS JUST A COOL IDEA TO START A BOOK WITH. Elsewhere is merely an idea transformed into a book and then left as is while Gabrielle Zevin finds ways to keep the story going for the sake of filling up pages. There is no story here no concrete plot that was supposed to carry the reader and the happenings forward Lizzy, the main character, dies @ 15 and is transported to Elsewhere, a land where all dead people go. In Elsewhere you live just like on Earth, but instead of aging older you grow back / younger. Cool concept and idea, right? Zevin could have came up with more witty ideas to make something out of these concepts! But instead she just enumerates all through out and I eventually grew tired of all her enumerations. That's just it. Lizzy isn't even a character you'd sympathize with. She's just a whiny self-centered brat. And yet almost everyone still loves her and falls in love with her!!! WHAT THE HELL. She's blatantly petulant and self-involved, acting like the world revolves around her and everyone can't possibly live without her! It is not really well-written. I've read books that really are, and that's why I have basis to say so... Zevin's writing did not excel from writing Memoirs of a Teenage Amnesiac to here. Her writing style grew even more clunky and her descriptions aren't even moving anymore. Though I'm considering with my opinion that her ideas in this one is far better. Maybe these remarks are deeply rooted right from my expectations on this book's synopsis. Its summary at the back seemed good at the time. So buying it seemed like a good idea too, but it ended up with me finding out that: It was JUST a good idea, NOT a good story, NEITHER a good book. I feel bad for Zevin because she could've came up with a really cool story from her ideas on this one. I hope she recovers from what she's going through. x

4 1/2 stars. Much has been said about The Girls, the "It Book" of Summer 2016. The critics love it, as do many GRers, but some people have put it down, unfinished, because they feel it's overwritten. Maybe, maybe not, but certainly not as much as that other "It Book", Sweetbitter. Personally, this was one of the best novels I've read in a long time. The only thing that really kept me from giving it a five is the framing story, which even though I understood the point of, didn't completely work for me. Otherwise, I was completely taken in. It has much of that gossamer, dream/nightmare-like feel to it that The Virgin Suicides does. There's a lot to take in here, from the parents who think they're being there for their kids when they're really not, to the harsh, sharp-edged anger that the female characters feel towards the controlling men in their lives, all of it sadly visibly and almost palpable from the outside. Cline is a true talent, all hyperbole aside, that I will definitely keep an eye on.

The overall story is great, it's just me having a hard time with the frustrating side of it - the older self hiding things (even when it wasn't needed and it was causing more drama this way), the main character lying to the older self and keeping things secret in return, the best friend seeming so clueless after all these years of bullying, just because he liked a girl and wanted everything to be sunshine and rainbows. I just couldn't. There is some sort of mystery that prepares you for the worse and that is a plus, as it makes you want to see how badly things got before they got a bit better. So I assume that things will get better through the story, but I am a bit tight on patience right now... Maybe I will try it again some other time.

* I received a free copy on goodreads first reads for review* You don't realise how language actually interferes with communication until you don't have it, how it gets in the way like an over dominant sense. I was continually amazed at the level of complexity and emotion that Lily King was able to fit into a mere 250 page novel. And, true to her quote at the top of this review, reading between the lines at what was left unsaid revealed far more about the characters than their own musings and anthropological discoveries. Euphoria is about the relationships formed between three anthropologists studying river tribes in New Guinea during the early 1930's. Nell, the American, and most well known of the three, having published a rather controversial book regarding the sexual lives of tribal children. She never really states it, but we get the picture that she suffers abuse at the hands of her husband, Australian anthropologist Fen, who seems desperate to right the balance of his perceived power in their relationship by making a discovery that will eclipse the scholarly achievements of his wife. Add to this, Andrew Bankston, a British anthropologist and erstwhile suicide attempter, who latches onto the couple in the hopes that they can possibly save him from his misery. Of course, they may also be his ultimate undoing, which makes this book such a tension filled pleasure to read. The tribes in which the characters settle and assimilate are colorful and fascinating and King draws them in such a way that we feel like scientists of sorts just reading and observing their customs and interactions with each other and with the main characters. I felt like King gave them just enough "screen" time to make them a vital part of the story without letting them overtake the spotlight on the relationships between Nell, Fen, and Bankston. This book also made me realize that we readers are all anthropologists of a sorts. Studying and observing human life through the lens of literature. Not a bad sort of profession in my opinion.

Appearently, it's really hard for me to form a proper opinion on The Long Way to a Small, Angry Planet. I have so any different thoughts that I can't seem to be able to boil it down to a rating. In cases like this, I like to browse through the other reviews and see which sentiments and thoughts resonate with me the most. In the past, this has often given form to my opinion, by voicing my thoughts in a way that I apparently can't. Unfortunately in this case, I find that there's a lot of truth (for me at least) in both good and bad reviews. So, let's just make a list of those thoughts/sentiments, in no particular order. Even if I don't manage to come up with a clear opinion, at least I'll be able to reflect on them later, or they might even help someone else resonate a bit. This is definitely a character-driven book, and even though I knew that going in, for some reason, I wasn't exactly prepared for it. There is very little going on, which isn't to say that there isn't a whole world galaxy being built, complete with different races and politics, but it all (literally) occurs OUTSIDE of the spaceship, and therefor takes a major backseat to the overall story. The things that do happen, often feel tacked on as a mere plot device to build more character background / relations. Which bugged me quite a lot, every time it happened. 2 examples of this (but there are many more): * Space pirates turning up right after our newbie has arrived and apparently she's the only one that can 'save' their asses from 'greedy' pirates, using some tidbit of knowledge which she just happens to remember from that one class that she took that one time. All just to build her 'rep' with the other crew mates. * Apparently, the galaxy might be pretty large, but when they're flying out to the core (where almost no one else is), and they pick up a distress signal in the middle of nowhere, it just happens to be the ship of the other-species lover of our dear captain. What luck that the ships Technician is able to fix the alien ship with no trouble, and in the process just happens to spot the 34+ mines that are hidden in the wall, which she luckily can defuse with little to no problem. Turns out the universe isn't such a big place after all and coincidence is all over the place. Continuing on with the worldgalaxybuilding, it is actually, surprisingly good. Throughout the book you get a feel for the recent history of the Galactic Commons, for the different races that it's made up off and how the human species fit into it all. The different species are also described surprisingly well. Not only are they all sufficiently biologically diverse (not just different variations on bipedal humanoid), but they also have their own history, religion, motivation, politics, quirks, etc.. They all feel unique enough to make believeable backdrop for the main story. As usual I combined the ebook with the audiobook and I have to admit that Rachel Dulude does an EXCELLENT narrating this. Especially her impersonation of Kizzy, an adult version of a 13yo fan girl, was outstanding. The writing is solid and is easy to follow. Which, in a complex universe with different species and worlds, is actually impressive. I never felt lost in its galaxy and always got the right information when I needed it, without it being overdone and patronizing. One tidbit that I have to bring up though, it must have slipped through the editing process, but there was this one line that completely tripped me up. So badly in fact, that I had to look it up. He had been in homes like this before -- sturdy, ramshackle dwellings made from whatever a few hard-working pairs of colonist hands could scrounge up. I'm sorry, but there is NO way that I can envision what she means by that. Google even states that they are opposites. There was one other instance of this that jarred my immersion, but I couldn't find it again. I loved the philosophy behind sentient AI's and their right to exist and self-control. Even if it was wrapped in a cheesy 'we-can't-be-together'-love story. The thoughts behind it are very interesting to explore and the character of 'Lovey' Lovelace was very cool and her story arc was arguably the best. Maybe that's just because I'm a tech nerd that's really into SciFi and AI's at the moment, who knows. In my opinion there was too much emphasis on the characters that we are supposed to love and way too little on the other members of the cast, who seem to be a lot more interesting. Corbin, I'm looking at you here, the mini-arc he got was way to short (and a little too (ch)easy) So much cheesyness! At times it felt like watching one of those romance movies, with cliches all around and cheesy lines to tie them together. This is definitely not something I enjoy, especially not when it's stretched out way to thin. Hellooo Rosemary and Sizzix 'foreplay'. What the hell was that? I get that the author wanted to convey how awkward the whole inter-species culture clash can be, but does that mean she has to make the whole reading experience awkard too? I was literally exclaiming how boring it all was, only to climax the entire ordeal with a proper 'face-to-black-sex-scene'. Apart from the awkard foreplay, the whole relationship was so unbelieveable it made me cringe. There's also this whole 'Firefly' vibe going on from page 1 and it never really went away. Firefly really was a cheesy show with thin plot lines and questionable acting, but then again, so was pretty much everything from that era. If Becky Chambers was going for this athmosphere, she has succeeded. But just as when I watched Firefly (not that long ago), I can't help but thinking that I would have enjoyed it (the show) and this (the book) a lot more, if I had read it when I was about 10 years younger. I think that all the cheesyness, combined with the uncanny plot devices & the many ex machinas made it all so unreal that the magic of the characters simply went straight out the window and into the void. Look at that, it seems I have reached a conclusion, of sorts. I think I will continue with the next installment, hoping that my overal qualms will be silenced. I'm also really curious to see if the story arc of 'Lovey' / 'Lovelace' will reach a satisfying conclusion Rating wise, I think I'll leave it at a solid 3 stars. I liked it, but there was too much jarring to love it.

While a lot of action happened in this book compared to the first, it seemed to be less driving than the last book. I was still interested in the plot, but it seemed easier for me to get tired because of how much the action was jumping around without anything of true substance happening. It was kind of like a mystery novel where each piece of the puzzle had to be exposed with someone breaking into somewhere or getting captured or moving camp to escape someone. I really liked Four and Tris's relationship, and I liked that it got very realistically rocky while still showing that they were still affection for one another. It was much more realistic than some plots that make one of the people in the relationship the strong force that the other must daintily rely on. They're probably one of my favorite literary relationships simply because they called one another out for being wrong. Trust and honesty were highlighted and when one of them kept something from the other, the consequences were shown and they talked about it. It seems like in other relationships when one person keeps something from the other it's played off as that person shielding the other person and the other person remains completely oblivious. Four and Tris are in tune with one another, and I just really loved getting to see that shown.

**2 stars for the beginning (biggest info dumps EVER!) and 3.5 for the end** Full Blooded had an interesting premise but the author needs to do some serious work on her world building, characterization and plot development. The ending was good - thus the 3 star rating - but the first half had the most horrid info dumps I've ever read. EVERY CHARACTER talked in long paragraphs of 3+ sentences - in chapter 2, I counted 12 examples of such paragraphs. Don't know what I mean? Here's one an example: "Listen, Ray. I realize you think I had something to do with this whole mess." I jabbed my elbow into door, gesturing to my apartment. "And you think I'm hiding a big, juicy secret from the world. Possibly hidden somewhere inside there. In fact, you've been dogging me for a very long time trying to find out just exactly what it is, making my life hard and miserable along the way, but here's the truth--are you ready? I'm not hiding anything." Well, other than the fact I just turned into a scary werewolf. "I'm not on drugs, I don't deal them. I don't have ties to the Colombians, and more importantly, I haven't broken any laws. The truth is, my boyfriend and I decided to go camping at the last minute simply because the weather was beautiful." Thank goodness it wasn't tornado season. "It was just one of those happy, carefree decisions people make. He took care of bringing the keys, and I forgot to get them back. And while we were gone, someone trashed my place. That's the end of the juicy story." I kept imagining Jessica as Joe Friday in one of this infamous speeches. Everybody talked in the same way: Jessica, her brother, the neighbor, the Pack's second and even her father. There was no distinction accounting for personality or temperament as if everybody goes around the world speaking in speeches. Besides the crazy info dumps, there wasn't a clear explanation of the premise. Why aren't there any female werewolves? The author didn't delve very deeply into this - it just doesn't seem evolutionary efficient for a race to rely in other females for reproduction. There was some mention of the "shifter gene being coded into the second x chromosome" but then, how is Jessica a werewolf? My husband's explanation: she's a hermaphrodite. One of the worst issues with the characterization is that we have very little knowledge as to what Jessica is feeling. She's confronted with a lot of new situations but with a few exceptions, we almost never get to know her feelings. Is she scared? Happy? Sad? Envious? Grumpy? We know when her wolf is lusty (which happens quite often) or when she wants to fight but that's pretty much it. What is the point of writing a book in the first person if the reader has to guess the character's feelings? It was difficult for me to take Jessica seriously when she was so boastful during fights. At one point, a dangerous character is disabled and instead of finishing her off, she decides to have a drawn out fight with an enemy she could have dispatched quickly while having boastful speeches of the 'You're going to die!!' variety. At the same time, the dangerous character took the opportunity to recuperate and wreak further havoc down the road. WHERE'S YOUR BRAIN, WOMAN? Full Blooded have some really good male characters - Rourke, Callum and James were particularly yummy - and they only reason I'm reading book #2. I really hope the author has curbed her tendency towards info dumping in future books because otherwise, I don't think I'll be able to read further.

You know when something is so bad that it's kind of good? That was Hourglass for me. I began the book with low expectations and immediately the prose jumped out at me because it was so...unique. It was very formal (the seventeen year old main character used the word "buttresses" with no hint of irony,) and since most paranormal romances have sarcastic leading ladies I wasn't expecting it. But the writing was almost too formal, and the book felt like it was trying way too hard, especially since a teenager was narrating. Then of course, the main character did end up being a sarcastic know-it-all and her informal dialogue contrasted with the narration so much that it was just awkward. "Three years worth of orthodontia" was used on the same page as "freaking Scarlett O'Hara." I'd say the first half of the book was just ridiculously obnoxious, but at some point I started finding the awfulness funny. The characters were ridiculous (basically, "Let's hate this gorgeous girl for being acquaintances with the guy I'm crushing I'm on and for absolutely no other reason"), the plot was confusing (time travel plots hardly ever make sense, but in this case the author didn't even clarify whether they were in the past or present during the climax), and despite how much the author tried, there was no chemistry between Emerson and Michael. Commenting on how good looking Michael in every chapter isn't enough, and even though they can literally create sparks every time they touch it wasn't enough. Am I going to read the sequel? Probably, yeah, just so I can laugh at how bad it is again. But do I plan on liking it? Hell no.

What if Sleeping Beauty didn't fall in love with the prince? First off, I'm a huge fairy tale nerd. So an adaptation of the Sleeping Beauty story after she wakes from her curse, sign me up! And Sleeping Beauty who disregards the true love trope? Hell-to-the-yes, I will pick that up in a heartbeat. And that's what we get with A Wicked Thing. Thrown into a strange new world right along side Princess Aurora, where the story of Sleeping Beauty is one that everyone knows, because its a hundred year old tale. With a true love's kiss, her awakening is meant to bring prosperity and magic back to the land. But nothing is happily ever after for Aurora. She is engaged to the shy Prince Rodric, a stranger to her and one of many princes that have traveled just to kiss her lips and await her eyes to flutter open. Her family is dead, long gone from this world. Her home is a mystery to her. And Aurora is all alone, thrown to the dogs in this strange, new world. And home is a hundred years in the past. I was bored with A Wicked Thing. It took copious amounts of chapters for the ball to finally start rolling. The writing is smooth and the olden-time feel is definitely present, but alone its wasn't enough to reel me in. Aurora is practically a prisoner in her own home. Her kingdom is under the control of a ruthless king. She has no say in anything. She is locked in her room each night. Only allowed out at the beck and call of the queen, to engage with nobility, or to meet with Rodric. Her passiveness became unbearable. It felt like pulling teeth for little things to start moving the plot along. When she finally started to sneak out, stick up for herself, and put her authority ahead of her polite smiles and curtsies, Aurora became interesting. Sadly it took far too long for it all to happy, and my interest in the novel started to dissipate. Aurora is a hard character to place or really enjoy enjoy reading about until she starts to really grow a backbone. And I'm glad that she finally did, which is why I gave the novel a three overall rather than a two. Her capacity to care for her subjects knows no bounds, but the authority she has as a monarch is nothing as long as the rigid King John sits on her throne. And marrying Rodric would leave her in the same position--powerless. So i give Aurora an A for effort as A Wicked Thing progressed, and an A for keeping the boys at bay. There are three significant men that walk into her life: Rodric, her "true love"; Tristan, the vengeful rebel; and Finnegan, the sharp-tongued prince from across the sea. Out of all these boys, Aurora is able to keep her head secured atop her shoulders, though some lust does creep in every now and again. Her idea of love does not confine to the limit of fairy tales, and that made me giddy. Especially the more she bonded by Rodric or the deeper she bantered with Finnegan (who I really enjoyed reading about). So say goodbye to true love, because Sleeping Beauty will be having none of that! Final Summation: A Wicked Thing is like a boat ride, smooth with some bumps along the way, and then you don't notice the storm clouds coming in, but once they're upon you there is no turning back. The ending is what is keeping me coming back to read more. Aurora's growth as a character has me hopeful for the next book, and I hope she continues to surprise me.

Title : Incarnate Series : Newsoul #1 Author : Jodi Meadows Pages : 384 Release Date : Jan. 31st 2012 Publisher : Katherine Tegen Books Format : Hardcover Source : Bought - Owned My Opinion : Incarnate is Jodi Meadows' remarkable debut novel. Oh, you still get one for reading my review *hugs* But, if you want another, comment :D) Jodi Meadows' voice is strong. Her book was slow-paced (I like any pace, actually, but it needs to match with the book), and yet, it was all it take for me to relax and enjoy it thoroughly. It was VERY unique... I don't think I ever read a book like that. In Incarnate, with a dystopian setting, we meet Ana; the child of Li and Menehem. She's a nosoul (from what her mother, Li, believes and has taught her) and a newsoul (to Sam, who she meets after walking away from her mother). She meets Sam while she's trying to run from Sylphs; they are things that burn you (ouch!). And, she decides she'd like it better to drown than die burned (I guess everyone has their preference, even about death *shrugs*). But, Sam saves her. At first, she thinks he wants to use her, or something like that, since that'S what she has ever known; she hasn't been in contact with civilization in 18 years (or her whole life), because she wasn't Ciana's soul. Ciana was the one who died and never came back. She's the reason Ana was born. I absolutely loved loved LOVED Ana. She may have been mistrustful, but it made her a hard and strong female character; and those are the bests of them all. Even though she didn't feel like she had a place in The Heart (which is the ONLY city we know). I also really loved Sam; he may have hid some things from Ana, I thought it didn't feel like betrayal. I thought it was great of him to do that. Stef was a bit annoying. Like the jealous ex-girlfriend of someone who's trying to be nice to you so they can get their boyfriend back. But, aside from that, I liked her. Did you know you can reincarnate with a different gender... Sam did, once (or twice, thrice, etc. ), but every time I read that, I could only picture a guy in a dress and a wig (not a pretty picture, right? *cringes*) It may have been slow-paced, but it's what made the book wonderful. For no reason she can figure out, sixteen-year-old Lex Bartleby is one crazy angry girl. Previously normal and a good student, the high school junior can barely get through a day of school without punching someone out. The only reason that she isn't kicked out of school a week before summer is that her very loving parents devise a plan to turn her around. She has to spend the summer in the country (Adirondacks) with her Uncle Mort, whom she hasn't seen she she was six. Lex is sick about the idea of being taken away from her twin sister and forced into the boredom of the tiny town of Croak. But Croak isn't the hell hole Lex thought it would be. Or--rather hell holes are not really so hellish when she gets the insiders' version. With the help of Uncle Mort, Lex discovers she is perfectly suited to reaping the souls of the dead and helping them move on to the afterlife. And the afterlife can be quite entertaining, not at all what people usually envision. The downside to Lex's new job is its very long hours; the upside is her partner Driggs, who is clever, insightful, and hot. The push-pull of their relationship is very funny and brings a good deal of humor to the novel, which is more of a mystery than it is a horror book. Finding new friends, Lex may come to enjoy her reaping. But when there is no explanation for deaths of some of the people she and Driggs are sent to collect, things get scary fast, and no one is safe--including the reapers themselves. High school housekeeping: For a quick, engaging teen read, Croak is perfect. It has all the best elements of a novel. You may have to finish in one sitting. Mystery and romance are combined with perfect pacing, witty dialogue, and deeper questions about right, wrong and vigilante justice. A great summer read for all teens--don't miss this one! NOTE: This review is also posted on my blog School Library Lady.
