EDIT: THERE IS A SYNOPSIS "Eadlyn doesn't expect her Selection to be anything like her parents' fairy-tale love story" HA. If I do do remember correctly, there was a ton of unnecessary drama, crying, and fits.

Eadlyn isn't a Princess Diana who the public fawns over, nor is she her mother America. Eadlyn is cold, selfish, and condescending. She was raised behind palace walls, and is almost oblivious to how the world works. She shadows her father in his duties, and she knows how to run a country, but her isolation has made her unapproachable to the public. Eadlyn isn't a sympathetic character. She does have moments of redemption, which are quickly followed by her making an egregious faux pas. I wanted Eadlyn after talking with Kile, to make a project to help bring housing to homeless. The thought never crosses her mind. With the original Selection, there were more opportunities to test the candidates, but in the Heir there were no such trials... well there was the quiz event. I feel like Cass missed an opportunity here, instead the pages were filled with run of the mill dates, bland summarization of riots and how tired the king looks. It wasn't humanized enough. Random Notes: I'm flabbergasted that neither Maxon nor America ever divulged what happened during their Selection. How do you keep something like that a secret for so long? I don't really get the hatred between Josie and Eadlyn. It's childish. Why is there no back story here, besides saying Josie is obnoxious and takes my things. Henri is adorable. Eric is unfailing. Kile is brilliant. What happened to America's other two brothers?

I'm not sure how Cora Carmack does it, but whenever I read a book written by her, I can't seem to stop reading it! If I really have to stop reading and then continue later, I can't stop thinking about the characters or about the book in the time when I'm not reading. Just like with Losing It books, I'm sure that Rusk University books are going to be high up on my favorites list! All Lined Up is told in two POVs following Dallas and Carson as our main characters. Dallas is freshmen at Rusk University. With her dad being a football coach, she grew up with it. Until now, her dad was always a coach for high school teams, but this year he decided to move up to coaching a University team. No less, but the very same University Dallas goes to. To make things even worse, her ex-boyfriend Levi is the lead quarterback at the Rusk University football team. While attending a fraternity party her best friend Stella dragged her to, she literally falls into Carson's lap while trying to get away from Levi and one other guy. The connection between them is instant. You can see sparks flying all around. But after that night the two decide to just stay friends because Carson is the second string quarterback and has to focus on football and getting the scholarship. While I am not a fan of American football and have absolutely NO IDEA what is going on there, I have actually enjoyed it as an element here. Usually, when I see there is football in a book, I tend to stay away and not even glance at that book, but with All Lined Up being written by Cora, I knew I at least had to give it a try. So all you non-US people, like myself, if American football scares you, give this book a try and you maybe end up liking it in the end! "I will never be in that position again. I will never be the person who cares more because that person is always the one who hurts more." We already know that Cora has mastered romance in her novels, and All Lined Up is no different. She did it well! What starts like a slow romance, with a lot of chemistry and a bit of banter, turns out into finding the truth, accepting themselves and finding love. To sum it up, All Lined Up is one of my favorite reads this year, and I'm sure it will appeal to all the lovers of New Adult Contemporary novels! Blog | Twitter | Facebook | Instagram | Pinterest

DEAD ENDS is a novel about identity - the "who am I?" question. It's narrated by a brilliant, but troubled teen named Dane whose new neighbor Billy D has Down syndrome. Over the course of time, these two begin to see what they have in common - fathers who aren't living with them - and the pain it's caused in shaping their identity. The circumstances behind their absent dads are different, and each copes with the loss with varied reactions - Billy seeks his father while Dane wants nothing to do with him. Dane is an angry, frustrated, violent boy who lashes out at every verbal altercation. Dane is a bully. Somehow, Erin Jade Lange does an excellent job creating sympathy for Dane. That was a tough task considering he has a tough time keeping his fists from hitting others. I like that Billy D leads Dane to ask the question: why do people hit? Because others hit them? But that doesn't fit for Dane. He has a lot to figure out. This novel has some very strong female characters: Dane's mom, Billy's mom, and Seely, the girl who Dane falls for. Major issues addressed: bullying single mothers friendship special needs YA identity physical abuse This is a straight-shooting novel that doesn't shy away from tough issues and situations. It's an important read, one I hope will be in schools and libraries and YA's hands across the country. Recommended for 14 and up because of the violence. Thank you to Bloomsbury for the ARC copy!

Yep, I'm an incurable optimist. After seeing this title in the library, I thought: "Well, the first book in the series was lame, but the third one wasn't that bad. I'll give this on a go." As you can tell from the rating, I $crEURwed myself over nicely. Snow white must die is a bizzare hybrid of a poor crime investigation, an American soap opera and a particularly bad episode of Cheaters. Whereas Cheaters can actually be hillarious thanks to the oddly cool and factual narrator, the Cheaters elements in this novel are just fillers and melodrama. I wasn't drawn to the plot, but I kept skimming the pages just so I can see what awaits us next - perhaps an episode of The Maury show? (Oh silly me! That was the third book in the series!) When I've mentioned the plot... oh, the plot. To say that I wasn't drawn to it is an understatement. It's convoluted and far-fetched. I really can't believe that a conspiracy of that magnitude could have been kept a secret for about a decade. I'm sorry, but I refuse to believe that. That's not how it works in real life - in real life, conspiracies/plots that involve just two people blow up just like that *snaps fingers*, let alone with more people involved. And the people in this book, goodness gracious! The book is full to the brim with characters, but none of them are fleshed out, not even the leading two characters. Trust me, folks, I have no illusions about Bodenstein and Kirchoff as investigators. When I compare them to the brilliant detectives of crime fiction, they sit at the little kids table. They can't hold a candle to one Harry Hole, or one Jack Reacher, or one Harry Bosch, or one Lew Archer, or the old-fashioned commissaire Maigret. With that said, I've expected more from them - a bit more engagement, determination, decisiveness, or just plain ol' thinking. (Though that applies more to Bodenstein, as he spends the majority of the book as a protagonist of the bad Cheaters episode.) I simply couldn't connect with the characters because I couldn't understand them. The logic of those people is completely baffling. Exhibit A - A girl likes a guy, but he sees her only as a friend. What does she do? - Talks to the guy openly and honestly about her feelings? - No, Martina, you silly fool. She starts eliminating her rivals! Exhibit B - A husband has to cut the family vacation short because he has to solve cases. The wife is pissed off. What does she do? - She shares her thoughts and feelings on the subject with her husband, so that he can view the situation from her angle and possibly make it up to her? - No, Martina, you silly goose. She has an affair! On top of that, it seemed as if Neuhaus deliberately went out, made a list of all possible human flaws, corruption, immoral and criminal acts and proceeded to cram those into the book. There's nothing organic about it; it's a totally artificial construct. Almost everyone in the village of Altenheim is involved in, to put it mildly, shady practices. Heck, the favorite sport of the residents is victim blaming! That's right, folks, it's the dead girls' fault that they've ended up dead! I really could't find a redeeming quality in this book. From the over-the-top plot, one-dimensional characters, absurd motivations, victim blaming all to way to the writing/translation which resembles a lumbering engine. I'm done with this series.

If you read Stroked then you remember Bodi who was Reese's main competition. A loner and an enigma, but also the best swimmer in the world. Well, in this book, we find out why. And it will make you see this man with new eyes. And you will sympathise (or empathize) or be frustrated with him. But you will also fall in love with him. I promise because you can't help but love someone so good and earnest. Our heroine, Ruby Hearts (yes that is her REAL name) is fantastic and funny and has a kind compassionate heart. She saw past Bodi's standoffish behavior and saw it for the defense mechanism it was. Ruby knows what it's like to march to the beat of your own drum and she in instrumental in Bodi's growth as a character over the course of the book. The romance and intimacy is super charged in this book. The writing is stellar and the visuals are awesome. But there is so much more to this story. I loved that it reminds us that people are so much more than their beautiful exteriors and that we should be kind to people, because you never know what they are struggling with. Meghan Quinn knocked it out of the park with this book! I highly recommend it! 5 stars!This review was originally posted on Words We Love By

In this golden age of young adult literature, there are two distinctive audiences: the young people the books are intended to be read by, and the older generation who, perhaps beguiled by the excellence of the sub genre over the past couple of decades, have continued to read YA well into adulthood. I am one of these. When I read a YA novel, I try to evaluate it on two levels: would I have enjoyed it as a kid reader, and do I enjoy it now? There have been a number of books that meet the first criteria while being problematical for the second. This is not one of those books. I can see my teenage self reading this book by the light of the streetlamp down the street, well after my parents had gone to bed, because I couldn't stand to stop until I reached the finish. Magic! History! History of places not usually written about! Mythology! A pirate ship! A girl navigating the pirate ship! A girl who feels like an outsider in her own family -- her own troubled family -- who has her own goals and enough smarts to go after them. And of course a cute guy or two, who do not overwhelm the story. The adult me appreciated the vivid depictions of different cultures during various points in history, especially when overlaid with a palimpsest of mythological possibilities. I was fascinated by the glimpse of Hawaii in the 1880s, even knowing that the kingdom was doomed thanks to the greed of American entrepreneurs. The author demonstrates the cost without hammering the point home, all while keeping the action brisk, and the threats real. Nix Song, half-Hawaiian daughter of an American man who discovered he could navigate to other times and places if he had the right maps, and Lin Song, a Hawaiian woman, is afraid she will be erased from history altogether if her father's obsessive search for a map to take him back to Hawaii before Lin died, so he can rescue her, is successful. In much YA these days, one of the most common tropes is what is now called the love triangle. This is not new. I remember rival guys in stories back when I was a teen reader. They seem to be part of the expected landscape now, but I liked what the author did here: Nix does not want to get involved. Having grown up with her father's obsession, she is skeptical at best about the addiction of love. Very refreshing! And I liked the guys: artistic Blake, who loves Hawaii in spite of his deeply troubled family, and insouciant, clever, funny, compassionate and passionate thief Kashmir. I like Nix's wrestle with normal teen responses to cute guys, and her determination not to be suckered into surrendering her life to those responses. And I really loved the plot. I think if I had one criticism, it would be That Nix unaccountably never tells her father her quite understandable fear though they had several very raw and real conversations toward the end but that was small, as the overall unfolding of the story was so satisfying. Full of insightful observations and deftly descriptive character moments, I enjoyed this book enough to put it on my keeper shelf, old as I am. And as a kid, I expect it would have been among those I checked out repeatedly.

I read A Court of Thorns and Roses (ACOTAR) after seeing the title recommended so many times - a Beauty and the Beast fairy tale retelling? Sure, but I was really sold when my friend said how much more she loved the sequel, A Court of Mist and Fury (ACOMAF). This proved true for me as well. ACOTAR had some exciting moments, but the romance with Tamlin was exceptionally boring. (I wanted, and still want, to know more about Lucien!) ACOMAF was miles better - and I especially loved the Hades & Persephone vibe. ***Very MINOR spoilers below*** That said... Maas made some big promises at the end of the second book. Feyre walked away from her friends and family to go undercover at the Spring Court and make them pay for selling out Prythian/her family. Without going into A Court of Wings and Ruin (ACOWAR) spoiler territory too much, I can say that Maas failed at delivering any of that. I waited for ACOWAR, riding the waves of "TAMLIN SUCKS" but ended up just seeing Feyre as naive and petty. Yes, she was right to leave him... but wanting his people to be vulnerable to an evil king and terrifying army as payback? Risking Lucien's life? I can't get behind that, even if Maas really wants the reader to do so. But we don't even get undercover, vengeful Feyre - she spends the first couple of chapters being angry and then flubs her own plan and takes off. So that's my qualm with the beginning of the book. Plot-wise, my other major problem is that things go "oh shi- horribly wrong" every couple of chapters and then someone (literally) swoops in to save the day every time. Every. Damn. Time. And no one every stays dead - unless they're a minor, forgettable character. This inability to kill her darlings also crosses into Maas' writing style. I cringed every time a character "snarled," which means I cringed a lot. She also refers to people as "males" and "females," and it just sounds so weird. These phrases, coupled with too much tell versus show, made for a slow and boring read. The pace picks up at the end but it's too little too late. The main saving grace for me in this book was the minor characters getting time to shine. (Nesta, Amren, Lucien, Azriel. I'd like a book about them Scooby-Doo-ing their way around the world, please. Now.) My rating is 3/5. I enjoyed some aspects and returning characters, but the sloppy writing and plot hurt my soul.

You don't go to Houellebecq for cheery, uplifting stories with happy endings, and Submission is another cynical black novel about loneliness, the decay of western values and the emptiness at the heart of our culture. If that's your sort of thing, and it's definitely mine, then Submission is worth a look, but only after you've read (in order of importance) Atomised, Platform, The Possibility of an Island and The Map and the Territory. Each of these are, in my view, more interesting and rewarding novels. Still, Submission is an entertaining read - the hangdog, over-it-all central character's disillusionment and boredom is convincingly conveyed and the changes taking place in Paris of the future are interesting and, while not entirely plausible, convey an interesting point.

Stray has a fascinating setup. Cass Devlin is having a perfectly normal last day of school. She's looking forward to university and, more immediately, to some great graduation parties. And then, while she's walking home the same way she's done hundreds of times before, she's suddenly somewhere completely different. There's no explosion, no feeling of falling into a void, no sci-fi-type transitions, she's just suddenly in a forest. She's completely on her own, other than some strange animals, and even worse, it soon becomes clear that she's not even on Earth. Through entries in her diary, we follow Cass as she does her best to survive and explore her new environment, looking for... something, anything. We then also follow her as she's rescued by humans from a very technologically advanced civilisation and becomes what they call a 'stray'. She's not the first person who's accidentally stumbled through a 'gate' from somewhere else in the universe, although she's the first one from Earth. Cass is granted a sort of refugee status, but hasn't even began to adapt to regular life when it is discovered she's got a special ability, one that might of great value in this world's struggle against outside forces. There was a lot here that I liked. Cass is a great character, wonderfully sensible and insightful about herself, but at the same time believable as a teenager. She reacts to the really strange circumstances in which she finds herself in ways that I felt made complete sense. Also, the concept is one that I think is absolutely fantastic, and I really liked the directions in which Host took it. The ways in which this other world differed from Earth and the implications of the technology all make perfect sense and were really thought-provoking. And yet... frustratingly, I ended up DNFing this after reading about 60%. The problem was the format, I think. Here's the thing: the diary entries were done in a way that was completely believable. That is a positive thing, in a way, but it also meant that the book was mainly exposition, as there are lots and lots of sections of Cass writing what she's learnt and reporting, in blow-by-blow fashion, what she did that day. I didn't have a problem with the format in the first sections, as Cass is wondering through the forest with no idea what's going on. In those sections Host manages to convey a lot of emotion through the writing, even as Cass is trying hard to be brave and sensible when she writes. Later, though, the emotion felt very distant and I found it hard to care. I'd even go as far as to say it became a bit of a slog. I did persevere and read on for a few days, but I didn't feel I was getting anywhere, and ended up putting it down. MY GRADE: It's a DNF. But DNF or not, I would still read more by Host, I think. I like her ideas, and maybe something not in diary form would work better for me.

Scooby Doo meets H.P. Lovecraft? Who wouldn't want to dig in with a book being marketed this way? Certainly not me since that seemed quite the, um, interesting pairing. Teen detectives (The Blyton Summer Detective Club) are well known for solving a particular case, and their last one at that, in Sleepy Lake. Somehow, something resonates horrifically with each of them - the invariadubitably (hey, if the author can make up words, so can I - it's fun to say - try it!) large pink elephant in the room! Thirteen unlucky years later, they reunite to go back and face this metaphorical elephant head on. I am so torn with this novel. I want to love it. I really do. But I just... don't. What I liked about it: various ha ha moments with nods such as "Nancy Hardy, journalist", Arkham Asylum and Zoinx River. Cute, very cute. And going in with Scooby Doo being the main factor, it was easy to see how this was more humor and nostalgia than anything else. For that, I can appreciate it. However, what didn't work for me was the writing style. I felt it was all over the place. Set stage one, scene one... and then back to novel style... then screenplay... sometimes dispersed sporadically throughout a section written like a (dare I say) "normal" book. I also learned more about the proper way to destroy a man's testicles than I ever needed to, though I found myself smiling during this part and I'm not sure what that says about me as a person or if I'm just in a mood... *wink*. And that was just in the first 50 pages. Ultimately the story line was fine - I can totally appreciate what the author was trying to do and found my love (again) for the Scooby Gang, er... BSDC, that is. I think the writing style hurt my brain a bit though. I'm off to find the Mystery Machine and Shaggy for some Scooby Snacks.

Not only was it a book lover's dream, it wasn't predictable. I didn't know who, how or why as far as the romance and Nina's business went. There are some sex scenes later on. She is one of those characters who puts everything behind a mask, hiding behind a tough persona. That isn't to say she isn't tough - she is - but she isn't as unfeeling and stoic as she portrays. Her brother and sister were fully fleshed characters, as well as Ann, Cole and Adam from the village, which was really great. Gabe, an injured Farther Lia and her family shelters and cares for, was pretty fascinating as well - it was easy to see why Lia is interested in him. I really liked this book. I want more of this book. It has the dystopian feel to it without the hopelessness. I am seriously looking forward to reading the sequel.

So no matter how much torment and misery this Class A douchebag has thrown her way over the past few years of her life, Tatum still wants him. Why? Seriously, though--why? Jared tosses hellish 'pranks' toward Tatum, but they are all actually harassment and ASSAULT. Speaking of Jared, let's have a look at him, shall we? He is a bard when it comes to romanticism. Examples of his swoonworthy-ness: "I think we've moved beyond friends, Tate, but if you want to play that game, then fine. We can have a sleepover, but there will be fucking involved." This is said as an actual THREAT, by the way. How romantic. "I wouldn't care if you were alive or dead." "If I ever lay my hands on you, you'll want it." "Are you still talking? Go home. No one wants your stuck-up ass here." Not only that, but Jared confronts Tatum alone in the girl's locker room at their high school (after first ordering the other girls to leave them both, like the egotistical asshole he is) and threatens her. Then later, after somebody tries to sexually assault Tatum, Jared stupidly risks both of their lives by speeding in his car with the headlights off just to show her 'real reckless behavior' because of how much she seems to like it. But oh, it doesn't even end there! He grabs her against her will and AGAINST her protests, forces her on the hood of his car, and tells her: "Don't try to get away. As you remember, I can keep you here." Gee, no wonder Tatum likes him! If you think that Jared's past and method of dealing with his anger both justify the way that he treats Tatum, please do not even go to the comments section and try to convince me that I'm wrong. You need to reevaluate your thought process when it comes to abuse. I also hated Douglas' descriptions. "His lips devoured me, hard and fast, like I was being eaten alive." Am I supposed to be romanced or horrified? "The campfire in my belly had turned into a bonfire in my core." Plus, I hate that Jared acted like an asshole--no, WAS an asshole--and still got what he wanted in the end. Tatum: "He can't win. He can't treat me like shit and then have me." Then BOOM. He does. I cannot stand this book. The writing, the endless list of plotholes, Jared, Tatum, K.C., Ben, EVERYBODY. Absolutely no character in this book is likeable. Skip it, unless you want to lower your IQ.

3-3.25 stars. This was an interesting read. I had not read a "daddy kink" book before, but I was curious and went into it with an open mind. This is Laine and Nick's book. Laine is out with her friend on her birthday, when her friend ditches her, leaving her without her purse and phone. She ends up walking home, is almost attacked by a creepy guy and Nick saves her. Laine's mother is on vacation so she has no where to go or way to get in her house. Nick takes her home and she ends up staying with him. Nick wants to take care of her and sees that no one else has taken care of her before. Laine is drawn to Nick, having grown up without a father, and likes that he wants to take care of her. Nick is 42 and Laine is just turned 18. Laine wants a daddy and sees that in Nick, but she also is attracted to him. He feels the same with her. He wants a child, because he lost a child, and sees Laine as a chance to have one, but he is also attracted to her. Laine stays in his deceased-sort-of-step-daughter, Jane's, bedroom, which is a pink, frilly 5 year old's bedroom. She loves it and wants to stay with Nick forever. She makes a move on him, sexually, and he resists, but eventually, gives in and they begin a relationship. He treats her like a daughter, except for in the bedroom. They do have some issues to work out, but by the end, they have everything worked out. I like Jade West's books, in general. Most of the time, I feel like there is a lot of emotion and not just lots of sexy, kinky, boundary pushing times. But I didn't really feel the emotion in this book. The characters didn't have a lot of depth. They were interesting characters, but kind of one-dimensional. I didn't really like either character or feel a connection to them. Laine is just turned 18, and a young, immature 18, at that. She practically raised herself with a mother who was never around and didn't know who her father was. But she doesn't come off as someone who raised herself. She is really naive and seemed not very smart, in general. She has huge daddy issues. She always wanted a father to take care of her. I understand her being drawn to Nick because he feeds that want in her. She doesn't have any experience with men or boys. She still wants Nick though as a daddy figure to her and sexually. I didn't think she really understood that that was a kink or a play that some people like sexually. It just came natural to her. Nick had "child issues". He had lost a girlfriend and her 5 year old daughter, Jane, that he was a father figure for, in a car accident. He felt like he was missing out on being a father and taking care of a child. So he was drawn to Laine in that way. But I was conflicted in that he was using Laine as a substitute for Jane (and I just noticed that their names even rhyme). So, was he sexually interested in Jane? Was he interested in daddy kink before Laine? I didn't think that was clear. I thought a lot more mature discussion needed to happen outside of "play" between Laine and Nick so that Laine understood that this was a kink they were doing. They did seem to work through their relationship on their own, but I still felt like it needed more discussion. I did like that they both worked out what they really wanted by the end of the book. And Nick did learn that sometimes he needed to treat Laine like a women, instead of a child, and that Laine needed that too. They were looking towards the future, instead of the past, and were even thinking of kids. (Although, I wondered if Nick could be a father without feeling sexually turned on by it) I don't think that all people who are into age play do it because they have daddy issues (or child issues), so I wondered how it would read to someone who is into age play and if it was offensive to them. I have no comparison since this is my first book of this type. I don't think age play is something I would mind reading again, but because of the characters and their issues, I didn't love this book. I am still a fan of Ms. West's though and will read her work in the future. *I received this book in exchange for an honest review.

I toyed with rating this only four stars because I generally reserve five stars for my all time favorite books... But I couldn't come up with any reason not to give it five stars, and as I considered the question, it occurred to me that it might actually be one of my favorite books. I'm still thinking about it, I just finished it a few hours ago, and I'm mulling over where the holes might be in my enthusiasm. I am overenthusiastic because it's the best book I've read in a while? Is my position skewed because I haven't read anything that funny in a long time? Is it just that the stuff I've been reading hasn't been up to snuff or is it that it's just that good. Better break it down and see how I feel about it on the other side: Characters: I loved every single character in this book, even the antagonists and secondary characters. Every one of them had a very distinct feel, they were clearly defined, consistent with themselves, and came to life off the page. Even if I couldn't identify with all of them I could see where they were coming from as people, because they were all represented as real people, even if they were real people who were parodies of themselves (these people exist I've met them, so I buy it). I loved the characters and they drove the story. Plot: Honestly, despite the bizarre kick off to this whole thing the plot unravelled in a way that was hilarious, ridiculous, but strangely believable given the circumstances. Though I saw parts of it coming, it was not predictable and, I felt it twisted in all the right places. I was happy to keep turning the pages, not necessarily because I was dying to know whodunnit, but certainly because I was dying to know what was going to happen to our heroine next. Pacing: As you might suspect from the way I described the plot, the pacing was spot on. Fast enough to keep you intrigued but slow enough to let you get to know the main players. Writing: I enjoy the hell out of Wirestone's style and sense of humor. The description and dialogue had me laughing aloud at times and generally smirking throughout. I will say this, the humor might not hit the mark if you are not a gamer or if you're unfamiliar with a few popular fandoms. I found it hilarious, but then, I used to play D&D before they added the A to it, and I've dabbled in the occasional MMORPG. If you have no idea what either of those things mean then you might not enjoy the book (but you might anyway, who knows). Formatting: I'm mentioning this just because I often critique formatting in my reviews, but in this case the formatting was impeccable. A big thanks to the publisher for doing it properly even for a galley copy. Errata: This was a galley copy and consequently is likely to undergo another round of proofing before it goes to publication. I certainly hope it does as there were more typos and errata than I would like to see in a final proof. Overall, I enjoyed this book from cover to cover (even down to the acknowledgements and bio) and very much look forward to the next in the series or anything else from Max Wirestone. I wholeheartedly recommend it to fans of humor, mysteries, and geekdom. *I received a free galley copy of this book from the publisher, through Netgalley, in exchange for an honest review*

These tropes tread brutally close to the language of victim / abuser, and the titular Rogue of this story goes far beyond alpha male bad boy, traveling deep into Inconsiderate Scumbag territory. I love a tale of childhood crush turning into adult affair, but the execution of this was too painful. MacLean made it clear she was working on a sort of Greek mythical tale mimicking Hades and Persephone, as the too-perfect Penelope descends into the dark abyss of Michael Bourne's pit of sin, but even Persephone got to feast on pomegranate seeds and visit her mom for six months of the year. This poor chick is living on a starvation diet of crumbs of affection and occasional bouts of sexy times interspersed with lots of being abandoned like yesterday's cold potatoes for what feels like 80% of the book. The inevitable turn --Hero realizes that Heroine is in fact his entire reason for living and that he's been a total chump-- is such a heavy swing of the emotional pendulum in the other direction that it reads as fake and excessively syrupy, like something soap opera stars would be embarrassed to watch due to the over the top declarations of undying love and addict-level worship. Again, it's a real shame so much of this was uncomfortable and awkward for me because the author's craft is considerable - she knows how to write dialogue and steamy scenes, she can move things along and her period detail is good, but too many hang ups stopped me from doing much beyond trudging grouchily to the finish line. Alas!
& it's over :( the wait is on. Truly epic book! Review to come.

I expected so much better. Alexandra Bracken's previous series, The Darkest Minds, is one of my all-time favorites. This is mainly because of the deep emotional connections I felt with all of the characters, as well as the amazingly written romance. This book gave me none of that. I wasn't able to really click with any of the characters (perhaps due to the 3rd person narrative? ), and the entire romance just felt rushed and forced. In addition, many of the conclusions that our two adventurers drew confused me. I was often left wondering how their trains of thought went from "here" to "there", and in a mystery-driven book like this, that is not good.

Incredible. It's written with such attention to detail, both in the icy landscapes it depicts and the characters, that every moment is captivating. I'll admit, it is somewhat repetitive. It doesn't leave its couple of locations, and yet I never found my attention wavering. The Snow Child is a stunningly poignant, human, and engaging novel.

I enjoyed SCARLET so much more than CINDER. And that's not to say I didn't enjoy CINDER, but I while I liked Cinder and Kai, I loved Scarlet and Wolf, so I think this just comes down to character/reader preferences. And plot. This one feels more like an epic quest/search, and I've always had a soft spot for these types of adventures. SCARLET picks up right where CINDER left off. While Kai deals with the Lunar Queen, Cinder escapes prison, taking with her the pompous (yet still loveable) Captain Thorne (who I'm pretty sure will end up a love interest for one of the future heroines). The bulk of the story focuses on Scarlet though, who is searching for her missing grandmother. Enter Wolf, a mysterious fighter whose help she enlists even though she doesn't fully trust him. I loved Wolf-his dark, mysterious past; his brooding nature; his inner demons/battles. Above all, I love how Meyer twists traditional fairytales to fit into this futuristic, tech-rich world. The threads of the original stories are easily recognizable, but her stories also stand on their own. Very much looking forward to CREST. Originally posted here.

** spoiler alert ** I forgot that I once attempted to read this until I was browsing the shelves at the bookstore today. And I picked it up to remember why I never finished, and then it hit me--it made me very angry! The first 75 pages are so beautifully written, and develop this story intermixed with Chinese culture, and it just pulls you right in. But then it just got a little too weird for me when she died and there was still 200 pages to go! And I just couldn't bring myself to read any more after that--despite the beauty of the language. I just couldn't read another page. I am sure that the book is good, but I just couldn't handle it at all. And it's not just because it dealt with life after death, because I loved The Lovely Bones just fine. This book just angered me so much that she died so soon that I just couldn't read it anymore.
Good, but not as fantastic as the first one. Still very interesting writing and world building. Yay for dragons!
I just love her books and her writing. I can't wait to get started on the next one.

I just couldnt finish this one. I dont understand how it got so much praise... It started off good, and I was engaged in the story, her living with the kids, them sneaking out for food, surviving in this new vampire world. etc. It was interesting. BUT THEN, then she was turned into a vampire and I just went For christ sakes, being a vampire is supposed to be all badass, kicking other vampire butt etc. (this is what book loads up for when she starts to learn how to fight, But meh!) And it just wasnt, there was no awesome-sauce. I mean maybe im not entitled to criticize too much, since I didnt read the entire book. (got to like 30 % into the book, before I threw it into a corner) But I read to be entertained, enjoy myself and have fun, and this book soooo wasnt it.

The Naturals is one of the best series of all time. I feel like we do not have very many YA authors who write about crime. It is sad, considering that I absolutely love anything involving crime drama. I am an early to bed, early to rise kinda girl but I stayed up very late to finish this book. It was just COMPLETELY captivating. The story line was genius and the characters were great. I would of given it five stars, but I read the first two books quite a while ago, therefore I was confused about a lot of things. I plan to reread all the books though, so this might be bumped up to a five later on. If you are currently in a reading slump, I suggest that you pick up the series. Okay yes, most of the time, people in a reading slump want a shorter book. However, these are all so action packed and exciting, so you'll fly right through them. I actually just suggested this series to my 13 year old cousin last week. She takes a little while getting through books, but she texted me yesterday asking for the title of the third book, because she already finished the other two. Jennifer Lynn Barnes had a lot of schooling in Psychology, and you can tell by her writing. You'll be put into the killer's head, and it'll be an exciting and crazy read.

Leigh Bardugo is an awesome writer. Her Grisha world is marvelously explored in her series and such a joy to read. But to be honest, Six of Crows just didn't cut it. Too much fat obstructing the meat of the plot. This book didn't have the easy rhythm of her previous books. One doesn't get lost in the story but rather they find themselves drifting away with the dull descriptions. The story doesn't even end and there's nothing as offputting as an abortive climax. Leaves one unsatisfied. I still love you Leigh!
I didn't like this author's previous book but I am very intrigued by this. It's on my list right now to read and I'll see how reviews start to come in before I pick it up.
The concept of the book was good but it didn't deliver. The romance was lacking and that was the main reason I chose to read it. Disappointing.
Finally Adrian finds love and happiness! Sydney is so kickass, smart, and brave! She's my new heroine!

My goodness, I don't even know where to begin with this novel, it's just... wow, I seriously don't know how to, I'll just start throwing things and see how it goes: The story follows Clay Jensen, one day, he receives a pack of mysterious tapes, old-school stuff, and he's anxious to listen to them, and the he discovers that they are Hanna Baker's detailed journey, and somehow diary, to death. Her last words. But, wait, Hanna Baker killed herself. How is it that he received tapes from her? Well, she made a whole plan, where she would record in seven tapes (thirteen stories total), the thirteen reasons why, she would kill herself, in the end, a why she killed herself. Each side of the tapes, or each story, explains one reason, and she mentions a person in each one, naming them as contributors to her decision. So Clay - naturally - is completely freaked out, What did he do to her? He had always had a thing for her, but other than that, nothing. And the story begins. He listens carefully to each one of them, a few of her stories are quite horrible and hard to believe, until the moment she finally finishes, and kills herself. At some parts of the story, I was so desperate, just like Clay, wanting to yell at Hanna to fight! To keep living! To stop! And then you realize... she's already dead. The idea that a person can take the time, days, weeks, or months, to make tapes detailing their way to suicide, is just twisted. Why would someone do that? And why did Hanna killed herself? The answer: she wasn't strong enough, she was never able to see beyond her current situation and realize that, she wasn't always going to live in high school. By the end you can see how she practically wants reasons to kill herself, looking for reason to give up. And it's easy to see, that there was nothing to do for her, her mind was made up already, she was already dead. Jay Asher's writing style is straight-forward, it's hard to tell if it's his writing style or if it is because it's his debut novel. But it worked perfectly. Jay Asher's novel will open your eyes. It lets us know that this matters are to be taken seriously. I think It's brilliant, and a must read. You won't be able to see death and suicide the same way. Ever. A valuable lesson, a strong novel, and a heartbreaking choice.
630 pages of road trips, 40 pages of plot.

I hate getting this far into a book and not finishing. What's amazing is that when I did the Kindle sample, I didn't pick up on some of the things that annoyed me from the start. I mean, sure, the actual zombies don't show up until later (I know they're all undead, but there's a difference between that and flesh-eating zombies), but the problem with Wren was evident from chapter 2 to me. She was supposed to be near emotionless, practically a robot. Everyone tells you so, including her. It's what excited me about the book. And yet, right from the start, she's making emotional judgements during her exposition on the Reboots and how they live. In fact, she's full of fear, and we see it at every turn. Look, there's nothing wrong with a fretting protagonist, but don't sell her as emotionless and suggest that the love interest is the first to give her a reason to feel. Anyway, I was just getting annoyed between the zombies and the protagonist, so I have to give it up.

This is like crack for your brain, if you're an idiotic female such as myself. It's poorly written, its characters lack depth and appeal, but it is written specifically for the impressionable, stupid tween girl we try to keep on lockdown. The protagonist is never described in much detail or depth and has very little sense of self (i.e. none) beyond her object of obsession/romantic interest. Said individual persists in doing things that would - to an adult - seem stalker-esque, obsessive, controlling, manipulative and co-dependent. However, to girls of a certain age, these actions may appear terribly, terribly romantic. I know better than to like this sort of book, but it doesn't seem to matter - I have an inner tween that can't seem to help herself.

I was looking forward to this and may revisit it. As it stands now, I couldn't get but a few pages in before my disbelief became unsuspended--it was the eggs that did it. The main character pretty much forces the cashier to ring up a dozen eggs that are all smashed and dripping out of the carton. She does this so as not to draw attention to herself and thereby get out of the store quickly. What? She stands there arguing with the cashier about ringing up the eggs so as NOT to draw attention to herself? Come on...give me a frickin' break here. Real Life Books don't have to be 100% life-like to be enjoyable, but they do have to bear some--at least SOME resemblance to real life. From the get go, this book failed, and so back it goes to the e-library. Far too many good books out there to waste time on junk.

From the way everyone raved about the book, I thought I would be hungry for Oreos, but I'm left a little homesick for Waffle House. They're just not up here on this side of Canada, and I have yet to find another place that can make a satisfying pile of greasy hashbrowns all the way. I read this book in three freaking hours - sorry, not sorry. It's hard to pick a spot to start from in raving about this. Simon, the funniest teenager with the funniest family full of in-jokes and made up worlds about Oreos? The diverse characters who existed because they were there with their own lives outside of Simon's personal world, not because the author went through a check list of diverse characters to include? The humorous but touching and courageous e-mails between Simon and Blue? I won't delve into Blue so much because I don't want to give away any hints about the mystery, but I have to say that from the very beginning, I knew I would not be disappointed in who Blue ended up being. Simon crushes on him so hard, and it's adorable and sweet. Anyone who could make Simon that twitterpated without revealing their name or face was not going to disappoint me when the reveal happened. Simon himself is a fantastic character. He's awkward sometimes. He's funny. He's introspective. He's a teenager. An honest-to-goodness teenager who doesn't want to make a big deal about his sexuality. His family really had me in stitches, and much of Simon's humor is developed because of them. Their reality show obsession. Their dog named Bieber. The Halloween costumes. The thing they did on Christmas Eve day was the only time I put the book down since I started reading because I had to go to a different room and laugh so I wouldn't wake up my spouse. It was kind of terrible but it was so funny. The story is a little on the simple side, but it's addicting like Oreos because all the characters are so well-crafted. Especially Taylor.
Looking for a book that makes you want to call in sick to work so you can keep reading? This is it. As with the first book, Collins grabs you hard and doesn't let up. This is a hell of a page turner.

I think I enjoyed this installment of the Pendergast series more than the last Crimson Shores however I feel like these last two books do not hold a candle to the previous in the series. The Obsidian Chamber has the same fast pace that is typical and it was entertaining but for me was missing one BIG thing. Any kind of twist I wasn't expecting. This book is really just a continuation of the last book and the two major twist were presented fairly flatly in the begging. If you did not know who the mystery man was from the end of Crimson Shores you have probably just started the series. If that is the case I beg you to go back and read the earlier books. The other major reveal should be pretty fairly easy to guess. We see a lot more of Constance Greene which previously I have found almost as interesting as Pendergast. I am having a hard time with how her character is progressing since the last book. Maybe it is because the curtain has been pulled back on her and she is not the mysterious subterranean dweller from the previous books. I feel like something was missing from Pendergast. I have always thought of him as a cross between Bond and Holmes. It seems like he was missing the "Holmes". It's possible is was the great mystery missing I guess. Either way a bit of a disappointment. I will continue to read the series in hopes it returns to it's former glory.

I liked this more than I thought I was going to. Primarily because ... the interaction between the h/h was fantastic. Sharp, witty, and snapping with chemistry. There were parts where I wanted to shake Amanda, though, either because she was so fucking obviously making a mistake, or because I felt like she could have done something - written something - to improve her situation. I think she has more tools than she realizes. But I really did enjoy it, despite moments of frustration. It's a bit soap-operatic, but still fun. Also, "womanizing douchelord" is my new favorite insult.
The New 52 reprisal of Wonder Woman is epic!
Never read anything like this. Its really good yet the sequel failed to keep my attention. But the maze runner is definitely worth a read.

Non-spoiler, but this is a sequel so if you haven't read Pivot Point...well omg go read Pivot Point. This is the sequel to and last book in the Pivot Point duology. It takes places shortly after the ending of Pivot Point. Characters: While I really liked the main characters - Addie, Laila, and Trevor, the new characters like Connor I wasn't super attached for some reason. Basically, I was rooting for Addie the whole time. I love Addie and Laila's friendship a lot. Addie is just really level headed and I think that's why I like her alot. It's so funny how much I hated Stephanie in Pivot Point, but kinda liked her in Split Second. Plot: A really interesting plot and boy I didn't see that big reveal coming at all for some reason. So I was thoroughly surprised. Really fun. I wasn't super into Laila's plot or Connor's though. I really just wanted Addie's perspective all the time. It had a very heist/Ocean's 11 feeling to it at the end. Writing: While I appreciated a different POV, I really wasn't super into Laila's chapters, but I understand why it was necessary. Romance/Feels: .5 Not quite as good as Pivot Point. I was just rooting for Addie and Trevor the whole time and I get that he didn't remember her, but MY GOSH I WAS JUST LIKE KISS ALREADY. lol Ending: Pretty satisfying. Possible Laila spin off? I could see it happen. Overall Enjoyment: Once I really got into it, I was back in Addie's world and I just loved the addictive fun quality that Kasie West has in her books! Rereadability: maybe. I would reread Pivot Point for sure because ADDIE/TREVOR FEELS, but then I'd have to reread Split Second. Final Rating: 3.75 stars to be exact! I highly recommend this duology as a whole. It reads like a contemporary but you get the special powers aspect as well.

Sounds like a great story. But there is too much literary waffling going on and too little snooping. After 172 pages of poetic soul searching by the members of the Dante Club I gave up in frustration. "Captivating thriller"? Not likely. "Sparkling with erudition" - I asked some very educated people whose mother tongue is English, nobody could even tell me what that means. All around a very unsatisfying experience.

This novel has received much notice and accolades recently, and I've been excited to read it since I first saw it. Told by the main character, she describes living through a "slowing" of the orbit of the earth from when it's first discovered until days and nights stretch on for days, even weeks at a time. Definitely well-written, I enjoyed the coming-of-age story. My only complaint is, even though it's told from the viewpoint of an older character looking back on her childhood, it still doesn't seem like it's the story of an 11 or 12-year-old, but someone significantly older. Would a child notice certain subtleties or nuances? I doubt it. Also, the ending is bleak and sad, hopeless in the same way The Road is. I don't mind that if done well, but it didn't seem to fit the tone of story that came before it.

Very early on I debated DNFing this book...but yet again, I pushed through because I had high hopes that it would get suspenseful and intense. It didn't. I thought that this entire book was incredibly boring. Summary: This book is from the perspective of two characters- Adele and Louise. Adele is having trouble with her husband. Though they have just moved to town for a "fresh start" things don't seem to be going very well. Louise is a single mom who hooked up with a man at a bar one night. This man turns out to be married... and her new boss. Yes, the husband and the boss are one in the same. When the two women become friends without telling the man, things get complicated. My thoughts: I liked that this book swapped between the two perspectives while sprinkling some flashbacks in here and there. It added a nice layer to the story and at least kept me reading and interested for a short while. Beware, the negatives: So first off, both of the main characters whose perspectives the book is written from are horrible people. One is manipulative and the other is just plain pathetic. The main male role is also a disgusting human. So there was absolutely nothing I liked about any of the characters in this book. I also didn't like the storyline. It was so boring to me. And really, not much happened. It wasn't suspenseful to me in the slightest. This book was horribly repetitive. It was all the same old thoughts by the same person over and over and over again. I mean, holy god... How many times do I have to read that Adele loves David, or that what Louise was doing was wrong? When things blew up in the characters faces, I wanted to scream "WELL WHAT DID YOU THINK WAS GOING TO HAPPEN?!" And take this line for example, "Suddenly, this is all very real." What?! Are you joking?! What was it before? A game? I so unimpressed. I had heard that there was a twist, so I kept reading. When I finally made it, I was not thrilled. I definitely felt like I wasted my time reading this book (and I absolutely hate saying that! Favorite passage: My feet are already aching in my two-inch heels. I always thought it was something you grew into, that ability to walk perfectly in high heels and always dress well. As it turns out - for me anyway - there's a small phase of that in the nightclubbing years of your twenties and then it's mainly jeans and jumpers and Converse with the ponytail, accessorized with life-envy of those who can still be bothered to make the effort. My final thoughts: I did not like this book. I gave it one star. However, I think this type of book simply isn't for me. I would recommend this book to fans of Gone Girl. This is the first time I have ever made that statement... but it is very fitting; horrible characters making stupid decisions and sticking their nose where it doesn't belong, complete with a silly "twist" ending that really isn't that interesting.
The only strong feeling I have about this play is the desire to never meet anyone like any of the characters in it.

Going into Queen of Hearts, I had high expectations. There is so much potential, so much to work with if you're writing an Alice in Wonderland retelling. I was especially excited because it was from the POV of the Queen of Hearts herself, and I was expecting a badass female character that rivaled Cersei Lannister. I also expected quirky side characters and a really colorful plot. Alas, I didn't get any of these things. In fact, I spent most of the book waiting for something to happen. And nothing did! There were a lot of little things going on throughout the plot, such as Dinah's abusive relationship with her father--The King of Hearts, plus the story's one-sided romance, and a dark secret within the castle itself. And yet, I was not given any concrete details to understand any of these things. They were just . there. I had no idea which details were significant and which were not. By the time I reached the really dramatic end, I simply didn't care, and I was happy that I was done with this book. Read my full review of Queen of Hearts

Honestly, I've tried to write this review for two weeks and have had no success. With as much hype around her as John Green, you would expect this book to be nothing more that spectacular. I wish it was that scenario. Reading the description on the back, I assumed the novel to be charming and engaging. What I found was it to be good but not to what people praised it to be. I don't entirely dislike the book, I found it quite funny and quirky. Parts of the novel held my interest for an incredibly long time. The plot and characters began to be more enjoyable as it progressed, most good novels do acquire that trait. The beachy theme made me miss summer tremendously. Sadly, there were some things I just could not ignore. Austen's family was horridly unbearable, I do realize this was Dessen's motive but every time I came across them I felt immensely agitated. I will compliment that Dessen's idea of her unbearable family helped me understand why Auden was snobby as well, and even made me pity her. Eli's character in the beginning had an odd way to him that made me dislike his character for a while. The potrayal of girly girls in this made me cringe due to the exaggeration that she included in this book. The fact of the prom situation happening again for Auden felt slightly cheesy as well as the final scene when Auden surprises Eli with the 'jump'. Overall, this book is a perfect summer read! Most faults I encountered in this were most likely meant to seem that way. I might just not like the faults due to the fact I'm not a big fan of quirky books and movies. I recommend to anyone in need of a chick flick and/or someone who is missing summer. It also teaches you it's never to late to begin again
It comes out on my birthday and it's from Jennifer Armentrout. I'm going to read it of course. It's like my own little birthday present. Hopefully, the date doesn't move.

Judging by the cover I expected a cute, sweet ghost story, something along the line of a YA Casper maybe. But fear not, that's not what you get! Don't get me wrong, the cover is good. Perfect, actually, because a) the models look exactly like I pictured Alona and Will (she was right, he sure has a nice jawline [image error]) and b) before reading it, you would never guess that the story has a dark touch to it. I loved the hint of darkness and creepiness. Although Alona and Will can't stand each other at first, you practically see sizzling sparks flying between them right from the beginning. I'm a sucker for hate-turned-love stories. I'm really looking forward to see what's in store for them in the next book. June can't come soon enough!

Skip this book and read My Butterfly instead. Much better. I hated Julia. I felt bad for WIll. I wish he could have moved on and found someone else. Why he didn't and kept loving Julia is beyond me. I mean...I hated her so much! She is the one who broke up with him, then she is all poor me when he tries to move on? And the end - he pours his heart out to her after the concert how he still loves her and always will and has never been with anyone else and will never be with anyone else because she is it for him, she still loves him too but instead of saying something is all sorry. No can do! Again she pulls away. Then I don't really know how or why that scene with the interview with Will makes her change her mind...that made no sense to me. Then the time jump was horrible. I hated that chapter. She just annoyed me so much. You can't keep pushing people away, then get angry because they don't fight to keep you. I mean if you break someone's heart into a million pieces, then hook up with someone else for years, and almost marry that other person...ugh! I hated her. I hate the poot me attitude when you are the one who caused the issues and could fix them easily. Besides that I also disliked the way it was written. You get random bits and pieces so you don't really know the characters at all. I don't even know why they were together, why they loved each other. The author told instead of showing which I dislike. And each chapter, especially at the beginning, I spent the first few page trying to figure out when/where it was. Like the chapter after the bonfire - was that the same night? Did they go out? Where are they? What are they doing? There wasn't much information really, just little snippets which didn't help. It didn't make me invested in the story since there was not a lot of story to be invested in.

I am so annoyed right now. I love Adam, but this isn't the Adam I've come to know over the past two books. The only thing that felt Adam-like was his love for his brother. This guy, whoever he is, thinks Juliette is some weakling who needs protecting: "I knew she should've stayed behind. She's not built for this-she's not strong enough." "The smart thing would be to hide her somewhere. Keep her safe. A weak link can bring everything down with it." "Kenji and Castle are always blowing smoke up her ass when they shouldn't, and honestly? It's dangerous. It's not good to make her think she can do this kind of thing when really, it'll probably get her killed." These thoughts both shocked and angered me, because the Adam I know wouldn't think such things. The tagline on the cover says "I will not lose her" and about half way through the novella he says he's not ready to give up on her or whatever, but towards the end it seems as if he has given up on her. Apparently he's not sure if he wants to rescue the girl who broke up with him and left him and his brother. He also doesn't want to be on the run again and put his brother in danger (which is fair enough, but it completely goes against his character. I thought he didn't want to lose her?) So, Kenji who is desperate to find Juliette (and btw, seems more worried about her than Adam does) has to convince him to come up with a plan to brake her out. Yes, you read correctly. He has to convince him: "Dude, what the hell are you talking about? Aren't you in love with this girl? Where's the fire under your ass? I thought you would be dying to get to her right now-" What happened to the Adam that once said: "You have no idea how much I've thought about you. How many times I've dreamt...how many times I've dreamt about being this close to you. God, Juliette, I'd follow you anywhere. You're the only good thing left in this world." Also, when Kenji and Adam were talking about how ruthless Warner is, Juliette's reaction kind of irked me. I get that she saw a softer side to him in Unravel Me, but she can't honestly be surprised at the things they were saying. The only good thing about this novella: Kenji's awesomeness. Prior to reading this I at least had some hope for Adam and Juliette, but now? I'm not so sure. I have this horrible feeling that maybe Alia will become Adam's love interest in Ignite Me. This novella has made me a feel a bit angry towards Adam, and that, quite frankly is upsetting. This review also appears on my blog The Page Turner.
Really loved this one. It's a retelling of The Turn of the Screw with a male nanny and a different ending. Perfect for spooky fall reading!

I wish these books were simpler. There's a really cool story in here I liked about America coming into her own and giving people hope without knowing it and figuring out the good she could do as a princess, but then there's love triangles and rebels and secret history coming to light and, as a result, I don't like the book as much as I could. And can we PLEASE do away with the Mean Girl trope? It's awful and I hate reading it. I did mostly enjoy myself reading this, though. And I liked that Maxon called America on her tendency to jump to conclusions and not let him explain himself because that was REALLY bugging me.

3 1/2 stars. Mr. Penumbra's 24-hour Bookstore was different in all the best ways. Original, mixing computer jargon and futuristic ideals, that are at times daunting and scary, but also exciting and slightly unimaginable. Along with this is fantasy laced secret society with a serious mystery. This book makes a great effort at combining every bookish genre into one terrific novel. If it weren't for the real fear of losing human connection and the onward decline of actual the written word that is so greatly evidenced in this novel, I probably would have rated it higher, but the fact is it presents the readers with serious fears for the future of paper. At the same time it does give evidence at the end that it was only through actual human interaction and stepping away from the all-mighty computer, that any of their progress could be given a result. I'm up, I'm down. Aw heck, just read it!
Sometimes I felt that she just found a thesaurus and copy-pasted the words in. Meh.

A somewhat breathless blurb led to this being chosen for our book group. Otherwise I would not have made it past the first few chapters. The plot and world are a hideous mash of all the worst genre cliches, the main character is a clunky Mary Sue, and the main magical systems are contradictory at best and plot moves at worst. The writing itself is amateurish, combining plot holes with the very worst of telling not showing and some serious pov problems that make me question how it was ever picked up, let alone ever edited. Uncritical fans of genre pap and poorly researched 'steampunk' will possibly enjoy it. Otherwise not recommended.

I was fascinated by this book and loved many aspects of it. I loved the fact that it is one of those rare books which does give consider the mental effects of playing with metaphorical fire and allows it to come through. It shows not only the submissive's side from an emotional perspective but, far rarer, the Dominant's. Even better, both partners are given space to be human. No idealistic stereotypes here (though both characters are stereotypes in their own). The fails for me in two ways: a) I prefer feeling the touch of a hand, the sting of a flogger on my skin - I do not just want to be told that this is happening. and b) I feel the book lets the reader down at the end. The two characters have just learnt that you can really screw up when you don't pay attention. They got off lucky though both of them have taken from this some emotional damage. Their lesson from this: do not play alone until you know what you are doing, at least if you do not trust yourself. Fine. But in the next sentence he then removes the safe word from their relationship for anything but pain. With this one sentence any awareness of the amount of emotional and mental damage one can do is removed and they are walking back into exactly the same problem they just thought to avoid. Overall I would recommend this book to everyone even with the problems I saw for myself. It is a good book, in places more interesting than arousing, and worth a read. I am just not sure if I would ever read it a second time.

Manga Classics: Great Expectations captures all of the things that makes Dickens great. The characters are complex and full of contradictions, and the story both frightens, frustrates, and inspires. The artwork does a good job of capturing these complicated characters and taking me through their journey. It's surprising just how much of the plot fits into a 300+ page manga. It captures the feel of Dickens' prose and whet my appetite for more. Manga Classics Series Review: The Manga Classics series is a set of five classics (so far) presented manga style. To try this series (and decide whether to order it for my library), I read two titles: Great Expectations and The Scarlet Letter. Great Expectations, which I haven't read, to see if they make sense when I don't know the story. The Scarlet Letter, which I adore, to see if they're satisfying when I'm already a fan. Both passed the test, and both include resources at the end to shed light on the adaptation process and unique traits of the original stories. The Manga Classics series is recommended: * To revisit or remember a favorite classic * For manga fans looking for something different * To enjoy classic stories in a short, fast format The Manga Classics series also includes Les Miserables, Pride & Prejudice, and Emma, with more titles to come. I received Manga Classics: Great Expectations as an ARC from the publisher, free through Netgalley. Reviewed on Come Hither Books

Another third went to boys stumbling back and forth through the city going "shhh!" and reminding us yet again that their masks are uncomfortable and they can't see very well. Captain Cly, a wonderful character, gets one scene but it felt like something put in because his contract requires it. At least we get to wonder if he might be half Sasquatch! When the boys finally meet rotters I had the feeling that the editor noticed there hadn't been an actual encounter, and asked Priest to put it in. Zeke meets sick fox. Aww. Squee! Guess how the inexplicable bit will end? Clumsy foreshadowing; again, as if written for the inexperienced reader. This is also the first in the series that felt like a Young Adult. At times I wondered if it was meant for the Teen or Precocious Child section. What should have been the main plot, bad guys horning in, is excellent and might have been explored more. I liked Hoijin (I wanted to call him Hoisin because he was saucy) and his idea of how to make a certain dramatic thing happen. He has potential, he does. Others have suggested that this book lays down a base for future stories. At times, I wondered if it's supposed to be a new entry point to the series, for a new and younger audience. If it is, I'll read them all, I'll expect a new, capable and non-whiny Rector, and I am sure they'll get back to the five-star level.

To prepare for this book, I read The Shining a week or so ago, and I am currently listening to the expanded version of The Stand. What fun to be immersed in King! He does it all so very, very well. The depth of his characters, the rhythm of his words, the power of his descriptions. I could hardly wait for the release of Dr. Sleep. How fantastic! King returning to one of his classic stories. This was going to be good! OK. It started out slow, but then again King starts slow. I kept telling myself to wait. It was going to get better. Surely it was going to get better. Wasn't it? The more I read, the worse it became. It got slower and slower and slower, and if that wasn't enough, it continued to spiral into mediocrity. The characters had no depth. The words no rhythm. The descriptions flat and uninspired. The plot dragged on and on. Two characters would do something, decide something. Then, in excruciating detail, recount to other characters what had happened, what they had decided. These would then find other characters and explain the same things over again, in the same detail. He was padding...blatantly, openly, atrociously padding. And even the padding was padded--there were what felt like whole passages lifted from an AA brochure. The big climax was a cheat. I'm not complaining that the foreshadowing was too subtle. It just flat out wasn't there! Not once. NOT ONCE! Was the reader made aware that Dan could hold a dead person inside him. NOT ONCE! Giving Dan a bad stomach doesn't cut it. Just doesn't! Not fair, Mr. King. Not Fair! You can't pull solutions out of your butt like that. You just can't. And after the big battle--gimme a break! Talk about tied up with pink ribbons. The bad guy orderly being run over by a car was bad enough, but it just happened that the hospitals were full? That the only place for him was the Hospice? That Dan was there just in time? That....oh forget it! It's too over-the-top for words. I have been disappointed in King's endings before (Under the Dome, and especially It ), but never have I been disappointed in his writing. NEVER! If it had not been for the book's cover, I would have never guessed this was written by King. And, if I had not known it was King, I would never have wasted my time reading it. I would have tossed it after the first 100 pages. What a sad, sad day.

So, I was surprised to discover we owned this book, since it's a very well known book but nobody in my house had ever mentioned it to me. Turns out my wife bought it, tried it, found it too slow, and gave up. I've convinced her to give it another go. I enjoyed Locke Lamora and his lies quite a bit. Immediately I liked the writing, which combines wit with solid prose. Like my wife I hit a bit of a soft patch early on, though for me it was that I was finding the point of view very 'surface' sharing almost nothing of Locke's thoughts or desires, leaving him a bit of a blank. Lots of fantasy fans quite like a blank to project themselves onto - but I'm not one of them. Fortunately Locke's personality continued to develop and the point of view seemed to settle a little deeper into him as things progressed. The real strengths of the book are the plotting, the dialogue, and the atmosphere. The dialogue (banter) brings the Gentlemen Bastards to life, the plotting keeps the reader on their toes, and the city is very well imagined. I was surprised to find that the light-hearted tone (set primarily by the banter between Locke's gang) actually allows a slew of quite dark themes/scenes to slide past with less impact than they might have. The child prostitution, the gruesome torture scenes, and the mutilation dealt out by our hero are all absent in my own debut which is often called out for being very dark. In any event, I found it to be a rewarding read, well written, and entertaining. I'd recommend any fantasy fan to give it a try. Join my 3-emails-a-year newsletter #prizes

"The only way out of the labyrinth of suffering is to forgive." I have had this book for so long but didn't really have the urge to read it until after I read The Fault in Our Stars. That book was fantastic. So after reading that it pushed me to read more of John Green's books and one of which was Looking for Alaska. I actually have to reread it because the first time I did, it didn't appeal to me that much. As they always say, "second time's the charm." Miles wanted a change. He wanted to move to boarding school. He wasn't running away from his family, he just wanted to have friends and fit in for a change. He was also determined in finding out what Francois Rabelais called the "Great Perhaps". He was sure that he will find this in boarding school. He was right. He found Alaska. The thing I liked about John Green's books is how easily he creates relatable and realistic characters. John Green has this ability to make hard sensitive topics very easy to read. When I first read it my initial reaction was all negative. I didn't like it at all. There was nothing there that I could connect to. But when I reread it I started to see things differently. Being a teenager is not easy. To adults it may seem that teenagers didn't have much to think about but they do. Adults may have work, money and personal relationships to worry about and teenagers have those too just not in the same level. Teenagers worry about fitting in and making friends. Honestly, not having friends at school would really put you down. Not having any friends may lead you to think that you are nothing because no one wants to be friends with you. You may say that it's a very shallow reason but it isn't. Fitting in and being with other people helps a lot. I didn't mean just being with people but being with the right people. At first, I didn't really like Alaska. I didn't like her for the reason that she was reckless and mostly don't think of what she was doing. But as I reread this book again I found myself empathizing for what she has gone through. Alaska might seem carefree at first glance but she was not. She hides behind this facade. She lets everyone see she's this fearless girl who loves to play pranks, have sex and drown in alcohol. But deep down you will see that there was this other side of her that had to be kept hidden away because of what happened in her past. I felt her pain and how she kept drinking and smoking herself to death just to forget all her worries for a little while. Why didn't I like her the first time? Because somehow I saw myself in Alaska. Miles was a different story. I liked Miles the first time I read him. He was the new kid and immediately got along with his room mate. Since he never had many friends back in Florida when he got some in boarding school he decided to try some of the things he never done. I liked his POV. There were no barriers in how he tells the story and I liked it. Miles was the typical new kid who would do anything to fit in. He desperately wants to fit in that he'd join in the stupid pranks that Alaska, Chip and Takumi had planned out eve if he doesn't really want to. He was a little gullible which was cute. I don't know how Mr. Green does it but all his characters were three dimensional that it's pretty possible I might meet one of them on the street. Everyone was whole and complete. You'd know each and every character in this book and its one of the strengths of this book for me. There were however parts in this book that I hoped weren't included. It was a bit dragging on the initial part of the book which I didn't really appreciate. I am okay with slow paced books but only if its necessary and in this case I didn't feel like it was. I was okay with this book being cut in the before and the after of Alaska's death but again so many unnecessary stuff here and there. All in all I think it was still a good book. Not as good as The Fault in Our Stars though but I still liked it. I have to change the rating from 3 stars to 4 stars
