I haven't read the first in this series, so this is a proper test for The Elite. Can it stand out as a good book in its own right? The answer? No. Warning: this review is a little angry, I didn't enjoy this book as much as that overly-fussy yet still pretty cover made me think I would. Boo for pretty covers and my judging a book by its cover. But it's still got (almost) 3 stars, so it's not all that bad. It's a decent enough story, if not terribly confusing, as it apparently picks up exactly where the last one ended. I often pick up a book and read it without checking to see if it's part of a series - and usually that's perfectly fine, it's great, it makes me want to read all of the other books. In a series there is usually a run-down of what happened in the previous book(s) if not only to remind you of what happened. Even House of Night managed that (but, you know, nowadays that'll be a book in itself. FINISH IT ALREADY!). It's the mark of a strong series, that it's easily accessible. The Elite just isn't unless you're already invested in the series. And then on to the characters. Dear god, America, what kind of girl are you? Do you want him or don't you? She's all "oh I don't want to be with him!" and then he shows the slightest interest in someone else and she's all "back off bitch!" and angry. Not everyone loves you, you spoilt Mary-Sue, who's only redeeming quality seems to be that she was once poor and is a bit of a slag. Maxon is a spoiled brat pretty much until the very end, and Aspen just needs to go away and stop screwing with Mer's head. I liked the queen though, and Marlee. The world seems very flat too. For a dystopian novel this isn't good at all, oh no. This story seemed to focus on the mansion and all the pretty things and the lavish lifestyle. There wasn't much of the hardship displayed, only a few raids during which all the characters are tucked away safely. Except for America of course, she's a Mary-Sue so can run faster than anyone, ever. Good points? Yes, there are some. The story was sweet in places and I really felt for Marlee. And for Kriss, as it feels like she's being led along. And America's maids, she was quite nasty to them, even when they devoted themselves to her. And by the end I was beginning to piece the obscure world together a little and better understand the motives driving some of the characters. Maxon's not all bad, but he's not all good either, I'm definitely team Maxon. There was tension and conflict between the characters, they weren't all 2D, they had emotions. The ending was a bit of a relief for me. It was predictable, yes, but a good predictable. It wrapped up well but kept enough back to set the scene for another book, you know to resolve the whole Selection process. And there was even more tension added, you know, because it's the end. If I had read the first I'd probably like this story more, as I'd know what was going on. I received a copy of this for free via NetGalley for review purposes.

[I also reviewed this title on my blog: Ishari's Bookshelf] There is a lot of love out there for Angelfall. I think it's well-deserved love. Angelfall is one of those books that hooks you by its bat wings and drags you along for all 247 pages until you finish and go "whoah!". It's compulsively readable and so fast-paced you feel like you are sprinting away from the killer angels right along with Penryn. So you may be asking - if you liked it and if it's such a readable book...why knock it down two stars? It lost a star because it was just too short. Yes, 247 pages is not enough for this book. It easily could have had another hundred pages to flesh out the world and the situations Penryn and Raffe found themselves embroiled within. Because the book IS so readable and fast-paced, it felt like I was flying by each plot point within the book. I know it's set in a modern-ish world, but I still felt like more world-building and more building up of the plot could have really made this book a lot more satisfying. It also lost a star because there wasn't much character development. It's hard to feel anything for a romance or for a character's suffering when you hardly know the character. I think the lack of character development may have been a result of the book being too short...again, another 100 pages would have allowed Ee to really establish the characters. As it stands, I could really care less whether Penryn recovers her sister and/or she gets together with Raffe. *shrugs* Don't get me wrong - I really enjoyed this book. Despite my ambivalence towards the characters and their plights, I already went out and got my hands on the second installment. It really does deserve all the love it's been receiving as well - it's one of those books that makes you scratch your head at publishers wondering why they chose to pass on this gem. It's always great to see an indie book make such a huge splash. Bottom line - check out Angelfall. While I may have not liked its shortness and/or lack of character development, I am definitely in the minority. It's a fun, quick read with an interesting premise.
The ending was not what I wanted from this book, but everything that came before was fantastic.

DNF at 45% + some skimming I can't do this anymore. I'm suffering with this book and I cannot continue reading it. Second DNF of the week, but I don't feel sorry. I hated everything about this: The MC, the plot, the writing, the world building, the other characters, etc. EVERYTHING. Seriously, I can't think of a single thing I enjoyed about this. At first it reminded me a bit to The Hunger Games, then to Red Rising and last but not least The Selection. I don't really know how to say it, but lately, I have not been into "normal" YA (meaning the popular books that have many tropes). I've grown tired of it to the point where I'm seriously thinking if I should continue reading YA fantasy/dystopian or anything that's not contemporary. Plus, the synopsis for this book didn't catch my attention. When this got released, it was compared to Red Rising, but I had not read that book before, so I couldn't agree. Now I can see where the comparisons are born. Let me present you the synopsis for Red Rising: The Earth is dying. Darrow is a Red, a miner in the interior of Mars. His mission is to extract enough precious elements to one day tame the surface of the planet and allow humans to live on it. The Reds are humanity's last hope. Or so it appears, until the day Darrow discovers it's all a lie. That Mars has been habitable - and inhabited - for generations, by a class of people calling themselves the Golds. A class of people who look down on Darrow and his fellows as slave labour, to be exploited and worked to death without a second thought. Until the day that Darrow, with the help of a mysterious group of rebels, disguises himself as a Gold and infiltrates their command school, intent on taking down his oppressors from the inside. But the command school is a battlefield - and Darrow isn't the only student with an agenda. All you need to do for obtaining a accurate synopsis for Red Queen is change the next words: * Darrow - Mare Barrow * Golds - Silvers * Mars - Some alternate universe of which we know absolutely nothing. (Is it the Earth? Is it another planet? Is this high fantasy? Well, all I know is this wasn't set on Mars... or was it?) * + add a Selection-esque concourse that includes girl-hate and a lot of drama. But I didn't hate this because it was similar to Red Rising. I mean... I didn't like RR, but it was MUCH better than this. At least RR had an underlying message and it was not loads of stupidity, unlike this book. So why did I give up on this book, even when I was telling myself to continue? Mare: Oh, Jesus Christ, she's so freaking annoying. All she could do was whine, whine and whine. My God! Again, I remember that causing pain is all I'm good for. Besides, she's oh-my-god so different. She's the only Red with superpowers, the only one fit for everything... she's the most special person to ever exist. World building: This seems to be my most common complaint in the last books I've read... and it's again something I'm complaining about. You see... there's little to no world building. They mention a war, but we never know why or who they're fighting, the caste system is vague - red with red blood, silver with silver blood, and that's all? Sorry, but that's not enough for me. Girl hate: God, why must all YA books have girls hating each other? Gah, it's annoying and it only makes us look bad! MB (because I won't say her name - I freaking hate it) always responds obnoxiously to all the girls! And the other girls hate MB for no reason as well. Nose Graze -- Book reviews & blogging tips I'm bummed that Tiger's Promise was only a novella; I could have read a whole book about Yesubai! I adored Yesubai's story. It was inspiring, but tragic. There was a constant feeling of dread as I was reading the book (like "I think something bad is going to happen") and that really kept me hooked! It also made me sad though because I loved Yesubai and Kishan together and I so desperately wanted things to work out for them. I will admit, Yesubai and Kishan's relationship was a bit insta-lovey. I guess that comes with the territory of a novella though. It's a short book and there's not a whole lot of time to develop a romance. But despite the insta-love nature, Yesubai and Kishan were adorable together. I like how Yesubai could have chosen anyone--she could have been a queen! But she actually felt a strong connection to Kishan and she was prepared to give up everything to be with him. And she eventually did give up everything to save his life. This novella also gave me a whole new perspective on Lokesh. Seeing him mistreat Yesubai was heartbreaking! But it was interesting to get a lot more backstory on him as a person and his motivations. Also, I have to say, this book really made me feel bad for Ren. :P Poor guy can't even have an arranged marriage without the girl falling for another guy. It made me really glad that he gets Kelsey in the end of The Tiger Saga, haha. Also there was this part at the end that was so fitting.. when the goddess tells Yesubai that she'll look after Kishan for her. Yes there are two guys in the picture, but there's no love triangle in the sense that Yesubai is not sitting around trying to decide which guy she likes more. She decides basically immediately that she wants Kishan. Thank heavens!

Wow, what a slide this series took. Not even a slide so much as a plummet to its death. After enjoying Divergent quite a bit, I was a little disappointed with Insurgent. But Allegiant is really another step down altogether. My gripes: Tobias and Tris are more or less insufferable to me. They think the stupidest shit about each other; I was rolling my eyes at least once a page every time they were together. Provide examples, you say? With gusto. "My Tris should look pale and small - she is pale and small, after all - but instead the room is full of her." "I feel the urge, familiar now, to wrench myself from my body and speak directly into her mind. It is the same urge, I realize, that makes me want to kiss her every time I see her, because even a sliver of distance between us is infuriating." "'Do me a favor,' she whispers into my ear, 'and never have pure motives again.'" "I watch her blond head until it disappears around the bend, and I feel bare, like there's nothing left to protect me against pain." There are about a zillion more of these, particularly every time there's a horribly contrived make-out scene (of which there are several), but I figure that pretty much sums it up. Blergh. Plus, no one gazes into each other's eyes like these two do. I swear to god, it's like every time they're not stroking each other's faces, they're gazing longingly at each other. And it's really, really irritating. Also, what's with YA novels trying to throw in a jealousy-inducing third party intended to cause dramatic tension that never actually goes anywhere? In this book, you get one for each of Tris and Tobias: Matthew and Nita. Both are good-looking, and both Tris and Tobias are like, "ZOMG what if he/she likes him/her!?" Or, if you'd like an actual quote to illustrate how codependent/insecure they are, here you go! "I don't know where I'm going, but it's away from Nita, the pretty girl who talks to my boyfriend when I'm not there." Tobias has similar bouts of insecurity that are annoying, but his are more like little twinges, and there aren't as many good quotes like the one for Tris. Anyway, as with most YA novels, that jealousy doesn't actually go anywhere, because god forbid the relationship be tested by anything that normal people are tested by. It has to be something life-threatening before the waters get even a little rocky, and even then, these characters are so solid (even though they're 16ish) that nothing can hurt their love. It's a little hard to buy. But I guess my curmudgeonly colours are showing. It doesn't help that I didn't really even like the characters this time around ("I may like to run, but I hate climbing stairs." What the hell is that, Tris? No one likes climbing stairs! This is not a character trait!). But still. In terms of plot, this story was also waaaay slower than in the previous two books, and all the crap about genetic damage and stuff was a very feeble attempt to give the story a message about discrimination so that it wouldn't just be another teen identity book. Personally, I liked it better when it was just a teen identity book. Finally, I know a lot of people apparently hated the ending, but I actually thought it was the strongest part of the entire book (even though that's not saying much). That's the only time I actually felt anything, because the characters were forced to develop a little bit, and it didn't feel so fake. It seemed more plausible than the rest of the book, and I actually approved of ending in a way that didn't just tie everything up in a neat little package. I certainly don't think it was a particularly good ending, but it was better than I'd hoped given the rest of the story. I've tried to avoid giving any spoilers here, so I guess I'll end it there (probably this has gotten too long anyway). I really can't recommend this, even if you've read the other two (maybe even especially not then).

No book has ever moved me to fall head over heels for it except for this. I am so unmistakably in love with this book. I can't even fathom how Ahern brings about something so connected between an imaginary person to a real one. Relentlessly, it counts to experience something similar. After the Unapologetic Romance Readers group read Slightly Married for one of our July reads, I thought I might as well continue on with the series, as some of the other side characters seemed interesting. Unfortunately, the hero of this book, Rannulf, wasn't one of them. He wasn't nearly as prominent in the first book as some of the other Bedwyn siblings, so I was a bit disappointed to see the second book was about him; I might have liked him more if there'd been more of an intro to him in the first book. The plot here follows Rannulf, of course, and our heroine is Judith Law. Judith has been exiled from her family home to go serve as a poor relation to her aunt, because Judith's brother has run up bills that are driving her father into poverty. On the way to her aunt's, the stagecoach Judith is traveling in overturns and the passengers are stranded. Rannulf comes along and offers to fetch help, and to take Judith with him to another town; she agrees, wanting a bit of adventure, and immediately makes up an alternate identity--as does Rannulf. The two have a brief, steamy affair, and then part ways...only to find out that they're to be neighbors, which also leads to them discovering each others' true identities. Oh, and Judith's aunt is trying to marry Judith's cousin off to Rannulf, a plan that his ailing grandmother supports. Drama ensues. Ultimately, the problem with this book is that neither Rannulf nor Judith is that interesting of a person. Judith is a long-suffering young woman resigned to being a spinster and suffering for her family, who tell her that she's ugly and that men leering at her is because she's doing something wrong, though clearly it's only because she's gorgeous. And Rannulf is a long-suffering young man who wants to party but has decided to settle down and make his grandmother happy. His family, who are full of colorful characters, also isn't very present here. The side characters, instead of running the whole gamut from amusing to annoying like they did in the first book, are instead just insufferable. Judith's entire family deserved a good punch to the face with the exception of her grandmother, who instead just deserved a slap. Rannulf's grandmother was equally tedious. There's a sub-plot here involving Judith's brothers debts and a lecherous step-cousin, but it's not enough to salvage a story full of boring characters. And because Judith and Rannulf hook up so early in the story, there's no real tension there to pull the story forward, either. Ultimately, this was a boring second book, and it manages to suffer from second book syndrome in a series that doesn't even have a continuous plot. It's not terrible, but there's nothing there to make it really sparkle. The first book was good, but clearly served a launch for the rest of the family characters, and this one is boring. Hopefully the third book will be better or this might be a series that I'll be abandoning. 2 stars out of 5.

I enjoyed this book very much and gave it 5 stars. It is an intriguing tale of the survival struggle of a human colony that encountered some significant problems on a very unique world. The entire book is written in the first person of the colony psychologist, who's first waking moment is being expelled from the vat he was grown in at the age of fifteen years old. All the colonists are vat grown until they are 30, and then birthed to form and build the colony. They are taught their respective skills by the colony AI via virtual lessons implanted in their brains while growing in their vats. Also, the physical and psychological characteristics of all the colonists are specifically designed to correlate with their roles in the colony (large, loyal security personnel, extremely intelligent scientists, attractive leaders, etc). Something goes terribly wrong and a mere 10 percent of the colony is prematurely "born" at 15 years old. The colony AI, named "Colony", destroys all the other humans before they are born, and sets the survivors to the task of building a rocket to send a mysterious message and payload back to Earth. The story of why this takes place and how the survivors discover the truth is very interesting and classic science fiction. However, what I thought was interesting was the character development of the survivors, and the unique character development of the protagonist. He struggles with homosexual thoughts throughout the book and discovers at the end that he was intentionally designed to be a homosexual via DNA by the colony's creators. While the book doesn't center around this plot point, the discovery goes a long way to explaining the methodology of "Colony" and is fascinating, in my opinion. I felt this aspect of the book very interesting and added some very believable tension to the protagonist's interactions with his fellow survivors. Though this book is short, it was one of my favorite books of 2013. I would very much like to see a continuation of the story in a series. There are plenty of natural, technological, and political hazards left for the survivors to battle in subsequent novels. I gave this book 5 stars.

Flight Behavior starts out so promising--a new Barbara Kingsolver book! A young woman about to embark on an affair stumbling across some sort of shimmering magical forest! (Okay, when I write it out like that, it doesn't sound so promising after all.) Quickly, it all falls apart. It commits the worst crime a novel can commit: It is boring. Very boring. Still, I soldiered on. The scenes are completely inert. Pages and pages will go by in places like a dollar store or a secondhand shop. During these scenes, the main character Dellarobia and her friend will have a long, meaningless conversation. She'll scope out the stores' wares and muse on the prices and the way the objects were manufactured. The kids will run around and she'll keep them in line. And fifteen pages later, they'll leave the store, after having bought a few knickknacks. The book also offers descriptions of several things most readers already know all about. There's a paragraph about how Google maps works. Many, many pages about global warming--what it is, what the effects are. A list of ways middle class Americans can go greener. A little lesson on "correlation does not imply causation." All of this is to help characterize Dellarobia--she is just too rural and uneducated to understand this stuff!--but it only serves to annoy the reader (me). There is no storytelling here. I am shocked because I know Kingsolver is capable of good storytelling. I've read most of her other novels and she can pull off a basic narrative arc. So why does this book go nowhere? In absence of plot there should at least be interesting characters and relationships between characters, but this book is missing that as well. Dellarobia and Cub's marriage is lifeless. The reader figures this out instantly, but it takes Dellarobia about 400 pages to understand. Dellarobia and Ovid's relationship lacks any sort of tension whatsoever; it does serve as a vehicle for those global warming lectures, though.

However, even though she isn't sure she loves Jason, she sure likes him a lot, so they begin an epic months long spree of oral sex that lasts like 200 pages. Two unattached, normal consenting adults shouldn't have had this much trouble. Just not enough conflict outside the characters unexplained immaturity. Jason especially was hard for me to figure out. However, this book does contain several things that seem to be trends in new romance novels, including platonic sleeping, animal nicknames and an extremely long epilogue. All of these things piss me off, especially the platonic sleeping. If you like it though, good for you. I would rather read about real adults.

Curl up with this book in the dead of night, read it by the flickering light of a torch, hidden beneath the covers, ready to hold the warm embrace of the blankets closer to you, as ghosts call out to you in the vain hope you might hear them. I'm in a daze after finishing this book. Nova Ren Suma's writing is superb and utterly engrossing. Lauren is an excellent protagonist, and you feel for her and the people around her as she slowly unravels under the weight of what's happening to her. The characters are all so believable and real, they feel so fleshed out and though Suma has gifted them maybe a sentence or two of description, they spring fully formed into the reader's brain. The plot races as the mystery deepens and you hold your breath restless for resolution. There are only two things that bring this story down. One is the ending. It's a twist, so I won't spoil, but I will say that it felt really out of place. The book seemed to be leading up to one place, then tumbling down to another, with no real lead up or clues spread throughout to make the end easier to swallow. The book also seemed to fairly obviously push an agenda - that is, the vulnerability of young girls in today's society - which is a good and honourable agenda, but was somehow presented in a way that made it quite obtuse and kind of irritating. I honestly wish I could give this book five stars, I enjoyed it so much, and I will definitely read the rest of Suma's work - I need more of that delectable prose - but unfortunately it just didn't quite get there for me.

She isn't stereotypically awkward and shy and "delightfully" clumsy - she's a real girl who wants to make friends but everyone at her school is already in well-established cliques. Anna's neighbour in the dorms invites her to join one of these cliques - and we get to meet Meredith, Rashmi, Josh and *sigh* St. Claire. These people becomes Anna's best friends, and they are there for her when she needs them and sometimes when she just wishes they would go away! I love that the supporting cast all have lives away from Anna, they are realistic, rounded characters. They each have small issues and none if them are perfect, but together they are an awesome group of friends. I loved St. Claire. I can understand why some people would be annoyed with him, he didn't break up with his girlfriend when he realised he was interested in Anna, but are people out there who want something comfortable and I understood why he wouldn't want to leave a steady relationship for the unknown. He and Anna have some really beautiful moments, and you can tell that they genuinely care about each other - they aren't just attracted to one another on a superficial level. I loved everything about this book! It's been a wonderful read when I needed a break from the Speculative Fiction I usually read, and I am hoping to read more of Stephanie Perkins in the future.

** spoiler alert ** My Sister's Keeper is what I like to call a "cheap book." It lures you in with its controversial topic, keeps you reading with endless mini-cliff hangers and moves you to tears with passages calculated to stir your emotions. Of course, that's exactly what one should expect when they pick up a book by Jodi Picoult, a writer who is probably making money angels right now in the piles of cash she's earned from capitalizing on the tender hearts of women. I don't even mean that in a bad way. It's what everyone knows they're getting when they open a book like this- a book where the author's name is printed bigger than the title. A script for a chick flick. Truthfully, if you're looking for a fast-paced, interesting, easy read, you could do worse than this book. It's just that a book like this has a ceiling on how good it can be. This book centers around a 13 year old girl named Anna Fitzgerald. She was conceived using in-vitro fertilization as a perfect donor match for her sister Kate, who was diagnosed with a rare and tricky form of leukemia. The original intention of her parents was for Anna to donate only cord blood to her sister, but when Kate's cancer returns, she is expected to donate more and more genetic material (like blood and bone marrow) in the hopes of curing her. When she is asked to donate a kidney, she decides that enough is enough and hires a lawyer to sue her parents for the right to make her own medical decisions. First, the good: No matter your feelings on books like these, this is an interesting plot. I read this one quickly to see how the story would unfold. It asks a lot of interesting questions about parental responsibilities, maturity, and self-sacrifice vs. self-preservation. The characters in the story are put into an impossible situation with no true good choices. They all seemed like good people who were trying their best to survive under extraordinary circumstances, and it put me into the mindset of constantly wondering what I would do if I were in their shoes. So it had a promising storyline. Now for the bad. I have a few points to make here. The storyline with Campbell, Anna's lawyer and Julia, Anna's guardian ad litem was boring and completely unnecessary. I found myself feeling very irritated when I would get to a section dealing with them. Honestly, what are the odds that these two would have been old flames back in high school with a rocky past? It was a coincidence that felt very forced. Their inclusion in this novel seemed like a ploy to make the book longer or to draw out fake suspense by getting away from the Fitzgerald family every so often. While I'm on these two, are seizure dogs really a great mystery to anyone anymore? I knew that's what Judge was for when I realized that Campbell wasn't blind. Also, is epilepsy something that a normal person would consider to be a deal-breaker in a relationship? The idea that you would have to abandon a relationship because you have epilepsy and don't want to tie someone down is ridiculous. Their story didn't make sense all the way around. So boring. Anna was written inconsistently. She was too smart and sassy in her internal monologue and too childish in her external actions. Her inside and her outside just didn't match up and that continually bothered me. It's like Picoult made her smart and rational when it was convenient to the story and made her scared and weak when she needed to create tension. The ending was a betrayal to the reader. That sounds awfully dramatic, but it's how I feel. Throughout the story all of these great, interesting questions are raised. Anna wins her medical emancipation case and is finally in charge of her own body. She had to make a hard decision in the story, one with difficult consequences. It would have been nice to see the natural outcome of those decisions. t would have been nice to see how Anna and Kate and the rest of the family came to terms with what happened. Instead, here comes the surprise ending! Picoult destroys the moment she has been building up to by killing Anna in a car wreck on her way home from the courthouse. Good thing her kidney is still okay. After all that, Kate winds up with the kidney anyway and she miraculously gets better. Obviously, an organ transplant is not a cure for leukemia, so the cure really is a miracle. Kate closes the book by saying that Anna took her place in heaven. I think I just threw up in my mouth a little. This could have easily been a 3 or 4 star book without the ludicrous manufactured drama of the ending. Why bother to ask the hard questions and explore such difficult topics if you're just going to throw it all away with a "shocking" ending? It's a trap designed by Picoult to trick her readers into thinking she's done something profound and edgy. All she's done is throw away anything that was good about her story. What a waste. Not a favorite of mine, especially due to the ending. It wasn't bad for a quick read when you aren't in the mood to think too much.

3.5 rounded up for effort. Fair warning, I'm going to kind of rip this story apart because a whole bunch of things bugged the hell out of me, but I want to say in advance that despite my issues, I really enjoyed the book, I thought it was well written, I loved the characters, and so forth. I think it was longer than it needed to be and could have done without quite so many scenes, especially in the getting close phase. The author has talent and I laud her desire to address such a difficult issue. The book still made me cry even with my frustration. My main issue with the book is the complete inconsistency and inaccuracy about autism. The characters talked the talk but they didn't walk the walk. (Forgive me.) It felt to me like the author did a lot of research reading about autism but didn't actually observe or interact with any autistic children, like the knowledge is there but without really understanding it. This kid is not autistic at all. At most he has Asperger's, but even that didn't quite fit. He really sounded to me like he just had Sensory Processing Disorder. Kid is very high functioning and not just for someone with autism. The kid is less "shy" than the average four year old. Well, he's referred to as shy, but autistic kids aren't shy. Shy means an awareness of what people think about them. Autistic kids are oblivious to social cues and in general pretty oblivious to people. This kid noticed people and had conversations. He's not just smart he's beyond brilliant. He's four. He should appear delayed because so many of his skills would be behind and those are the ones people see. The intelligence, the number work, that wouldn't be obvious, so people wouldn't look at him and say, "Oh he's so smart!" These children are not regular kids who are shy and hide. They just ignore what they don't like and get angry when their ordered world is interrupted. (And age doesn't matter. At the end, the kids is only seven or eight which is just as traumatic if not more so for him to move across the freaking country . Autistic children have a hard time with expressive skills and have to work on it much harder than a child without the disorder. One of the hardest things for parents who have children with autism is that there is no emotional feedback. They don't get the cuddles, and "I love you"s and gifts that other parents do. The children act as if the parent doesn't matter. For a child to draw a picture for someone is beyond huge. It takes years of therapy for an austitic child to be aware enough of someone else's needs to give something. Autistic kids do not pick up on moods. That's nonverbal communication which they don't have. They don't seek approval because they're not that invested in anyone else. Seeking approval comes from caring what other people think of you. They're the ultimate introverts. And this kid is four. He hasn't had time to get the therapy to get past things yet. If you want to read a good book about an austistic person, read Elizabeth Moon's The Speed of Dark. She actually has a child with autism. In the afterward, she talks about how incredibly high functioning the character is and he is completely oblivious to social cues. (It's an amazing book.) A close friend of mine's husband has Asberger's which is more highly functioning than autism, and he can't hold down a job because he is unable to focus. He's very smart but takes twice as long or more to do anything as everyone else. He will go to the store and get so distracted on his way that he'll never make it and have no idea hours have passed. He doesn't understand why he has to bathe or wash his clothes. He's oblivious when she's mad at him, completely unable to read body language. And this is an adult male who is so highly functioning, his Asberger's wasn't diagnosed until middle age. The stuff that the kid does in the morning that's supposedly so trying, is just typical stuff for an intense little kid. Many children have temper tantrums in the morning with parents frazzled before even leaving for work. It was also odd how everyone was so weirded out by the kid rolling himself back and forth on the ground. It sounds no more disturbing than watching an hysterical child having a temper tantrum. Other nitpicks: Why is the fact the waiter dark complexioned relevant? He has an unintelligible accent and is mean. It wasn't necessary and since he was the only one who's ethnicity was even mentioned, it really bothered me. The MC supposedly lives in such a poor place that he doesn't have a bathroom. But he has a separate bedroom and a kitchen. If he didn't have his own bathroom he wouldn't have a kitchen. That's ludicrous. And if he can't afford his rent, he should be in a studio, or sharing a flat, or living in a rooming house. A one bedroom apartment is a luxury, especially in a big city. There was some head jumping mid scene which just drives me crazy. The MC is supposed to be illiterate but he doesn't talk like he's uneducated. He said things like, "utterly engrossed." I read a book a day, have a graduate degree, am a writer, and highly ranked in Scrabble, and I don't talk like that. A writer named Castle? Isn't that kind of tacky? Or is it an "homage"? I don't like how the incident with the John was just dropped like nothing happened. There should have been more there. Simon should have found out at some point . What kind of school doesn't check visitors, especially a private special needs school? It's really hard to get in to see kids in regular grade school. The writer is rich because he's written a couple of novels? He claims he's fast because he only takes a year to write a story when most authors take two to three years to write one. Huh? Most authors with contracts on a series are supposed to produce one a year. It may take years to write The Great American Novel, but with a genre like horror, and with the fact the man is a full time writer, I think a year is quite reasonable and actually a little long. Stephen King writes two or three a year. The history and science pieces of the GED are just reading comprehension. The whole GED is just reading, writing and math. The science and history portions are just multiple choice questions where you read a passage and have to answer questions about it. You also get your results the next day (it may even be the same day in places) for everything except the written piece because it's computer graded. There are five tests so only one test would take longer. That test should take at most a week to get back. It's not like the SAT. The separation was totally contrived. He could have applied to local schools as soon as the relationship got serious. Public schools almost always have rolling admissions. He could enter second quarter or semester. If they didn't, he could start taking a few classes in community college until he got in and them transfer. I get what the dream meant to him, but to just toss away such a wonderful relationship was stupid, too. There should have been a happy medium not all or nothing. The forced holding thing is weird. I would thing a blanket would work better. Anyway, I think it's a book worth reading and I would definitely read a sequel, but I really hope the author has more exposure to children with autism before writing it. Again, I think it's wonderful she's trying to make the kids sympathetic while also explaining just how hard it is to parent them. But I just don't feel like she got it.

Out of the entire Throne of Glass series, this book is now my favorite. It was so beautifully written; the words just fell out of the book and smothered me with emotions. All of the characters, both major and minor, were given remarkable depth and development, the plot once again thickened, and finally, there was non-stop action. From a fantasy series, you really can't ask for much else. The transition from Celaena to Aelin was pretty much flawless. There were parts of Heir of Fire that I felt dragged on, but this is the reason why: Queen of Shadows. Celaena had to be shed away, and I can imagine that it is not a slow process to kill off THE main character in a series, and replace her with someone else. If that sounds bizarre.... well, it kind of is. Celaena and Aelin are two different people, with two personalities, two different homes, but they happen to share one body. As far as the other characters go: I love how much depth Maas gives them. Kaltain was amazingly unexpected, Aedion was fiercely loyal and lovable, Arobynn's was perfectly sinister and despicable, and Lysandra was just perfect all around. I love how Maas twists and turns and manipulates my emotions when it comes to thinking "I've got them figured out". For Rowan though, he is still growing on me. I think I liked the strictly platonic relationship he had with Aelin better, and I really don't see an end game with them considering the whole immortal thing, so I will chalk their relationship up to hormones and the natural need for physical closeness. And finally, I absolutely loved how Dorian's story line played out. At first I was not optimistic about his fate, but him teaming up with Aelin at the end of the novel and bringing down the king... oh god yesssss. RIP Chaol and Celaena. I am ok with this simply because I embrace the idea of Celaena and Aelin being separate persons. I didn't really like the progression of Chaol's storyline, I thought he was bitter and mean for unclear reasons. It was like every time he would justify his actions and feelings to the reader, I couldn't see from his point of view. Unfortunately, his partnering with Nesryn felt forced and a little predictable, so I am secretly hoping that love 'connection' doesn't pan out. I loved Aelin. It took me until Crown of Midnight to really like Celaena, but I always thought she was immature and unattractively whiny. One of reasons that I loved the transition to Aelin, was she shed that immaturity and started speaking/ reasoning more like an adult, like a queen. I really liked that I no longer had to use the "well she's only 17," justification in my head anymore. The ending of this book was a little odd to me. It almost felt like the end end. Quite a few story lines were wrapped up, and the new plots that were introduced were so fleeting, they don't hold any merit yet. With Aelin and the beginnings of her court finally moving away from Rifthold, there was a distinct feeling of closure. The fact that there are two more books in this series is borderline mind blowing. Don't get me wrong, I'm excited. I'm pumped. It has been too long since I have read a series as it comes out, too long since I have felt the anticipation and agony of waiting for the next installment. I plan on gobbling up those books as if the fate of Erilea rests on how fast I can finish.

I wanted to love Given to the Sea SO so much. I mean an all-consuming love for a book that I knew was going to be magical and original and all things right with the world. And I think my expectations were a bit too high. Let's start with the basics: the multiple points of view. It's common enough in fantasy, not a shocker. But when you do that, ALL the characters need to be strong and I just don't think the members of this cast pulled their weight equally. You have Khosa and Vincent, both told in first person PoV, who seem to be the major players while the other two appear in third PoV and are more designated as secondary. Was that the intention? I don't know, but I didn't care about the characters equally and, in fact, I didn't really about any of the characters at all. This is a struggle because I've read another book by this author (The Female of the Species) where the characters were SO strong and yes, I can't compare books especially in different genres but it's hard having read both to not see the differences. I felt like the author focused so much on this unique idea of the Given and these different cultures and her unique way of telling the story because, yes, this book was not like any fantasy I've read before. But in all that, I felt the characters suffered, and even the world-building. Given to the Sea has such a rich, beautiful world it's situated in but you barely get a glimpse. You see more of the people and I've established that I wasn't a fan of that so that doesn't bode well. But the world had issues too. We talk about problematic books and I was a bit surprised that an entire group of people had disabilities and were seen as lesser for it. The Indiri are seen as uncultured and their entire race save for two people wiped out. The Pietra send any who are remotely weak, body or mind, to die at sea. The Stillean are the "perfect" people. Though the book addresses some of these characteristics, I can't say it sat well with me. Also, if you are triggered by rape, there is both discussion and a pretty detailed scene so fair warning. Now back to those characters. This book featured romance that seemed to wind its way through most of the characters which was crazy but alright. Let's see how that goes. Well... we got a love triangle-square thing. I don't even know. It was a mess and felt completely unnecessary. And in the middle is Khosa who can't bear human touch because of her genes but has to get pregnant to fulfill her destiny and I'm just sitting here like WTF is actually happening. Honestly the whole plot was like that. You have Khosa, Vincent, and Dara (3 of the 4 PoVs) at the castle along with Dara's twin Donil. And they're just chillin' there dealing with their angsty emotions. And then there's Witt who's supposed to be heartless but isn't completely leading an army in the fringes but they don't really accomplish anything in the end so his character and most of the others didn't hold much weight for me. This book was all over the place. I was never grounded in the world and never connected with the characters. And for a fantasy, that's really important to me. Perhaps I'm harsher about this genre than others because I read it more frequently than most but my expectations were high and this Sea couldn't rise to meet them. This review originally appeared on NovelKnight Book Reviews

Shadowfae was as interesting as it was hot. Jade is your perfect gritty character. She was a nun who has pretty much turned into a paranormal crack-whore. To live she needs to feed off the energy of a person's climax and the energy of her demon master, Kane. Our story is set in Melbourne, Australia. Melbourne is infamous for it's dangerous night life and gang land wars. According to Hayes, a lot of the side gangs and drug runners are supernatural beings. We see their stories unfold in the Chronicles to come. But for now it's focused on Jade the succubus. As soon as Kane wills her to do something, she must do it because of the bands that circle her arms, she is indebted to Kane for a thousand years, after which, she will die. For Jade it is a lonely existence because she hates Kane for his part in what she has become. Enter Rajah, her sexy rival who is an incubus, for Jade to be free Rajah must die, but can she kill the man she is beginning to love? Rajah is sought after by nearly as many who want Jade as he himself wants her. Together they embark on a journey to freedom and also to each other. Only they know what it feels like to be indebted to Kane and so they find solace with eachother. Shadowfae was a hot read, the intimate scenese between Jade and her patrons had an edge of darkness to them, whilst her and Rajah made the pages steam with the intensity of their joining. I love how the book flowed smoothly, even though we were constanly changing characters between Rajah, Jade and Kane. For Kane being such a bad guy, i started to like him aswell, with his vulnerability and soft-spot for Jade. The trip into the Supernatural underworld that lies beneath the lights of Melbourne was intriguing, it's like a paranormal Underbelly, but better. The scenery was vivid and detailed without taking time out from the story, everything just flowed together and it was an intense read. I will definitely be picking up Shadowglass as I would love to read the next chapter in the life of Melbournes supernatural crime. Find this review at storywings.blogspot.com

I would consider this story sci-fi (very different in my mind from paranormal), which is a genre that I typically avoid. It also relies heavily on alternate universes, which I detest as a rule. Neither of these aspects endeared me to the book, in fact the whole story really disturbed me. I also felt like I never got all the information I needed - it drops you right in the middle of something and you have to figure out what happened, but you only ever get pieces of the puzzle. Even at the end, I felt like I was looking at the story through a fog. I have no idea if this is part of a series - it certainly didn't leave me with a settled feeling for the characters - but if there are more books, I will definitely not be reading them. The message seemed to be: the world is a scary place no matter when/where you live, so fight for love as hard as you can. Not a bad message, but the way the author got there was a complete mess. This was my first Elizabeth Scott novel and it completely threw me off of wanting to read any more of her work. I know this isn't her usual genre - she does a lot of Contemporary YA - but it made me not want to even try those.

An awkward tale that is so sweet. It rings true to how we can all feel a little out of step as we battle through high school and adolescence. Even though this is a contemporary romance, I felt it had more to do with finding a happy place with who you are - accepting yourself - rather than finally getting the girl or guy; or a coming out story. Even though it's all of those things, the undercurrent with Anything Could Happen is like a resounding boom. I loved it. It's upbeat, quirky, and written to a familiar soundtrack. Halcyon (by Ellie Goulding) is featured prominently, and you can hear the lyrics singing up at you from the pages. With an easy to read narrative, this is one of my favorite GLBT books at the moment. I've read half a dozen in this genre in the past month to experience a protagonist apart from young heroines - and it's been fun. Walton's book is a positive story, much like a warm hug, but oozing realism. A totally authentic account of Tretch's journey. I particularly loved how he danced without abandon in his room... so cute! The cast (notably Tretch's family) are beautiful and very prominent in the story line and not in the periphery like in much of YA. And while there were some surprises around their story, the plot is a little predictable. But in a good way. I'd definitely recommend this book for an afternoons reading in the sun - something to leave a smile on your face.

If you have managed to make it this far without any spoilers on this book, I congratulate you. There is a reason people are talking about it. Even in the broadest strokes, it's impossible for me not to convey that things go really wrong here. That doesn't mean everyone hated The Shadows. To the contrary, it's got its fair share of 5 star reviews floating around. You'll find readers who love rolling around in the kind of misery only "true love" can precipitate. You'll find others who find beauty in despair. And there are still others who feel like JR Ward could rub dog shit around on a piece of white paper and call it art. I fall into none of those categories. To explain how this book is a failure for me, I am going to have to tell you why. I'm not going to spoil every single thing about it, but I am going to talk about the big twist at the end that has split the reading community. Here is your last chance to look away. JR Ward kills the heroine. She is still dead when the book is over and she is not coming back to life. They burned her corpse and sent her off into the Fade. It's the forever kind of dead. And for that, I say JR Ward has broken her covenant with readers. Romance books are supposed to end with a working relationship between the hero and heroine. There is supposed to be happiness there. One isn't supposed to be dead while the other is left a shadow of himself. No pun intended there. I'm too mad. I've actually seen other people claim that these books aren't romance; that they are more urban fantasy. To that, I call bullshit. Yes, Ward has broadened the scope of the series to multiple POVs (too many) but each book follows a core romance. Remember how much it sucked when she killed Wellsie? And she was a secondary character. This is so much worse, and honestly, has about a quarter of the emotional impact. I didn't cry. I wasn't even tempted to cry. I was too annoyed. The move was so very wrong that it pulled me out of the story entirely, just wondering WTF? Meanwhile, we've got iAm percolating a very second-string romance with a ridiculously predictable outcome, and that is supposed to be satisfying? IT'S NOT. I can't even blame the ending as the only problem in the book. Rhage is prominently featured here, which some readers may be excited about. But I swear, he acts like he is losing his marbles. This plot thread recurs over and over and then it is totally dropped with no explanation. It made the character look like he had a personality disorder and then it had no impact on the plot. (And don't get me started on his self-love in the pantry.) We also get a Scribe Virgin sighting; then she is dropped like a hot potato. The romance, itself, between Trez and Selena (before Ward killed her) was kind of meh. I had some issues with how she got so modern so fast. But my real complaint was in the melodrama. It didn't ring true. Maybe that's another reason why my emotions weren't engaged. The most interesting parts for me were in the few cut-scenes with Qhuinn's brother, Luchas. He is a messed up guy and with good reason. --And in the b-plot of Xcor and Layla. I feel something there. I liked where it was going, until he stomped all over it with a hooker. In the end of it all, I was just left tired... and disappointed. This is not what I signed up for as I committed myself to these 576 pages. After wading through all of the predictable, trite, and even downright ridiculous parts of the book, I should have had something to show for it. A happy freaking ending. Instead, I got a big, fat fail. If you want total spoilers from beginning to end: http://twitter.com/tweetasiread *ARC provided by publisher

I was disappointed with this novel. When I read the description I thought it the idea seemed like a really good one. A coma patient with a previous head injury awakes and finds himself with physic like abilities. I think that sounds like a great story! There were several things that I didn't care for with this particular Stephen King novel. The first being I felt the entire story was being told one long ramble. There were so many extra tangents off the main plot line that I felt were unnecessary. One example of this being keeping Sarah, the love interest for Johnny, involved in the book. I understand the sense of lost love between these two characters, but I felt like after the "What If" moment they shared after Johnny was discharged from the hospital should have been the end of her character. She had the opportunity to be released from the rest of the book as she drove away that evening. But instead, she kept popping up randomly in the future. Another thing I had trouble with was the exponential character growth for Greg Stillson. I have a hard time seeing how he went from Bible Salesman to a foreseen presidential winner who is going to drive the world into nuclear war. It was like The Omen, except with a backwoods bumpkin at the helm. It just didn't seem plausible to me. Personally, I felt the best part of the book was when Johnny gets involved with the small town strangler. I thought that Frank Dodd was a successful version of the growth style that King used for Stillson. He was portrayed in the same glimpses into random points in the characters life, however, I felt that the development of Dodd was way more believable than Stillson (This fact alone maybe why I didn't care for Stillson in the first place.). It makes sense, to me, for a young boy to be so effected by his mothers abusive treatment of him that it shapes a murdering rapist. That is a psychological path that makes sense. I feel like this book would have been a lot better if the main plot was dedicated to catching this killer. The biggest problem I had with this story was King's interpretation of religious fervor. Johnny's mother was a very religious woman and her coping mechanism to her son's terrible accident was to turn to her god. To me, this is a very normal thing to do. People often seek the comfort in the graces of their religions when the ones they love are in danger. Sometimes it comforts them and gives them strength, other times, it breaks them and sends them into a dangerous spiral of cult like proportions. What really bothered me was every encounter with the devoutly religious (letters and correspondences to Johnny after it became general knowledge that he had some sort of psychic ability) that King decided to write down, were letters from people who were grammatically illiterate and unable to spell things correctly or consistently. One particular letter that comes to mind, the sender misspelled the same word several times, but each time the word appeared it was misspelled differently than it's previous dictation. I felt it is the author's way of telling the world how stupid he thinks people of religion are. That idea itself is very one sided and narrow minded, the very thing he seems to want to emulate about these type of people. I am coming to the conclusion that King doesn't respect anyone of religious background. Carrie's mother was an extreme devote woman who's abusive suppression of her daughter's natural curiosity of the world killed them both. Mother Abigail from The Stand was a supposed to be the religious leader after the superflu killed most of Earth's population. Instead, she ran off into the wilderness to pray and fast and it pretty much killed her. All of these characters of religion met brutal ends. I would love to see him write about someone of faith who isn't 1. crazy 2. unintelligent or 3. fodder for a death scene. Personally, I don't subscribe to any organized religion, but I do feel that they are being unfairly portrayed. But that's just my opinion. I intend to keep moving forward through the works of Stephen King and hope that I find his next book better than this one.

A Visit From the Goon Squad is nowhere near the book I expected it to be. Since it won the Pulitzer, it seems to have gathered a lot of buzz, and it also seems to have gathered a lot of hate. "Indulgent hipster crap" is what a friend of mine referred to it as. I've also heard many people say that Goon Squad is among the best they've read. I personally found it to be a breath of fresh air. So many of the novels I've read recently have been dense, depressing, and dull (*cough* Norwegian Wood *cough*) and here Jennifer Egan made me laugh a lot and made me smile by the end of many stories. Jennifer Egan is clearly an innovative author. She is also clearly aware of the fact that she's clearly an innovative author, and therein lies most people's problem with this book, clearly. The "novel" (I hesitate to call it that) is composed of 13 short stories told from 13 different points of view. In the mess of different perspectives, two clear narratives emerge. The stories are of Sasha, a kleptomaniac, and Bennie, a former punk rocker. The glimpses we catch of them make them feel so much more real than if a whole novel were devoted to them. By the end, Bennie and Sasha seem like friends who you know a lot about, and yet are still a little of a mystery. Overall, the novel gives just enough to care, which makes it very interesting. Here's the only problem I have with the short story setup: the quality of what I'm reading varies from story to story. Without spoiling too much, I found the story of the genocidal dictator and the story told as a powerpoint to be some of the most interesting and compelling fiction I've read. However, the Africa story and the last story in the novel drag, and I would personally do without them. All in all, though, this novel was well worth the read.

Fate of Flames is a kick-ass, girl powered, diverse superhero novel. I know, what on Earth is not there to like?! In a world almost identical to our own, incredible monsters known as phantoms stalk the Earth killing indiscriminately and causing mass chaos. They can take any form from small to large, serpent to wolf. But all are terrifying and all are capable of inflicting massive damage. The world has managed to develop anti-phantom technologies that can keep entire cities safe. But there are also four Effigies, girls chosen by what force we do not know, and imbued with the power necessary to fight and destroy phantoms. There are only ever four Effigies at any time; when one dies, her replacement is called up. An Effigy could be any girl, and you'll never know until it happens that you will become one. Find the rest of my review at The Midnight Garden.

I need to be careful here as to not totally bash this book. It was a freebie and after seeing all the four and five star reviews I decided to give it a try. I had to wonder (as others have said) if I was reading the same book, or was it just me? The actual plot had so much potential, but there were significant problems with the writing and timelines that left me scratching my head while saying, "Huh!?" Sorry, folks. I just didn't like this one. Since this was written in 2011, I'm sure the author has grown over time, but I hesitate to spend money on a book that could end up like this one. I'll start with the good and do my best to address my issues constructively. The Good: It had a happy ending and Mac was very sweet to the baby, although it was a little creepy how quickly Maddie handed her son into his care. Mac was a stand-up guy when it came to the important things. Mac's father was actually my favorite character in the book, but I don't understand why he was given such a cheezy name: "Big Mac." The chemistry between Joe and Janey peeked my interest. For just a few pages out of a 500 page book to stand out like that, the author is doing something right, but there was so much of... The Bad: I'll start with Maddie. I did not like her. At all. I prefer my heroines to be fighters, not victims that "give up" and wallow in their misery. Yes, she was treated unfairly in high school, but she gave her body image, specifically her overly large breasts, far too much negative power in her life. IMHO, this book was insta-love (actually, it was insta-lust) with little to no realism. Mac learns that "...someone in his family had done this woman wrong, and if it was the last thing he ever did, he'd find out who." Okay. He's known her an HOUR. The book was riddled with scenes and scenarios where I simply couldn't suspend belief. Like this exchange: Maddie: "I pictured you as a real playboy. Different day, different woman." Mac: "That might've described me at one point in my life, but not anymore." Maddie: "And when did this miraculous change occur?" Mac: "About nine o'clock this morning." The writing pulled me out of the story over and over with comments like "fingers fisting in his hair" and "the wicked scent of summer flowers." To me, fingers curl, hands fist. When I think of wicked, flowers aren't in the picture, unless they're dead or black. Some of the language and descriptions in the sex scenes I found to be trashy and vulgar. Since when is breast feeding sexy? Reality in this book was he'd known her ninety minutes and it was: the sexiest thing he'd ever seen and then he tells her "I have a very vivid imagination." Another problem was Maddie's behavior. If she was so self-conscious of her sexuality, why was she always "[rubbing] against him as she walked by" and so open about past sexual encounters? Then there was the father of her child. She'd just told Mac that this man had lied about a vasectomy, took her virginity without even noticing (another reality stretch), and broke up with her via text message. But WAIT! She NAMES her BABY after him?! WTHeck? In summary, the book was over sexualized for the actual plot. If this hadn't been on a list for one of my reading challenges, I wouldn't have finished it.

It's a setting that just full of possibilities: the Greek Gods of Olympus are still around and most of the principles are living in a rundown house in modern London. With characters like Apollo and Athena and Hermes, there's no end to complications and plot twists, right? Phillips does come up with jobs suitable of her cast - Aphrodite as a phone sex operator just makes perfect sense. And if Apollo and Aphrodite live in the same house, they probably would end up having sex with each other, considering their particular strengths, and despite being half siblings. Altogether, wouldn't we expect the whole clan to be just as dysfunctional in this age as the one they originated in? But that's the problem with this book - the characters do act all too often just as you'd expect. They have almost no arc. I guess that's the problem with characters so deitic - they have no where to go but down, and if that's not your ending, you really don't have much of a story. There are two mortals that get mixed up with this crazy family, and they do have a journey, but you'd think with people like Zeus and Hades getting involved, the whole thing would be more.....epic?

2.5 / 5 stars rating This review is also posted at http://readingnookandcranny.blogspot.... I have still yet to be blown away by Aimee Carter. It seems she is just another author in the vast array of young adult writers out there. Though her fundamental plots are often unique, the execution of them throughout her series has been so far tired and cliched. Queen is no exception. While it wraps up the series well, the ending for the rebellion was a bit predictable, and the romance was a little too heavy considering the dire situation they are all facing. Granted, I now realize this series is published by Harlequin Teen, so of course it's going to have a strong dose of romance. Unfortunately, the romance in Queen seems to come at the cost of the plot. Kitty (still a terrible name for the main character) is limping along with the Blackcoats, trying to find a way to prove that Prime Minister Daxton is not who he says he is and to overthrow his power. They struggle at every turn to make a mark and find a foothold for the rebellion, and yet there is still an emphasis on this love triangle between Kitty, Benjy, and Knox. I don't think it would be so bad, except there is no real chemistry between any of them at all, so it makes it that much more glaringly out of place. Overall, I think this series fails to deliver on expectations I started with in Pawn. For such a crazy dystopian and an unique world and idea, the possibilities were endless. And while there is a bit of suspense and excitement through the series, it's heavily weighed on by other issues that aren't quite as gripping. So while I bought Pawn and got an ARC copy of Captive, I probably won't add Queen to my collection to complete the series in my personal library.

This book was amazing. I read the entire thing in two short sittings, but not because it was overly simplistic or juvenile. I just couldn't put it down. It was that good. The feed tells you what to watch, where to shop, what music you might like. It can look up anything for you at any second. There is no need to write anymore because you can virtually chat with anyone. There is no need to remember things, because a world of knowledge is at your fingertips, no actually, already in your brain. I think what I found most interesting about this book was the fact that it was published back in 2002. iPhones weren't out yet and very few people were getting online via their phones or hand held devices (maybe business folk were, but certainly not your average teen). Back then, it was still all about laptops and computers. I find it amazing that in just a few years iPhones, iPads and Blackberries have became huge and this book managed to jump right past that, to a time (a possible near future) that this information is not just in your hands but literally in your mind. Implanted. Always on. There's no longer any down time. You are always connected and something is always being marketed: places, products, music. While the book was filled with interesting commentary on consumerism and technology, they were still the backdrop to a story of adolescence and knowing (or struggling to know) one's self. Anderson's carefully crafted, futuristic teenspeak is wonderful. It is a bit overwhelming at first, but it does so much to ground the teens in this novel and introduce you to their world. The relationships he builds between both Titus and Violet is a tumultuous one, but also very realistic, and speaks strongly to the emotional roller coaster of growing up and deciding not only who you are, but what you want from life. The ending was rather grim, full of little hope, and yet I didn't mind at all. In fact, I commend Anderson on writing this ending. I imagine many will not like it, but I believe it shows a true journey of a character in a way a more upbeat ending may not have. Titus and Violet are changed forever, in ways both good and bad, and as a reader I was left thinking not just about them, but also myself: How my iPhone is sitting right beside me as I write this, how I am no longer able to read a full article online without my attention span drifting, and what these things say about my own relationship with technology, and information, and data... It's like, so meg deep, unit. Like, you have no idea. Originally reviewed here

Disclaimer: My thoughts on this book are my sole opinion and mine alone. Please be respectful and mindful of that. *INITIAL REVIEW* Yet another bland, 'New Adult' contemporary that follows the exact same pattern as all the rest. Don't get me wrong, I love NA, but when three quarters of all the books follow the exact same format, it's kind of hard not to be pissed off a bit. When can I get something original to read? I'm not going to keep ranting, because this isn't my review just yet (and I'm actually writing a discussion post on NA and stereotypes for later in the week! Sad and disappointed with this one. *FULL REVIEW* I'm not going to sugarcoat this review. This book bothered me. Okay, wait, wait. Before I start getting the cries of "Why!" and "OMG are you crazy!" let's just clear one thing up first - the only reason I gave this book two stars instead of one is because, love or hate a book, I really can't fault Colleen's writing style. She definitely has a way with words, and it was really the most outstanding thing about the book for me. To clarify as well - all my reviews are based on my own personal opinion. I know this review is going to sound like me just moaning a lot, but it is my own views. I know so many people who really enjoyed this book - which is great! Good for you. I'm happy that you liked it. I'm just sad I didn't. Things that irritated me. Okay, deep breath. Realism Okay, so I've talked to some people, and they loved the plot. Don't get me wrong again, I enjoyed it also. Until, well, it started getting so cheesy and cliched. Hopeless shows that the world isn't perfect. That it's full of people that do bad things, sometimes for no reason at all, sometimes for stupid reasons, or even because they think they are doing the right thing. Which is great and all, but when you sugarcoat the ending to make everything look as happy as larry, the point you are trying to put across becomes void. Catch my drift? The ending was too sweet. Too, everyone except the bad guy gets their happy ending. Life isn't a Disney movie, and for me, the events that play out in Hopeless, while yes, I understand this is a novel, I was left feeling like none of the characters had any actual growth or development to them. It was as if the drama was completely void. Characters. Sky, for me, lacked any credibility right from the start. First, she had the worst choice in friends. Breckin was okay, but Six, God. If I ever met someone like Six, I know I'd be staying well clear. Why would a person let herself be defined by her friend's actions? Sky says she isn't a slut. And okay yes, so maybe she isn't. But if you don't want people to label you as such, then don't go fooling around with as many guys as your best friend does. Yes, Sky has the 'I don't care what people think of me' attitude, which is great and all, but seriously Sky, have a bit of back bone. A bit of character and self respect for yourself. And I find that as someone who is the victim of sexual abuse, she would consent to be used like that. Sure, I understand that what she does with boys is because she needs to numb the pain. But seriously? Are we so much the weaker sex that we need to numb the pain of being sexual abused by letting guys feel us up? Why not take a kick boxing class. Why not tell someone about what happened? Okay, I understand that in Karen's case, it had been reported once and the case fell through. That Sky's dad was a cop, but that does not make it okay. Really, what is so wrong with society that we can justify rape like that? To just be so blase about the idea that oh, nothing can ever be solved by it. I just don't understand why people cannot stand up for themselves. Why they give up. And really, it makes me sad. Unfortunately, no-one seemed to learn from their experiences. Karen abducting Sky at a young age was emotionally unstable. Her parenting skills were classed as 'liberal' because she let Sky do whatever she wanted, but God forbid if she ever asked for a phone, the internet or a television. Holder was mediocre at the best of times. I point blank refuse to believe that he had such a close relationship with his sister and yet he had not one inkling what had happened to her. I also find it hard to believe that despite both Holder children attending counselling sessions, Lesslie's sexual abuse wasn't discovered. I also...and, sigh, I just...suicide. Okay, I'm not going to express those thoughts. Everyone in this book seemed to be running away to escape their problems. Holder gets all moody at Sky for weeks and not once does she confront him, but at the slightest touch of affection, he's all forgiven. Names This was the big one for me. For the love of God, what kick do people get out of having crazy made up names? Lesslie. Less-lie. An adapted version of Leslie, for what reason? So that the main character could have a tattoo on his arm that said Hopeless (which you'll discover the point of later). What's wrong with Leslie? I mean, really. Les. Stick it with Hope and it's still Hopeles. Hopeless. Point made. And Six. Her real name is Seven. For Christ's sake, what do people get out of calling their child a number? And then let her retaliate by nicknaming herself with another number? In Divergent, by Veronica Roth, Four's nickname makes sense. Four fears. Here, nothing makes sense. Sex & New Adult Labelling. So firstly the sex. Why was it that it felt like this book was just one big teenage girl's wet dream with a semi-interesting plot thrown in? Do people have nothing better to do in their lives than lay on a bed on a Saturday night and make out with someone? Not just that, but the whole we aren't really going to have sex sex but we will do everything else under the sun thing is kind of off-putting. It makes me feel dirty reading it, and that's not necessarily a good thing. Now don't get me wrong - I love a good sex scene, but when it happens every five pages...does anyone else feel like they've walked in on someone doing the dirty? Over and over again? My second point was the age thing. Is the only reason this novel is New Adult because there is so much sex? Why? It's not even like the characters fall into the NA age bracket (18-25) for most of the novel. They are still in high school for heaven's sake. Wrongly classifying New Adult is starting to get to me. This, at best, is mature YA. Books for Older Readers. Overall, as you can see, this was a really big let down for me. The bland story line that most New Adult contemporaries now follows has really gotten up my goat recently, and that was really something that set me on edge here. It'd be really nice to read something for a change where the main girl doesn't fall head over heels for the main guy in a matter of glances. But I'm discussing that later in the week on the blog, so I won't go into it. A story that fell flat because of the plot holes and unrealistic situations and characters, Hopeless made me feel that this novel was just that. Toto, we're not in Monument anymore. The Monument 14 kids have finally been rescued and taken to a refugee camp in western Canada. It's not the best of situations. In fact, it's not even as good a situation the kids had in the Greenway store from the first book. It is believable but sad, portraying the bureaucracy of the management of a natural disaster. It is reminiscent of the way FEMA handled the survivors of Hurricane Katrina but with a heavier hand. The camp is a place of refuge certainly, but it is also contained. The refugees aren't able to immediately leave and there is some funny business going on. This final installment encompasses escape, adventure and serious danger in a way that goes beyond the first and second books. There is an element of the horrors of a concentration camp. There is a madman with a bit of power who is determined to wield it in a demeaning, destructive way. There are victims of the chemical weapons spill who are left to deal with the devastation they have caused while under its influence. And there are Dean, Astrid, Jake and Niko who are determined to rescue Josie and ultimately find their way to true safety. The great thing about this book is the way the characters have naturally evolved. They still aren't adults but are teenagers who have been weathered by circumstance. They've gotten tough and have cast off any illusions about their situations. They don't condemn or hate adults but are smart enough to be wary of them. Dean is still struggling with a jealous resentment of Jake. Jake is still a jerk. Astrid is still conflicted. Niko is doggedly determined. The action is steady as is the pacing. This is a page turner. Things get pretty desperate and some adult themes are referenced but not completely explored. It is age appropriate. On audio the book is narrated by Todd Haberkorn, who has been the voice of Dean throughout the series. He was the perfect choice for a narrator. His ability to interpret the dialogue and narrative are absolutely expert. This is a wonderful end to a great post-apocalyptic series. I'm sad to see these characters go! There are a series of novellas that go along with the series and they are worth checking out. They only add to what is already a thrilling tale of survival. Don't miss this series.
