Defy caught my eye because its cover reminded me of Graceling by Kristin Cashore, one of my favorite YA fantasies. Its premise also got my hopes up: Girl dresses as boy and joins the army, and in the end saves her kingdom from a sorcerer. Clearly, Larson drew some inspiration from Tamora Pierce's Alanna quartet (another of my favorites). Novels with genderbending heroines are irresistible to me, but I wish I had resisted Defy. Instead of a kickass warrior heroine who challenged gender roles, I got Alexa, a hormonal weepy teenager who can't decide between two hotties. The worst part is, I felt cheated of the all-important reveal of "Alex's" true gender, because apparently the guys Alexa had been ogling for most of the book knew since the beginning. How convenient, since that means neither Rylan nor Damian ever had to feel-god forbid-gay for a fellow soldier. Alexa must be the worst girl in disguise ever, because not one person was surprised by her "secret," nor did they punish her for it. Actually, the worst part of Defy was probably the inclusion of the breeding houses, or rape prisons where refugee girls are sent once they get their first period to breed more soldiers for the king's army, even though the king conquered Antion a mere 20 years before. I truly wish I were shitting you. Setting aside the faulty logic of such an institution, I despise when rape is used as a device to make a villain seem more villainous. Apparently, we're supposed to believe Alexa's main reason for pretending to be a boy is so she's kept out of the breeding houses. Just how many women are kept in these houses, then? What keeps noblewomen out of them? Why haven't the king's people rebelled against him already, if he's such a shitty ruler? I know that cliched tropes aren't necessarily bad, if they're executed well, but the love triangle in Defy is even clumsier than Twilight's Edward/Bella/Jacob, which is saying something. Every time Alexa daydreamed about Rylan's "chocolate brown eyes" or Damian's sky blue ones, I wanted to bang my head against a wall. Alexa's so busy mooning over these two dudes that she barely has time to do any world-saving. But no worries, because guess who's the most skilled swords(wo)man in the king's army? That's right-perfect little Alexa. She beat the captain of the king's guard years ago, no big deal. At least Alanna had to work for her swordsmanship. As soon as we meet Alexa, we know she could beat any enemy one-handed. And then there's the worldbuilding. Hello, tired old medieval English society-but in a jungle! Aside from the humidity and danger of the jungle, we learn nothing about Antion's culture, history, or people. All we know is there's some kind of distant land that the king came from, there's desert-like Blevon, and then there's Antion. Great job, Larson. I can really picture the setting. I can't even say that Defy made up for its many flaws with the plot, because there was none to speak of. The melodramatic love triangle took up so much space, I'm surprised there was even room for an assassin subplot. The writing was equally painful, especially in the romantic moments (of which there were many). I never felt compelled to keep reading, and god knows why I managed to finish this book. I guess it was some form of masochism. Let's see how many times I want to strangle the protagonist? Go! In short, don't pick up this book unless you're eager for a stale, overdone love triangle padded with some magic and swords. It doesn't even come close to measuring up to my favorite YA fantasies, from Alanna's First Adventure to Graceling-and even Disney's Mulan would blow it out of the water. I wasn't expecting the world's greatest novel, but I wasn't expecting to be so hugely disappointed either. Note to self: Don't judge a book by its cover. Check out this review and more on my book blog here.

His late caretaker was Sunny's uncle and has made Jackson promise to care for her when she's released. This is a great premise for a novel, and I was completely hooked into the story from the beginning. But I felt Hellenga kept a bit too much distance between the reader and his characters. I wanted to know more about the WHY of what they did, and I didn't get any answer to that. I was confused about some of their actions ... again, why did they make certain choices or react certain ways. Instead I got a lot of information and miscellaneous facts - about serpents, or indigenous peoples in Africa, or field dressing a deer. Still the story kept me riveted, and there were twists in the plot line that I really didn't expect. I would definitely read another book by Hellenga.

4 Stars Read full review here: https://5171milesbookblog.wordpress.com/ What I admire most about YA dystopian authors is their massive imagination and their creations of new worlds, new societies, new rules and new ways of thinking. Nothing is impossible. Some dystopians focus on a new world and a society that was only recently formed as a result of a war that our current society caused. Other dystopians focus on a world and a society that existed for hundreds or thousands of years because our world as we know it never existed in the first place. The Winner's Curse by Marie Rutkoski is one of those dystopians. It focuses on seventeen-year-old Kestrel and the world she lives in. New worlds, societies and rules in dystopian novels need to be explained to the reader. And while some authors explain those worlds in long discriptive passages in a few chapters, Rutkoski revealed the Valorian and Herran society mostly through dialogue and only through a few descriptions. The revelations were scattered throughout the book and the reader learned bits and pieces here and there, which I really enjoyed. It was confusing yet fascinating to watch Kestrel and Arin interact with each other. With each chapter it became more obvious that Kestrel and Arin's initial master-and-slave-connection merged into a more affectionate one. But as quickly as their initial connection changed into a more intimate one, they were just as quickly to put their feelings on hold. You see, on the outside it looks like they come from different worlds, but the more you learn about their respective societies (especially before the Valorians started the war), you quickly figure out that they are not that different after all. Although they have a lot in common and share feelings for one another, they both want what's right and best for their people. Their struggle to stay committed to that was difficult. They were always tempted to decide against their societies and their way of thinking was a constant back an forth which resulted in a few sacrifices at the expense of their societies. The possibility to escape from our everyday lives into a completely different world is great. I enjoyed getting to know Arin, Kestrel and the world they live in. I'm eager to pick up The Winner's Crime soon to see where the journey will take them. Review to come!

This book makes an excellent essay. Simply fantastic. But a novel? I'm a little more dubious there. Written in 1948 and set in 1984, this book is essentially a prediction of the future. There's a bit of a cautionary tone to it - Orwell was telling readers not to let this happen to the world - but the logic on display behind how the world came about suggests that it was a prediction. And, like most predictions of the future written for political purposes, it isn't bright. This book helped shape a lot of the dystopia tropes that we're familiar with today, from the constant surveillance, to the attempted control of thought, and, of course, the evil government. It certainly wasn't the only dystopian book to use these tropes (The Giver seems to have influenced how these tropes are handled just as much), but 1984 is particularly important in what it uses these tropes to say. Here's the problem: Orwell is too busy pushing a political message using these tropes to worry about using them to create a good novel. That makes the reading experience fascinating in some places, but boring in others. I'll be blunt here: the worldbuilding sucked gigantic asses. All day long. Because the political message is more important than creating a fast-paced story or being true to how his characters think, Orwell doesn't care the slightest bit about subtlety in his worldbuilding. And as a result, he relies hugely on infodumps. Some lasted as long as ten pages. It's my firmly-held belief that infodumps stop the story for information that, while often essentially, could be more subtly interwoven into the dialogue and narration. There's no excuse to stop the story for ten pages to explain anything, ever. The world itself was interesting - and I'll get to that later, believe me - but the way it was presented could've been much better. Orwell's lack of care in the story aspects of the novel are also reflected in the characters. Winston is a very bland character, defined entirely by his role in the story. He has to be a trapped, discontent, critical person - otherwise the plot doesn't work. He never develops beyond that; not once do we see anything else human about him. Likewise, Julia serves her role in the story equally - she's a clever, also discontent person who loves Winston. The only thing we learn about her that the plot didn't require is that she's horny. O'Brien is the same way. Orwell could've added to his political commentary by populating his world with real people, people that the reader could feel sympathy for. But instead, they're blank slates. I feel as if they're supposed to be hypothetical people that Orwell can use as an example, as if Winston and Julia's story is just one of the many in this world. But it falls flat, because it makes it feel as if Orwell's world isn't populated with real people. All this accumulates in a plot that just doesn't work. It's incredibly slow in the first 200 pages or so. Instead, these pages are packed with political commentary, climaxing in Emmanuel Goldstien's book at the end. This would've worked fine, except that the plot takes a sudden and dramatic turn around the 200-page mark, and it suddenly speeds up. For the last 100 pages, there's next to no political commentary - instead, the entire thing is dedicated to plot, and it moves at a surprisingly quick pace. They left me with confusion - I'm honestly unsure as to what Orwell was trying to accomplish with this book. Is it a thinly-veiled essay on what could happen to the future if current (as of 1948) trends continue? Or is it meant to be an intense psychological thriller with accompanying political commentary? If it's the former, then the last 100 pages feel completely tacked on and unnecessary - Orwell says what he came to say in the first 200 pages well enough. If it's the later, then the entire book is a failure, because the slow pace and lack of character development in the first 200 pages completely undermine any intensity that it might've had. But I think this is an essay, because that's where Orwell exceeds. Some of his insights on how societies work and what the future will be like are simply spot-on. Quotes like this one really rang true for me: Throughout recorded time, and probably since the end of the Neolithic Age, there have been three kinds of people in the world, the High, the Middle, and the Low. [...] Even after enormous upheavals and seemingly irrevocable changes, the same pattern has always reasserted itself, just as a gyroscope will always return to equilibrium, however far it is pushed one way or the other. The aims of these three groups are entirely irreconcilable. The aim of the High is to remain where they are. The aim of the Middle is to change places with the High. The aim of the Low, when they have an aim - for it is an abiding characteristic of the Low that they are too much crushed by drudgery to be more than intermittently conscious of anything outside their daily lives - is to abolish all distinctions and create a society in which all men shall be equal. There are uncomfortably socialistic undertones to it, but on the whole, Orwell demonstrates a very strong understanding of how capitalism and societies work. And that's what makes the message of the novel so powerful - not the plot or the psychological intensity, but Orwell's understanding of how societies work. And that's what makes this world genuinely believable. Because make no mistake - regardless of how badly the world was established, it feels chillingly accurate to how societies work. I honestly do feel like a world similar to the one Orwell creates might happen - it's a feeling even the best dystopias (The Giver, The Hunger Games) have failed to instill in me. Most good dystopias feel like they could be real, in an alternate universe where power structures, the laws of physics, ect. work differently. But here, I felt like this society might actually happen someday which is a scary feeling. Orwell's prose is also some of the best I've read. I've read essays of his about the English language before, and the thought and care that he puts into his word choice is reflected here. The prose is smooth, efficient, and completely fitting to the essay-like structure that much of the novel has. Even though some aspects of the novel fall flat, Orwell quite clearly knows what he's doing as a writer. Overall, though, this felt at times like two books in one, like it didn't quite know what it was trying to be. This novel might've worked very well if it had been entirely Emmanuel Goldstien's book. There, Orwell could've fleshed out his opinions on this world and how it came about to his heart's content, all without worrying about sounding too much like an essay, because the book is an essay in-universe. But the way it was now, it felt broken - very interesting insights and good prose, but lacking in strong worldbuilding, character development, and plotting.

Oh Millennium trilogy, two books in and I am so torn with you. Lisbeth Salander is a most intriguing character who is worthy of being the center of these books. And unlike the first book where she shared the spotlight with Blomvkvist, she is most definitely at the center of this one. I almost thought the title was going to be another misnomer, but it ended up making sense about 3/4 of the way through, maybe a little later than that. My frustration with these books lies mostly in the extreme depth of detail Larsson goes into for EVERYTHING. Almost all of the first 200 pages of this book lend nothing to the actual plot. An entire page is devoted to detailing Lisbeth's complete IKEA shopping list (the fact that IKEA keeps popping up is somewhat hilarious). Every single device used or food eaten or whatever is specified by brand and all the components for all the computers are listed seemingly to sound impressive (and their mid-2000s specs are so not impressive today). When there are finally murders to solve to get the story moving, instead we get a whole lot of boring and sloooow police work that does nothing to even start to find the actual killer. Because of this, this book (as well as the last) is at least 200 pages longer than it needed to be, and I kept finding myself getting distracted to do little tasks around my apartment instead of reading. However, unlike the first book's slow and perfect ending, this time there's action right up to the end (although it still ends up being rather perfect, despite some bruises). I will soldier on to book 3, but these books just haven't gripped me the way I was expecting them to based on all the hype. I think I was expecting it to be a similar reading experience as Harry Potter (though obviously a completely different story), and that just hasn't been the case.

I absolutely loved Nina LaCour's 2012 YA book The Disenchantments and when I saw the cover of Everything Leads to You, I was dying to read it even though I had no idea what it was about. I wasn't disappointed. I thought that Everything Leads to You was a magical book -- a love story that deftly explored themes of illusion and reality in both movies and romance. Emi was a fascinating character. She's the biracial daughter of two academics, brash and self-assured, and just knows she'll have a fantastic career in Hollywood. She's well on her way, having just landed a job assisting a well-known set designer. Her confidence gets her into trouble sometimes, and I loved the way that this story showed both the positive and negative side of that personality trait. She's trying to extricate herself from a not-great relationship with a co-worker. And one day, she gets a call from a friend who tells her about an estate sale of an actor, a Hollywood legend. That sale will lead Emi on a journey of self-discovery and love. There was just something about this book that made me -- an HGTV addict -- want to climb inside it and live there. Emi spends her time hanging around cool flea markets, finding stuff to use for her design projects. While this is an LGBT story, it's not a coming-out-of-closet one. Emi is completely comfortable with herself and her sexual identity. But the girl Emi falls in love with is having major identity issues -- can't say more without spoilers -- and I loved the way the story took Emi's job -- she has to take fictional film characters and figure out how to translate those characters into objects to be used on set -- and uses that job to explore issues of identity and social class.

Despite her reliance on "tell" rather than "show," her tendency to date her work with long and drawn out descriptions of fashion and technology, and her cheesy dialogue and even cheesier romance, she does write escapism at its best. It's almost like her publisher told her to write a story as good as Perfect, and instead, she just recycled Perfect. Only this time around it seemed like her heart just wasn't in it. The story and the characters were mediocre, and the above mentioned writing flaws were so much more pronounced ... and much less ignorable. This is not an example of her best work. That being said, I wouldn't not recommend it. It did have me sighing and giggling as the characters fell in love, which has always been Ms. McNaught's forte - even if it's not up to par with her earlier works, it's still heads and shoulders above a lot of the other drivel out there. So, if you are interested in reading it, and you've never read any of her other works, I'd say read this first. Then, if you want to see this story when Ms. McNaught is in peak form, read Perfect. You'll see what I mean.

My translation says these are 3rd year B class (second semester) junior high students (9th grade) but I can't help thinking that they are really supposed to be 3rd year middle school students (7th grade). This would make an enormous difference; but let's not quibble. The omniscient narrator probes the head of his male students pretty well (not so well with his female students) but the writer also assumes an eighth grade (let me split the difference) mentality. Shuya might fantasize about (**spoiler alert**) overpowering a boatload of trained SDF soldiers (with a bullet in his shoulder, no less) but this stretches credibility beyond anything reasonable (I can believe that, with enough exposure to junior high student, many people might be willing to send them to The Program). I did like the ending, although there was no need to (**spoiler alert**) kill off any potential epilogue-love-triangle with Shogo. What Takami doesn't explain, however, is why The Greater East Asia Republic is sponsoring The Program ("instilling paranoia" is not good enough). I think it might be better explained as a means of controlling the underclass. We traditionally think of the underclass as limited to the chronically unemployable--but really, we should extend this classification to anyone doing a job that is relatively meaningless (unrewarding, with positions easily filled through the minor training of random individuals). A successful society has to breed a fairly extensive underclass (you never know when a war or plague might make it useful). I believe it was Voltaire who suggested that whenever European nations fought, 100,000 men would be facing each other, half of them being ravaged by syphilis. War and disease were the means by which nations traditionally controlled the size of their underclass. But our wars are now too small, internal medicine too successful, and our population too great. In some parts of Japan, only the Xiong (oldest son) was traditionally allowed to marry and have a family (see The Ballad of Narayama--1983). While this left the Chang Nan Yi Wai noNan Xing horny-but-non-reproductive, I can't imagine anyone remaining so un-copulative today. However, if you had enough of these programs (Takami is almost there) you could use them to cull your underclass. This might be a better explanation--in fact, this might also be a better explanation for the Hunger Games--although, then, I suppose, you'd lose The Capitol's network coverage. But why junior high schools? Why not nursing home? It wouldn't be as interesting, but might solve the nation's social security/aging populace problem. Maybe they could call it The Chronic Constipation Games--give them bedpans instead of gladii.

This book and I never quite connected. The premise was intriguing. The main character, Ciel, and her buddies are "adapters," people who take on other people's auras and thereby imitate their shapes, voices, and appearances. Let's start with what I liked about the book. I liked Mark, a man Ciel has had a crush on for most of her life. I found her feelings for him and her hesitance to act on those feelings to be believable. I appreciated that her attraction to him was more than just physical and was based on a lifetime of encounters. It was easy to become invested in their relationship, and I rooted for them to get together. I also liked Ciel's reactions to taking on new auras. While using an aura, her body took on characteristics of the person she was copying. For example, as Mina, Ciel was prone to crying because Mina is a crier. As "Boner Benjamin," Ciel was horny for no good reason. That was a fun and interesting side effect of adapting. Sadly, I had trouble connecting with Ciel outside of her relationship with Mark. I suspect this was partially because she wasn't herself enough; she was too busy playing other people. Her internal monologue remained intact when she took on other auras, but without actions connected to that dialog--actions that were true to Ciel as opposed to the person she was playing at the time--I never bonded with Ciel. I also had trouble with the fact that, although the issues presented in this book were serious, Ciel didn't take them seriously enough. Multiple times, she was held captive and her life was at risk. Her associates were also held captive from time to time, as well. These should have been intense situations. Ciel should have taken these situations seriously. But it didn't work out that way. The book was just too light-hearted for its content. Ciel kept her good humor too well, and she rushed into things without thinking. I never felt the suspense or urgency that these situations should have created. Also, the theme of being held captive was a bit overused, in my opinion. It was like events kept repeating themselves. I wanted to see new scenarios from one chapter to the next, but I didn't get that. It was like an ongoing game of catch and release. For those who want a light-hearted read with a unique premise, I might recommend this book. But it simply wasn't for me. I stopped reading at 50%.

The Eleventh Plague is about a world destroyed, not surprisingly, by plague, and the remaining people are scavengers just trying to survive. At the start of the novel, Stephen must suddenly fend for himself after his grandfather dies and his father is badly injured during an accident. He joins up with group of strangers who take him to a hidden town that has managed to maintain some semblance of order and safety. However, this isolated village is not as perfect as it seems, and Stephen begins to wonder if he'd be safer on his own. The main problem with The Eleventh Plague is that it is boring. Books don't need constant action to be interesting, but they must have some believable tension. Hirsch was trying to portray a very insular community where freedoms were restricted in order to ensure social cohesion, but the stakes never seemed that high. The expectations were pretty low (contribute and don't be disruptive), and readers were only given one example of a family being banished. Additionally, an adopted Chinese teenager named Julie lived in the town, and she faced mistrust and racism from the community, but not nearly as much as I would have expected given the fact that China unleased the plague. Julie refused to participate in community functioning, and caused a lot of havoc and disharmony by fighting. However, the town let her skip school and do her own thing most of the time. She faced little punishment for her indiscretions, and this is surprising as I would assume that fear and distrust could cause people to react violently to a person that they see as an enemy. Many authors have used isolated villages to really explore the horror of human emotions under pressure, but The Eleventh Plague only brushed the surface of human depravity. For a dystopia, it was pretty lightweight, and there are a lot of better books that deal with the subject in a more nuanced and in-depth manner.

We were heading to shitsville during the prologue but the proper DNF is at 15%. I'm a masochist. This book should be renamed to "All Girls Are Trash, But Have You Met Caroline?" First, let's meet the heroine: Without her parents and no close friends to keep her there, California didn't have the appeal to Caroline that it used to. Caroline thought about the man sitting next to her. He probably had a lot of close friends. He looked trustworthy. Caroline almost snorted at her own thoughts. How the hell could someone "look" trustworthy? It was ridiculous. Didn't all the crime shows talk about how the killer always looked like the "guy next door?" Caroline shook herself. If you haven't already realised, the heroine's name is CAROLINE. She's ordinary, ordinary and even more ordinary. Oh and she's also very plain. Caroline was nervous. She wanted to talk to the over-the-top masculine man sitting next to her, but she didn't want him to look through her as most men did. Caroline had faded into the woodwork most of her life. No boyfriend in high school, she hadn't gone to any of the school dances, not even prom. One guy had the nerve to tell her that she wasn't "girlfriend material." Thinking back to that comment, made without thought, still hurt her today. Caroline knew she wasn't model beautiful, but she didn't think she was a troll either. She wasn't tall like men seemed to want in a woman, but she wasn't short and cute either. Caroline was average from the top of her brown-haired head to the bottom of her normal sized feet. This goes on for a loooooong time. Here we are, 4 pages later: Caroline could feel the man's eyes on her. It discomfited her. Shifting uneasily in her seat, Caroline wasn't used to men looking at her that closely. She was plain and uninteresting. She knew it and so did everyone else. Caroline wasn't the type of person who got special favors because of her looks, and she wasn't one to draw the attention of any man. She'd long ago learned to accept it. Caroline had a pretty healthy self-esteem, even with her plain looks. She'd had a tough time growing up, what teenaged girl didn't, but when all was said and done, Caroline learned to actually like herself. She was smart, had a good personality, and even if she didn't have men lining up to take her out, she was mostly content with herself and her life. I especially love the "Caroline had a pretty healthy self-esteem", "she learned to actually like herself" and "she was mostly content with herself" parts of that paragraph. I mean, we only spent 6 fucking pages reading about how she was ready to throw herself off the nearest horizontal surface higher than a sidewalk to end her misery. Anyway, we've met CAROLINE so it's time to meet the hero Matthew, aka Matt, aka Wolf, aka Mr. Paranoia. The woman turned away from Wolf to buckle her seatbelt. It didn't seem like she was trying to flirt with him or to get him to notice her. But the fact that she wasn't, only seemed to draw his attention to her more. Maybe that was her plan all along? Matt/Wolf also thinks the supermarket cashier is a Russian double agent and that the elderly lady living across the street is actually a Colombian drug lord. As the military's finest, he's onto them. Hoping she'd reciprocate and shake his hand, he waited for her to give him her hand. Wolf learned a lot about people by their handshake. Many women felt as if they shouldn't squeeze a man's hand when they met, so they just let their hand lay limply in his as they shook. He hated that. Wolf had no idea where that had come from, but if women knew how much it turned men off, they'd certainly stop doing it. All women are trash... Caroline tentatively took his hand, but shook it with strength. ..... but have you met Caroline? Caroline might be ordinary but she's very perceptive: Caroline looked over at Matthew and saw he also wasn't sleeping. He had one leg stretched out into the aisle and one under the seat in front of him. His eyes were closed and his hands were intertwined, resting on his stomach. NOTHING gets past her. He'd met too many women that were all about the money, or fame, or fashion, or whatever. All girls are trash.... "Sounds sensible." Wolf agreed, happy to hear she seemed like a reasonable woman. .... but have you met Caroline? Wolf knew he had to be careful about talking about his job. "I and two buddies are headed for some leave in Virginia. We're between missions...er...jobs right now." Aced. It. "So, what is this new job you're flying across the country for?" Pleased he was showing interest in her, Caroline told him, hoping it wouldn't turn him off--some men didn't like smart women. "I'm a chemist." She's a picture of self-confidence and security. "Something's wrong with the ice. I can smell it. It smells off, like something's in it." "I don't smell anything." Great, now he thought she was nuts. But she wasn't. She was a chemist dammit, and this is what she did for a living. No honey, that's a sniffer dog. What a trainwreck.

First sentence: "They say the fearsome thing doesn't always work well." What if Marie Antoinette left a hidden diary in her cell as she left for her date with the guillotine? A diary that detailed her thoughts and feelings for 20 odd years of her life, from a teenager in Austria to the new dauphine (and later queen) of France to Citizeness Capet, despised by a France in revolution. I was not impressed with this book, which makes me sad because I did like the author's biography of Elizabeth I. Anyone wanting a novelization of Marie Antoinette's life would be better served by reading Juliet Grey's Becoming Marie Antoinette. Erickson calls her book "historical entertainment" not a historical novel, which I guess gives her free rein to make stuff up. In the book, Marie and Axel von Fersen go on a romantic getaway to Sweden where they stay out in the country by themselves for months. There is also a scene where Marie Antoinette's jailers let her go away with him for her health. I did not like the diary format at all. Months and sometimes years would go by between entries. The book is supposed to span Marie Antoinette's life from the time she is a teenager to right before her execution. The tone never changes and the character doesn't seem to grow at all over the course of the book. Some important and historical events that happened to Marie Antoinette are completely left out. The book was entertaining though and a quick and easy read, so Erickson did accomplish that much. Not the best novelization of Marie Antoinette's life.

Heinlein hits upon several very interesting issues in this book. Included in this are polygamy, incest, the rise and fall of societies, immortality, computer evolution, and establishing colonial frontiers to name just a few. On the whole, I felt that this book tried to do too many different things and deterred itself from the more compelling themes. Lazarus Long was a man who wanted to- OMITTED -establishment of colonial frontiers was another interesting concept presented in the book. The book did a wonderful job to show that no matter how advanced things are in the future, you often times will have to toss the technology aside to reduce how much weight you have to carry. Survival is the most important fact. However, when compared to the casually discussed description of the fall of Earth- OMITTED - I found it would have best been included. Another issue with the book is the often choppy jumps in plots. Be it from the removed sections of OMITTED text or from what are supposed to be intentional, none OMITTED jumps. The story that I liked in Time Enough for Love is the story of a man who has done everything and is bored. He meets an interesting computer named Minerva and, in the course of figuring out what to do, Minerva decides to go into the body of a genetically created women. This was intriguing. However, what Heinlein thought was more interesting was his attempt to break down the taboo of incest and polygamy. The approach for focusing on both of these lost me along the way with the dozens of other parts to this book. Come the conclusion of the story, Heinlein failed to convince me to the breaking of any of these taboos when he might have had some success in the way he has had with other books. My final opinion of this book is- OMITTED

I'm a plot girl through and through, but there are certain authors that can make me sit down and read a book that's pure character study and absolutely nothing else. Melina Marchetta is one of those authors. I love how she manipulates words. Sometimes, I still feel like crying myself to sleep over The Piper's Son and Froi of Exiles only improved on the second reading. On the Jellicoe Road is a different animal. The stories of Taylor Markham, Jonah Griggs, Ben Cassidy, Narnie, Webb, Tate, Fitz, and Jude never really came together for me. Marchetta does try to fit all the puzzle pieces together in this disjointed novel, but even the best explanation falls flat when the reader doesn't care about the characters. Of a character driven story. See what I did there. When I'm reading a character driven novel I need to be able to connect with the secondary characters if not with the--unreliable--narrator. Every fragmented scene was merely an anecdote that had happened to someone else, to people I don't know or wish to meet. It was all so far, far away from me. I'm not talking about the fact that I live in Northern Europe and the author with her characters lives in Australia, I'm talking about the emotional connection that never was. I did not care. On a technical level I can admire what Marchetta was trying to achieve by indulging in non-linear storytelling and I wish there were more books like this--only better--to challenge readers of all ages. The problem is she's not good enough author to pull it off. Neither was Hal Duncan, come to think of it, no matter what the award committees might think. If the soul of a book is sacrificed at the altar of writing craft, the book fails. On the Jellicoe Road fails.

I am a 14-year-old girl who is absolutely, positively childish. So in this Theresa review, I shall review about how much I SERIOUSLY COULD NOT UNDERSTAND THIS BOOK. I didn't know what other shelf to put this book on besides my "read" and "fo-shizzle" shelf (fo shizzle isn't really a . good thing). I usually read romance and YA books--but Lord of the Flies is neither. And I didn't know what rating to give it either. I would have given it a 2-star, but 2-stars means it was "OK". It wasn't OK to me . because it gave me torture. It seriously did. AND TORTURE IS NEVER OKAY. Now, the review part of this review--which is for my fellow review readers that are wondering if they should flip open this book--is basically: I can't understand this book and if it wasn't for my English teacher and my english class full of smartypant-wearing people, I wouldn't have understood a single word. NOT. EVEN. ONE. So unless you're surrounded by smartypant-wearers OR you are a smartypants, please......just put this book back onto the shelf and search for another. Anyway, I want to explain that I had to read this book for my 8th grade English Honors (I don't know how I got into honors!!! I like to read. I like to write. This doesn't necessarily mean that I can withstand books like these!) class, and I had to do book reports, as well as a project (that I didn't do--but I still passed the semester somehow) on this freaking book. Now I'm just gonna say the life lesson that this book teaches straight out in human language. "If there is only passion, but no logic, destruction is unevitable." Err--I think it's "destruction". I'm not entirely sure--I totally forgot what it was. BUT ANYWAY, this is a valuable life lesson--don't get me wrong! The story was just sorta creepy. First the kids are stranded on an unknown island. They decide to work together to survive and to signal for a boat or an airplane or SOMEONE to come and rescue them. But then things start to go wrong, and some people die, and then they get rescued at the end--the end. This would be an interesting story but it was just really creepy. And I wouldn't have been able to understand anything if I hadn't done this for English class where we would discuss the book as a class together and I had like 28 other fellow classmates helping me. And it seems like everything the characters do represents something totally figurative. Like there's the fact that Piggy (plumpy character) has specs (glasses). Those glasses represent society, right? When things start to go wrong, Piggy starts frequently cleaning his specs. My english teacher and english classmates kept saying "Oh, Piggy cleaning his glasses represents that the society is getting more screwed up." And now that I explain it to you guys, I do understand what the representing thing is coming from, but during THAT MOMENT in english class, I just sat there in my own little island with my mouth hanging open. Because truthfully, the only thing I thought was that a plumpy character was cleaning his glasses. I clean my glasses too. That's what you do when they get dirty. When I clean my glasses, it doesn't represent anything but the fact that my glasses are dirty and I'm trying to clean them so I can see. I don't know where the representing thing came from. So apparently a lot of things in the story represent something. So when you're reading, this story is one of the stories that uses the characters to represent something that the author is trying to teach. This is one of the good things about this book. I love books that teach life lessons. Those are the best kinds. This one was just really hard to understand, but I had my classmates and teacher help me so I ended up understanding it. But I didn't LOOOOOVE this book...I didn't really like it...but that's just my opinion!! I think it teaches a valuable lesson that I will keep in my head forever and ever and ever, but I will NEVER forget the torture this book brought to me.........maybe it's because reading it was classified as homework or something. But anyway, yeah, if you're really smart and you enjoy books that teachers recommend and you're not as clueless as I am, I think this book MIIIIIGHT just be the one you're looking for.

I AM Ultimately Conflicted So, let's do this like an Amazon review for a skincare product: PROS: Beautiful Writing Genius Premise Entertaining Mystery Fantastic Ending Highly-Researched Worldbuilding CONS: Boring as FFFFUUUUU- Not-so-Connected Characters Plot Confusion Timeline Confusion Overall WTF-Confusion The Night Circus is one of those books that you love but at the same time you really don't, for the reasons lifted above. UNBROKEN, BY LAURA HILLENBRAND Recommended by Trisha Cook, on Goodreads. Actually, I was very vague when I asked for recommendations, and I get the feeling that she recommended many, wildly varied, radically different books, probably sure that at least one of them would please me... I definitely appreciate her efforts :) even if I didn't quite enjoy this book in particular. I'm a fiction fan. I read nonfiction sometimes, but the bulk of my reading is fiction. For me to enjoy a nonfiction book, it has to have two things: a subject that deeply interests me and superb writing. I love survival and personal victory stories, so it had the former, but the writing was atrocious. The parts are disconnected, the pacing varies drastically between them. It's so repetitive I often wanted to throw the book out the window in frustration (the only thing that stopped me was the fact that I have a digital copy). The details of Zamperini's ordeal are described so often (and so repetitively), and with such excruciating minutiae there's no way they served any purpose other than shock value. Top it off with the shameless attempt of distorting the truth to make the atomic bombing of Hiroshima and Nagasaki justifiable, and I just can't bring myself to say I liked this book. It's a shame. Zamperini's story, and of his companions, is truly heroic and fascinating; it deserved a better telling. Up next: Death at la Fenice, by Donna Leon

Am I alone in finding this book really terribly written? I am no literary fiction snob, far from it, but I thought it was awful. I managed two thirds of it before ditching it. I just couldn't face the idea of it droning on and on with the contrived prose (that'll explain why the book is so long), done-to-death cliches, and ridiculous characters straight out of the 'Big Book of Nasty Nazis' for another several hundred pages. What grated most with me with regard to the prose was that it was, well, extensive, in that he's clearly a writer unafraid to ratchet up the word count in describing a scene, yet at the same time, it managed to be lazy, and uninspiring, too often reaching for the more predictable, formulaic turn of phrase. It is hard to explain this properly, but I was very aware whilst reading it that this was an American depiction of Europe, it just read like someone describing a place in much the style you'd find in a travel magazine, it never really made me think he was describing Europe from any deep knowledge or experience of it. I appreciate that's probably because the author is American, and maybe that's understandable - similarly, you wouldn't expect a British or French author to write the great American novel. Still, it never really made me think I was reading a book written about a place the author had any real experience of, or more importantly, feel for. The Second World War is in one way an 'easy' period in which to set fiction - you have the events of six years, multiple conflicts, set in almost every corner of the globe, to choose from. What's more, it is an era we are very much aware of, having lived through it in many cases, or through the ongoing huge interest in that period (we are still making films about it, 70 years on). On the other hand, it is difficult to get it right, and lots of writers reach for the cliched characters far too easily. The ultra nazi Hitler Youth, the monocle wearing Gestapo man screaming to see someone's papers, the Wehrmacht man dutifully following the orders of his superiors, the whole "for you, Tommy, the war is over thing". Maybe I am just being too sensitive about these things, or overly critical, but for me this book belongs in that category.

Linked by Imogen Howson was not terribly convincing. Usually I have a pretty open mind about YA now, since the whole paranormal/sci-fi movement has mass produced stories that can sometimes be identical to other stories. I won't say that Linked was identical to other stories, even though it did have pieces of other stories here and there. What I will say is that it was disappointing. It took too long to get into Elissa's world and understand that this was dystopian. When beginning this story I was under the impression that Elissa was sick (like terminally ill, maybe) and she needed a cure. Come to find out the girl is suffering from hallucinations, as she thinks. What in reality is happening is that she is linked to another person. She doesn't know who this person is, all she knows is that this person is tortured regularly and her hallucinations feel as if she were "linked" to someone and seeing things through their eyes. Also, come to find out that this story takes place in the future, on a different planet, one that does not recognize twins. I would say that the author needed to work on a couple of things for me to have just liked it: first, she should have done a better job of world building. Secondly, I really did not appreciate the rushed sentiment of humanity. Sure the whole premise is about what being human truly means, but the overall way it was conveyed in the story lacked conviction. The world building would have helped with understanding what the hell was happening from the start but instead we find out about a third into the novel what kind of alternative universe the book was set in. Overall I give this book 2/5 stars.

I wonder about the 5 star rating system here at GoodReads regularly, wishing for half stars most often. Books like This Savage Song, by Victoria Schwab, make me wish for 6 stars. They make me question how I could give 5 stars out to other books, question my entire book ranking system, because this book was nothing short of brilliant. How can I say this? I'm not even interested in monsters, but Schwab made me fall in love with one. I hate dark stories, violence, and cruelty, but Schwab's words sucked me in from the get go and gave me a tiny light to follow through the darkness. She made me think. She made me feel. And if I'm throwing my hand over my mouth at the end of the story--an exceptionally rare thing for me, rarer than tears which almost never happen for me--you know she did something right. We have Kate Harker and August Flynn, a young woman and a monster, someone who wants to be like her father and emulate a monster and someone who wants with everything he is to be human. They couldn't be more opposite. When Kate sets out to prove to her father that she can be as ruthless as he is, she crosses paths with August, one of three Sunai--monsters who feed on the souls of sinners. August is sent to follow Kate because she could prove useful if the truce between the 2 sides of the city of Verity breaks down, since Kate's dad, Callum Harker, runs the north half. When the monsters start attacking, August and Kate find themselves as unexpected allies as they try to figure out who is behind the attacks. Wow that was hard to put into words, to avoid spoilers but give enough info about story to make someone interested. And that's just it. I picked this up because I really like Schwab's Shades of Magic series, not because of what This Savage Song was about. Her writing is amazing, as are her world building and characterizations, and This Savage Song is no exception. But it was splendidly different: deliciously and achingly dark, like that sort of darkness that leaves you hopeless and aching. I mean yes, there was darkness in Shades too but TSS went deeper and darker. I found myself considering the light and dark in both August and Kate, comparing and contrasting, trying to figure out what each was capable of. I loved them both. I can't say I've ever loved a monster, but if August were here, I'd ask him to be my book boyfriend. And I say this admitting there is no romance to speak of in this story. There's just so much good in August. And Kate? My god the girl is kickass. She was an utterly amazing heroine/villain. And that's another thing. I'm not entirely sure who the villain was and who was the hero, AND I DON'T EVEN CARE. I love them both. I love them regardless, good or bad, light or dark. I loved the whole Flynn family. I mean how could you not like 2 humans who call 3 monsters sons and daughter? Ilsa was so full of love and sadness, and Leo so full of anger, but what wonderful and interesting siblings they were to August. On Kate's side there were so many people to hate, none more than Sloan save for one, both the embodiment of cruelty, characters to send your rage at. And you will be rage-y, or something, because Schwab's writing brings the emotions to the surface the same way a Sunai's music brings the soul to the surface. Did you see what I just did there? Yep, I went there. I can't say enough good things about this book. The writing was beyond words, with characters to love and hate and an unimaginably creative storyline. THIS ONE IS A MUST READ. Please pardon my yelling. I simply want EVERYONE to hear that they should drop everything and read this now!

A different world, a new star crossed love affair This Shattered World is the second book in the Starbound trilogy. I have to admit I'm really enjoying the trilogy thus far and probably because each book has given me a new world and couple to get to know. I have really been craving more stand alone type YA fiction and while these aren't exactly stand alone they fit the bill quite nicely. It would not hurt a reader to read the first without the second nor the second without the first so far. I suppose only time will tell if the third book in the trilogy could be read alone as well. Setting the scene and the players Kaufman and Spooner are a really great writing duo. I can't tell which parts are written by whom. Maybe each writes from either Flynn or Jubilee's perspective? Either way it's extremely well done. The world building sucks me into the setting and I can feel the tension that is lit through the two opposing groups of peoples (the military and the locals / rebels). Avon is a world that is still in the terraforming process but should be much farther along by now then it is. Right now it's stuck as a swampland. There are some parts I don't quite understand though - like really why are so many things denied to the locals? Education, decent medical care, off world broadcasting access, heck even same world broadcasting abilities. It seems like there are any number of things that the government and military are withholding from the local people of this world that is causing more unrest and thus making the situation worse then it needs to be. I just didn't get much of this until the end and I would have appreciated if it were explained better more throughout the novel rather then it feeling a bit glossed over. I'm fascinated by the idea of terraforming and would have loved to hear more about that and the infrastructure for the local populace. I'm just greedy and want more information on a planet so different from our own. What was there though was great in setting the atmosphere. Logically I want to pick some things apart but emotionally I was like yes, oh yes! So that's what happened with me in regards to the romance between Flynn and Jubilee. When I stopped to think about it at all for a few moments on a logical level the budding romance didn't make much sense to me and I scoffed and went 'yea freaking right no way would I be falling for the other if I was either ends of that equation.' But then emotionally I'm like 'oh heck yes, you just happen to be exactly the right piece that was missing and ooo la la dangerous attraction.' I can only say that often as evidenced by real life - love and romance do not take anything even remotely resembling logic or common sense into account. So it works, it just does - roll with it. I think fans of young adult fiction romance will enjoy this one. However, I did enjoy the romance between Tarver and Lilac from These Broken Stars much more so then Flynn and Jubilee's. What's up with those after each chapter interludes? I have to say that initially those between chapter interludes really bugged me. At first they were ok and then they started getting tiresome and annoying because I just didn't see the point and then at the end came the "ahhh ha" moment when the reason for them being there makes sense but it didn't quite make up for my impatience with them. As I was reading I didn't feel the need for them and the info they were giving to me felt a big repetitive and nonsensical until I reached the end of the book but then I'm also notorious for being impatient with non linear sequences of events and flashback type scenarios. So you can probably take my opinion on these with a grain of salt. Whispers and plot points Admittedly I felt there were a small handful of holes in the plot points where the whispers are concerned. While I think the whisper entities are a really interesting thread in the story arcs that connect the two books I felt like there were some inconsistencies between their abilities and behaviors in the first book versus the second book. Perhaps some of these things might be explained in the last book or maybe even these things can be explained away via the progression of time in research and experiments but I just didn't feel like I was given enough information. For this reason and a few other concerns I feel like my rating sort of wavers between a 3.5 and a 4. I enjoyed the action but there were so many little things things that kept sticking for me. But for the most part I rolled with it and still enjoyed the overall reading experience. Are teenagers really that mature in the future? These books are young adult but the characters don't exactly feel young adult. The explanation for that is built into the story line because teens can join the military as early as age 16 and these character have also seen their fair share of hardship in life. Now I'm going to get snippy on the military points - In the Unites States teens can join the military as early as 18 (or 17 if they have a parent sign off on a waiver). As I joined the military at the age of 18 I don't believe 2 years of service could give the level of maturity that these teens have unless there is a HUGE mortality rate and if the ranks had a high turn over because I find it hard to believe they would be able to achieve the military ranks that some of them have. I know that life experience also helps to speed up the progression of any characters maturity but still the behavior to age balance didn't seem to fit perfectly. Because of this I wish they would have just made these adult novels and given them more realistic ages to match their maturity levels. Maybe like 20 to 24 would have been better for me. Even though I had a few concerns, This Shattered World was a great addition to the Starbound trilogy. Full of action, suspense and romantic tension, I'm eagerly awaiting the final book!

2.5 stars "Sunai, Sunai, eyes like coal. Sing you a song and steal your soul." I find myself in an awkward situation of holding a converted ARC, agreeing it's well-written with a creative concept--and feeling nothing. Maybe it's because I'm a little over black-and-white morality in YA. The stuff I've read of late, The Rose Society and Six of Crows, all feature criminals in sweeping shades of grey and compared to them, our resident monster August feels a little... vanilla. "Why would you even want to be human? We're fragile. We die." "You also live. You don't spend every day wondering why you exist, but don't feel real, why you look human, but can't be. You don't do everything you can to be a good person only to have it constantly thrown in your face that you're not a person at all." August, accept this Edward Cullen badge and stand with Akiva and the rest of the self-loathers in the corner. It's such a shame because the world-building is lovely. Longtime fans of Schwab will swoon. This is the first of her books I've read and if it's a taste of what to expect in A Darker Shade of Magic, sign me the hell up. Right from the beginning, we're thrown into a post-apocalyptic world where monsters roam free. There are three kinds: "Corsai fed on flesh and bone, Malchai on blood, and whose it was meant nothing to them. But the Sunai could feed only on sinners. That's what set them apart." August is a Sunai, which makes him more of a sack of flour. He and his siblings live under their adopted father Flynn's protection in one of half of Verity. The other is run by a mafia boss-like guy called Harker, who is our heroine Kate's dad. The meet, sparks collide and stuff happens. I genuinely don't remember the plot anymore. It leans towards formulaic, no memorable twists or like. Those who are tired of the same old love will be happy to know there's next to zero romance inside. Kate and August have some chemistry when they first meet, but it doesn't blossom into something more. Next book, maybe. Kate is strong, badass and utterly forgettable. Think any typical dystopian/High Fantasy heroine and you have Kate Harker. I am, at my core, an emotional reader. I need to connect with characters and This Savage Song just didn't do it for me. I picked this book up at my local library (Thank god) because I heard so many people loved it and it had such a high rating on goodreads that I figured it must be good! I was wrong of course... To begin with this book is like every other YA paranormal romance out in the market. You have the "average" girl protag who isn't like other girls because she listen to cool indie music and doesn't dress like a "slut" or anything. Also she happens to have some interesting magical or paranormal power, and if she doesn't people are just attracted to her because she's so "different". Then you got the boy who's usually rich and attractive and falls in love with the girl protag because she isn't falling at his feet to worship him, even though she secretly is but doesn't show it. Then you got them falling in love somehow, and also a basic ass plot or no plot at all, and there you have it that's the book. The reason why I picked up this book, besides the high rating, was the interesting premise, but of course it was wasted by the terrible writing and dull characters. I felt like the book had many opportunities to explore and go deeper into the paranormal aspect of the story but Hodkin instead chose to explore the cliche romance. I felt that the paranormal aspect was overshadowed by the romance in a really dumb way. Like you have all this crazy paranormal shit going on around you but you're worried about a boy??? Like come on?? The romance was also terrible, unhealthy, and controlling. Almost like what I've read in "50 Shades of Grey." Noah is a controlling bastard at best, and for some reason Mara swoons over that??? Why I will never know I guess. I honestly don't know what else to say about the romance other than it is basically a combo between "Twilight" and "50 Shades" so there you go that's all you need to know. Mara's view on mental illness was very disgusting honestly. She referred to herself as "crazy" , "psycho", and "broken" a lot of the times, and as a mentally ill person myself I felt offended and that she wasn't really educated well on the topic of mental illness at all. Also she believed that Noah could somehow save her from her mental illness which is a really negative and terrible thing to think, and I'm honestly shocked this is somehow still a popular trope for YA literature. The writing wasn't good. I have no idea why people are calling it beautiful and lyrical. The writing was juvenile at best, and at times I felt that the author was trying way to hard to make things seem deep and meaningful. Also there was no plot? Like at all? Till maybe the end where they were setting up for the second book. Nothing was explained, nothing was resolved, and everything was terrible. I have nothing else to say about this other than I just didn't like it. It was a bad book with no real redeemable qualities. The only reason why i'm interested in the second book is because maybe things will be explained finally, and maybe a plot will exist. For now though I think i'll take a break from this series.

Shall I point to the cliche-fest, the predictableness, the flatness of characters, or the unremarkable writing style? Which one should I start with? You tell me. They're all there, and I'm going to talk about them anyway. Or better yet, how about I start by voicing this question that has been burning in my mind since I popped this book open: How the hell was this .. this thing published in 2017? Because, honestly, if you were to give this book to me blind and ask me to guess it pub year, I'd say, with absolute confidence, late 2014 to early 2015, maximum. Why? Because it's too similar to releases back then, such as Victoria Aveyard's RED QUEEN (Feb 2015, which I loathed with a burning passion) and Sara Raasch's SNOW LIKE ASHES (Oct 2014). FROSTBLOOD is not just similar; it's the same damned story cycling again and again and AGAIN. So FROSTBLOOD's luck must be terrible as hell (ahahaha look at 'frost' and 'hell' and tell me my juxtaposition isn't hilarious) to be born in the wrong year. *deep sigh* I'm more resigned than angry, honestly. For the sake of making sure we're all on the same page here, let me list the cliches for you. Something tells me you want to see them clear as day, so here you go. - A social system stratified into just 2 groups; in this case, it's frost vs. fire - A skinny brunette girl who is 'weak' and 'unremarkable', and snarky as the lead - "Don't practice your powers, Ruby!" "You ain't the boss of me!" = plot ball starts rolling - Disobeys parent and causes their death (Why are parents so allergic to High Fantasy??) - Mysterious dude who functions as love interest #1 - Oh, and that mysterious dude also has the pleasure of falling into the Pretty Boy With Tragic Past trope (look at the membership grow in that group! I'm impressed! [not] ) - MC cannot control her powers at all and is clumsy/uncoordinated/trained by the aforementioned Mysterious Pretty Boy - Love interest is quite sexist and believes in locking the girl up to save her [<-- can this trope die a tragic death, please? That is not (!!!) romantic. It's actually quite demeaning and condescending to girls. So stop it.] - OH. And there's an Ancient Prophecy saying MC shall save the world - So MC had now been elevated to Special Snowflake status - There's a makeover session in which the MC emerges gorgeous - And gains another love interest (which leads to random kissing that had no place whatsoever) - Also, there's a fight-to-the-death magicky tournament - .. need I go on? [I totally could, by the way. I haven't even hit half of the tropes in this shindig] I wholeheartedly believe that the points I have cited are sufficient in convincing you that I am very, nay, COMPLETELY AND 100% annoyed. The worldbuilding was interesting enough, I guess, with the four gods and their rivalry and whatnot, but the way this was explained was quite info-dumpy and had me blinking blankly at times. I mean, is there anything else that needs to be addressed? Even the writing style was bland and unimpressive. It's not bad by any measure - in fact, the descriptions of the palace and the throne were quite pretty and well-done - but it's just nothing new. And guys, when you read as much high fantasy as I do, you find yourself reading the same-old same-old every so often, but I've honestly never seen something as bad as this. Will I be reading the sequel? It depends on whether I'm caught up with all the things I actually WANT to read, honestly. Especially as I'm hearing quite negative things about the 2nd book (a love triangle? A love triangle!) and lately, I've just grown used to reading snappy duologies rather than the traditional trilogy with middle-book syndrome and all that fun stuff that makes me want to scream into the void. Do I recommend this? Yes, if this is your very 1st YA high fantasy book. If you've even read 1 and a half, then you'll find this incredibly cliche. Now, if you'll excuse me, I'm going to build a time machine and transport FROSTBLOOD back into 2015 where it belongs with the rest of its outdated family.

Ceony has just finished her schooling to become a magician and now it's time to start her apprenticeship and bond with a material. Unfortunately, there's a shortage of paper magicians at the moment, so that becomes her material. She would rather have done just about anything else. Her mentor, Emery Thane, isn't all that impressive at first, either, but as time goes on she discovers he has more depth than she expected. She learns some basic folds and spells. Then the world pretty much falls apart as an Excisioner (magician bonded to human flesh=DARK ARTS!) bursts in, steals Emery's heart out of his chest and runs away. Ceony fashions a rudimentary paper heart to take its place, but she knows it won't last for long. She calls in help from the school who soon arrive to watch over Mr. Thane. Meanwhile, Ceony can't just sit around and watch him die. She sneaks off to find the Excisioner with only a packet of paper, her basic knowledge, and a gigantic paper airplane/glider as transportation. There's a confrontation in a cave, and that, my friends, is about where the action stops. I thought this would be a spoiler, but as it mentions it in the Goodreads blurb, I guess I'm okay. She spends the rest of the time tromping through Emery's heart! Yes, literally inside/through it. There are memories and flashbacks to be had at every step, and meanwhile, the Excisioner is in there as well chasing her...in slow motion. [WHY? She has the girl trapped inside this heart--why on earth would she feel the need to go in after her? Makes no sense to me.] As a diversion for a chapter, maybe two, it could have added depth and interest to the story. However, it just kept dragging on and on, piling on the tedium. Nearly every question that had been brought up by the plot up to that point was answered quite neatly in one flashback or another. Then the Excisioner's shadow or face or something would show up across the room and so Ceony would hurry out of one flashback directly into the next...[yawn] repeat, repeat, repeat. There was the beginnings of a interesting world going. Too bad it got sucked into the Vortex of Eternal Flashbacks.

This novel... It was like the regurgitation of every other fairytale known to man. When I read the synopsis, I thought PRINCESS AND THE PEA! Yeah... Basically, this author thought that one fairytale wasn't enough, no. Instead, she just stuck a bunch together and made 'em pop up randomly throughout the book. Another thing I didn't love about the book was the insta-love. After spending like one hour with said frog prince, she falls in love with him, instantly assumes he's human in some way, and finds that he's like her new bestest friend ever. And it's just like ... no. There's also a lot of evil fairy, nice fairy, surprise fairy, and all that, and I'm here like C'MON! Think all of those fairytales above mixed with a large amount of YA fey mythological stuff all kind of rolled up and forced to fit together. The characters were interesting (they'd have been a lot more interesting if there wasn't a million of them... I mean, they're the seventh daughter of the seventh daughter, or whatever, but on top of that there's like three brothers, and a royal palace of people...). I liked one character, and everyone thought she was insane... The prince's name bugged me, but I could live with it... and I liked Trix, Velius, and Erik (i.e. the three main supporting characters) more than the main ones... Speaking of this main character, she left nothing to mystery. Instead, within, like, the first 20 pages, you know the name of every single one of her family members, what they do, what their specialty is, what she does, why her family hates the royal family, some stuff about fairies and how they work, the king, someone's father, and this frog who's her new best friend. TA-DA. Honestly, this book would be so much better if the author stuck to one fairytale and expanded and worked at it to make it something amazing. But she didn't... so well... In Partials, Dan Wells creates a realistic future in which humans have suffered through a couple more wars before being decimated by the RM virus. Now, the remainder of North America, at least to Kira's knowledge, has retreated to Long Island. Humanity is now divided in their argument for how to fight for the survival of humanity even as they guard themselves against the Partials, super soldiers they believe to be responsible for the release of the RM virus. It is eerie how Dan Wells is able to create such a realistic future in light of the events that have passed in his world. The Senate is made up of older people who survived the attack of both the Partials and the RM virus unleashed upon humanity, and they are unwilling to take risks with the remnants of the human population. Instead, they decide to use statistics and pass the Hope Act, forcing women eighteen and older to have a baby every year in the hopes that one will be immune to RM. Kira and her younger friends believe that something else can be done, and her friends take little convincing to go along with her outrageous plans that follow. The medical focus of the novel interested me the most. Kira first trained to be a medical intern in the maternity ward, because she thought that the dying newborn babies were the ones she needed to observe to find a way to save humanity, before deciding to research Partials. Kira's conflicting scientific and emotional views give her a unique voice. While there is a lot of scientist in her, Kira will let her emotions get in the way when there are lives in danger, and she will jeopardize more lives along with the mission to save a single person. The events in the novel take time to unfold, and more questions are raised than are answered. Partials is the start of what promises to be a thrilling series about a girl's journey to find herself and the reason behind humanity's destruction. Original post at Imaginary Reads

I have huge issues with stories that try to normalize or justify or romanticize relationships between high school teachers and their students. But that doesn't mean I think it's not possible to write a thoughtful -- and hopefully disturbing -- book about the subject. The best I've read so far is Boy Toy by Barry Lyga. While I think that Unteachable did romanticize Maise and Evan's relationship, I did appreciate the fact that it also seemed to suggest that their relationship was a form of sex addiction, just as other of the book's characters suffer from drug addiction. I thought it was pretty gutsy to make Evan a repeat offender who changed his name to try to flee his first messy mistake... and then went and did the same thing all over again. I think that's probably realistic; I just wish that icky revelation had made Maise open her eyes about the fact that, hot or not, Evan's a creeper who can't seem to find a sex partner who isn't one of his students. For that reason, I didn't love the ending -- what happened to the Casablanca ending that the book was hinting at? How can tough, fierce Maise justify fleeing from her crappy life while dragging messed-up Evan around with her like a ball and chain? This can't end well -- with their seventeen year age difference and general effed-up-ness, I don't see the two of them making it through her freshman year of college. This book was definitely gripping, but in the end, I couldn't see it as romantic and hope I wasn't meant to. However, I absolutely loved this author's writing style and will definitely, absolutely, without question try her future books.

Originally posted at The Book Nympho The setup Figure skater Matty Marcus is struggling to not only recover from a back injury but also his failure to medal at the last Olympic Games. A benefactor reaches out and offers him an opportunity to earn some serious money while continuing to heal and get back into competitive shape. He moves to Montana to house sit a home that has the handsome rancher, Rob Lovely, as a neighbor. The issues With Rob, the flamboyant Matty finds strength, courage and confidence to do what's necessary to prepare for the upcoming Olympics. He also learns how to be submissive in the bedroom, being able to relinquish control without losing himself. Even though their feelings are deepening towards each other, Matty's eventual departure looms over them as they struggle to come to terms with the probable end date for their relationship. And, Rob has a 12-year old son who shows promise as a skater with Matty's help, complicating an already tough dilemma. Winning an Olympic medal and doing everything he can to reach that goal is Matty's primary goal. What worked for me Matty forced me out of my comfort zone with respect to m/m romances. He's effeminate, dresses outrageously and wears makeup, leaving no question as to his sexual orientation. I was unsure if I could connect with him and here was the power of the story. Matty had to not only excel in his skating but also overcome the judges (and others) stereotypical thinking about his style. I loved that he never felt compelled to change any aspect of his identity, with full awareness of what it might cost him and the reactions of those around him. Rob's embrace of all that was Matty and his patience with him made him so appealing. Their romance was at times sweet and always sensual. I loved their relationship, even when Matty made it difficult. He got under my skin and I ended up adoring him. What was a challenge for me Be forewarned that the sex is graphic, which doesn't really bother me normally but there were some dom/sub scenes that pushed me beyond my limits. I actually found myself skimming over some of the encounters as I found them confusing to the story. The bottom line I loved the story, the romance and the sometimes bratty Matty. It's my understanding that the author was channeling the Olympic skater Johnny Weir and this book helped me develop a new level of respect and appreciation for him. My perceptions were completely altered and that's pretty powerful. I'm thrilled that the author created Matty and wrapped this wonderful story around him. (I received an ARC from the author)

It is a truth universally acknowledged that there is no point to writing a review of this book, because even if you haven't read it, you probably already know what it's about. It is also a truth universally acknowledged that "truth universally acknowledged" Austen jokes are pretty played out, but I proceed in defiance of both of those pieces of wisdom to tell you that Pride and Prejudice is, you know, really good. The suspense of any romance is not "will the couple get together?" but "how will the couple get together? ", and Austen elegantly and wittily draws tension out of that with Elizabeth Bennet and Mr. Darcy. There is, throughout, a very real feeling that personal flaws can get the better of even good, well-meaning people, and ruin their happiness, especially when the rules governing their interactions are so strict, and allow so little directness. Austen knew that Regency-era courtship was an intricate game played for very high stakes, and here you get both the sense of fun and the sense of tremendous investment. And aside from all that, it's a funny, sharply-observed novel, with a great way of putting things. Here, for example, is the narrative's treatment of Elizabeth leaving her parents and home for a few weeks' visit: The only pain was in leaving her father, who would certainly miss her, and who, when it came to the point, so little liked her going, that he told her to write to him, and almost promised to answer her letter. It's social comedy as much, or more, as it's romance, and if you like clever banter and the occasional bit of cringe comedy from someone making a fool out of themselves at great length, you would like it. There is also something moving, and useful, about the way the novel presents two people discovering their failings and trying as best they can to work to change them. (And, given that their example is surrounded by examples of people never realizing their faults, realizing their faults and doing nothing about it, or realizing their faults and trying to change and failing, it's a very realistic optimism.) The satisfaction of the ending, where everything comes together neatly and amusingly, is perfect.
