One of the worst books I've ever had the displeasure to read. I only really picked it up because I adore Jake Abel, and he has a part as Mark in I Am Number Four's film adaptation, but it wasn't worth it for several reasons. This book is a cliche piece of drivel. It has almost every overdone young adult trope EVER in its tree-killing pages: 1. a mysterious new student with incredible powers, 2. a gorgeous, sweet, popular girl, 3. love at first sight, 4. the popular girl's jealous ex-boyfriend and other muscle-head jocks, 5. a cute, quirky best friend/side-kick, 6. a mentor figure, 7. an action girl, 8. an evil force hell-bent on destroying the world, etc, etc, etc. And the thing is, you can subvert cliches; you can turn them on their heads, poke fun at them, and/or reinvent them into something interesting. For example, look at Kendare Blake's Anna series. It has a ghost hunting boy starting at a new school, where the popular girl and quirky kid are both immediately drawn to him, the jocks hate him, a powerful creature's after him, and so on. But the sardonic self-awareness of the text, and the characterization, makes it all better. Cas tells Thomas he's not looking for a tag-along, because he knows tag-alongs, like Four's BFF, somehow stumble into the protagonist's affairs. He knows Mysterious New Drifters catch the eyes of Queen Bees, but he uses that to find out more about doing his freaking job, and you know what? Carmel wants to know more about him because she's the Queen Bee, she's actually really smart, and she keeps tabs on what's happening in her school. She and Cas become really good friends, instead of a couple! She surprises him with her ability to be badass, her brilliance, and her determination. That's NOT what we get in IAN4. Which feeds into my next point: the characters. Anna Dressed in Blood and its sequel, Girl of Nightmares, aren't perfect. I had my issues with both. However, the primary characters were wonderful. Cassio's POV is snarky fun. Thomas is adorable, and not just relegated to sidekick status; often, he's the voice of reason, and there are points where he acts on his own, for his own reasons. He has plot-threads that are only for him, not Cas. The female characters, though, are even more wonderful! Here's something I wrote in my review of the first book (which is spoiler-y): "Anna Dressed in Blood has many badass, amazing female characters, who have agency in their actions, rather than being mere, passive receptacles for male characters. Anna, like Cas describes, is a fierce goddess. She is the one who stops the ultimate antagonist in the end, not Cas, and is aided by Carmel's titanium bat, while a cursed Cas looks on." In the second book, we get the enigmatic Justine, who gives Cas a run for his money when it comes to being a competent hunter. She's beautiful and clever and young, and you know what? This doesn't intrinsically mean she needs to be thrust into the position of romantic interest in order to be valuable. She cares more about being successful at her job than that, though she and Cas do have some chemistry. All the characters of Anna are great! In comparison, IAN4's characters are card-board cutouts of the same tropes. Four and Sarah are perfect and beautiful and meant for each other, really, BECAUSE THEY HAVE NO PERSONALITIES WHATSOEVER. Why should anyone else have to suffer them? Four is one of the most boring protagonists I've ever had to read. He and Sarah have no interesting flaws, like Carmel's inability to easily give up her status at school, and Justine's desire for power, or even Cassio's habit of making the people who care about him unhappy because of his obsession with saving Anna. None of this is accepted by the narrative as good, but it's there as an opportunity for good growth. IAN4 TRIES to give Sarah some depth by saying she used to have an alcohol problem and was mean to the people in her school because of it, before Four came along. You know how? With a dull info-dump. And Mark doesn't have much depth to him, though my baby Jake did manage to make a few expressive faces when his character wasn't being a shallow dick. He eventually helps Four, but he's still mostly a two-dimensional, overly jealous jock. You know where you belong, Mark (and maybe everyone else)? In a 70's flick about mean, poopie-head jocks keeping the odd, but ~oh so speshul guy away from the girl of his dreams. NEENER, NEENER, NEENER. THE PLOT. It's a cliche plot, but it could have been SO COOL, if pulled off properly. Motherhugging ALIENS want to destroy other planets and screw shit up! Four is one of earth's only defenses! Instead, most of the story was stupid, romantic, teenage angst about characters I really had no reason to GAF about. Four and Sarah are drawn to each other for no real reason, except that Four thinks she's the most beautiful girl ever, and I assume she finds him hotter than Mark - which, Imo, what? Jake's face > Pettyfer's, any day. BUT that's beside the point. There was no buildup in their relationship whatsoever. Almost as soon as he meets her, Four thinks Sarah is his soul-mate, because on Four's planet, people imprint or something. YES, like in Twilight, because Frey wants to write JUST LIKE TWILIGHT FOR THEY MUNNIES! This is why, I guess, the world-building and explications for why the aliens do what they do is so vague. He just has a shell of a concept that he's trying to sell. And this ties into my final point: THE AUTHOR SUCKS. Not only is his writing boring, simple to the point of eye-rolling, filled with no descriptions whatsoever, and the antithesis of show-don't-tell; he's honestly an asshole. He's James Frey, of A Million Little Pieces's infamy. Basically, he wrote a "memoir," and lots of people found it moving, but it came out that he lied through his teeth in it. He's really in writing only for the money. Wanting lots of people to enjoy your work the way they do, say, Harry Potter is one thing. It's nice to dream about. But wanting to write ONLY to be famous and make money? He apparently has a writing factory where he takes naive young writers, makes them sign a contract that hands much of their rights over to him, and sticks his name on their work. He even writes under the pen-name Pittacus Lore, who happens to be the greatest alien leader on Four's home planet. How arrogant can one guy be? He had IAN4 created to be the next big thing in the YA franchise - to get movies and products and all that other crap. Not because of a love of writing. TOO BAD IT SUCKS, FREY. AND THE MOVIE DOES, TOO (aside from Jake Abel's face, of course). ;P

"The right steps with the right dancer can wreck havoc." Vanessa's sister disappeared from the New York Dance Academy, but she's not the first one. 11 girls have gone before her, and all in the same way. They were told to master an odd dance- La Dance du Feu- before they went missing. Something is wrong, terribly wrong within the 4 ashen walls of the dance theatre and Vanessa must find out, or the world will spin away into the hands of a sinister force as she dances. Mark my words, the disappearing girls will keep you spooked out... and still guessing. Yelena Black is really good with her world-building, from the studios, to the ballet, to the ancient folklore and dark magic, I held my breath the whole time because I was so afraid that shadowy hands will grab me from the book! The element of fear and suspense transcends every page, not to mention how the intoxicating ballet atmosphere feels like the best cake treat for a kid, if only I can try those steps and pirouette my way cross country! However, as I dug deeper into Dance of Shadows, I realized there was nothing amazing or particularly outstanding. It didn't convince me how so many missing girls from the same institution could go unnoticed by the public, and it was sad to see how the high school drama watered down the gripping mystery I was ready for. I read this book very very carefully, not skipping a single punctuation because I couldn't bear to miss any details that points to a possibly mind-blowing revelation. And... There was none. Throughout the whole story, the characters continually disturbed me. I like how Vanessa is a girl with a mind of her own, but her stubbornness and lack of judgement is infuriating. It's those moments when you know exactly what's wrong with what the character is doing but she won't do anything about it. The clues are screaming into her ears, the abnormal behaviours can be explained if she stops to reason, yet she pushes away the person trying to help her and confide all her secrets to the big bad guy. Don't even get me started on the love triangle. Both boys were equally douche and I had no idea, absolutely NO IDEA how that mushy little relationship could be love!! *RAGES* If not for the final paranormal twist and beautiful ballet, this wouldn't even be a 2-star book. "Kissing you is.. I tried so hard for so long to deny myself. I tried to do the right thing. But ever since we kissed on your birthday I knew once I started I'd never be able.. even through we can't.." - Lincoln ***Mild spoilers*** THE GOOD: The story: To be honest I was a little wary about starting this one. I have only read 2 other Angel stories in the past, Halo & Fallen and hadn't really enjoyed them, I was starting to think maybe angel books are not my think. But Embrace is simply amazing, the concept of Grigori's & their partners was good & Shirvington has obviously done her research into the mythology. This is not just a romance with a few mythical/paranormal creatures thrown in for fun - there is a really strong mythical storyline pushing the book forward, with an even balance of romance. It's an adventure as we follow Vi discovering her identity & having to make the choice of wether or not she will 'embrace' her Grigori powers. The romance: Wow, this books is just dripping with sexual tension, seriously *fans self*. The tension between Violet & Lincon was so intense, they just had to be in the same scene for you to feel it. What's best about their relationship is that it began as a really strong friendship, which makes their love so much more real (no insta-love, yay!!) "Did you ever think we would be anything other than unbelievable?" - Lincoln There is also somewhat of a love triangle, however I personally believe there is only one obvious choice (team Lincoln here!) I usually loath love triangles, but this one actually works and just adds to the sexual tension building between Vi & Linc. The characters: I found Violet to be such a relatable character. She responded to situations in realistic ways - like when confronted with the idea of being a Grigori she didn't just suddenly become a kick-ass ninja warrior, she was scared & unsure what to do. Lincon is the perfect hero, caring, protective (but not in a stalkerish way) & of course hot!! But best of all he actually knows Violet - not just the obvious or superficial things, but all the little quirks that make a person who they are. Phoenix is the 'bad boy' sort of guy, but it's not as simple as him just being the evil guy. He has so many layers & I really believed that there is some good in him (and I still do). He can be really sweet to Violet, but then can turn around & do something so evil. It's almost like he believes that because of who he is, he is meant to do bad things, and therefore does. Like he has no choice & isn't allowed to be good even if he wants to be. The Writing: This is a beautifully creative & incredibly well written novel! Jessica Shirvington's writing style is clean & sophisticated. The story is well structured and flows so naturally. There has also been a lot of research put into the mythology of angels, which was great to see. I also felt Shirvington handled the religious side to the story very well - at no point did the story become either preachy nor disrespectful. Weather your religious or not this book shouldn't offend anyone. With so many books being published in the YA paranormal romance genre, I feel that books are being rushed out too quickly that they lack the proper research & editing. It's so refreshing to see such polished writing - great work Jessica! THE BAD: I really can't think of anything I didn't like about this one...nope...nothing! FINAL WORD: This is a superbly written paranormal romance and Jessica Shirvington's beautiful writing makes this one a must read! I cannot wait to read the sequel! After reading Pawn and Carter's past novels--as she always writes in a manner where you feel the strong need and ability to go on and purchase her other books, I found that I was unable to wait any longer for this sequel. It turns out, there wasn't a lot to wait for except for more instalove and having to choose between two men who both suck. Captive is a very romance-based story where the love is most of the problem. I mean, we all have Knox and Benjy on our minds, trying to figure out who's the best for Kitty.You know, they both know about her secret... and Benjy is working for the palace to see Kitty... Doesn't this ring a bell of The Selection? Like, I understand that it isn't a completion to fight for love or whatever, but this is most definitely something that's unknown between the two men who are fighting for the same girl. Just saying, people... "Everyone in this place is an enemy." I turned away and began to pile my plate with bite-size desserts. "I'm not." First thing's first--this really should've been a standalone, to be honest. Why are trilogies suddenly the new thing? This was barely a dystopia, and now we've gotten a full-blast series that continues and not much happens? You may think that I'm crazy for giving this a three-star rating if all I'm doing is raging for now, but it's the truth in some ways. This takes place right off where the first book left us off, in a miniature plot twist/cliff hanger. Kitty's just discovered that her role as being the PM's niece is there for a reason and she begins to have trust issues. Obviously, who wouldn't? You're sitting there, basically in a prison where you don't understand why you were placed in that position in the first place. Isn't there a reason for everything? I still have a ton of questions on what will happen in the end, as I was often left confused and wondering while reading. It was as if Carter was focusing on the steps leading off to Kitty's romantic adventure with Benjy in the end where she can just let loose and forget that there was so much trouble behind her--for things she didn't even do. The way this book left me in the end was weird. I felt like something was missing, and that this book took my dignity and expectations for any future stories of Carter's away. I'll probably read the third book, just to see what'll happen, though. "I invite you into my home, feed you my food, let you sleep in a warm bed, and this is how you repay me?" He flipped a switch, and yellow light filled the room, revealing walls lined with rack after rack of gleaming metal objects. Some I could name--knives, saws, screwdrivers--but others looked like they were relics from some ancient time." I do have to say that there was a major character-development phase over here. Kitty has become stronger and wiser, as she now knows her rebellion and what and who's against her in her world. She's so fucking kick-ass and is definitely is Carter's best heroine to date. I'm just sitting here, wondering who'll she pick in the end, especially since both guys don't really seem to catch my eye. I'd probably go for Knox, though. There's more love with him! *gushes* Boom--that was the plot for you. What we got here was a pretty good showcase of the plot, with a few boring moments in the middle where my mouth was aching of my yawning, to tell the truth. I was wondering what the ending would give to us (and the truth was that it was really eye-popping) and I guess you could say that I do have a few theories in mind of what'll happen in the end, or the future for that time being. With a great heroine and a strong plot and ending, I'd say we've got an okay novel over here. It's most definitely not the best book of the year so far, but I'm going to say that I'm captivated to read the third and final novel to see the fate of the characters--because hey, everyone deserves a happy ending.

Pretty Fierce is a thrilling story, with plenty of action and drama. It took me a few chapters to situate myself within the story, but the action soon grabbed my attention. But while this book has plenty of dangerous situations, high speed chases and guns to the forehead, it retains a sweetness and playfulness. The title is therefore apt, it is both Fierce and Pretty. Eighteen months ago, while on a mission with her parents, Kaia and her mother were attacked. Her family was destroyed, her parents were both missing presumed dead, and Kaia put into action the plan that was only to be used if everything went terribly wrong. For the past 18 months, Kaia has been living with her 'grandparents', colleagues of her assassin parents. She has the most wonderful boyfriend, Oliver, and she is no longer endlessly plagued by nightmares. But all those fears resurface when she is brutally attacked and Oliver sees her take out her assailant. Now her secrets have been revealed and she isn't sure Oliver will want to stick by the crazy girl who was raised by assassins. Kieran Scott says this story was inspired by a dream starring Chris Hemsworth - I knew there was a reason I enjoyed this story. It's fun, playful and still has all those elements of a high-speed, action blockbuster. When the story starts it has been 18 months since Kaia's parents were killed and Kaia started a new life. She already has a strong relationship with Oliver, so Pretty Fierce is not about the start of a romance but instead the journey of a romance as Kaia and Oliver face death and an unknown future. Kaia, as the daughter of two assassins, is of course strong, resilient, and proficient with weapons and self defence. But she is also not unbelievably talented. She is still recognisable as a teenage girl. She misses her parents, fears for her life, and makes mistakes, but she can also shoot a gun and handle a knife. Oliver, too, knows how to protect himself. At first he doubts his ability to keep up with Kaia. He is so surprised, and hurt, to discover the secrets she has been keeping from him, but as they face increasing danger, Oliver knows that he can protect Kaia just as she can protect him. I liked that Oliver was a strong character. I like that Kaia is strong enough on her own without needing a weak character to make her look strong. Oliver also has his own story, just as Kaia has hers. I liked that his backstory gives him depth, motives, and desires for the future. He is more than just Kaia's sidekick and their relationship is solid, despite the challenges they face and the changes they need to make. As Kaia discovers more about her family and their secrets, she also learns about the secrets Oliver has been hiding from her. Together they face assassins, sometimes in the strangest of forms. At times the story was a little unrealistic, but its balance between playfulness and threat makes this an interesting and fun book to read. The publishers provided an advanced readers copy of this book for reviewing purposes. All opinions are my own. Find more reviews on my blog Madison's Library.

While polite society shuns him and his antics, they can't help but keep him around because he's a whiz when it comes to investing. Everyone loves money and Roderick ensures money continues to flow. He's charming, good-looking, a touch dangerous and a lot passionate. He tries to do right by Emma until he realizes right by anyone else's standards doesn't mean right for him or for her. Emma doesn't expect to end up working for Roderick or for the flare between them to ignite into a raging inferno. She is doing what needs to be done to pay off her father's debts and ensure her sisters can find suitable marriages. When things take a turn for the worst, Emma makes a decision that leads her to not only fall into Roderick's bed, but also to really finding what she's been missing her entire life. The story is interesting, mildly fast-paced and definitely sinful. I was entertained, engaged and delightfully intrigued. This book presents fascinating theories and research about a number of topic ranging from the oft-repeated "Intuitions come first; strategic reasoning second" to how the Democratic Party fails to appeal to the full range of moral tastebuds. Haidt is very persuasive and makes a number of points that seemed intuitively correct (thank you elephant). His intentional shortcoming is choosing to omit opposing evidence for some of his claims (because confirmation bias would cause the reader to selectively choose the information that we already agree with). Unfortunately, to someone brand new to moral psychology, I just kept wondering what else could be out there. I didn't know the other side, so even though I found Haidt persuasive, I retained a healthy dose of skepticism knowing that I was only getting one side of the story. Still, this is a fascinating, well-thought out book.

So where to start. This was a great book! I started reading thinking it was about something else (I had seen it as a recommendation and I don't usually read blurbs) but soon discovered it wasn't historic fiction but fantasy - which was fine because I love both! This series has three main protagonists though there was a chapter also from another character. The characters know each other but don't join forces until the end, I'm not sure if this is common in fantasy novels but I found it refreshing. The characters know each other from a Kiriath-Human alliance against the scaled folk. Now, the plot is about gods or other superhuman beings wanting to take over their territories. This is a dark fantasy, it describes things in great gruesome details. I didn't have much experience reading this genre and I winced but I liked it! I can see so many parallels to real life in it! As for the characters: Ringil, Archeth and Egar (of which I can only say the last name, the others I am still confused about) are veteran war heroes. Ringil was a leader, Archeth who's half-Kiriath (the black folk) a good engineer and Egar a Steppe-Nomad dragonslayer (but so was Ringil). It took me a while to get used to their world because they kept referring to previous events, of which there isn't a book about. After the first 100 pages it was ok. I loved Ringil's sense of dry humour and the fact he was openly gay - people hated him for it but also kind of feared him. He's asked by his mother to find his cousin who was sold into slavery. The end wasn't so much of a shock, there were hints but I liked that he took it as a challenge. He's the referred dark lord that will rise. His love life although active - good for you Ringil! - is kind of sad. He killed TWO of his lovers and had flashbacks to another. Archeth, who's also queer! (I knew there was one but not two!) is a practical person but she tries to protect people from disasters. She's practically the right-hand person of the Yhelteth Throne Ethernal. She uses diplomacy but is frank. She's also one of the only persons with morals although she, like the others, has dark internal fights apart from external. It's one of the reason this is so gruesome. Egar, I didn't much like at first. He's actually not a good leader although he cares. He's too selfish and sex-minded. He does have a caring aspect but I just didn't like him, especially at first. Once he leaves the Steppe, he becomes a nicer character to like. Although he like many calls Ringil a 'faggot', it's done in a chamaredie way. He sides with Ringil at every turn and I liked their friendship and the soft way he ended presenting himself (asking about his crush). There were aspects that I didn't like. There was too much sexism, too much homophobia, too much death and pain and too much evil things condoned by law. But I also understand that it's a dark fantasy and that these aspects where all leading us to understand why the characters where changing before our eyes. Still, simply because it's fantasy, doesn't mean there should be so many hating and stereotyping comments:/ There were things I liked! The characters that understand the world they live in but not wanting to be part of it and wanting to change things, the realistic (although not wholly human) sex and that bad-ass Ringil bottomed but also topped once. The fact that Archeth held her impulses. That it didn't end with a massive cliffhanger- a chapter was closed- but that we are led to be anxious to see how things turn out. In conclusion, great read but be ready for some really dark content. It includes reference to rape (even one that happened to a main character), slavery, torture, war, hatred in all kind of ways, unsupportive family and so on. Already bought the other one to see what happens.

There has been a long history of explorers searching for lost cities, and here Preston brings that same sort of exploration (although technologically updated) to his readers. This "lost city" is located in the Mosquitia region of Honduras, in a god-forsaken place to which access is pretty much impossible. After going through a brief history of attempts to discover this lost city, Preston's account reveals how he joined an expedition to the area after a documentary filmmaker named Steve Elkins had decided to make a search of the area using lidar technology. The cost to do the whole area was prohibitive, so Elkins settled on a search area of about fifty square miles. Not only did Elkins and his team discover one large site, they discovered a second one as well. Most of the book details the ground expedition -- pitfalls, surprises and discoveries, etc., -- as well as its aftermath. I have to say that I was glued to this book as far as this expedition goes because of my fascination with this sort of thing, and I do believe he does a fine job relating events for armchair travelers like myself and doing it in a way that transmits the excitement, the frustrations, the hard work, the perils etc. involved. I also enjoyed reading about the history of other attempts at finding the Lost City that he provides which puts the search for this particular site in a larger context. But having said that, I do have a couple of big niggles. Aside from a couple of issues re sources, my major complaint is that quite a bit of space was used by the author in this book to discuss a horrific illness that some of the expedition members picked up, brought on by bites from parasitic sand fleas at the team's camp. I didn't mind that so much, since it was interesting, but he uses this potentially-deadly illness to bring up dangerous effects of global warming. Now before anyone gets huffy, does the eyeroll, and starts calling me a denier, that's not the case at all. In fact, I totally share Preston's views about climate change and global warming. It's just that it came across as out of place in this book, and left me thinking that perhaps this is not the correct venue for that particular discussion. Another thing: the history of diseases brought to this area that he offers in making his point as to what may have caused the disappearance of the indigenous population of the "Lost City" is certainly compelling, but Preston is a journalist/author, not a scientist, and once again, his own speculations seemed misdirected and out of place here, especially without evidence from the site itself to back them up. I will say that while sticking to the past history of explorations, and to the challenges of the expedition of which he was a member, the author managed to keep me turning pages, so in that sense and during those times, it was a good read. Keeping in mind my caveats here, I'd recommend it (although to be very honest, I'm not bubbling over with great enthusiasm here) to other readers who enjoy this sort of thing. http://www.nonfictionrealstuff.com/20...

*I was approached by the author, who gave me the opportunity to read and review this work* Taboo subjects don't bother me. I actually respect authors who are brave enough to write about controversial subjects, as many people are turned off by these types of things. I am someone who isn't bothered by illicit subject matter as long as it isn't ridiculously vulgar. This book is indeed about incest. Make no mistake, this book was written for adults. There are many mature themes and scenes depicting sexual acts between brother and sister. Lillian and Elm had an interesting family dynamic. Obviously, they're sexually attracted to each other, but other than that, their sibling relationship is quite normal. They bicker and pick at each other like any brother and sister pairing would do. Lillian was spunky and sassy, while Elm seemed a little more soft spoken. The members of the band that they are each contribute a little to the story, but The Sinister Urge is very much the story of Lillian and Elm. Though I quite enjoyed the story itself, I felt like the delivery was a bit lacking. There were a few grammatical errors, and I came across quite a few points in the story when the writing just seemed a little broken and disjointed. I wasn't really thrown by the flashbacks, but that was probably because they were in first person, when the rest of the book was not. I personally would have preferred the book to be entirely in first person, as it would have given a bit more insight on what the characters were thinking. Considering the end was a bit of a cliffhanger, I'm assuming there will be a sequel coming out sometime. I will be reading it. Overall, this first installment was a solid 3.5/5 stars.

4.5 stars, rounded up to 5 Mary Robinette Kowal really impressed me with Shades of Milk and Honey - a very Pride & Prejudice-esque novel with a magical twist. Needless to say, I was very excited to continue the series with Glamour in Glass. While it was quite different, I'm happy to say I wasn't disappointed! Whereas Shades of Milk and Honey had a plot focused around societal pressures, family issues, and finding a husband, Glamour in Glass has themes of gender equality and political intrigue. While I wasn't expecting such a dramatic shift, I have to say I really enjoyed it! It actually reminded me a bit of Sharon Cameron's The Dark Unwinding (which I really enjoyed). Now that Jane and Vincent are married, the two are under a bit of pressure to have a child. I'm sure other newly weds can relate to this! I've started telling people I'm not having children until I'm 50 so that they stop. asking. me. Sheesh! Jane's sentiments toward children strike me as very modern, and therefore much more relatable than I would have expected. A pregnancy would mean she can't practice glamour. She loves glamour so much that the idea of being cut off from it (and her work with Vincent) terrifies her. As much as I enjoyed this element of the story though, Jane's inner dialogue did get a bit frustrating at times as she is still fairly insecure of Vincent's feelings...even though they're married. There is a ton of political intrigue in this story since it takes place in Belgium just after Napoleon has abdicated his thrown. The setting actually helps Jane grow a lot as a character as she finds she prefers the way women are treated in Belgium a bit more than she does in Britain (after the culture shock wears off of course). There is a great deal of talk among the characters of whether or not Napoleon might return to power, and quite a few shocking events that stem from the Bonapartist movement in Belgium. Glamour in Glass is a stunning sequel to Shades of Milk and Honey. It takes the characters from the first book and really expands upon them and lets them grow in new situations. While the characters have a special place in my heart, the plot was absolutely fantastic and well beyond what I was expecting. Mary Robinette Kowal has clearly grown a lot as an author after her first book and I am so excited to see how her writing, as well as Jane and Vincent, grow as the story continues. I want to root for someone. I didn't feel that here. It was not fun. JH says he is not a fan of Dudley Do-Right heroes. I'm sure many readers will appreciate that. In SK's "It," Bill rides like the wind on his bike yelling Hi Ho Silver - Away (or something like that). When Vic rides her bike, bats hurt her, something slips, the bike loses a part, she is injured, she hurts. OTHER THINGS: I was frustrated when the heroine tries to convince herself that she is insane. She doesn't believe the truth when Maggie tells her something. Warning: This is unpopular opinion review post. It is okay for you to love this book as it is okay for me to hate it. If you feel like this review might offend you, you don't have to read it. This book is about Molly a self-proclaimed "fat girl", her 27 unrequited crushes, a stupid "love-triangle" and Molly's fixation about being the only person on the planet left without a boyfriend. This was suppose to be a cute, fluffy, contemporary, feel good romances and I never felt cute or fluffy reading this. The amount of body issues in this book, was overwhelming. The sister hate in this book, was overwhelming. The need to validate who you are through relationships, was overwhelming. Maybe in Cassie's world, you can do that and have it end in making out. But I'n not sure it works that way for fat girls. I don't know I just like to be careful about this stuff. Really, I could just let the quotes speak for themselves here. Because if Mina thinks Olivia's body is noticeably curvy, I'd like to know what she thinks about mine. No. Actually, I would not like to know. She is letting her weight rule her, her need for a relationship rule her. To the point where she needs it to validate who she is as a person and feel better about herself, more confident. She had twenty six? Twenty seven? Unrequited crushes? But Molly is 17 now, it's summer, she has a job and somehow ends up with possibility of two different boys suddenly being an option. One is a skinny hipster named Will (aren't hipsters in their 20's, 30's?) the other is a "husky" geeky co-worker named Reid. These people, where the most generic characters ever. Cause apparently, when you see geek, Reid had to be a total package. It's like she looked up what geeks liked and combined it all together, Tolkien, Game of Thrones, World of Warcraft, Ran-Fair. I was like, cue some serious eye roll. Guess who Molly ends up with? Can we just mention a quick fact that Reid is just there? And has like no freaking character development whatsoever? Especially when he plays such a major role in this book. The book felt stale, forced, boring, and it went nowhere. The entire time it was Molly whines about her weight and being the only person who doesn't have a boyfriend. Am I repetition that? Well, that's okay because the book itself, was super repetitive. If it is a glance about me, I will die. We are amused by the sad chubby girl who is clearly enchanted by our hipster beauty. And like there was so much diversity in this book (again, felt generic. It's like, oh what will make people praise this book.) I did not understand how can everyone be so accepting about the sex in this book, but not the person's weight? Like her grandma was so rude and downright mean about it and then she goes to a party, where apparently another kid mentions her weight. This book put me in the dark place. It made me feel shitty about my own body. Like when Mina says that Reid is not the kind of person you have sex with, but a type of person you marry. Like ... what... the ef? Did I connect with the book? Somewhat, I guess. Not in a good way. It brought back really shitty memories. I don't think I'm fat. I might be a little overweight. But what is considered fat these days? Because by media standard anyone above size 1. And then this happens Here's what I would never, ever admit out loud: a part of me always thought it was some kind of a secret compliment when someone got called a slut. It meant you were having sex. Which meant people wanted to have sex with you. Being a slut just meant you were normal. Really, like what did I just read? Are you kidding me? These kids didn't read like 17 year old's. I felt like they were 15 based on their behavior alone so when Molly's age got mentioned I was a little baffled. Dude, you are not mature enough to have sex. Get your stuff straight first. Why was having a relationship ruling her life so much? Like it felt like Molly had no personality in this book. I get she is crafty and likes pinterest. But what are her aspirations? Like, why is having a boyfriend in high school so damn important? Like it's a small blip in your life and most relationships don't last past that when you go your separate ways to colleges and discover yourself as an adult. Why did this book focus on her body issues? I was surprised that the author works with teenagers and has a degree in psychology. Because if she was writing a book to make it feel like they can relate in a good way, she should have stuck with maybe avoiding body issues and body shaming in her book? It felt overwhelming and did she even realize that it can trigger some bad memories for these teens? I myself spoke to teenagers about body issues in books and although some would love the MC to be curvy, they don't like being constantly reminded how others treat them because of it, and the dark thoughts they might have because of that.They would much rather the focus was on the personality of the individual and let that rule who they are. I found I can relate to that way of thinking. I don't like being reminded of this kind of crap in books. I read them to escape that's why it's called FICTION. Even in the end, the nastiness was unnecessary. But like, things smoothed out just because Molly finally had a boyfriend. Oh, and get this. Molly feels better about herself when she get's a boyfriend. All the sudden, she sees herself as a beautiful girl. So... You need a boyfriend to feel better about your body? Really? UGH This review Is choppy and it sucks, but I just... I did not understand the love this book received. I guess I felt like, if the author's first book is a hit that she can do no wrong. So this is gonna be a tough one to review. I want to cover what I thought of Gemina as much as I can without going into any real spoilers for those who haven't read it yet. I'll be expanding on those points in the spoiler tags, and I'm just going to warn you all now that IF YOU HAVE NOT READ ILLUMINAE AND GEMINA YET, PEAKING BEHIND THE CURTAIN WILL BE SPOILERTASTIC!!! DO NOT CLICK THE SPOILER TAGS WITHOUT READING BOTH BOOKS FIRST!!! You have been warned. To start off, it was great to be back in this world. I loved getting to see some different aspects of society that we didn't see in Illuminae. The idea of using the toxins secreted from a dangerous parasitic alien creature as an in-demand narcotic is my favourite new thing in this book. As is our constant Analyst ID 7213-0089-DN getting too grossed out by them and Kady having to get AIDAN to become a second analyst for Illuminae Group so he can describe the scenes involving the Lanima. I had heard of the real-life lamprey eels (which inspired the Lanima) once before on a top 10 list of the most horrifying animals on earth, but I'd forgotten what they looked like until I set the book down and Googled them. Thanks for the nightmares, Amie Kaufman and Jay Kristoff. After hearing about the Heimdall so much in Illuminae, it was cool to find out more about a jump-station in this world and how it works. The majority of reviews praised the last part of the novel as the best part that really bumps the rating back up and helps Gemina earn many of those five-star reviews. They aren't wrong. Kaufman and Kristoff really do try to go all out to tell the best story with this premise, and the climax is enormously creative. Hats off all around. Marie Lu illustrated Hanna's journal, and those illustrations are a lot of fun and a great new way to tell parts of the story. I intend to finally get to some of her books next year. And, speaking of fellow YA authors, it's a lot of fun searching for the names of other authors in the group-name segments. So many dead writers! The first issue I had with Gemina is that it shares a lot of striking resemblances to Illuminae, and I'm not talking about format and the fact that's it takes place in space. I don't think I can be any more specific about this without going into heavy spoilers for both, and I don't want to give any big hints for those that have read Illuminae but not Gemina yet. For those who have read both already, here we go: While the storylines of Illuminae and Gemina are different, a lot of the overall story and character beats in Gemina are lifted right out of Illuminae. Such as: A monster gets loose on the ship/jump station and starts attacking people: Illuminae: Zombies Gemina: Lanima The leading man getting killed off halfway through: Illuminae: Ezra making it to the wrong escape shuttle. Gemina: Nik getting killed "valiantly"(?) by pausing his running from kill-crazy Kali for a second so he can pick up the journal Hanna just dropped. The leading lady deciding to save everyone else anyway, likely sacrificing herself, even though her love is dead: Illuminae: Kady agreeing to stay with AIDAN, who will be blown apart by the Lincoln and doesn't want to die alone, so he will set the rest of the uninfected free. Gemina: Hanna staying behind on the Heimdall to fix the broken universes, even though if she does save everyone there's still a second drone strike incoming to blow everything left. The twist reveal that the leading man was still alive after all: When I read Illuminae, I was impressed that the story took such a turn, and enjoyed seeing Kady have to grow because of it. I was hooked so much by everything in it that I didn't mind when Ezra turned out to still be ok. I thought the book had earned that back-pedal happy ending. Plus, AIDAN made it out ok, so who cares? (In case anyone hasn't been able to guess my favourite character in these books.) Gemina managed earn its happy ending too, with enough foreshadowing to tell you that something is off here even before Nik apparently gets killed off. I'd initially thought there was something going on after the wormhole malfunction, but after a while of nothing coming of it, I forgot it and started to wonder if this was going to be some clones thing. I'm so happy I was wrong, and the twist was far more creative than that. And yet, Gemina tried to pull that same trick a again shortly after Hanna and Nik are reunited. Only this time, Jackson comes in and kills all three of our new main characters, only there's a twist (again) that their still alive. I understand the explanation for this twist existing, but I didn't like it. Let me explain. There's a show I used to watch called The Mentalist. A lot of it was about using mind games to solve crimes, and I would say that unfortunately probably over half of the episodes would have the characters play the 'Oh no, something terrible has happened to a main character!' card in order to get the villain of the week to mess up and reveal themselves. But they wouldn't tell the audience. Week after week, you'd learn to stop caring pretty quick when something apparently awful happened to the characters you cared about because you knew it wasn't real. Almost ever. You would watch an episode an think, 'Well, there goes the writers playing that card again. I wonder if any new viewers somewhere will get punked?' The point is, if you play that card to many times, especially if there's no real consequences, your audience is going to get annoyed. This is why I'm now worried about Illuminae #3 following too closely to the formula a third time. Speaking of that second twist: The 'other guy' who was the/one of the antagonists having a change of heart because lurv and letting the leading lady go save herself (and her friends, in Gemina's case) and sacrificing themselves in the process: Illuminae: AIDAN revealing that he wasn't really going to let Kady die and giving her an escape from the Lincoln. Jackson deciding that it's time to do as Hanna asked earlier and prove himself with his actions. The difference is that Jackson is most certainly not one of the greatest AI characters ever created (though I hear he has a lovely voice), while I was plenty invested in what was going to happen to Kady and AIDAN. There were more I could think of, but this section is too long already. Whether these similarities bother other readers is going to depend on the individual. For most people who loved Illuminae, I don't think it will be a problem. I'm generally a tough critic. And then there are the new characters. I seem to be alone in this judging from the reviews, but I wasn't a fan of Hanna and Nik, although when that beautiful climax happened I really wished I was. They are the reason Gemina is missing a half star. Hanna and Nik were far too similar to Kady and Ezra. Essentially, when you subtract the character quirks and history, they are nearly identical to the couple we met in Illuminae. Both as individuals and their relationship: She's a girl who's already made up her mind about him, and is now immune to his charms. She's a complete badass at something (Kady = hacking, Hanna = 'ninja skills' and battle strategy), which make her valuable in a crisis. She will do whatever it takes to find the truth after her parent is killed. She is independent and can handle the threats well, even when she is alone. Meanwhile, he's a well-meaning jokester who keeps striking out with the girl of his dreams, and greatly lacks her level of skill at anything. Our Constant Analyst is much less favourable when describing him (Ezra = clumsy klutz, Nik = slow and dimwitted) and he's the butt of the jokes of many characters. He's the devoted screw-up in way over his head compared to Madam Badass, and he's gonna use his charms in this crisis to open up to her and win her over in the end and she'll realize it was him all along. I was disappointed that Gemina was doing nearly the same thing over again, and just decided to hope that Hanna and Nik would end up working for me the same way Kady and Ezra did. Here's why it worked for me in Illuminae and not in Gemina: When we meet Kady and Ezra, they're exes. They have history we don't see and we don't need to see. We know they worked, at least for a time, and what brings them together in the end is the both of them coming to terms with why they broke up. We get to learn so much about them this way. In Gemnia, we get to see how Hanna and Nik met: He hit on her, she didn't like it, she told him so, he didn't listen, she broke his arm. The End. Yet now, according to her diary, she thinks of him as this great puzzle to solve and she does plenty of flirting with him when we see them together. I felt like I'd missed a chunk of the book here. I think this is one of the unfortunate downsides of this format: we don't get to see how they see each other from their point of view. We don't get to see why they are interested. After reading the whole novel, I still have no idea why they are interested in each other. He likes her because . she's hot and rich and badass, I guess, and flirts with him. But I have no idea why he's got this deep devotion to her. He never says why he's into her and so we never learn. Hanna doesn't really say why she's attracted to Nik either, but from what I can discern, it isn't very flattering. First off, Hanna already has a devoted boyfriend! I don't care if he turned out to be the bad guy, she didn't know that, and neither did Nik (who also knew she had a boyfriend). Yet, she keeps stringing Nik along like her and Jackson are in an open relationship (Jackson definitely doesn't seem to think so). That's not fair to Jackson or Nik, and to make matters worse, the book has several brief discussions on how wrong it is for a guy to cheat on his girl, but there's nothing about what Hanna's doing. I don't like double-standards. Anyway, at the start of Gemina, Jackson appears to be the perfect guy. Perfect looks, great voice, devoted, good job, Dad approves, etc, while Nik is the scoundrel drug dealer. Then, some reveals later, we find out that Jackson is working with the bad guys and Nik, who first appeared to be a murderer, is innocent of all charges and selfless enough to confess to his little brother's crimes, so it turns out Nik was the perfect one all along. Now Hanna chooses Nik, because he's the perfect guy now. Side-note, I'm really tired of the apparent bad boys who, it turns out can do no wrong. They brush the crime off when it turns out to be his brother's crime, like he didn't know what he was doing and was misled. If they were going to make that excuse anyway, why not have it that Nik did the crime, and use those excuses on him. I think it would add another detention to his character if he did the crime (maybe lessen said crime slightly, if that makes everyone more comfortable), and genuinely regret what he did and try to recover and go straight from then on. But then he wouldn't be perfect enough for Hanna, I guess, meaning she'd either have to: 1) Come to some realization that somewhere along the line she wasn't so perfect either, and grow from this knowledge, or, 2) Realize that the other true perfect character was really Ella all along, and Hanna has to go to extreme lengths to win over her true equal. Even with these problems, I loved a lot of Gemina and I look forward to Illuminae 3. Definitely check Gemina out if you were a fan of Illuminae.

When I pick up romance, chick lit, love stories - whatever you want to call them - I understand that I am reading a certain formula and adjust any expectations I might have accordingly. Despite having done this, I was still unimpressed with Jojo Moyes' Me Before You. But first, let's recap the (formulaic) plot: Louisa Clark, a working class woman in her mid-20s with no qualifications, has just lost her job at the local cafe. She eventually finds work as a caregiver for paraplegic Will Traynor, a smart and sexy businessman paralyzed from the shoulders down after an unfortunate motorcycle accident. Will is understandably grumpy and difficult, Louisa lacks worldly experience; the two don't get along. They eventually begin warming up to each other and bond in a way that bolsters Louisa's confidence and expands her small-town horizon and unburdens Will, if only a little. The real challenge comes when Louisa learns of Will's intent to commit suicide and dedicates herself to changing his mind. Cue the rest of this oversized, at times boring, at times legitimately tear-jerking, novel. So what is so wrong with this acknowledgedly predictable story? Let's start with the writing. The novel is told mostly from Louisa's first-person point of view, with occasional shifts, still in first-person, to other characters in the novel like her sister Katrina and Will's father Steven. Despite these shifts, the narrative voice remains the same simplistic tone that is also oddly refined for a lowly-educated, working-class, exclusively tabloid-reading girl like Louisa. Granted, we can assume Louisa may be writing this story later, after she's had time to polish herself, which is the trajectory the novel sets Louisa on by its end. But I would still expect Steven's portion of the narration to read differently. Then there's the plot. Predictability still has to be done right. Some instances are so pointless or unnecessarily dragged on that I skimmed pages at a time. In terms of characterization, Will is the only character that is nicely fleshed out, perhaps because of his paralysis, which gives him a depth that the other characters lack. The rest, including our dear Lou, are just stock characters. This may be in line with the romance formula, but it doesn't make it memorably so. Overall, this story doesn't work in writing. While it won't take that long to read (especially with the skimming), it'd certainly go by faster in visual form that is guaranteed to yank even more tears out of you. So it's fitting that the movie adaptation is being released in June (for the Netherlands), co-written by Moyes, which is where Me Before You should have gotten its start. Written by Laylan Saadaldin

I am not going to lie and say I liked this, or that it was OK just because everybody else praises it. No, I did not like it. I feel like I was played with. I feel like I was meant to feel miserable. I did feel miserable reading this. I feel manipulated. I detest those who try to manipulate me. Grisly, gory details are easier to take than the implied horrors of this book. Innuendos are worse than specific details because our own imagination takes wing. We are delivered a mix of fantasy and horror. Horror of our own making. This was way too fantastical for me. Sorry dear friends, but I cannot classify this under the benign category of magical realism. Realism in this book is minuscule. The author heaps on misery to an extreme! Example: not one but two leading characters have retarded mothers. The warden's wife had to be dying of cancer too? And don't tell me the horses are anything but pure fantasy! Sure you can think about what the author is implying, but the primary thrust of this book is to partake of the suffering in today's penal institutions and to wallow in the depravity of man. It doesn't help me that the author throws in some sparks of hope and love . These are merely pasted on. There is no depth in any of that which we are delivered Sorry, but this book totally rubbed me the wrong way. The narration by Jim Frangione was fine. I have no complaints on that front.

Hummm... Yummy So, this is a very short story about how Lia and Evan meet. You can pretty much figure it out what happens here by the synopses... He's stuck in the middle of nowhere, obliged by his boss, waiting for a message saying that he can come back home... She's lost and finds him... They have a wild night together, she goes away and he gets the message he's been waiting for.. Believe me, the writer tells the story better than I can... I started reading this series because I've read Surviving Raine, and Evan is suppose to appear in the second book and cause the fight of the century... So I figure I should know who is this Evan Arden guy... Since he'll try to kill one of my favorite characters and everyone is going crazy because no one wants either to die... I get it... Evan is a really great character... And so is Lia... At first she seemed like the typical damsel in distress... A abusive victim, agrees with everything, need someone to show her what to do... Sweet, but weak. Not that Raine is so much different... But I liked how she manage to deal with Bastian bad moods... Raine is patient, but without being a doormat. But this is not Surviving Raine! Why am I talking about her? Let's go back to Lia, Shall we? Yes, well... At first Lia did not called my attention... And then, there's this coin scene.... And it's so funny! And because of this one scene I could see Lia as a fun and confident girl... I'm hoping I won't be disappointed farther on... Now, comparing Evan with Bastian... Evan is not as much of a asshole as Bastian... He's a lot more civilized, but also very closed and with a strong interest in prostitutes... He seemed smarter and quieter, somehow... He's a lot more calculist, and a better observer... He's one of those people that can read body language as if it were a children's book... You know, like in the Show The mentalist or Lie to me ... I absolutely hate those shows, but I love these kind of characters! What I liked more about Evan is that he doesn't have a little sad story as a background to explain why he became a hit man... He doesn't call himself broke or bad or anything.... He's a ex-military, a war hero, but he hates being called a hero... He has survivals guilt, but he doesn't keep crying over it... At least not in this book... He got in this life because he said that if he doesn't do it, somebody else will... So, whatever... I think he says that in the second book, but you might as well know now... It's not that he doesn't have a conscious, it's just that he's lines are very blurred... He's very pragmatical, unlike Bastian who's very much driven by emotion(rage, mostly), which makes Evan seems a lot more dangerous... I've read 335 pages of Sebastian Stark... And in 56 pages, Evan Arden already got me convinced... If these two are up against each other? I would put my money on Evan... No doubt about it... Even though it would break my heart because Bastian is like a mistreated Pit Bull... Angry, distrustful and very protective of his bone... And I love dogs! So can I not like Sebastian? Wow! I've just realized that Raine makes the same comparison in the book! I swear that didn't cross my mind when I said that... It only shows the writer really does makes him look like one.. Even if Raine haven't point that out... Specially at the end when Raine is sleeping when he puts him self on top of her, covering her as much as he can, and pretty much growling at anything that makes noise or try to come close to her... That's a funny scene... I should really stop talking about Surviving Raine on Otherwise Alone's review... But it's only natural since one lead me to read the other... I'll stop blabbering now... In a nutshell? This book is good, Evan is badass, Lia is fun, and you should read it!

I have mixed feelings about the third installment of this series. I still find the world-building to be extremely compelling, as well as relevant to today. Each successive book drives home the tensions between the Silvers and the Reds and the moral repugnance of the way the Silvers enslave the Reds. There is no clear way forward for these factions but the newbloods show there might be a third way and the new alliance in this book shows the Red Guard, Montfort, and Command working to integrate Silvers, Reds, and newbloods. This was fascinating and while the analogy doesn't hold up entirely when we think about race and privilege in our world, there's a lot for us to take away. Mare's character growth was incredible. She was getting on my nerves in the last book but here, through terrible circumstances, she starts facing her own demons. The scenes with Maven were heart-wrenching as she battled what he used to mean to her, the monster he is now, and the monster she fears she is. I want Maven to be redeemed so badly and maybe this will happen in the final book, though I hope Aveyard won't take a conventional approach in doing so. Cal has finally- finally!- picked a side but the stakes remain high for the former prince and the decision he's faced with at the end is brutal and OMG if he makes the wrong choice it is going to haunt him forever. This alone is what will make me want to read the next book. So all of that is pretty positive but here's what I wasn't feeling so much. Whereas the first two books have been from Mare's perspective, this book gives us two other first person accounts: Cameron and Evangeline. Granted, their perspectives were interesting and gave us a lot more information, which was useful since Mare was a prisoner. At the same time, my paranoid instincts kicked up because this had Allegiant written all over it. Maybe nothing Allegiant-like happened this time but I'm girding my loins for whatever might happen as the series wraps up. (While I loved Allegiant and appreciated that bold move, I do not want that to happen here. No thank you.) The book also started dragging around the middle and I found myself only skimming the battle scenes. It wasn't as much of a page turner as the first two, though as I noted above it remains a compelling story overall. I look forward to seeing what Aveyard will do next because I have no idea what a happy resolution might look like for the kingdoms or these characters. Also, be sure to read her acknowledgments: the last four paragraphs gave me goosebumps.

What I Expected: A cute contemporary romance. What I Got: So much more. As someone who is not a big fan of instalove, I was a little skeptical of the concept of two characters falling in love over the course of one day. Really, the only reason why I gave this book a chance was because I loved Everything, Everything so much. But Nicola took my suspicions and slapped me across the face with them. Seriously, the way the romance was done in this book absolutely blew my mind. I was rooting for two characters who had just met only hours before. How is that even possible? Not only was the romance amazing; literally everything else about the book was. The POVs switch between Natasha and Daniel, as well as many other minor characters throughout the book. Another thing that I thought I wouldn't like, but it turned out to be my favorite part of the novel. Getting a glimpse into characters' lives that you otherwise wouldn't think twice about was such a cool experience, and these chapters even tied into the ending of the book. The whole set-up of this novel is extremely clever and well-done. Yet another aspect of this novel that I enjoyed was the diversity. Getting to experience new cultures and live from the POV of someone facing deportation was truly amazing. It made me wish that more books addressed topics like this. Overall, this is probably the best contemporary I've ever read. This is one of those books I know I'll read over and over again and never get tired of it. 100% recommend this book to everyone! I know it seems weird that I'm going to bash this novel about how it deals with cheating when the synopsis more or less says that it's about cheating. And that's fine. I'm not here to dictate what kind of book should or shouldn't be written about. If we can read novels about murderers, incest, and stalkers then cheating isn't really that big of a deal. Plus, the book promised to be funny and I love laughing so I was looking forward to this. Sadly, it wasn't funny. It was just a big pile of hypocritical nonsense that tried to come off as feminist rant about gender and sexuality. Lily Wilder is a lawyer, not a good one though, who is getting married to the man of her dreams, who she thinks she loves, but she's worried about their relationship...mainly because she loves sleeping around, even though she's engaged to him. Her family tells her to reconsider, because they know how she is, but it only makes her want to marry Will all that much more. But does she love him? Can she love someone who doesn't truly know her and can she love someone who she doesn't know either? You know what would solve that, sleeping with some guy at the bar. So she does that a few times to clear her head and get her mind back in the game. I guess she's like Chloe from Apartment 23, only she's engaged and not as funny or as awesome as everyone's favourite B. Damn....I really wish that show wasn't cancelled. It was great. Anyways, it turns out that her fiance knows that she hasn't been faithful so he lets her know that it's okay. Why? Because he hasn't been faithful either, but that's okay! His reasoning is stupid, but it basically boils down to them loving each other and yadda yadda yadda. Unfortunately, Lily doesn't take it well and calls off the wedding. She can cheat and yell feminism, but when it turns out that he's cheating then it's wrong and dirty. I mean, he slept with one of her bridesmaids...even though she tried to sleep with the best man and two of his friends, one of which was his boss. But who cares! Women are allowed to be sexual beasts and follow their desires. I am a woman, let me have sex even though I'm engaged to someone!! I don't get it. If Lily didn't try to justify her cheating or wasn't engaged to someone she thought was monogamous to her and who she thought he thought she was monogamous...then I guess it would be funny? In a, "Oh God no...never...what are you think??" kind of way. I was looking forward to the laugh out loud moments and a look at the double standards when it comes to cheating, because there is one. And while the book tries to touch on these issues, it fell on deaf ears because you can't justify crappy behaviour and say "feminism" when it's just you being a poopy person. The entire book seemed to make a case about how great cheating is as long as everyone is in the know. Lily's father has cheated on all of his four wives and is currently cheating on the fourth one with the previous three. But that's okay, because the first three ex-wives are okay with it even though the fourth one finds out about it while away...because she's taking care of her sick mother who has cancer. *sigh* Then there's a trial thing that I think was meant to come off as empowering and funny, but it didn't. The way she acted was unprofessional, insulting, and rude. I should have read the comments before reading this one. It would have saved me some time. The only thing I got from this book was that cheating is fine and normal and everyone is going to do it whether you like it or not. Awesome!

4.5 stars I was pleasantly surprised with how this Little Mermaid retelling went, like REALLY HAPPY that all the reviews I read of The Summer of Chasing Mermaids lived up to the book. This is truly a diverse novel, with a person of color who has a disability (in that she is mute). For me, seeing Elyse without her voice, with all her dreams and plans crushed because of it, literally crushed my heart. It constantly made me think of my own future, and what would happen if that was all taken away from me. However, I realized, like Elyse, that having a home and finding your family is what really matters. Which is why it is not only the love interest, Christian, that helps her recover what she's lost, but also her family and friends. Even though the plot revolved around Elyse helping Christian fix up his boat to win the Pirate Regatta, a race that the both need to win due to an idiotic bet his father made with the mayor, it mainly focused on Elyse's recovery. As she hung out with both Christian, his adorable little brother Sebastian, she learns to look forward to the future again and face her fears with the sea. Speaking of the adorable little child---I mean brother, I can't really put into words how much of an impact he had on Elyse. First off, CHILDREN. You don't normally see such well developed children in YA, especially in the form of a younger brother. And he definitely had a personality. He loves mermaids, and he always wants to go searching for them in the cove. My favorite part is that this is not gender stereotyped at all, especially his love for dressing up as a mermaid. And everyone's support for him (Except the father and the mayor because ugh). So here's a sum up so far of all the amazing things going on in this book. - Diversity - Feminism in Gender Equality/NO Gender Stereotypes - Awesome friendships and family - Romantic interest is not a jerk, and actually APPRECIATES Elyse for who she is, even though she can't talk. Oh, and I forgot something. An actual mention of self-pleasure AND I AM SO HAPPY because it was in a positive light (why wouldn't it be?) and though it wasn't super detailed, it was very easy to understand what was going on. I think this is such a good message to the target audience (and I mean everyone, really) because it shows that masturbation isn't this taboo thing, and it's good to explore your body. So yeah, this made me incredibly excited because I honestly thought this novel wasn't going to get any better. I think I'm going to stop here because I have done so much talking about the awesomeness of this book. However, before that, I do want to mention that it has kind of bothered me that the model on the cover seems whitewashed. Is this just me and my thinking? It was mentioned that Elyse was dark-skinned, but I'm not sure how dark. Anyways, it has nothing to do with the content of the book. Overall, everyone needs to read The Summer of Chasing Mermaids, because even though it is a contemporary retelling, it sure does a good job in tying it back to The Little Mermaid. Like a REALLY good job. So yes. READ. READ IT.

This was such a fantastic book, I almost don't even know how to begin to review it. First and foremost, for a tale about a dark and debilitating mental illness, The Vegetarian was beautifully written, and worthy of the highest praise. The characters in this novel were very interesting. There were small moments when readers could relate to the characters or sympathize with their actions, but at no point do readers feel as if they are part of this world. It is very clear that readers are not meant to be a part of this story, but to simply observe it. None of the characters in this book are very likeable. Yeong-hye's husband is a complex character. While readers will agree that he acts in ways which we find to be immoral and violent marital rape , his character is fitting to the portrayal of Korean men in literature (not that I agree with this stereotype, it's just that it is often found in literature). Yeong-hye was our silent protagonist, the vegetarian. While some may argue that as a character with no real vocalized thoughts of their own couldn't be our main character, I argue that her actions speak louder than any of her words could. Her vegetarianism is believed to have spawned from mental illness, but I think it originated from a place of control. Kang gives off the impression that Yeong-hye had very little control of the things going on in her life, and this was one of the ways in which she could try to regain control. I think reader's will try to like Yeong-hye's sister, but for me her actions were first selfish, and then a little too late. While no part of this book would classify as a traditional suspense or a mystery, there was something very suspenseful in the writing and pacing of this novel. I think readers can sense the outcome of this novel, and are held in suspense while they wait for confirmation. While the novel does end the way readers may predict Yeong-hye's death it does not occur the way readers expect it to, and there are glimpses of hope met with despair until its very end. This book is not for the faint of heart. I will admit that parts of this book triggered very real emotions and memories from my own battles with mental illness, so this is something readers should consider when picking up this book. This book isn't quite contemporary, or mystery, and while it's kind of creepy, it isn't horror, so I believe it best belongs in the genre of Weird Fiction. I highly recommend this book, and I plan on giving all my weird-fiction-lovin' friends a copy for whatever significant gift giving holiday comes next! 4.5 / 5 stars ** Reread and reviewed for Blogging For Books on October 15th, 2016**

This actually does contain spoilers, but I find that spoiler warning annoying. How can you tell whether you'll want to read this review, if you don't get to see any of it? I came very close to giving this three stars. I did. There are good things about it, and I will probably check out the sequel, because I understand it doesn't deal with the same characters. Parts were exciting (parts were the opposite of exciting). The world is interesting. The idea of it being several generations past the Zombie Apocalypse, of knowledge of the world before being lost, is interesting. Here's what's not interesting: love triangles (quadrangles?) where you can't connect emotionally with any of the participants. That's what took up far too much of this book, and is the reason I just couldn't give three stars. I was also not in love with the writing style, which I found sparse and repetitive. I don't think it was bad; quite the contrary, it was very effective. It helped create a feeling of claustrophobic greyness. It was kind of dead itself, oppressive almost, shambling. I thought it worked, I just didn't like it that much, and I'm baffled that so many found it elegant. Apropos, yes; elegant, no. I am willing to give these characters the benefit of the doubt, somewhat. Say you'd lived all your life surrounded by walking death, hemmed in by a fence and by religion. You might very well end up stunted, emotionally and in your capacity to imagine. Maybe these characters, who all seem incapable of complexity, are utterly realistic. At the very least, they are one person's deliberate vision of what people under such circumstances might be like. Still, I really don't enjoy spending time with these people. The most interesting person in the book was the Outsider, and she gets maybe two speaking lines before she's undead. Even undead, however, she manages to have more personality than most of the living characters. ETA: stumbled across a really interesting explanation of the love triangle at the author's blog: http://carrie-ryan.livejournal.com/60... That makes me reconsider my response to the love triangle a bit, I have to admit. In the end, though, I'm not sure that understanding the author's intention better would help me connect emotionally with the characters any better.
