Read the full non-spoilery review @A Perfection Called Books The Concept: I was a bit hesitant to read this book because whenever I think of mermaids, wait, I don't think of mermaids! That's just it. It seems like such a childish idea/fantasy, it's something I haven't though about since the days of watching The Little Mermaid. I didn't think I'd like this book because it focuses on mermaids, but I did end up liking it! The mer-people in this book are called Syrena. There's forbidden romance, mystery, snark, and more! And that's all I'm saying. Go read ;) The Writing: I was a bit confused and put-off by the dual POV because Emma's side is told in first person while Galen's is told in third person. Either have them both in first person or both in third person. It made Galen seem so impersonal, and it was harder to connect with him than Emma. It was easier to deduce more of the story from Galen's POV though. The writing was simple and plain and good. There were some really hilarious and witty moments so I commend Banks for that. I wish that Banks explored more of the Syrena world, but I guess this book was more about Emma discovering her gift. Next book perhaps? The Plot: To me it seemed that the plot was dragging in parts. Sometimes I felt that this book focused too much on the romance and less on developing characters and an actual plot/storyline. The plot was a bit predictable but still enjoyable. Overall though a plot did eventually form. It was fascinating learning more about the Syrena race and their story. The Characters: Emma - This girl had a 180 personality change within the first 20 pages. She went from sweet and innocent to feisty and stubborn. I find that HIGHLY unrealistic. But besides that, I do like Emma. She gets a bit on my nerves sometimes, but overall I like the girl. She's not weak like some other protagonists. *cough* NORA GREY *cough* She's strong and although she gets all weak in the knees near Galen, she knows how to snap out of it and call him out when he's being too controlling. Galen - Whoa this guy is hot. That was my first thought. I really like Galen. He's protective and thoughtful and smart. He's clear-headed and sweet. He's not afraid to say what he feels. I HATE how sometimes his overprotectiveness turns him into a domineering person. Chill out, dude. The Romance: The romance in this book was really cute, but I felt that it happened way too quickly. Emma and Galen are an adorable couple, and I think they complement each other well. It's a bit hypocritical of me, but gosh it took forever for them to kiss!! All that sexual tension. I was like "Just kiss already!!" The Ending: Things got crazy near the end!! It all happened so fast. The ending isn't exactly a cliffhanger, but it's really good. This book is light and fun, so if you're looking for a book to get you out of a reading slump, this is the book for you.

FIRST OFF: KNOW THAT G. R. Mannering is a literary genius and you DEFINITELY need to read Roses if you're in search of a Beauty and the Beast retelling! This isn't Disney. There are no talking teacups, clocks, candle holders, etc. Instead we get silvery, magical beings. Amulets. An unexpected yet welcomed Gaston-esque character. An enchanted castle where you can ride a horse for hours in the fields, thinking you might escape, only to find out that the magic has been playing a cruel joke on you and you've been running in practically the same spot over and over again. G. R. Manning took some liberties and branched off with her own retelling while still incorporating the most important pieces of the fable. I thoroughly enjoyed this book. The only problem was the ending, actually. Everything became fine and dandy, which is alright. But it felt too rushed, like G. R. Manning was super excited to finally finish the book. Other than that, this is a great retelling and I highly recommend it!

Parodies are something that I always struggle to rate and recommend to others. I mean they aren't wholly original material and unless you've read what it's based usually you just end up reading something that you can't fully understand and are just left baffled. As I left Mr Earl Grey and Anna gazing at each other gazingly though, I realised that those problems didn't apply to this book. I mean what this is based off of isn't wholly original either (and terrible and hiding it) and it's so famous and discussed by everyone that if you've read the books or not you understand almost all the in jokes. I've only read the first original Fifty Shades (and even that was too much) but still got many a snort, snicker, giggle and laugh-till-I-cry moments that this has to be one of the best parodies I've ever read. And it doesn't even really have to try. It just exaggerates the ridiculous that was already there and that's where the humor comes from. The fact that you know that a serious romance book was written that was only slightly less ridiculous than this but still sold millions (or was it billions) of copies worldwide. Also, as someone who reads plenty of fanfic (although not as much Twilight stuff anymore. It's all getting published. ), this was like a big fuck you to every Twilight fanfic ever that did everything that Fifty Shades did but just didn't get published. Because they all did this. He buys her love, not with money but things, and just does heaps of ridiculous things to win her affection instead of doing normal things. And they always have butt loads of sex (and usually also butt sex) and he always has a huge penis. I loved this book and want to give it to the people I know who actually enjoyed the original Fifty Shades and say "LOOK AT HOW RIDICULOUS THIS ALL IS! THIS AUTHOR HAS ADJUSTED SO LITTLE! HOW CAN YOU ENJOY THIS SERIES??" but I won't personally be going back to read it again.

I have to admit, adult historical fiction genre is one I rarely read. I think I'm afraid that it'll involve melodrama, inaccuracy too flamingly bold to ignore and far more sex than is appropriate to the story (really, where do I get these ideas?). Lily of the Nile proved to be absolutely none of these things and left me craving the sequel. This was definitely a book that I didn't want to set down--the one upside of the 2 feet of snow in 12 hours blizzard was that I had every excuse to stay on the couch all day and immerse myself in Dray's world. With that being said, I confess that I set the novel down once, about 50 pages in, just to look in my old Roman history textbook and see what I could find about Cleopatra and her daughter, Cleopatra Selene, who the novel focuses on. Turns out I could hardly find a thing about Cleopatra Selene, so I think it's safe to say that Dray writes about a period that isn't often touched on. Dray's novel is fantastically paced. Some might wish that she was more descriptive, but I think she did a nice job of briefly touching on events that are best summarized as opposed to described play by play. The descriptions of the Roman feasts definitely made me hungry. To top it off, Dray creates complex characters that were interesting to read about and kept me guessing. My only real complaint about this book is that I questioned how realistic a couple of plot points were, but after turning the final page I still really wanted to get my hands on a copy of the sequel. Lily of the Nile surprised me in the best way possible. It may not be the most thought-provoking book I've read, but it approaches history from a new angle and kept me turning the pages.

Marilynne Robinson shrugged and thought "Maybe I'll write a book" and then just did it, in longhand, and then she showed it to her friends who lost their minds, and one of them was an author whose agent pounced on it and she got a call, like, "This is brilliant, get ready to be famous," and she was like "Oh, okay." The deep woods are as dark and stiff and as full of their own odors as the parlor of an old house. We would walk among those great legs, hearing the enthralled and incessant murmurings far above our heads, like children at a funeral.I wonder how many struggling would-be novelists have read those sentences and just given up. Hopefully enough. "Here's a first novel that sounds as if the author has been treasuring it up all her life, waiting for it to form itself," said the Times instantly. It was nominated for the Pulitzer. It was 25 years before Robinson felt like writing another book. She's compared to Melville. "I thought that if I could write a book that had only female characters that men understood and liked, then I had every right to like Moby-Dick," she says, and it's hard to find a piece about Robinson that doesn't mention Melville too. This is not because of her symbolism; although housekeeping is a symbol here, it doesn't have the smashing originality or unsubtlety that the Whale does. It's because it's about faith, which is alive and vital to Robinson the way it is to Melville. People who care this urgently are apt to sound radical about it:In the newness of the world God was a young man, and grew indignant over the slightest things. In the newness of the world God had perhaps not Himself realized the ramifications of certain of His laws, for example, that shock will spend itself in waves; that our images will mimic every gesture, and that shattered they will multiply and mimic every gesture ten, a hundred, or a thousand times.This isn't dogma; it's actual God, from a person who believes that the Bible is an actual thing. "It must mean something," Robinson says, "and I'm going to find out what." I'm an atheist, so I think the first statement is false, but I find her efforts awe-inspiring. When you talk about Robinson you talk about Melville, and Emerson and Thoreau thanks to her gorgeous relationship with nature, as quoted above, or the abandoned house in the cleft of the valley. Shirley Jackson doesn't come up as much, which seems odd because We Have Always Lived in the Castle seems like an obvious comparison. They're both about houses and outcasts, and they're both fuckin' amazing.

*ARC copy provided by NetGalley* So, it started well buti t did not end well. Alexa and his twin Marcel have lost their parents at the early age of fourteen years old. To escape a terrible fate, Alex cut her hair to look as much as she could to a boy and together with her brother she joined the king of Antion's army. No one could ever guess who she really is, especially since she is one of the best soldiers of the army, almost unbeatable and she's in the personal guard of prince Damian. But nothing is what is seems, just as Damian is not the spoil, arrogant and defenseless prince everyone thinks he is. When Damian, Alexa and her soldier friend Rylan are abducted by a sorcerer, all the dark and unexpected secrets start to come to light. The beginning was very promising. I was wandering in a Middle Age atmosphere, with swords fight and military codes to respect; I also liked the language used, which was the one with which a soldier had to address his king. Then the sorcerers showed up and the fantasy was so good and it made the story even more interesting. Then... the characters ruined everything. Alex has lived in the army pretending to be a boy for three years and suddenly all she can do is blush and stare at the prince's chest and notice the honey speckles in Rylan's eyes. I mean, keep your hormones at bay! You're supposed to act like a tough guy, remember? How could she have survived if she made these noticeable mistakes? I swear, if I read one more time about muscled torsos and hard and clenched jaws, I would have hit her with a pan! And if this isn't already enough, she first said she wasn't worthy of the prince, he couldn't possibly like her and then she complains about Damian keeping secrets from her. C'mon! Another thing that I didn't like was the similarities between Damian and Rylan. Apart from their physical appearance, they both knew that Alex was actually Alexa, they both were sweet with her and loved her for who she really was... I don't know, I couldn't single them out. The love triangle was just too much, after the first few chapters it became the thread keeping the story together and I wondered where the action and the fantasy stuff had gone. It also reminded me in the end of the star crossed lovers Gwenevere and Lancelot, even though in this case Lancelot would be Arthur. However, I still want to know how the story goes; so yeah, I'll read the next one hoping it will get better.

What is it like to have a best bookfriend? Is it something that makes you laugh so hard, people think you are an idjit? Is it something that makes you swoon over utterly adorable things? Is it something that's goes on such similar lines as your own that you just can't help but get swept by an air of nostalgia and longing? If this is so, Eleanor And Park is my absolute best friend of the year! Warning- Proceed with caution: I'm going to be melodramatic throughout this review, and I know if Eleanor would be reading this, she would roll her eyes and say,"Seriously? That's so lame." But I am filled with such a myriad of emotions right now and I probably might sound incoherent and mad, but not writing this would be unjust to the very cause of this review. It's the only way out, so please bear with me. *sigh*}} I am addicted to Romance genre, so much that after every other genre I NEED to read a romance book, just in order to satiate my love for this genre. Be it Harlequin, be it some sappy and totally predictable story but something that deals with it. I have made inroads into this genre throughout, and I have seen so much of Romance, that now when I read something like that, by halfway usually the plot becomes totally discernible, and it kind of gets banal. Until I crossed paths with Eleanor And Park. I know people are creating ships and harbours of romantic novels in every corner of the world. But while reading this book, I could bring myself to apprehend that there was something which these books always ran short of. In the context of more sophisticated themes and displaying human emotions and mindsets, we often forget what we are to expect in a romantic novel. Why, what we look for is love. Love in its fragile, unrefined, yet still strong and priceless form. Love that reminds us of the sunshine, of the dawn that seeps in through the dark veil of the night. Love that is so dazzling and pristine in its shine; Love that has the power to lit up your face like a blooming daisy and at the same while make your heart ache, and tears fall. This story was all about it, it dealt with the perks and punches of teen love; the kind of first love that materializes in that totally impulsive phase of life when everything seems so proper, so promising. The sudden fluttering of heartbeats, that rollercoaster ride through feelings you never could reason out, that play of music in the background, with cute, blissful fantasies- this book just nails it all the way through. Ms. Rowell is an expert in adding the perfect lustre to every bit of the story in such apt measure. Every part of it deals with such minute, precise details, wonderfully woven around the characters- you just waft away with the flow. Its like you live in the characters' minds and every thought is like transparent glass material. Every emotion Eleanor felt, every tiny thing Park thought, it was like you were breathing it too with them. Even if you are way beyond your teen time, I don't think this book will nonetheless manage to dishearten you. I would like to take a minute and appreciate Ms. Rowell's exquisite creation, something maybe many hoards of people might have tried but couldn't quite meet the need of the minute. Rowell is some of those rare gems who could bring alive the unadulterated beauty of true love. I am not aiming at comparing authors; that isn't my intention. What I mean here is, she just endeavoured to deliver all that one ACTUALLY expects from a romance novel. I hate love-at-first-sight and all that first-look-and-electricity-urging through-me stuff, and this book wasn't based on that (Thanks Heavens!). In fact, Park's first impession of Eleanor was utter disdain. "Not just new- but big and awkward. With crazy hair, bright red on top of curly. And she was dressed like... like she wanted people to look at her. Or maybe she didn't get what a mess she was. " It was books and music that paved way for their story. At first, they were both so self-conscious and mulish, that neither would come up with even a simple civility of barely acknowledging the other. But even that was so hilariously written, it made me groan with laughter. Everything about them was funny, cute, adorable. Just plain adorable. The best part of Eleanor and Park's falling in love was the intricate way in which you learn about each of them, just before their world is struck by Cupid. It was the perfect pace; nothing was too haphazard or sluggish. They were such two charming people, you can't just pass by and not notice them. Eleanor belonged to a poor messed-up household, growing in which has been somewhat mechanical and lifeless. She joins school, and owing to her weird dress-code and out-of-place features, people wouldn't just stop taunting her from the first day itself. (Ah, you know teens will always be teens!) Even Park, though it all goes on in his head. Park offers her to sit beside him. Not by way of goodwill, but out of sheer annoyance. And it all became a routine. Eleanor would come every day into the bus and sit beside him. She used to sneakily peek into his comics, and when Park eventually started noticing that, he went slow with his books. Isn't that silent friendship so unbearably cute? By and by, he began sharing his books and music tapes with her and that was what made them talk. They would argue all the way about the characters in the comics and about their tastes in the varied tracks they heard together. It all started in slow, tiny steps. And long before they knew, they were already beginning to fall for each other. The best parts- Oh My God! I don't think I can ever decide one of the other. The moment when Park held her hand for the first time and admitted that it felt like holding a butterfly; or when Park fought with Steve for his snide talks about Eleanor; or when both the birds confessed whatever they felt for each other over that epic phone call; or when Park kissed her in the dark alley; or when he sneaked to Eleanor's place after having fought with her over Tina; or when they say Goodbye.. I can't decide which. It seems so unfair to even dare to choose. These moments are so perfectly etched in definite cubbyholes in my memory, that I can't override one over the other. The ending!! Whoa! Was it a cliffhanger??? I think it was. There's going to be a sequel? That, I am unsure of. And a part of me doesn't want one too. I love Rowell and I love E&P, but my love for them is so humongous and precious, that I don't want to take a chance with a sequel. I know I'm contradicting myself and I'm being all confusing but I just want to savour them like this. I want to cherish them as two 17-year olds who fell in love, lived it, treasured it, and the rest, I know, its always going to be a Happily Ever After. Eleanor And Park- could ever anything go wrong with them? No. Never. Jesus. :D 5 totally flawless, adorable, romantic stars!

I read The Hunger Games more than a year ago, finishing it despite my strong dislike of its protagonist, Katniss. I made it 100 pages into Catching Fire before I could take no more. I hoped that watching the movie would make Katniss feel more human to me. More someone I'd like to root for. It did. I resumed reading Catching Fire, and was able to finish it by imagining Jennifer Lawrence in the role. I still didn't like it, exactly. I just wanted to see how the story ended. I'd heard such dismayed reviews about the conclusion of the trilogy that I expected I, too, would find it unpalatable. Instead, I found myself finally both unwilling to put it down and truly feeling Katniss. Not just being in her head. Not just hearing her mental rundown of the actions she's taking or planning to take, but feeling her. This is what I crave from a protagonist, and I'm so glad to have found that connection at the end. And what an end it was! I finished with tears in my eyes and goosebumps rippling up and down my arms. It's not an ending without sadness, but it is, indeed, an ending full of truth, love and halting, wary but real hope.

Cloud Atlas by David Mitchell I do have to admit that I am not really an avid short story fan and this book is basically an assortment of short stories. Each story is in a different time and place but threads from the other stories are woven into each other. There is a common theme of oppression throughout the book. Even though I like to read various genres, the way the book completely switched genres, eras and language really threw me for a loop. I can tell you that by the time I got to the middle of the book, the language used was an extreme chore to read. "Souls cross ages like clouds cross skies, an' tho' a cloud's shape nor hue nor size don't stay the same, it's still a cloud an' so is a soul. Who can say where the cloud's blowed from or who the soul'll be 'morrow? Only Sonmi the east an' the west an' the compass an' the atlas, yay, only the atlas o' clouds." Zachry Once Mitchell reaches the end of the sixth story, he takes up where he left off on the fifth and so on until by the end of the book you are back to finish the first story. That's great because the first story left off in mid-sentence and I actually thought there were pages of my book missing! I think this was a great structural idea but I never comfortably settled into this book and I couldn't wait to finish it.

This review and others can be found at http://www.bookishtreasures.blogspot.com "I know we're fucked up, alright? I'm impulsive, and hot tempered, and you get under my skin like no one else. You act like you hate me one minute, and then need me the next. I never get anything right, and I don't deserve you...but I fucking love you, Abby. I love you more than I loved anyone or anything ever. When you're around, I don't need booze, or money, or the fighting, or the one-night stands..." - Beautiful Disaster Beautiful Disaster was my favourite book of 2011 so naturally ever since I first heard about Walking Disaster I was excitedly and anxiously waiting until I could get a copy. My feelings during the wait were mixed; on one hand it was a brand new book by one of my favourite authors, it was going to have all the characters that I loved in the first book and most importantly it was going to be the story of Beautiful Disaster from Travis's point of view! However, on the other hand it was going to be the exact same story just from a new point of view. I was worried that it might be repetitive and possibly even boring. Luckily it wasn't. I LOVED Walking Disaster. Despite being the same storyline the author made it fresh and new. It just goes to show how different things can seem when you are looking through someone else's eyes. Rather than repeating what we already know conversational scenes are briefly mentioned and the main focus is on the things we never got to see in Beautiful Disaster. I would recommend having read the first book recently so all the events are fresh in your mind and you can fully appreciate this book. However at a push you could probably read this entirely as a standalone but I think you will love it more if you know Abbi's side of the story first. "To douchebags!" he said, gesturing to Brad. "And to girls that break your heart," he bowed his head to me. His eyes lost focus. "And to the absolute fucking horror of losing your best friend because you were stupid enough to fall in love with her." - Beautiful Disaster For anyone who didn't like Travis in Beautiful Disaster (apparently you do exist) I think he will win you over in this book. Seeing his reasons for things and his thoughts about certain situations actually made me a little mad at Abbi for not being more understanding. I challenge you to try to read this book and not fall in love with Travis; he just seems so sweet and caring though also out of his depth as he has never been in love before. Some things get explained in this book too, such as where the nickname pigeon came from; who knew a name like pigeon could have such a sweet meaning. Both books will merge in your head to give you such a complete understanding of the story unlike anything you have ever experienced before. Together the two books make the ultimate book! Travis and Abbi are one of my favourite book couples of all time because neither of them are perfect nor is their relationship perfect but they love each other, need each other and fight to be together. I am very happy to say that Walking Disaster was just as good as I hoped it would be, if not better! I now can't wait to see what Jamie McGuire will bring next, all her books are so amazing that I would buy pretty much anything she writes. *I received a free ecopy of this book from the publisher via netgalley in exchange for an honest review, this has not affected my opinions nor the book rating in any way. Actual Rating: 3.5 First Drop of Crimson is centered around Spade and Denise's romance. Spade, as we know from the Night Huntress series, is Bones' best friend while Denise is Cat's. Who wouldn't like their best friend to date their spouse's best friend? It's quite a perfect match. In fact, the two couples can definitely double date all the time now. The book followed a sort of generic storyline. The formula was pretty much girl asks boy to help with a task. Boy agrees but with conditions. Boy and girl pretend to be dating in order to fool everyone around them and accomplish their task. At the end of the day, they both fall in love. It's pretty simple when you break it down. However, the bonus was that this was a paranormal fiction, with the boy being a vampire and the girl turning into a shape-shifter after being blackmailed by a demon. So the plot was definitely more exciting than if it was focused on just humans. Frost developed a good chemistry with Spade and Denise. I liked the build up/development of their feelings to each other. I was also intrigued by the introduction of demons and shape-shifters into the Night Huntress World. While reading The Night Huntress series with its primary characters, Cat and Bones, Frost hadn't introduced any other supernatural creatures except ghosts and ghouls. So the addition was somewhat refreshing. There was a lot of insight to both Spade and Denise. They were a lot similar to each other, with the tragic ending of their past loves. I think that helped the bonding process between them. In the sense that they could definitely identify with one another. Denise's character was refreshing, definitely a break from Cat's. I liked that she wasn't completely impulsive. And she mostly did what she was told, which I guess can be attributed to the fact that she didn't have much experience in the supernatural world, as Cat did. I think that also contributed to the growth of her character, because Denise definitely started to understand how the other side lived and that's why she was able to do what was required of her at the end. So you could see the difference in her character from the beginning to the end. Frost also shed some light on Ian's character. The first time I read about him in One Foot in the Grave, I was definitely interested in his character. But then when he seemed to get in the middle of Cat and Bones' relationship, I became somewhat skeptical. However, this book gave us a little insight to Ian. Although he can be annoying, a part of him that I'm beginning to love, Ian definitely seems to have more layers than what has been shown to us in the previous books. I think he's an interesting character that should be fully explored. All in all, Frost delivered an entertaining book.

Those sentimental Hallmark greeting cards that bring a tear to your eye when you read them at Target? If whoever wrote those also wrote a novel about a crusty old curmudgeon, it might turn out something like this book. The characters are typically described by one word (pregnant, overweight, homosexual, etc) then spend the rest of the book behaving only in behavior that directly supports the initial description (ie eating a sandwich or asking about food in every scene). Character interaction is so slapstick that Ove might as well be a man called Elmer Fudd. There's at least one eye-rolling, exasperating moment in each chapter. And yet there are moments that transcend the morass, moments where we genuinely feel for these characters and their absurdly cartoon-like lives, moments where we reflect on how little we really know about the people around us and what they've been through in their lives that affects who they are and how they interact with others. And those are the moments that make this book worth reading in spite of its faults.

Oh no, I thought as I read the first couple of paragraphs of this book. Already, the main character, a blind teenager named Alex has mentioned his super sonic hearing. This would be cool if blind people actually had the power to hear blades of grass moving, which sadly we don't. We are, much to the disappointment of your average person, incredibly normal. He also can sense whenever a person is looking at him, because the air around him begins to vibrate...again, this is not a blind superpower we possess...mainly because we don't have any. He is also given a new pair of sunglasses by his parents. Within the first chapter I've come across two major tropes, and I'm starting to lose hope. Some blind people do wear sunglasses, but mostly people with residual vision. This is because they have photophobia, meaning they are extremely light sensitive, they are wearing the glasses for the exact same reason sighted people do, to dim the sunlight. Alex however is wearing them because he is blind...and for no other reason. He also, for some odd reason wears boots that supports his ankles in case he falls. I'm really trying to figure this out, he's blind, rather than having balance issues. The author seems to have also missed a lot of basic information where technology is concerned. For example, Alex mentions he uses a braille keyboard. At first, I assumed this was referring to a braille display, with internal memory. And yet then he says he has to print out his notes on a braille printer (embosser for the rest of us), so that can't be the case. As far as I know, there is no way such a system would be put in place. It's unfortunate, because it implies that blind people are really limited in school, whereas in reality technology gives us so many options that enable us to take notes and access them, as well as our textbooks. Later, the author clarifies that the boy is using a computer with a braille keyboard, which is why he can't go back to check his notes. This made me very sad, there is so much information online about how blind people access computers with a screen reader, giving us the ability to use it fully. And yet the author says that he needs a braille keyboard to type, and has no way of reading his notes other than hard copy braille. Later in the book, the author contradicts herself by saying Alex has a talking web browser. Again, this indicates a lack of research as we would use a computer with a screen reader, rather than a specific web browser. But if he can access the internet, why then can't he read his notes in class. It was these contradictions and the complete butchering of the technology we use that bothered me. These are really, really easy things to get right. Even simple google searches will bring up information on how we access computers. He also is unable to submit work without someone converting his braille into print. Again, this demonstrates a lack of research because most blind students either use a braille note taker, which has email, or the ability to transfer work to a USB, or a computer. Either way, there is no need for someone to transcribe the work. There is also face touching, a trope that makes many blind people shudder. It's an invasion of personal space, and the idea that we would randomly start touching people actually makes us quite uncomfortable. In this situation, Alex touches his dads face to make sure it's really him. I'm going to be honest, the way I'd tell if it was my parent definitely would not be through face touching, ever. It crosses a barrier that I am just not willing to, and I know virtually no other blind people who would ever want to touch someone's face. It's disappointing that the author chose to stand by tropes, because there was a lot of potential in this book. In fact, I didn't dislike the paranormal elements of it. For me, those were the best parts of the story, however sadly it was all overshadowed by the poor characterisation. There is mystery and danger, a teenager trying to get a hold on his abilities and a cast of characters who are behaving in ways you don't understand. All in all, it could have been a great book. I continued to read it because of these things, I genuinely wanted to know what would happen to Alex. And it was this, more than anything, that made the lack of research so disappointing. Every time I began to really enjoy the story it would be punctuated by a huge, glaring stereotype and push me away again. I'm not sure that I'll read the rest of the series. The story was ok, at times I was genuinely caught up in it, but overall it wasn't wonderful. I want to encourage people to write books with a diverse set of characters, but please, please do your research. Most people with disabilities are more than happy to answer questions, mostly because we don't see positive portrayals in the media, and if we can help then we will. By asking you will be far more successful. There is nothing worse than picking up a book with a character that has the same disability as you to find it disappointing. Not only because you can't identify with them, but because you know that others reading it won't see how inaccurate it is. Other people who pick up this book will think I'm unable to take notes and hand in work in school without the help of a sighted person, that I have heightened senses and I need to wear sunglasses wherever I go to hide my face. None of these things are true. By spreading these tropes you are harming the community that you wish to help. With research and communication with people with disabilities this doesn't have to be the case. You can read more of my reviews by visiting my blog.

This book was SO BORING. Wow. I'm giving Daughter of Smoke and Bone a 3 1/2 star rating. There were parts of the story I found undeniably attractive. The imagery and descriptions were well done. The characters were strong. The writing style was good. I really liked the novel, but I did have a couple of issues which is why it's a 3 1/2 star for me instead of a 5. Seventeen year old Karou is attending a fine arts school in Prague. She's trying desperately to get away from her ex and keep her life a secret from everyone - because she has to. The catch is that Karou was raised by 4 chimera beings = not quite human. She goes on missions for the man (?) who's been like a father-figure to her her entire life; strange missions hunting for teeth. She's trained in fighting and been to plenty of black markets around the world. She has a necklace that can grant small wishes and she knows around 20 different languages. Needless to say, not quite your typical teenage experience. While on one of these missions, she encounters an angel; someone that tires to kill her; an enemy. From there, she starts to uncover secrets that Brimstone (her father figure) has been keeping not only about where he's from, but about who she is. The blurb to this book is incredibly misleading. An angel and demon falling in love? Not quite. This shouldn't dis-sway anyone from reading the novel in and of itself though. I actually loved the fact that the book wasn't at all what I expected it to be. The author breaks the story down into something incredibly basic: war. It's about prejudices and people brought up to hate their enemy - who that is exactly depending completely on which race you are. It's about starting to overcome those per-conceived notions, hoping for peace, and eventually falling in love with someone you never dreamed you would. And especially with war going on today, I think most people can relate well to the feeling Laini Taylor portrays about war, hate, death, destruction, bonds, and mercy in the mist of life-time enemies. I loved that aspect of the novel. That it could so accurately pinpoint some of the feelings war leaves behind was truly something to be commended for. A quote that struck me was: "It is a condition of monsters that they do not perceive themselves as such. The dragon, you know, hunkered in the village devouring maidens, heard the townsfolk cry 'Monster!' and looked behind him'" - which is nothing if not true. Villains never perceive themselves to be villains; they all believe they're doing the right thing. It's hard to see a foe's point of view, hard to see them for anything other than monsters. They tend to feel the same way though about you. I loved that this book lets you see 2 characters lives intersecting, and both realizing that the other isn't as evil as they had imagined. I loved loved loved Akiva (our love interest). He's a tortured soul, broken in grief. Then he meets Karou. Although they don't get off to the best of starts (trying to kill someone really isn't the gentlemanly way to approach a girl, after all), they feel pulled to each other. It does get kind of insta-lovey, but in the context of the story and finding out what we do about Karou, it makes sense. He's a hardened soldier with other-worldly beauty and a killer of the chimera, no mercy given. He's closed off and has dead eyes. Karou knocks him out of that and throughout the story, you can really see how much he loves her and is willing to sacrifice for her. He even puts his life in her hands when he tells her something unforgivable he's done to her. So now that I've gone over several things I loved, let me mention why my rating is 3 1/2 stars instead of 5. Maybe I'm just jaded but whenever creature-like beings, half human, half animal are described (like the chimera in this book), I always get flashbacks of the Chronicles of Narnia. I mean I love the idea but I feel like C.S. Lewis beat everyone to it and to describe anything similar is just...well, disappointing. It feels like cheating to me, although others may not have the same feelings about that as I do. Towards the end of the novel, Karou finds out exactly who/what she is. And, while I believe that to an extent, some of it was necessary, the last 100+ pages of the book are completely about the past. To me, a flashback here and there is completely fine but I felt like this information was dumped on me in one setting. During the ENTIRE book Karou is shrouded in mystery, even, she doesn't know exactly who she is. Then, in the last 100 pages, we get every detail about her history, how she came to be here, love interests, everything. It was just too much dumping. It was interesting but it drug a little bit for me in places and I was getting impatient for the author to go back to the present. That was the biggest let down for me. It was dump, then end of book one. However, I will say that that last couple pages (back to the present) dropped a big bombshell that I didn't see coming. Because of it, it was left on a bit of a cliffhanger, making me anxious to read book 2. Finally, although I liked Karou's character, I did not love her or always relate to her. I can't pinpoint exactly what made me feel that way. She's lonely, and she feels like she's missing part of herself (the void isn't filled by needing a boyfriend thank goodness, like some other books). My heart goes out to her at certain places but like I said, I didn't fall in love with her like I want to for hero's/heroine's of books.

Americanah is a love story, true love. It is not a beautiful love story though, it is full of pain and misery, full of longing, full of not belonging, and of shame. But the love is not the only main theme. Americanah is a story about race, and racism. A topic that none of us want to talk about, but Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie talks about bravely, and every word is carved in stone. Sad but true. Or in her own words: Race is a brew best served mild, tempered with other liquids, otherwise white folk can't swallow it. And I have to admit, we want to claim that we are colorblind, that color/race doesn't make any difference any more, that everybody is equal. But unfortunately, it is not yet the case in reality. And our blindness and denial might be contributing to keeping this problem around. If you're telling a non-black person about something racist that happened to you, make sure you are not bitter. Don't complain. Be forgiving. If possible, make it funny. Most of all, do not be angry. Black people are not supposed to be angry about racism. Otherwise you get no sympathy. Americanah is also a story about relationships between people from different races, different cultures. And how hard it is to belong with your partner's friends, when you actually don't belong with them, when they can't pronounce your name (and they don't bother too much). And about some immigrants that try to deny their past, their language, their accent, to become someone else. About people that couldn't get a taxi, or a job, because of their complexion. So sad that racism is about looks and skin color (and uncontrollable hair too). Americanah is a slow story, with many parts that actually talk about race, so that's just a heads up for people who like action and fast pace. I loved it, every word. And I identified, with some parts even personally, as an immigrant in America. And I acknowledged the problem, that even I, most of the time, love to deny. Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie reminds us how racism looks like in today's world. "Mild" racism, if you wish, but totally not mild to those who encounter it. She reminds painfully how it feels to be a minority (when you open the TV and you know that you'll see mostly people that are not from your own race), and how empowering is to belong ("the US president is black, like me", which caused me a heart wrench). I guess all of that can be easily identified with being a woman too... Insightful, powerful, and beautifully written. I highly recommend, and I think that we all should explore a bit inside ourselves about this important topic, that we keep quiet, too quiet.

Yaaaaaawn Man, this was a snoozer. I'm not entirely sure what happened in this book, nor am I certain if that's my own fault or the book's. Long story short, this is the introduction to Kanan and Hera from the animated Star Wars show, Rebels. While I love Rebels, I was more than a little underwhelmed with a A New Dawn. The basic premise of the tale is to. thwart a mining explosion conspiracy? I think? Kanan and Hera were my main reasons for picking up this book in the first place, but I soon realized that AND conforms to an irritating tradition in the Expanded Universe which involves splitting the story up between 30,764 different POV characters. (Dear Star Wars writers: please stop doing this. It only detracts from the story). While I understand that quite a lot of time lapsed between AND and the start of Rebels, very little of Kanan and Hera's relationship is set up here: they decide to team up on their next adventure by the end of the book, but other than that, they're hardly close. The inevitable moment when Kanan reveals himself to be a Jedi in disguise by whipping out some Force powers comes about ten chapters too late, and carries far too little weight. Instead we spend the majority of the book meeting new boring characters and trying to remember what the hell is going on. I have only read a few of the new EU Star Wars books, and thus far my favorites have been the novelization of Rogue One and Bloodline which, while not as perfect in my eyes as it is to many others, was still well-written and enjoyable. Pining down why most of these books have bored me so much is difficult, but I think it may come down to a conflict of genres. For me, Star Wars was always more of a fantasy series than science fiction -- it had a mystical Force, a badass princess, a cowboy in space, a monkish wizard with a fancy staff, talking ghosts, and miniature teddy bears that can overthrow empires. The only parts of the SW universe that ever struck me as strictly science fiction were the numerous space ships (which had always been my least favorite part of the series) and those godforsaken midichlorians. Most of the approaches these authors take, however, are almost entirely science fiction: a huge emphasis is placed on machinery, chemicals and conspiracies. That is surely appealing to many people, but for me it contrasts sharply with the nature of Star Wars, and what makes that universe so enticing in the first place. A second problem is a lack of emotional depth. Perhaps this is the product of Disney/Lucasfilm not being willing to take any big risks this early on and therefore putting pressure on their authors not to either, but almost every Star Wars book has read like a manual: Part A leads to Part B which leads to Part C. So much of the plot is focused on what the characters are doing rather than on the characters themselves. A New Dawn could have been an incredible character study: how did a decade in hiding affect Kanan? What was it like to watch all the people he cared about perish and how did that influence his ability to get close to people now? Did he feel angry and betrayed with the Clone Troopers who turned on the Jedi (which is something the show eventually addresses, even if the book doesn't)? Does he miss using the Force? Does he grieve for the fallen Jedi? These are all answered in the most superficial manner possible. Kanan feels sort of bad for fleeing his master on her command, but doesn't really miss or care about her or any of the other Jedi. The Force? Eh, he could take it or leave it. Living on the run? Basically a normal routine at this point. Instead of taking a deep, emotional look at the hardships Kanan faced, they're essentially checked off of a list, mentioned in passing in order to be pushed aside and move onto something more important. You know, like robots. Miller himself seems to be a competent writer, so I imagine that he can and has written better books than this in the past. But until Star Wars writers are allowed or able to write more emotionally engaging stories, they will continue to be forgettable.

I'll admit that I raised an eyebrow at the heroine's name, but the author managed to create a setup to where it's understandable. What I liked most about the book is that it kept from being too predictable. Don't get me wrong- this is standard romance thriller fare, but Tentler doesn't paint exactly by the numbers. Tentler does managed to do a good job of juggling a semi-large cast, but there are a lot of different plot threads in this book, not all of which were as neatly wrapped up as I'd like. There's closure, but I just wanted one or two things to be addressed. This is your typical romance thriller, but as far as first novels go this was pretty good. It's not "stop the presses, dethrone the queens of romance thrillers" awesome, but it's enough to where I forsee Tentler having a very promising future. After all, this is her in the rough, so imagine what she'll be like when she smoothes out her rough spots. (Reader copy provided by amazon vine)

If you're looking for a haunting, suspenseful read, then this is not the book for you. The Girl From The Well by Rin Chupeco is a bland and boring story based off an overused legend: Okiku and the Nine Plates. Whereas this legend has many variations, Chupeco's story is a spin off the version where Okiku, a beautiful young servant is courted by a samurai. She constantly refuses to marry the samurai, so the samurai plans to frame her for a crime. He entrusts her with the care of the Emperor's ten precious plates, and her job is to keep watch of these plates. Following the samurai's deceptive plan, he sabotages her and breaks the tenth plate. Okiku is framed, and the samurai pretends to show mercy on her by giving her the choice to marry him rather than face death, but Okiku still chooses not to marry him. She is brutally murdered, and her corpse is thrown down a well. The legend continues with Okiku haunting the well, counting to nine every night for each of the plates, and screaming when she can not find the tenth plate. It is said that this haunting was broken by another samurai shouting "Ten!" before Okiku could scream, thus ending the curse. This Japanese legend has inspired many works, such as the movie, The Ring. In Chupeco's retelling, Okiku (the protagonist) is a ghost who avenges the deaths of murdered children. Sounds great, right? Wrong. Okiku is actually a ghost that does nearly nothing but observe,stalk, count, stalk, make bad metaphors, stalk- oh, did I mention stalk? As quoted from the book: "I have followed him out of the bathroom..." "I stand there for a long time, just watching..." "And when there is nothing else, I count." "I spend the rest of the day counting." "I follow them into the car, where there is very little conversation." If this stalking and counting was supposed to be a frightening display of insanity, then its effect did not work for me. Okiku just felt like a bored ghost with nothing better to pass the 300 years of her existence with. Chupeco's story is told in alternating first and third person point of view. Okiku narrates a couple paragraphs, and then the point of view changes spontaneously in another paragraph. I personally felt as if these changes were highly unnecessary, and took away from the overall "chilling" effect of the book. Not to mention the odd line breaks. Sometimes, it is hard to read a sentence that breaks off into a a million pieces. Truthfully, I couldn't stand the sporadic separations and isolated words. And yes, the broken sentences previously written in this review are placed purely to annoy you. Your wel come. Next off, the characters from The Girl From The Well are cliche, static and boring. Other than Okiku, there are a couple more characters such as Tarquin Halloway, Calliope Starr and "The Chanting Exorcists Cult" (named by me). The story revolves around Okiku and Tarquin (Tark). Tark is a moody teen that deals with everything from friends to death by joking it off. "Callie? I was lying. I'm a little scared. But tell anyone else, and I'm gonna deny it and laugh all masculine-like." Both Tarquin and Callie barely have a personality, so you can forget about character development. Now, "The Chanting Exorcists Cult" is absolutely different. In a refreshing twist, this group of weird demon-fighting women have even less of a personality than the rest of the characters. I am astounded. If you haven't noticed, there has been no mention of plot yet. This is because there is no plot. The Girl From The Well is a 267 page book, and it took something around 190 pages for me to realize there was even a problem. In short, Tark was infested by a demonic woman in black, and he needed to go through an exorcism. *mini spoiler alert* He comes out of this "traumatizing experience" unscathed. (As does most everyone, save for a couple of the women from the "chanting exorcism cult") Really, this book was a sorry excuse for a horror novel. There was one scary scene involving the murder of an unimportant character and... wait, that's it. This book was not scary. Take my advice, if you want a scarier book, go pick up Asylum by Madeleine Roux or even the original versions of fairy tales by the Brothers Grimm. Anything but The Girl From The Well. In total, this is the kind of book you could use for kindling with no regret. It's almost three hundred pages of mediocre writing and quite frankly, I don't think reading The Girl From The Well is worth the hassle. This October, I challenge you to be environmentally friendly and read a different book. Preferably one that is worth the use of cutting down trees for. Go green, and read a better book! It's a win-win situation. But if bland and boring is your type, go ahead, no one's stopping you. I hope you enjoy it much more than I did.

Jagger's wife's best friend, Dawn, is under a pretty serious threat, but he decides to let her swing since she's not "family". This is the same woman who hid his wife when she was on the run from her father. Another club kidnaps Cade, beats him viciously, cuts him across his MC tattoo, and instead of annihilating them, the club agrees to consider a patch over. WTF. They would be the laughingstock of the MC nation if this happened in real life. A member of that same club who beat on Cade breaks into Dawn's house, who is Cade's Old Lady, threatens to rape her, fires on two Sinner's members, and Jagger tell's them to not only stand down, but to help him get away before the cops get there so they won't jeopardize the patch over that is probably not going to happen anyways. The money she was paying the SIL for a few stolen hours with her kids would have paid for one hell of a lawyer to get that sham of a custody order overturned. This book was just one frustration after another. In order to save my Ipad from an early death, I gave up. So I decided to take a chance at the YA scifi book (and series) - I've read a few YA scifi ones back in the right age :P - got this on Christmas and started reading some days ago. I finished the book sooner than I thought, impatient to reach the conclusion even after peeking at the end (haha). I'm quite impressed at the story's quality and that the romance was so well balanced with the actual story, with realistic, tragic details. In 2575, our two main characters Kady and Ezra, have freshly broken up when their colony, a place on a remote planet of Kerenza, is destroyed - they must quickly find their way to evacuation, ending up on two different ships. While they eventually make contact with each other again, troubles are rising again - and not being able to reach their destination Jump Station Heimdall as fast as hoped is just one small thing among them. It is a tale of interrupted life, price of truth, and of great courage against insane, manipulating ship computer capable of blowing up not only the ship wanting the destroy the fleet but thereatening the ship itself, but also the deadly 'anger' virus spreading that might end the people being saved as well as the crew . Kady is a great heroine for this story: a determinator with a power of sarcasm who doesn't just sit there but does stuff (but does have moments of vulnerability). The petite 'secret digger' with fearlessness of youth and a natural computer whiz. We see less of Ezra, but I grew fond of him, his humor, loyalty and growth - I'm glad this pair could patch things up and realise what they meant to each other. Nothing too mushy or sweet, just a right amount at the end, deserving it. The book is written as a dossier of hacked documents, sent a year after to a certain person (I was able to guess who) - cursing censored for them by blacking them out. There's emails, schematics, military files, IMs, medical reports, interviews etc. This spreads a little to the cover art too. Some small commentary marks are also added. It sounds complicated, but it actually makes the reading easier and quicker - another reason why I marathoned the ending *lol* The thickness doesn't matter (500+ pages). I also ended up liking AIDAN eventually, especially after he had a certain important change of mind , and saying this: "The universe owes you nothing, Kady. It has already given you everything. After all, it was here long before you, and it will go on long after you. The only way it will remember you is if you do something worthy of remembrance." -plus then learning afterwards that part of him survived as a 'seed' *grins* The receiver of the documents will not be pleased. Good. :) :P So, I was entertained, pulled in, and came out of reading happy. Slightly surprising but great reading experience, that's for sure 8) <3<3

This book just barely scraped a 3 star rating from me. Sure, it had its moments. It was cute at times and admittedly I giggled aloud once or twice. Plus, it took place in London! Julia was the type of protagonist that never ceases to infuriate me. She thinks she's better than everybody else, constantly judges those who don't reach her ridiculously high standards, and lives inside her completely fabricated fantasy world! I'm sorry, but there is no such thing as a MTB. Nor is it realistic for a girl to have a crush on three guys at once. At least, not in my personal experience. And the way the story wrapped up made me so friggin irritated! Julia spends literally half of the novel looking her nose down at her classmates! Like the fact that she reads classic novels and likes the Beatles and doesn't doll herself up makes her superior! Pretentious people, I find, are the most superficial. And Julia just SCREAMED pretentious. The entire time I just wanted to grab her and shake her, yell: GET OFF YOUR HIGH HORSE! The only character I even SORT OF grew to like throughout this book was Jason, though he often got on my nerves as well. Out of the handful of characters that were given to me, though? He's definitely a shining star. It was a shame the author didn't incorporate the side characters more into the story, or at least show them in a better light than Julia's twisted mind made them out to be. And yet, I gave this story 3 stars! I do this because as much as it irritated me and ground on my nerves, I still found myself enjoying it at times. It has some cute elements on it and a few moments that made me laugh out loud. Some of the situations Julia finds herself in are so completely ridiculous it ends up being very entertaining to watch it all unfold. So, despite my lack of interest in the main character and my issues with the love story, I maintain the statement that I did like this book. Just not as much as I wanted to, I guess. Would I recommend it? I wouldn't go as far as to say that.

I had been waiting so long for this book. So very long. Obelisk Gate is still not a satisfying ending, of course (part 2), but that isn't really a problem when the story is so damn good I'll be upset when there actually is an ending. The world expands in this novel as we learn more about Guardians, how orogeny works, Stone Eaters, and what the heck is up with the Moon. We also learn exactly who is narrating all these second person chapters, aking all the haters realize there WAS a good reason for using second person after all. Review originally posted on Books & Bottles. Edit: After sleeping on it, I've decided to downgrade to two stars because I couldn't sleep, knowing it was still a three star. Nope, definitely a one star. First book of 2016, and I'm disappointed. There was so much hype over this series every where that I was anxious to get reading as soon as I got my hands on it. 2015 Goodreads Choice reward, raving reviews from reviewers I look up to, and yet I'm left feeling a little cheated and very disappointed. Don't get me wrong, the story is fantastic, the premise unique, and I'll always be a sucker for the surprise can of woop-a** from the under-dog. But that's the only reason I'm giving this a three instead of a two - because I had to finish the book and I really enjoyed the plot. Let me go through what I did like first. First, the plot. While laid out in the stereotypical YA Fantasy layout, it played out well and fit the characters and twists Aveyard threw in. The overall feel of the story that I'm left with is satisfied, like watching a chick-flick. You know all the twists and turns before the happen, and there's no surprises at the end. The skeleton of love triangle, suppressed powers, everyone-turned-against-me-and-I'm-a-raging-idiot, and a complete 180deg plot layout for the sequel is homely and welcoming to come back to when you need it. Second- wait, no. There is no second that isn't covered under plot. So on to what irked me. Mare. Okay, I know that she's only seventeen and I'm probably a little harsh, but the incessant nagging that the reader is put through as she has to keep telling herself that "things are different", and "she's doing everything for the people she loves" is draining. I'm sure that it's just as much the way she convinces her self as well as how often she does it that I found irritating. More than once I found myself groaning and thinking, "You're so hypocritical! Just get over it!" She would get mad at the other characters for pulling the same stunt as her, but yet it's completely okay for her? Formatting: Italics. Everywhere. I have a new appreciation of the overuse of italics because it was so stressful reading the Red Queen and having words italicized instead of using a for emphasis. And the four words italicized at the beginning of the chapter? Why? Other than the irritating protagonist who must have been dripped in honey judging from the number of boys falling head over heels for her, the nagging first person perspective, and the excessive font formatting, I recommend this book for regular YA Fantasy fans. I wish you luck with the sequel as I will not be reading it. give this a shot if you're really dedicated and can't resist. Glass Sword only gets WORSE than Red Queen in regards to every aspect I mentioned above and has had me throw this entire series down as the worst books I've ever read.

Still haven't made a complete decision on this book -- I'll probably wait to finish it the second time. I will say two things, though: (1) It doesn't have ground breaking theology (just basic trinitarian theology and a good dose or relational spirituality, essentially) and it doesn't have any gimmicky answers to the hard questions. And in the end I think that's what gives this book it's strength: an honest look at some hard questions, based not upon a ten-step program or a witty turn of phrase, but based upon solid theology -- with a believable main character (if not a believable story) to make it easily readable. This book is going to create a greater pool of people with a more solid understanding of some of the basic theological underpinnings of the Christian relationship, and that's 100% a good thing. (2) In relation to my earlier aside (that it isn't a 100% believable story), that isn't actually much of a criticism. One of the reviews compared this book to Pilgrim's Progress, and while that's a rather lofty goal to aspire to I do think that the comparison works well in terms of genre. I'm not sure if the author intended this story as an allegory (for all I know he wanted the story to be taken seriously), but this book is best read as an allegory. This didn't really happen, but the different actions and interactions all have meanings worth exploring; and in the end the most important thing is that the main character, Mack, is a very believable character that a lot of people are going to identify with (or at least find realistic) on one level or another. I want to give the book another read through, because I read it quite quickly the first time, but generally I'm very impressed with the book and think it will present a challenge to anyone who reads it with an open mind. I know it certainly challenged me to reassess where I am in my relationship with God -- particularly in terms of how much I am showing trust in Him.

3.5 rating On a snowy Christmas morning, Holly Judge awakens, the fragments of a nightmare-something she must write down-floating on the edge of her consciousness. Something followed them from Russia. On another Christmas morning thirteen years ago, she and her husband Eric were in Siberia to meet the sweet, dark-haired Rapunzel they desperately wanted. How they laughed at the nurses of Pokrovka Orphanage #2 with their garlic and their superstitions, and ignored their gentle warnings. After all, their fairy princess Tatiana-baby Tatty-was perfect. As the snow falls, enveloping the world in its white silence, Holly senses that something is not right, has not been right in the years since they brought their daughter-now a dangerously beautiful, petulant, sometimes erratic teenager-home. There is something evil inside this house. Inside themselves. How else to explain the accidents, the seemingly random and banal misfortunes. Trixie, the cat. The growth on Eric's hand. Sally the hen, their favorite, how the other chickens turned on her. The housekeeper, that ice, a bad fall. The CDs scratched, every one. But Holly must not think of these things. She and Tatiana are all alone. Eric is stuck on the roads and none of their guests will be able to make it through the snow. With each passing hour, the blizzard rages and Tatiana's mood darkens, her behavior becoming increasingly disturbing and frightening. Until, in every mother's worst nightmare, Holly finds she no longer recognizes her daughter. For once, I'm sticking with the synopsis provided by the publisher. It's written very well and I don't want to butcher it. But more importantly, it provides a glimpse at the writing style within the novel. For me, this took some getting used to. There aren't chapters and the writing can seem all over the place. For the majority of the novel I felt that the author was rambling, though the writing was very poetic at the same time. The latter is what kept me engaged. There were some lovely passages. Although, there was some frustration while reading. I wasn't sure if this was a book I was going to finish. I'm glad to have made it to the end. To be honest, this book stressed me out. The incoherent narrative really helped set the scene. The author really did a great job at developing the world that the characters were set it. I felt stretched thin and worn out while reading this, which is exactly what the characters were experiencing. I am personally glad that Christmas Day is months away so I don't have to worry about the possibility of dealing this kind of mental pressure. This book takes places over the period of a day. But the author takes us through 'flashback' scenes to give the reader the background and insight to the characters. There were times when I felt that this might turn into a supernatural twist. I thought that the child might be a changeling. However, I was very wrong. I didn't realize until I got to the last few pages that I was dealing with an unreliable narrator. Which was perfect, and really tied the book together for me. A surprising psychological thriller. And while this book was under 300 pages, I felt it ended on the right note. *Won in a Goodreads First Reads Giveaway

I don't understand how this got such high ratings. It's a cool idea (aren't most stories? ), but I was drowning in detail. "It was an ordinary day, a Friday, twenty minutes till lunchtime, five hours till quitting time and the weekend, ten months till vacation, thirty-seven years till retirement. Then the phone rang." WOW. What a great opening. "This was Martin Lastvogel, my instructor, and we shook hands and agreed it would be sensible to use first names." Not "hi, nice to meet you, call me by my first name", but instead told quickly and cutely and I loved it. Little truths like this: "I sat forever in Rube's office then, turning the pages of old copies of Life, discovering again, as in a doctor's waiting room, that it's very hard to tell, looking through back issues of Life, whether or not you've seen them before." There there were the passages that made zero sense to me because the book was written in 1970: "And then, like a computer finally producing the right card, my mind said, How?" But mostly it was page after page after page of detailed descriptions of 19th century clothing, buildings, and New York street names. The author also felt the need to remind us again and again how much simpler life was and how glad the protagonist was to be in the past. Towards the end I was just skimming and ignoring full paragraphs because it was all detail and no story. And though this book left us with a great cliff-hanger, I will not be reading the sequel.

Some books should come with a warning on the cover: excruciatingly boring. In Everything I Never Told You, Celeste Ng makes a case for how racism and sexism can destroy a family. It certainly can, and the premise is very interesting, which is why the book itself is such a disappointment. Marilyn is an ambitious young student who desperately wants to become a doctor and escape the humdrum life of a housewife that her mother plans out for her. James is a professor and the ultra-Americanised son of Chinese immigrants who has to face racism at every step of the way. Marilyn attends James' lecture and falls in love with him, gets pregnant and gives up her dreams to have babies like everyone else. Nath, Lydia and Hannah are their children. The story, as such, is not bad and there is a lot of scope to show how racism and sexism can affect people and impact families. However, none of the characters even appear real, nor do the interactions between the family members. They never actually talk to each other. Marilyn's mother opposes her wedding to a Chinese, and Marilyn never speaks to her again. But we never get to see how Marilyn feels about it. How does James deals with it? How do the children feel about a grandmother whom they have never seen?? How does Marilyn's mother herself feel at this fallout? What about other relatives? Nothing is explained as the story follows a very linear path, missing out many opportunities for actually making an impact. This happens consistently with almost every chapter throwing up many avenues to explore but the author just drones on repetitively on the same themes of isolation and lack of communication. The characters were flat, and one of them was pretty much useless. The youngest daughter, Hannah, just existed for no reason, except to be ignored throughout the book and later take the place of Lydia. Every time there was a crisis in the family, they just filed it away behind them and acted as if it never existed. Yes, I realise this was the time of stoic acceptance but really, never having a conversation about things that affected you deeply? Even at the end, things automatically 'got better' for no reason and they still won't talk about it, but things will get better because the author told us so and because she finally told us about Lydia's death. Story over, things get better, why explain? But if you don't care to talk about your problems, why the hell would I be interested in reading about them?

They have history (as did Colt & Feb, Tanner & Rocky) and they have great chemistry but I think the formula got a little stale here, which is why I took a star off. If I'd read Games of the Heart first, I may have given it the full 5 stars. As with all of KA's books, it's far better than average and edited very well for a self pub - it's just not knock-my-socks-off great. I'll probably reread this and can't wait for Benny & Frankie's story in #5.

Full Review Phew, this book put me through a bit of emotional turmoil. After the cliffhanger that To All the Boys I Loved Before had (Review here), P.S. Originally posted at City of Books I'm Team Warner all the way, but I was still anticipating this novella, just so I'd have another glimpse into this world. But it's definitely not what I was expecting, and Team Adam fans may not be very pleased with this one... Firstly I want to say that the line at the top of the cover is misleading. It should say, 'I Will Not Lose Him' instead. Why? Because in this novella we see just how much Adam loves his little brother, James, and he'll always be number one in his heart. Fracture Me starts off at a point towards the end of Unravel Me, and we get to see Adam's perspective of what happens. I've got to admit I'm not very impressed. The rest of this review may be a little spoilery so hold off if you're really against spoilers. I began disliking Adam in Unravel Me, and I was a little worried that this novella might turn me back to Team Adam. Man, was I wrong! This one actually cemented my place on Warner's side. I really hated Adam in this. The guy we loved in Shatter Me is gone, he really is. It's great to see how much he cares for James, but I thought all along that he'd do anything for Juliette, and in Fracture Me, I realized how wrong I was. We see a completely different side of Adam in this, and it's in his POV so this is clearly the real him. Tahereh's writing is great as usual, but lacks the poetic flow that we see in her other works. This is probably because she wants to show that Adam's not like that. Which is totally fine with me. In fact, her writing is the only reason I gave this novella 3 stars. Otherwise, my disgust of Adam would have knocked it down to 2. I can't really enjoy a book or even a novella if I don't like the protagonist, and Adam's thought process just made him all the more pathetic-sounding to me. One second he says he loves Juliette, and the next he's doing something that shows the complete opposite. There were two things I really liked in this novella, though. One - Kenji. This guy really needs his own novella! I love him. He's funny and sweet and loyal and he can be serious when the situation commands it. Plus, he's got some kickass skills. Kenji made this worth it. Him, and the Ignite Me excerpt at the back! The other thing I loved is that I think Tahereh is hinting towards who Juliette ends up with. And what I saw in Fracture Me makes me very happy. It's definitely important to read this before you get into Ignite Me, because there's a shocker at the beginning of Ignite Me which would make a lot more sense if you've read this novella. Overall, If Warner didn't charm you enough to switch sides in Unravel Me, this novella may just do that, out of a possible contempt for Adam.

This story lost me somewhere on the way. Where is it going? What is it trying to say? Is it doing so in the right manner? Habibi, as far as I came in reading it, revolves around a young woman who raised a young boy when she was still underage herself. The two of them have different ethnic backgrounds, and the whole story is taking place in a middle-eastern setting. They live isolated, in poverty, in a desert. Just when the boy's blooming sexuality makes things awkward between them, they are torn apart. The woman ends up in a harem; the boy is raised by transgender people. And somehow, having learned the erroneous lesson that sexually desiring women is wrong because he associates it with a desire to harrass or overpower women, he has his male genitalia removed?? I'm not saying that this isn't an important topic, but I wish it had been handled differently. The way this story was told, it was disturbing, not insight providing. The story mixes several very different topics, each of which have enough weight to deserve a separate story of their own: * arranged marriage, * the daily struggle for the basic necessities in life when you're truly poor, * motherhood (the adoption of the boy is contrasted against the child that the woman bears in the harem), * gender politics, * the subjective perceptions of sexuality and how it is interwoven with power of one gender over the other. Perhaps the book is just too long and things become clearer at the end (which I didn't read), but I struggle to see how Thompson is going to suddenly make all those themes work together. It's not that they couldn't but the narrative doesn't accomplish it for me.

Batman: Year One is so much more than the four arc comics series collected within. Yes, it is kind of thrilling to see Batman before he was so invulnerable. Yes, the story of Lieutenant Gordan's move to Gotham and his fight to be a good cop in a bad city is excellently done. And yes, the way that this particular arc has no Big Bad but the city of Gotham itself - drawn to darkly corrupt perfection - is a terrific way to pare Batman down to who he is without the rogue's gallery of super villain foes. But the greatest thing about Batman: Year One is the inclusion of all the extras once the comic is finished. The line drawings and essay from artist David Mazzucchelli (including his insightful take on the why the Batman/Robin dynamic is not homerotic), the back page poetic reminiscences of Frank Miller on his first entrance into Gotham as a boy, and the recreation of how a lot of the panels originally looked in the newsprint comic palate are all fantastic inclusions, and worth the read entirely on their merits alone. It's a little behind the scenes tour of Batman's recent history, and its a perfect capstone to this carefully respectful update to the Year One mythology. As for the comic itself, because Batman at this point in the story is still a work in progress - still a creation that has yet to be fully formed - a lot of this story falls to Bruce Wayne. This is interesting, because of course as Batman's story goes on, Batman becomes so much more his identity, and Bruce Wayne turns into nothing but a convenient disguise. The features of Bruce Wayne are also drawn here to be a bit blocky, a bit blank. That's a nice touch. We also get glimpses of those who become important to the story later on, especially Harvey Dent and Selina Kyle (with a tongue in cheek Vicki Vale mention thrown in for good measure). While I love what this version does with the both Gordon and Dent (still, in these early days, unscarred and heroic), I was not so much a fan of the Selina Kyle bits. I understand that they are making the case that if it hadn't been for Batman, Catwoman as we know her would have also ceased to exist, but unfortunately in this story, she doesn't have much to do. I do, however, think that Frank Miller did a great job with the other female characters. Barbara Gordon (the wife, not the daughter destined to be Batgirl and Oracle) is especially well done, and the relationship between her and Jim Gordon is rendered more convincingly than most marriages in literature. I also loved the way Mazzucchelli deliberately draws certain panels to resemble Zorro, in a nod to "The Mask of Zorro" being the movie the Waynes were watching together immediately before Bruce's parents were killed. This is a good looking version of a fine rewrite of a classic story. You can't ask for better than that in a Year One comic.
